SERMONS III (117-183) GOSPEL OF SAN FUAN, ACTS OF THE APOSTLES AND LETTERS
Topic: The Word of God (Jn 1,1-3). Location: Unknown. Date: Around 418-420.

1. The preamble, dear brothers, of the gospel that was read to us is demanding purity in the sight of the heart. In it Jesus Christ, our Lord, is presented to us; and to God, maker of all creatures; now man, repairer of the creature this fall. The gospel is from John, whose outstanding personality we know from his gospel itself; In the excellence, then, of the minister we can glimpse how high the price of the Verb—of the Word—that such a mouth had to utter. But what do I say? The Word, which surpasses all things, has absolutely no price; Well, in relation to its price, a thing is either equal, or below, or above. If someone buys it at its value, there is an equation between the price and what was purchased; if less, things are going down; If anything else, things are on the rise; But nothing can equal the Word of God, nor is it possible to lower its price nor for anything to surpass it. All things, yes, can be below SERMO
DE VERBIS EVANGELII IOANNIS, CAP. 1,1-3: «IN PRINCIPIO ERAT VERBUM, ET VERBÜM ERAT APUD DEUM, ET DEUS ERAT VERBUM», ETC. AGAINST ARIANS

CAPUT I.—1. Verbum Dei ut intellegatur, quo pretio comparandum.—Capitulum Evangelii quod lectum est, fratres dilectissimi, purum oculum cordis inquírit. Dominum enim nostrum Iesum Christum accepimus secundum divinitatem ad condendam universam creaturam, secundum humanitatem ad reparandam lapsam creaturam, evangelizador loanne. In ipso autem Gospel qualis et quantus vir Ioannes fuerit, invenimus, ut ex dignitate dispensatoris intellegatur quanti pretii sit Verbum, quod per talem dici potuit: immo quam nullius pretii sit quod superat om[662]nia. Pretio enim aut comparatur res venalis, aut subicitur, aut exceed eam. Quando tan quisque comparat quanto valet, aequatur pretium rei quae comparatur: quando vilius, subicitur ei: quando carius, superat eam. Verb autem From nec aequari aliquid potest, nec ad mutationem subici, nec superponi aliquid. Subici enim omriia possunt Verb * The translation of sermons 117-147, with the exception of 132 A, 136 B, 136 C, 140 A, 145 A, is due to Father Amador del Fueyo and has been revised by Father Miguel Fuertes Lanero.

Word of God, because they were all made by him; but they are not below the Word in terms of price, as if someone could make it their own by giving something. However, if it is not unreasonable to use this language, or this name of price can be canonized in some way, or if it were in use, we would say that, to buy the Word, its price would be the same buyer, if he gave himself the Word to acquire himself. When, in fact, we buy, we get our hands on something—money, kind—to give, and, giving the price, we get what we want. Now, what is given is outside of us, or, if in us, put it outside of us so that what is purchased comes to us. Whatever kind of price the buyer resorts to, this must be done in such a way that one gives what one has to receive what one does not have; but whoever gives the price does not change, he remains the same; exchanges—or exchanges—what is acquired at a price. Whoever, then, has the will to buy this Word, whoever wants to possess it, does not look outside himself for something to give, he gives it himself; By doing so, one does not lose—or alienate—, like the price is lost or alienated when one buys something. 2. The Word of God is offered to all; Those who can buy it, and those who piously want it can; The Word of God, in fact, is the abode of peace, and this peace is given on earth to men of good will. Whoever is willing to buy from him must give himself. This self-giving becomes the price of the Word, if speaking like this is, in some way, admissible; a price of such nature, that

He who gives himself and acquires the Word by whom he gives is not lost—or alienated—and even himself is acquired by acquiring the Word to whom he is given. And what does it give to the Word? Nothing that does not belong to the one for whom it is given, but what is made by the Word itself: it is returned to him to be remade. All things were made by him. If all things, then also man. If the sky, if the earth, if the sea, if everything that is in them, if every creature, it is more evident that also man, made in the image of God, is the workmanship of the Word. 3. We do not try now, brothers, to find the true meaning of the passage. In the beginning there was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. It can be understood in an ineffable way, that is, that human words are incapable of elevating us to their intelligence. We deal with the Word of God, and we say why it is not possible to be understood. We do not say what we say to understand him; We only talk about what prevents us from their intelligence. Because the Word of God is a certain form; an unformed form, whence, however, all forms are formed; invariable, stable, which lacks nothing; without time or place; that transcends everything, that rises above all things, the foundation on which they rest and the crown that covers them all. If you say that all things are in Him, you do not say wrong, because this Word was called the Wisdom of God, for the Scripture says: You made all things in Wisdom.

Dei, quia omnia per ipsum jacta sunt (lo 1,3): non tamen subiciuntur, quasi pretium sint Verbi, ut quisque det aliquid, ut illud accipiat. Tamen si dici potest, et admittit nomen hoc ratio aliqua vel loquendi consuetudo, pretium comparandi Verbi ipse comparator est, qui se ipsum pro se ipso dederit huic Verbo. Itaque quando aliquid emimus, quaerimus aliquid quod demus, ut habeamus rem dato pretio quam volumus emere. Et extra nos est quod damus; et si apud nos erat, fit extra nos illud quod damus, ut sit apud nos illud quod comparamus. Quidquid pretii invenerit qui emit aliquid, necesse est ut such inveniat, ut det quod habet, et accipiat quod non habet; maneat tamen ille a quo abscedit pretium, et accessat illud pro quo dat pretium. Qui autem vult comparare Verbum hoc, qui vult habere, non quaerat extra se ipsum quod det, se ipsum det. Quod cum fecerit, non se amittit, sicut amittit pretium, quando aliquid emit. CAPUT II.—2. "Pretium Verbi ipse homo.—Verbum ergo Dei propositum est omnibus: comparent qui possunt; possunt autem qui pie voluerint. In illo enim Verbo pax: et pax ín terra hominibus bonae voluntatis (cf. Lk 2:14). Ergo qui vult comparare, det se ipsum. Quasi pretium est hoc Verbi, si dici aliquo potest mode, when nec se perdit qui dat,

et acquirit Verbum pro quo se dat, et se ipsum in Verbo acquirit cui se dat. Et quid dat Verb? Non aliquid ab ipso alienum, pro quo se dat; sed quod per ipsum Verbum factum est, hoc ei redditur ut reficiatur. Omnia per ipsum jacta sunt (lo 1,3). Si omnia, utique et homo. Si caelum, si terra, si mare, si omnia quae in ipsis sunt, si universe creature; utique ille manifestius, qui ad imaginem Dei factus per Verbum factus est homo. 3. Verbum Dei forma quaedam non formata. Vorma sine tempore et loco.—Non moda, fratres, tractamus, quomodo possit intellegi quod dictum est: In principle erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum, et Deus erat Verbum (ib., 1). Ineffabiliter potest intellegi: non verbis hominis fit ut intellegatur. Verbum Dei tractamus, et dicimus quare non intellegatur. Non nunc dicimus ut intellegatur, sed dicimus quid impediat ne intellegatur. Est enim forma quaedam, forma non formata, sed forma omnium formarum: forma incommutabilis, sine lapsu, sine defectu, sine tempore, sine loco, superas omnia, existens ómnibus et fundamentum quoddam in quo sint, et fastigium sub quo sint. If you say quia omnia in illo sunt, you will not lie. Dictum est enim ipsum Verbum Sapientia Dei: habemus au[663]tem scriptum, Omnia in Sapientia fecisti (Ps 103,24). Ergo in illo sunt omnia: et tamen quia Deus est, sub illo

All things, then, are in him, and yet, because he is God, all things are under him. From what has been said, the incomprehensibility of the passage read can be deduced; But it was not read so that it could be understood by man, but so that man would be pained at not understanding it, seek to find the impediment to understanding, in order to remove it, and ardently covet the intelligence of the unchangeable Word, an intelligence that changes man, yes, from worse to better. The Word, in fact, gains nothing by being known; That you stay, that you leave and come back, he remains unchanged, your changes do nothing to him; renewer of all things, is eternally the same. It is, consequently, the eternal exemplar of all beings, an unfabricated, timeless and inspatial form, as we said. Everything contained in a place is circumscribed. The form is circumscribed by its limits, it has boundaries, within which it is. Furthermore, what is contained in a place occupies a space, has a mass and is smaller in the part than in the whole. May God understand it. 4. From these things that we have before our eyes, we see, we touch and among which we walk, it can be inferred that all bodies are in a place and have a shape. Now, what occupies a space is less in the part than in the whole. Let's assume a part of the human body: the arm. True, the arm is smaller than the entire body. Being, therefore, smaller, it occupies a shorter place. In this way, the head, part of the body, is in a smaller place and is smaller than the entire body, whose sunt omnia. Dicimus quam incomprehensibile sit quod lectum est: tamen lectum est, non ut comprehenderetur ab nomine, sed ut doleret homo quia non comprehendit, et inveniret unde impeditur a comprehensione, et removeret ea, et inhiaret perceptioni incommutabilis Verbi, ipse ex deteriore in melius commutatus. Non enim Verbum proficit aut crescit accesonte cognitore: sed integrum, si permanseris; integrum, si recesseris; integrum, cum redieris; manens in se, et innovans omnia. Ergo est forma omnium rerum, forma infabricata, sine tempore, ut díximus, et sine spatiis locorum. Quidquid enim loco capitur, circumscribitur. Forma circumscribitur finibus, habet metas unde et quousque sit. Deinde quod loco capitur et mole quadam et spatio distenditur, minus est in parte, quam in toto. Faciat Deus ut intellegatis. CAPUT III.—4.

Non minar in parte quam in tota.—Quotidie autem de corporibus, quae ante oculos nostros sunt, quae videmus, quae tangimus, inter quae sumus, possumus iudicare corpus quodlibet in loco habere formam. Omne autem quod spatium loci occupat, minus est in parte quam in toto. Pars corporis humani, verbi gratia, brachium: utique minus est brachium quam totum corpus. Et si minus est brachium, breviorem locum occupat. item caput, quia pars est corporis, in minore loco est, et minus est quam totum corpus, cui caput est. Sic omnia quae sunt

head is. Thus, localized things are less in the part than in the whole. Let us not feel anything similar from the Word, not even by dreaming. Let us not take spiritual things to the size of the flesh. That Word, that God, is not less in the part than in the whole. 5. If you cannot conceive such a thing, it matters little: pious ignorance is worth more than presumptuous science.' We talk about God, from the passage And the Word was God; we talk about God; What wonder you can't understand him? If you understand him, he is not God 2. Let us make a pious confession of ignorance rather than a reckless confession of science. Giving God a little with your mind is already a very great joy; understand him, encompass him, everything in everything impossible. God belongs to the mind, he is pure intelligible; the body is visible to the eyes. And even the body, do you think to encompass it with your eye? No; by no means. No matter where you look, you will never see the whole. If you look at a man's face, while you see his face, you don't see his back, and when you see his back, you don't see his face. Consequently, you do not see him comprehensively; When you set your eyes on another part not yet seen, either your memory assists you to remind you where you are leaving, or you could never say that you had understood anything, not even external things. You touch, you see, you walk from one side to the other, or you go around it to see in loco, minora sunt in parte quam in toto. Nihil tale de illo Verb sentiamus, nihil tale cogitemus. Non de suggestione carnis spiritualia imaginemur. Non est ille Sermo, non est ille Deus minor in parte quam in toto. 5. In rebus divinis pia ignorantia melior quam praesumpta scientia. Oculo cordis Deus incomprehensibilis. Dei cognitione fit homo beatus. Deus ex nostra cognitione non crescit.—Sed non potes such aliquid cogitare. Magis pia est talis ignorantia, quam praesumpta scientia. Loquimur enim of Deo. Dictum est, Et Deus erat Verbum (lo 1,1). Deo loquimur, quid mirum si non comprehendís? If enim comprehendis, non est Deus. Sit pia confessio ignorantiae magis, quam reckless professio scientiae. Attingere aliquantum mente Deum; magna beatitudo est: comprehendere autem, omnino impossibile. Admentem Deus pertinet, intellegendus est: ad oculos corpus, videndum est. Sed corpus oculo comprehendere you whores? Omnino non potes. Quidquid enim aspicis, non totum aspicis. Cuius hominis faciem vides, dorsum non vides eo tempore quo faciem vides: et quando dorsum vides, eo tempore faciem non vides.

Non sic ergo vides, ut comprehendas: sed quando aspicis aliam partem, quam [664] non videras, nisi memoria tecum faciat ut memineris te vidisse unde recedis, nunquam te dixeris aliquid vel in superficial comprehendisse. whole. In one go, therefore, you cannot see the whole. And on the way back to see it you only see part of it; By uniting these with those already seen, you seem to see the whole; but here what is shown is not the sight of the eyes, it is the retention of memory. What, therefore, brothers, can be said about the Word? If the bodies before the eyes cannot be embraced with the gaze, what eye of the heart understands God? It is enough to touch him, and this is pure. Now, if you touch him, touch him in a certain incorporeal and spiritual way; but he doesn't understand him. This is pure. And man becomes blessed by touching his heart to what is always blessed, perpetual Beatitude and perpetual Life, from which man derives his life; Perfect wisdom, from where it comes to man to be wise; Everlasting light, where man's light comes from. There you have it, then, now how, by touching him, you become what you were not; You don't make what you touch be what it wasn't. That is, God is no longer by being known; the knower is more knowing God. Let us not imagine, dear brothers, that we are doing God a favor by having said that we give, in a certain way, a certain price for him. We give nothing where it increases; You have fallen, he remains whole, and he is whole when you return, and ready to be seen to beatify those who return and blind those who are far away. To the soul that distances itself from God, the first divine retaliation is to blind it. Who closes

the eyes to the true light, that is, to God, is ipso facio left in darkness. He does not immediately feel the punishment, but it is already upon him. 6. The idea, then, brothers, that we must form of the Word of God, is the idea of ​​an incorporeal, inviolable, immutable Word; no temporal birth, but born of God. Can we hope to persuade certain men far from the faith along some path, since what we, Catholics, say in contrast to the Arians, who have so often put the Church to the test, is not opposed to the faith, if we are seeing that carnal men only willingly accept what enters their eyes? Because some have dared to say: "The Father is greater than the Son and the Son is less than the Father, who preceded him in time." And they reason like this: "He was born, therefore the Father existed before his Son was born to him." 3 Pay attention, and let him assist us, budget the help of your prayers and the lively desire to receive what he gives us, what he suggests to us; Help us, I say, to somehow be able to explain what is proposed. I warn, however, brothers, first of all, that if I cannot explain it, it is not the fault of the matter; It is the exhibitor's inability. So, I conjure you to pray, I beseech you; May God's mercy favor us to say things to the size of the audience and the person who says them. They, then, the Arians, say: "If he is the Son of God, he was born." We confess the same; He would not be a Son if he had not been born. It is evident, faith admits it, the Catholic Church approves it,

ut totum videos. One ergo aspectu totum videre non potes. Et quamdiu versa ut videas, parte vides: et contexendo quia vidisti alias parties, videris totum inspicere. Non autem hic oculorum visus, sed memoriae vivacitas intellegitur. Quid ergo de illo Verbo, fratres, dici potest? Ecce de corporibus dicimus subiacentibus oculis nostris, non illa possunt comprehendere_aspectu: quis ergo oculos cordis comprehendit Deum? Sufficit ut attingat, si purus est oculus. Si autem attingit, tactu quodam attingit incorporeal et spirituali, non tamen comprehendit; et hoc, si purus est. Et homo fit beatus contingendo corde illud quod semper beatum manet: et est illud ipsa beatitudo perpetua, et unde fit homo vivus, vita perpetua; unde fit homo sapiens, perfect sapientia; unde homo fit illuminatus, lumen sempiternum est. Et vide quemadmodum tu contingendo efficieris quod non eras, non illud quod contingis facis esse quod non erat. Hoc dico, Deus non crescit ex cognitore, sed cognítor ex cognitione Dei. CAPUT IV.—Ne putemus, fratres carissimi, quia beneficium praestamus Deo, quia diximus pretium I will give us quodam moda. Non enim unde augeatur, illi damus, qui et te span integer est, et te redeunte integer manet, paratus videri ut beatificet conversos, et aversos puniat caecitate. Vindicat enim primo in anima aversa a se, exordio poenarum, ipsa caeci-

tate. Who enim avertit a lumine vero, id est, a Deo, iam caecus efficitur. Nondum sentit poenam, sed iam habet. 6. Verbum coaeternum Patri asseritur contra Árlanos.—Itaque Verbum Dei, fratres carissimi, incorporaliter, inviolabiliter, incommutabiliter, sine temporali nativitate, natum tamen intellegamus a Deo. Putamusne possumus aliquo modo persuadere quibusdam infidelibus non abhorrere a vero, quod dici tur a nobis fide catholica, quae contrara est Arianis, a quibus Ecclesia Dei saepe tentata est, cum carnales nomines id facilius accipiunt quod videre consueverunt? Ausi sunt enim quídam dicere, Maior est Pater Filio, et praecedit eum tempore: id est, maior est Filio Pater, et minor est Patre Filius, et a Patre in tempore praeceditur. Et sic disputant: Si natus est, utique erat Pater antequam Filius illi esset natus. Attendite: adsit ipse nobis, adiuvantibus orationibus vestris, et pia intentione excipere cupientibus quod ipse donaverit, quod ipse suggesserit; adsit nobis, ut possimus quoquo modo explicare quod coepimus. Tamen, fratres, ante dico, si non potuero ego explicare, non rationem putetis, sed hominem defecisse. Itaque vos hortor et deprecor ut oretis: adsit misericordia Dei, [665] et ita rem a nobis dici faciat, ut vos audire oportet, et nos dicere. Hoc ergo illi dicunt: Si Filius Dei est, natus est. Hoc fatemur. Non enim esset Filius, si natus non esset. Manifestum est, admittit fides, approbat Ecclesia catholica, verum est. Adiungunt deinde:

That's the truth. They then add: "If a Son was born to the Father, the Father existed before the Son was born." Faith rejects this, the ears of Catholics reject it, it is a condemned proposition; Whoever thinks this way is outside, he does not belong to the society of the saints nor has he any part with them. The Arian, then, tells me: "Explain to me then how a Son could be born to the Father and have a simultaneous existence with the Father." 7. Now, brothers; When we make the spiritual known through the carnal, are we not, in doing so, of a carnality similar to that of the Arian, who, in the style of births here and the order that creatures keep, where some come and others leave, places differences in age between all those who beget and are begotten? Here, in effect, the son is born after the father and succeeds the father, who must die. We find this in men, and the same thing happens to other animated beings: parents are prior to children with priority of time; Children are after their parents. Having seen this, the Arians insist on applying the carnal to the spiritual, and with these rude things in mind, seduction is easier. Because the listeners of those who propagate such things do not reason with their heads; They judge, as a rule, neither more nor less than their preachers. What do we do? Shut up? I wish it could be done! Perhaps, in effect, silence was the only tribute worthy of understanding to the Ineffable; Well, if something can be expressed in words, it is no longer ineffable. And God is ineffable. If the Si natus est Patri Filius, erat Pater antequam ei Filius nasceretur. Hoc respuit fides, respuunt aures catholicae; anathematur, extra est qui hoc sapit, non pertinet ad participationem societatemque sanctorum. Ergo, ait, rationem mihi redde, quomodo et Filius potuit nasci Patri, et coaevus esse ei a quo natus est? CAPUT V.—7. Divina carnalibus insinuare difficile.—Et quid facimus, fratres, quando carnalibus spiritualia insinuamus: si tamen et nos ipsi non carnales sumus, quando carnalibus ista spiritualia intimamus, homini, assuefacto nativitate terrena, et videnti istius creaturae ordinem, ubi successus et decessus, gignentes et genitos aetate distinguish? Post patrem enim nascitur filius, patri utique morituro successurus. Hoc in hominibus, hoc in alus animantibus invenimus, parentes priores tempore, filios tempore posteriors.

If you cannot understand it because you are still very young, be patient while your wings gain strength; lest, pretending to fly without a feather, the aura of freedom is a fall of recklessness 4. But what would the adversaries object then? Well! Well! If Agustín had something to tell us, he would tell us. Bad payer excuses; He doesn't want to answer because he is overwhelmed. And when one is told this and does not respond, although he is not defeated in himself, he is defeated in the hesitations of his brothers. In fact, the weak brothers hear it and think there is really nothing to say; perhaps they think that there is really nothing to say, not that there is no matter to give an opinion; words necessarily imply a judgment in man; But there may also be in man a judgment that is impossible to translate into language. 8. Let us, then, also give some good similarities to refute them, although we are incapable of understanding the majestic ineffability of the birth of the Word. No one imagines that by giving them we are going to arrive, through the path of similes, to the complete understanding of what, little ones as we are, we cannot formulate verbally, nor even touch it with thought. It is true that some, older ones, are not so incapable Paulus, et dicit se audisse ineffabilia verba (cf. 2 Cor 12,4); quanto magis ipse ineffabilis, qui talia demonstravit, quae fari non possit cui demonstrata sunt? Itaque, fratres, melius erat si possemus tácete, et dicere: Hoc habet fides, sic credimus: non potes cápete, parvulus es: patienter tolerandum, doñee pennas nutrias; ne cum volate implumis volueris, non sit illa aura libertatis, sed casus tenieritatis. Quid illi contra? Or if haberet quod diceret, diceret mihi! Deficienti ista excusatio est. Victus est veris, qui will respond non vult. Ule cui hoc dicitur, si non responderat, etsi in se ipso victus non est, vincitur tamen in titubantibus fratribus. Audiunt enim fratres infirmi, et putant revera non esse quod dicatur: et forsitan verum putant, non esse quod dicatur, non tamen non esse quod sentiatur. Homo enim nihil potest dicere, quod non etiam will feel possit: potest etiam aliquid will feel, quod dicere non possit. 8.

The same image already appeared in sermon 51:6.

like us; but even these see it in part, in enigma and reflection, not face to face yet. Because also, when here we say that there is no impossibility and that it is perfectly intelligible that the Son was born and is coeternal with the one from whom He was born, they use similarities to reject it and prove to us—that is to say—that such an assertion is false. Where do they take them from? Of the creature; and they tell us: «The man, and there is no doubt, existed prior to the begotten son, he is greater than his son; The horse existed before procreating his son; the sheep and the other animals, the same. 9. All of which are appearances brought from creatures. That! Are we going to also work to find conformity to the statements we make? That! If I do not find them, could I not well say: "The birth of the Creator perhaps has no resemblance in the creature"? Because the same difference in highness that exists between those from there and those from here, the birth there surpasses the births here. Everything here owes its being to God; What things, however, are in proportion to God? In this way, God is the efficient cause of everything born here. Therefore it is possible that there is no resemblance to his birth, just as there is no resemblance to his nature, immutability, divinity and majesty. What, in fact, can be found here that is similar? Why, if perhaps no similarity of his nativity is found either, am I going to consider myself defeated because I have not found similes of the universal Creator, no matter how much I long to find something similar to the Creator?

10. I, of course, will not find temporal resemblances adequate to eternity; but yours, Arian, what are they? What have you found? That every father is greater in time than the son; and, because the son is found to be less than the temporal father, the Son of God must be less in time than his eternal Father. Have you found, perhaps, a son temporarily inferior to an eternal father? Stability being a characteristic note of the eternal and change being a characteristic note of the temporal (the eternal is permanent; the temporal, ebb and flow), you can find in the variable time a younger son who succeeds the father, just as this father, because of being temporary, succeeded another non-eternal father. Can we, in fact, brothers, find something coeternal in the created, if we find nothing eternal in the creature? Find me an eternal father in creation and I will find you a coeternal son. If, therefore, you do not find something eternal and created beings precede each other in time, we are sufficient for the similarity that we seek to find coevity. One is coeternity, another is coevity. Every day we call coevos those who measure the same time, one does not precede the other in time, but both have had a beginning in time: this is coevity. If we could find a coeval born of the one from whom it is born, if two coeval things can be found, one engendering, another engendered, we would have here, in the created, coevity, and there coeternity. If I find that the existence of one begotten here began

similarities adversus illos, unde illi refellantur, non unde illud capiatur. Etenim cum dicimus valde posse fieri, posse intellegi, ut et natus sit et coaeternus sit ei a quo natus est, ut hoc refellant et quasi falsum esse demonstrent, similaritiesines nobis dant. Where? De creature: et dicunt nobis, Homo utique erat antequam generaet filium, maior est filio suo; et equus erat antequam generaet filium, et ovis et cetera animalia. Similarities adhibent of creaturis. CAPUT VI.—9. Similitudinibus turnen non nititur nostra fides de Verbo.—Quid, nobis laborandum est, ut et nos inveniamus similaritiesines earum rerum quas astruimus? Crux? si non invenirem, non recte possem dicere, Nativitas Creatoris fortasse similarityinem in creature non habet? Quanto enim superat ea quae hic sunt in eo quod ibi est, mucho superat ea quae hic nascuntur in eo quod ibi natus est. Omnia per Deum hic sunt: ​​et quid tamen est comparandum Deo? Sic omnia quae hic nascuntur, illo efficiente nascuntur. Et sic forsitan non invenitur aliqua similaro nativitatis eius, quomodo non invenitur et substantiae eius, et immutabilitatis, divinitatis, maestatis eius. Quid enim simile hic invenid potest? Si ergo forsitan nec nativitatis similaireo inveniatur, numquid inde oppressus sum, quia non inveni simileines Creatori omnium, in creatura cupiens invenire quod esset simile Creatori?

10. Similitudes nativitatis Filii Dei imperfectae in creaturis. Coaevum et coaeternum.—Et revera, fratres, non sum inventurus temporal similarities, quas aeternitati possim comparare. Sed et tu quas invenisti, quid sunt? Quid enim invenisti? Quia pater maior est tempore quam filius: et ideo vis ut Filius Dei tempore minor sit quam Pater aeternus, quia invenisti minorem filium patre temporali. Da mihi aeternum patrem hic, et invenisti similarityinem. Filium minorem invenís patre in tempore, filium temporalem minorem patre temporali. Numquid invenisti mihi filium temporalem minorem aeterno patre? CAPUT VIL—Quia ergo in aeternitate stabilitas est, in tempore autem varietas; in aeternitate omnia stant, in tempore alia accessunt, alia succedunt: potes invenire minorem filium in varietate temporis succedentem patri, quia etiam patri suo ipse successit non aeterno patri temporalis. Quid ergo possumus, fratres mei, in creature invenire coaeternum, when in creature nihil invenimus aeternum? Inveni aeternum patrem in creatura, et invenio coaeternum filium. Si autem non invenís aeternum, et vincunt se in tempore; sufficit ut ad similarityinem inveniamus coaevum. Aliud est enim coaeternum, aliud coaevum. Coaevos quotitidie dicimus eos qui eamdem habent mensuram temporum: nonalter ab altero praeceditur tempore, both tamen esse coepisse, quos dicimus coaevos. Si potuerimus invenire coaevum quod nascitur ei a quo nascitur; si possunt invenid coaeva duo generas et generatus: hic invenimus coaeva

When that of the begetter began, we would deduce that, since the begetter of the Son did not begin to exist, the Son, certainly, did not begin to exist either. Well see now, brothers, how, perhaps, we find something in the creature that, being born from something else, nevertheless begins to exist when that from which it is born. This has existed since that from which it is born began; that, the Word, has existed since the one who never began existed, the Father from whom he is born. 11. It seems to me that your holiness has understood what I am saying; namely, that, although temporal things bear no proportion to eternal things, there is, nevertheless, between coevity and coeternity, a certain subtle resemblance. Let us try to find some coevities, and let the Scriptures reveal this similarity to us. We read of Wisdom in the Scriptures: It is the white splendor of eternal light. We also read: Faithful immaculate image of the majesty of God. Let us, therefore, call Wisdom the white splendor of eternal light, Let us call her the image of the Father; Let us take the similarity from there to try to find coeternal things from which we can get an idea of ​​the coeternal ones. Oh Arian! If I find a begetter who does not temporally precede what is begotten, if what is begotten is not temporally inferior to the begetter, it is right that you grant me the possibility of finding this same thing, begetting and being begotten, coeternal in the Creator, since it was possible to find him coevous in the creature. I imagine this has already occurred to you in va[667] ibi intellegamus coaeterna. Si hic invenero genitum ex eo esse coepisse ex quo coepit generator, intellegimus certe Filium Dei ex eo esse non coepisse, ex quo non coepit generator. Ecce fortasse, fratres, invenimus aliquid in creature, quod de allia re nascatur, et tamen ex eo tempore esse incipiat, ex quo coepit illud unde nascitur. Hoc ex eo ex quo illud coepit, illud ex eo ex quo iüud non coepit. Hoc ergo coaevum, illud coaeternum. CAPOT VIII.—11. In coaevis similarity quaedam Verbi coaeterni Deo. Ignis et lux coaeva.—Arbitrar Sanctitatem vestram iam intellexisse quod dico, non posse comparan temporaria aeternis; sed posse ex aliqua tenui et parva similitudine coaeva coaeternis. Inveniamus ¡taque coaeva, et de Scripturis admoneamur ad has similarities. Legimus in Scripturis de ipsa Sapientia, Candor est enim lucís aeternae. item legimus, Speculum sine macula Dei maiestath (Wis 7,26).

Ipsa Sapientia dictates this candor lucís aeternae, dictates this imago Patris: hinc capiamus similarityinem, ut inveniamus coaeva, ex quibus intellegamus coaeterna. O Ariane, si invenero genitorem non praecedere tempore illud quod genuit, si genitum non esse minorem tempore illo a quo generatus est; iustum est ut concedas mihi posse ista coaeterna inveniri in Creatore, quando coaeva in creatura inveniri potuerunt. Iam quidem aliquibus fratribus hoc occurrere

brother rivers, because, when I said: Wisdom is the white splendor of eternal light, they anticipated it with their applause. Fire, in fact, gives off light, light is given off by fire. If we wanted to investigate which takes the existence of which, an everyday fact, turning on the light, would bring to mind an invisible and unspeakable thing, where our intelligence could be turned on; Lucerne, let's say, that illuminates us on this night of the century. A man lights his lamp. The unlit skylight is not yet fire, nor is it the glow that comes out of the skylight. Now, then, I ask and say: "Does the brilliance take its existence from fire, or does fire take its existence from brilliance?" Every soul responds to me (since God wanted to plant in every soul the first principles of judgment, the first principles of knowledge), every soul responds without hesitation: "Splendor exists through fire, not fire through splendor." Let us now imagine that we are the father fire of that splendor; We have already said it before: we seek coevities, not coeternities. While I think about lighting the skylight, there is still no fire in it, there is still no glow there; but then, at the point when I light up, there is both the radiance and the fire. Give me fire without glare, and I grant you that the Father has been without the Son. 12. Pay attention. We have expressed a surprising thing as being feasible, and because God favored the help of your prayer and the good dispositions of your spirit, you made the most of your ability. That, however, is ineffable; Don't think anything of substance has been said for the same reason. Nam praevenerunt aliqui ex quo dixi: Candor est enim lucis aeternae. Ignis enim lucem fundit, lux ab igne funditur. Quid a quo existat, si quaeramus, quotidie cum luzernam accendimus, admonemur rei cuiusdam invisibilis et inenarrabilis, ut luzern aliqua intellegentiae nostrae in ista nocte saecuü possit accendi. Attende eum qui luzernam accendit. Non accensa luzern, nondum est ignis, nondum est et fulgor qui ab igne exit. I interrogate autem ego, et dico: Fulgor ab igne existit, an ignis a fulgore? Omnis anima mihi responder: voluit enim Deus inseminare omni animae initia intellectus, initia, sapientiae: omnis mihi anima responder, et nemo dubitat, quod splendor ille de ign existit, non ignis de splendore. Ponamus ergo ignem patrem illius splendoris: quia iam praelocuti sumus coaeva nos quaerere, non coaeterna.

If Lucernam accendere cupio, nondum est ibi ignis, nondum et ille splendor: mox autem ut accendero, simul cum igne et splendor existit. Da hic mihi ignem sine splendore, et credo tibi Patrem Fuisse sine Filio. HOOD IX.—12. Alia coaeva, imago et res unde nascitur.—Attendite: dicta est ut potuit a nobis tanta res dici, Domino adiuvante intentionem orationis vestrae et praeparationem cordis vestri, excepistis quantum capere potuistis. Illa tamen ineffabilia sunt. Nihil dignum putetis

that the coevous is compared with the eternal, the temporal with the always equal, the ephemeral with the immortal. But since the Son has also been called the image of the Father, let us take from there another similarity, although it varies so much, as we have said, from one thing to another. The mirror image takes its existence from the man who looks at himself in the mirror. (But this comparison does not help us at all in terms of making clear what we are trying to explain. In fact, I am told: "Whoever looks at himself in the mirror obviously already existed and was already born." The image, of course, is produced at the moment of looking at himself; but whoever looks at himself existed before reaching the mirror.) What will we find in order to obtain the desired resemblance, as we extract it from fire and its brilliance? Let's at least try it. Water, as is well known, often returns the image of bodies; When, for example, one passes over the water or is next to it, one sees one's own image there. Suppose, therefore, that a thing is born at the edge of the water: a wand, a herb; Isn't his image born at the same time? As soon as they begin to exist, their image begins to exist with them; They do not anticipate being born into the image; I don't see anything born next to the water and, appearing without an image, the image appearing afterwards; It is born with its image, and yet it is the image that comes from the plant, not the plant of the image. They are therefore born with their image and the wand and its image begin to exist at the same time. Don't you confess, perchance, that you are the image generated by the wand, not the wand by the image? Confiedictum, vel eo ipso quo coaeva coaeternis comparantur, temporalia semper manentibus, exstinguibilia immortalibus. Sed quia dictus est Filius et imago Patris, accipiamus et bine aliquam similarityinem in rebus longe differentibus, ut praelocuti [668] sumus. Imago existit de speculo hominis intuentis speculum. Non nobis potest suffragari ad evidentiam rei huius, quam explicare uteumque conamur. Etenim dicitur mihi: lile qui attendit speculum, iam utique erat, et iam natus erat. Existit imago mox ut aspector exstiterit. Nam ille qui inspicit, erat et antequam accesoet ad speculum. Quid ergo inveniemus, unde possimus eruere talem similarityinem, sicut eruimus de igne et splendore? Faciamus at minimum. Facile nostis quemadmodum aqua corporum saepe reddat imagines. Hoc dicimus when quisque vel transit super aquam vel stat, videt ibi imaginem suam.

Ponamus ergo aliquid natum super aquam, velut virgultum aut herbam, nonne cum imagine sua nascitur? Mox ut íncipit exístere, incipit cum illoexistre imago eius, non praecedit nascendo imaginem suam: non mihi ostendítur natum esse aliquid super aquam, et postea apparuisse imaginem eius, cum illud sine imagine prius appareret; sed nascitur cum imagine sua: et tamen imago ab illo, non illud ab imagine." Nascitur ergo cum imagine sua, et simul esse incipiunt virgultum et imago eius. Numquid non faterís imaginem esse de illo virgulto,_ non virgultum de imagine genitum? Ergo de illo virgulto confectionís imaginem.

You know, in fact, that the image comes from the rod. Then the engendering and the engendered began their existence at the same time. Then they are coevus. If you always change it, so does the image. But what exists through another, certainly was born from it; Therefore there can always be a generator and always with him what is born from him. And that was what made us restless and worked for us: to get an idea of ​​the everlasting nativity. The Son of God, consequently, is called Son insofar as there is a Father, insofar as He has someone to be from; not because the Father was prior, and the Son posterior. Always the Father, always his Son. And since anything whose being is due to another is a born thing, the Son is always born. Always the Father, always the image of him; in the same way that the image of the varica was born from the varica, if the varica were eternal, the image that is born from the varica would be eternal. You, Arian, could not find coeternal things with eternal begetters; You have found things born coeval to temporal begetters. In the Son I see him who is born coeternally to an eternal begetter. 13. And here, brothers, attention must be stopped somewhat because of the blasphemies. Because we always get this: "The radiance radiated by the fire looks less than the fire itself, and in the image of the rod, evidently, there is less property than there is in the rod whose image it is." In these things we see a certain similarity, but no absolute equation; so it does not seem to be the same substance. What are we doing, therefore, Itaque et generas, et quod genitum est, simul esse coeperunt. Ergo coaeva sunt. Si semper virgultum, semper et imago of virgulto. Quod autem de alio est, utique natum est. Potest ergo semper esse generas, et semper cum illo quod de illo natum est. Ibi enim aestuabamus, ibi laborabamus, quomodo intellegeretur sempiterna nativitas. Ergo filius Dei secundum hoc dicitur, quod et Pater est, quod habet de quo sit: non secundum hoc, quod prior esset Pater, et postea Filius. Semper Pater, semper Filius of Patre. Et quia quidquid de aliquo est, natum est; semper igitur Filius natus. Semper Pater, semper de illo imago; quomodo imago illa virgulti de virgulto nata est, et si semper virgultum, semper nata esset et imago de virgulto. Non potuisti invenire coaeterna genita aeternis genitoribus, et invenisti coaeva nata temporalibus gignentibus. Intellego coaeternum Filium natum aeterno gignenti. Quod enim est temporali coaevum, hoc est aeterno coaeternum. CAPUT X.—13.

In úmilitudiritbus allatis est inaequalitas.—Hic iam modicum est quod advertatis, fratres, propter blasphemias. Semper enim dicitur, Ecce dedisti similaritiesines: sed splendor qui funditur de igne, minus luzet quam ipse ignis; et imago virgulti minus utique habet proprietatem, quam illud virgultum unde imago est. Habent istam similarityinem, sed non habent omnimodam aequalitatem: quare non videntur esse eiusdem substantiae. Quid ergo dicemus si dicat aliquis: Talis est

What if someone replies: "Between the Son and the Father, is there the same relationship that exists between the radiance and the fire, between the image and the rod"? Now I have established that the Father is eternal, and the Son co-eternal; But have we said that it is like the brightness, less luminous than fire, or like the image, whose entity or consistency is inferior to that of the rod? No; equality is omnipresent. "I don't believe," he says, "because you haven't found a complete resemblance." Well then believe the Apostle, to whom it was given to see what I have said. And he says: He did not consider being equal with God to be a captured prey. Equality is an absolute adjustment. What did he say? He did not judge prey. Because? Because prey is something foreign. 14. However, perhaps through the path of these two confrontations and engenderings we will find in creation a way to understand how the Son is coeternal with the Father and in no way inferior to him. What we cannot find is in just one of the similarities; let's unite both types of similes. Like both? One, where they get their opinions from; another, where we have taken it from. They took the similarities of things born in time, where what is born precedes, with priority of time, the things from which they are born; v.gr., the man, who is born from another. The eldest of whom in time was born before; but both are men, that is, of the same substance. In fact, man gives birth to man, a horse to another horse, a sheep to a sheep. This gives rise to a substance by comego Filius ad Patrem, qualis ad ignem splendor, et imago ad virgultum? Ecce intelligence Non: sed aequalitas omnimoda est. Non credo, ait, quia non invenisti similarityinem. Sed crede Apostólo, quia potuit videre quod dixi. Ait enim: No» rapinam arbitratus est esse aequalis Deo (Phil 2,6). Aequalitas omni moda coníungitur. Et quid dixit? Non rapinam. Quare? Quia illud est rapiña, quod alienum est. 14. Filii Dei coaeternitas et aequalitas ex duobus collatis similarityinum generibus.—Tamen ex duabus istis collationibus et generibus duobus, similarityinem fortassis invenimus in creatura, quomodo intellegamus Filium et coaeternum Patri et nequaquam minorem. Sed non illud possumus invenire in uno genere similarityinum: iungamus ambo genera. How does both generate?

Unum unde ipsi dant simílitudines, et alterum unde nos dedimus. Dederunt enim illi simíltitudines ex his quae nascuntur in tempore, et praeceduntur tempore ab eis a quibus nascuntur, sicut homo de nomine. Maior ille tempore prior natus: sed tamen homo et homo, id est eiusdem substantiae. Homo enim hominem generat, et equus equum, et pecus pecudem. Ad eamdem substantiam generat ist; sed non ad idem tempus. Various sunt tempore; thirst non sunt diverse

full equal; but time is not completely equal. As for time, the engendering and the engendered are two different things; As for nature, they are no different. What is laudable in this birth? Without a doubt, equality of nature. What is missing? Equality of time. Let us now remain with the only laudable thing, that is, the equality of nature. In the category of similarities that we proposed, the radiance of the fire and the image of the varica, there is no equality of nature, but coevity. What do we praise here? Coevity. Missing? Equality of nature. Put the two praised terms together. In creatures one good thing is missing, in the Creator nothing good can be missing; Everything you find in the creature has the Creator as its creator. And, in the case of coevity, should you not attribute to God what you praise in it? The faults are not to be attributed to the Majesty, in which there is no defect. I put before you, as you see, generantes coevous to those generated; In them you praise coevity and dislike disparity. What you dislike, do not put it on God; Attribute to him what you please, and from this kind of similarity attribute coeternity instead of coevity, so that the born may be coeternal with the one from whom he is born. And of the other species of similarities, which is also a creature and must contribute to the glory of God, what do you praise? Equality of nature. Now, if you gave coeternity to the first type of similes, give it equality to this second, since being born from the same substance of the generator is also perfection. Is there greater madness, my brothers, than praising something in the creature that is not found in the Creator? Praise in homage. Quid ergo hic laudamus in ista nativitate? Certe aequalitatem naturae. Quid autem deest? Aequalitas temporis. Teneamus hic unum quod laudatur, id est, aequalitatem naturae. In illo autem genere similarityinum, quod us dedimus de splendore ignis et de imagine virgulti, aequalitatem^ naturae non invenís, invenís coaevitatem. What was laudamus? Coaevitatem. Who is this? Aequalitas naturae. Coniunge quae laudas. In creaturis enim deest aliquíd quod laudas, in Creatore deesse nihil potest: quia quod invenís ín creatura, a Creatore artífice processit. Quid ergo in coaevis? nonne hoc Deo dandum quod ibi laudas? Quod autem deest non tribuendum maiestati, in qua nullus defectus est. Ecce offero tibí genitis coaeva gignentia: laudas ibi coaevitatem, sed disparilitatem reprehendis.

Quod reprehendis, noli ttibuere Deo; quod laudas, tribue: et tribuís illi ex ¡sto genere similarityinum pro coaevitate coaetemitatem, ut coaeternus sit natus cum eo a quo natus tú. De alio autem similarityinum genere, quae et ipsa creatura Dei est, et deben laudare Creatorem, quid ibi laudas? Aequalitatem naturae. Iam propter illam distinctionem dederas coaetemitatem; da propter istam, aequalitatem; et perfection est nativitas eiusdem substantiae. Quid enim dementius, fratres mei, quam

about the equality of nature, and do I not believe it in the one who made man? If what is born of man is man, will not what is born of God be the same as the one from whom it was born? I put aside works not done by God. Let all his works praise the Creator, then. I find coevity here, I know that there is eternity there; here I find equality of nature, I know that there is equality of substances. Because there is everything here distributed among things. Everything is found there, and more than what is found in creatures: I find everything there; But as much as the Creator exceeds the creature, so much does he exceed this visible that invisible, this temporal that eternal, this changeable that immutable, this corruptible that incorruptible. And to conclude: what we find in the generation of man is man and man: two men; there the Father and the Son are a single God. 15. I give infinite thanks to God for having deigned to rescue me safely, thanks to your requests, from this very delicate and extremely difficult matter. But, above all, stay with this: that the Creator transcends indescribably what we have been able to grasp in the creature, whether with the sense of the body or with mental discourse. But do you want to touch him with your mind? Purify that mind, cleanse the heart 5. Cleanse that eye, so that you can touch that, whatever it is. Cleanse the eye from the heart, for blessed are the pure in heart, for-

that they will see God. Without purity, as we were, of heart, what resource could God excogitate or what more generous gift could he give us than that Word by whom all things were made (and of whom we have said such excellent things and in so many numbers), so that we can achieve what we are not? Because we are not God, but we can see God with the mind and the inner insight of the soul. Our eyes darkened, dulled by guilt, spoiled by illness, they long to see God; more so we are in hope, not yet in reality. We are children of God. all things were equally found in me before they were made, as in the virtue of immutable reasons your hairs are also numbered” 7. Did you think I would tell you this? No; What he said was that first: That I am meek and humble of heart. What you have to learn, brothers, you are already seeing, is the small thing. We crave the summits; To be great let's learn the small. Do you want to apprehend the excellency of God? Learn first the humility of God. Deign to be humble for your own good, since God also deigned to be humble for you. Take ownership of the humility of Christ, learn to be humble, do not be proud. Confess your illness, patiently allow yourself to be treated by the Doctor. When you have made his humility yours, you will rise with him; Let us not say that he rises in his capacity as the Word, but that you will rise so that the Word becomes your prey more and more. If at first your ideas were unresolved and hesitant and later become more resistant and clear, it is not he who grows, it is you who progresses; and then it seems like he gets up with you. That's the truth, brothers. Be faithful to the divine commandments, put them into practice, and God will strengthen your knowledge. Do not be petulant by putting, let's say, knowledge before the precepts of God; It would be to inferiorize you instead of fortifying you. Observe the tree: first it shoots downwards to then grow upwards, it digs its root into the humble to launch its pillory into the sky. Where but in humility is it strengthened? Quieet astra: omnia etiam in me, antequam ieront, numerata fuent; quomodo in virtute rationum incommutabilium etiam capilli vestri numeran sunt (ib., 10,30). Haec putabas et talia esse dicturam? No. Sed prius illud, Quoniam mitis sum et humilis corde. Ecce quod capiatis, videte, fratres, certe parvum est. Ad magna nos tendimus, parva capiamus, et magni erimus. Vis capere celsitudinem Dei? Cape prius humilitatem Dei. Dignare esse humilis propter te, quia Deus dignitatus est humilis esse propter eumdem te: non enim propter se. Cape ergo humilitatem Christi, disce humilis esse, noli superbire. Confitere infírmitatem tuam, iace patienter ante medicum. Cum ceperis humilitatem eius, surgís cum illo: non quasi et ipse surgat secundum quod Verbum est; sed tu potius, ut magis magisque a te capiatur. Intellegebas primo titubanter atque haesitanter; intelligis posts certius et clarius. Non ille crescit, sed tu proficis, et quasi tecum videtur arisere. Sic est, brothers.

Verbum aeternum apud Deum.—Dominum nostrum Iesum Christum factum esse hominem quaerendo perditum hominem, ñeque unquam tacuit praedicatio nostra, et semper habuit fides vestra: hunc autem Dominum nostrum, qui homo factus est propter nos, Deum semper Fuisse apud Patrem, et semper futurum esse, immo semper esse; quia ubi tempus non praeterit, non est ibi Fuit et Erit. Therefore God did not make the Word in the beginning, because in the beginning the Word already existed. Where was this Word that existed in the beginning? It continues: And the Word was next to God. Accustomed to hearing human words every day, we do not give importance to this name of Word. Beware of paying little attention to this word here: The Word was God. This, that is, the Word, was in the beginning with God. All things were made through her, and without her nothing was made. 3. Expand your hearts, make up for the poverty of my word. Verbum Dei non est factum.—In principle erat Verbum, et Verbum erat apud Deum, et Deus erat Verbum (lo 1,1). O praedicare! or saginam Dominici pectoris eructuare! In the beginning it was Verbum. Topic: The Word of God (Jn 1,1-9). Location: Hippo. Date: Easter day. 1. Beginning of the gospel of John: In the beginning the Word already existed. Thus began the evangelist, this he saw, and, rising above every creature, mountains, airs, heavens, stars, thrones, dominions, principalities, powers, angels and archangels; rising, I say, above all, he saw in the beginning the Word and drank him. He saw it above every creature, he drank it at the breast of the Lord. This John is the same holy evangelist whom Jesus loved with preference, to the point of lying on the heart of Christ. There was this secret, there he drank it to belch it in the gospel. Happy are those who hear and understand! And although not so much, blessed are those who, if they do not understand it, believe it! Who can explain with human words the greatness of seeing the Word of God? 2. Lift up your hearts, my brothers; Raise them as much as you can and discard any body images that occur to you. If you imagine the Word of God as the light of this sun, no matter how much you extend and diffuse it

everywhere and with your imagination you erase all limits, it is nothing with respect to the Word of God. As far as the soul can think, the part is less than the whole. Think of the Word as everything everywhere. Understand what I'm telling you. I am cringing for you as much as I can. Listen to what I tell you. See how the light of the sky, which is called the sun, illuminates the earth when it rises, extends the day, outlines objects and discerns colors. Light is a great good, an immense gift from God made to all mortals; glorify his works. If the sun is so beautiful, what is more beautiful than its maker? And yet, my brothers, observe that the sun spreads its light throughout the earth, it penetrates transparent bodies, but opaque bodies resist it; enter through the windows; But does it go beyond the walls? Everything is accessible to the Word of God, nothing is hidden from him. See in another difference the enormous distance that goes from the Creator to the creature, especially to the corporeal creature. When the sun is in the east, it is not in the west; It is true that the light, emanating from his great body, reaches to the west, but he is not there. When he is born he is in the east, when he dies he is in the west; and for these two works of his (being born and dying) he gave his name to the places. Because he appeared in the east when he was born, he caused this point to be called the east, and because he was in the west when he died, he caused that place to be called the west. what about the stones will cry out. We, in fact, come from gentility, and in the person of our fathers we have worshiped stones; for which we were also called dogs'.
