It is not fair to take the children's bread and throw it to the dogs. Have you ever watched dogs lick greasy stones? Such are the worshipers of simulacra; But grace came to us, and to all who received it, He gave them the responsibility of being children of God. There you have the newborns: He gave them the power to be children of God. Who did he give it to? To those who believe in his name. 4. And how do they become children of God? Which were not of blood, nor of the will of man, nor of the will of the flesh, but were born of God. In receiving that they received the faculty of being children of God, they were born of God. Note well: these were born of God not by the mixing of blood, as the first generation takes place, full of misery and the product of misery. What, in fact, were these new children of God? How were they born before? Of the blood: of the mixture of the blood of the male and the female; that's where they came from. Where from now? They have been born of God. The first birth is male and female; the second is from God and the Church 2. 5. They have, therefore, been born of God; but where did it come from?

tacebunt, lapides clamabunt (Mt 21,9.16; Le 19,39.40). Who lapides, nor who colunt lapides? Si parvuli Iudaei tacebunt, maiores et minores Gentes clamabunt. Qui lapides, nisi de quibus dicit ipse Ioannes iste, qui come ut testimonium perhiberet de lumine (cf. lo 1,8)? Cum enim videret ipsos Iudaeos superbire de genere Abrahae, ait illis, Generado viperarum. lili se dicebant filios Abrahae: et iste illis dicebat, Generatio viperarum. Abrahae faciebat iniuriam? absit. Ex moribus ibat eis nomen. Quia si essent filii Abrahae, imitarentur Abraham: Sicut eis et ipse ait, qui dicunt ei: Nos liben sumus, et nemini servivintus unquam, nos patrem habemus Abraham. Et ille: Si filii Abrahae essetis, boasts Abrahae faceretis. Vos vultis me occidere, quia veritatem vobis dico; hoc Abraham non fecit (ib., 8,33.39.40). Inde generati estis, sed degenerastis. Ergo quid Ioannes? Generatio viperarum, quis vobis otendit fugere a ventura ira? Quia veniebant baptizan baptismo Ioannis in paenitentiam. Quis vobis otendit fugere ab ira ventura? Facite ergo fructum dignum paenitentiae. Et nolite dicere in cordibus vestris, Patrem habemus Abraham. Potens est enim Deus de lapidibus istis suscitare filios Abrahae (Mt 3,7-9). Potens est enim Deus de lapidibus istis, quo, videbat in Spiritu; illis dicebat, et nos praevidebat. Potens est enim Deus de lapidibus istis suscitare filios Abrahae. De quibus lapidibus: Si isti tacebunt, lapides clamabunt.

Mode audistis, et clamastis. Impletum est, Lapides clamabunt. De Gentibus enim venimus, in parentibus nostris lapides adoravimus. Ideo et canes dicti sumus. Recordamini quid audierit mulier illa, quae clamabat post Dominum, quia erat Chananaea,idolorum cultrix, ancilla daemoniorum. What do you say about Jesus? Non est bonum tollere panem füiorum, et mittere canibus (Mt 15,26). Nunquam advertistis, quemadmodum canes lapides unctos lingunt? Sic sunt omnes simulacrorum cultores. Sed venit vobis gratia. Quotquot autem receperunt eum, dedit eis potestatem filios Dei fieri (lo 1,12). Ecce habetis moda natos: dedit eis potestatem filios Dei fieri. Quibus dedit? His qui credunt in nomine eius. 4. Nativitas duplex.—Et quomodo filii Dei fiunt? Qui non ex sanguinibus, ñeque ex volúntate viri, nec ex volúntate carnis; sed ex Deo nati sunt (ib., 13). Accepta potestate ut filii Dei ieront, ex Deo nati sunt. Intendite ergo: isti ex Deo nati sunt; non ex sanguinibus, qualis est prima nativitas, qualis est nativitas misera, veniens de miseriis. Sed qui ex Deo nati sunt, quid erant? What cousin was born? Ex sanguinibus: mixtis sanguinibus masculi et feminae, commixtione carnis masculi et feminae, inde nati erant. Unde mode? Ex Deo nati sunt. Prima nativitas ex masculo et [680] femina: secunda nativitas ex Deo et Ecclesia. 5. idem tractatur argumentum.—Ecce ex Deo nati sunt: ​​unde fac1 We have already seen the same thought appear in sermon 77,10. í See complementary note 40: The mother Church: vol. VII p.757.

that being born of God to those who were first born of men? How, how was it? And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us. Admirable barter! He becomes flesh and these become spirit. What does this mean? Oh goodness, my brothers! Lift your spirits, however, to expect and receive greater things. Do not want to give yourself over to the evil passions of the century. You were bought at a great price; for you the Word became flesh; For your sake, he who was the Son of God became the son of man, so that the sons of man might become sons of God. What he was and what he has become! What you were and what you have been made! He was the Son of God, and became the son of man; You were sons of man, and you were made sons of God. He took our evils from us to communicate his good things to us. But even as the son of man he is very much upon us. For we are children of man through the lust of the flesh; He owes his to the faith of a virgin. The mothers of all men have conceived by sexual union; all men are born of a man father and a man mother; Christ was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary. He approached us without straying far from himself; or better yet, he never departed from his own divinity, but joined to it what is proper to our nature. He approached, therefore, what he was not, without ceasing to be what he was; He became the son of man, without ceasing to be the Son of God. And that is the Mediator, being in the middle. What does "in the middle" mean? Neither above nor

below. How neither up nor down? Neither above, because he is flesh, nor below, because he is not a sinner. However, as God, always above. Because, when he came to us, he did not leave the Father. He left us and did not leave us; He will return to us and will not leave him.

tum est ut ex Deo nascerentur, qui primo ex hominibus nati sunt? Unde factum est? where? Et Verbum caro factum est (ib., 14), ut habitaret in nobis. Magna mutatio: ille factus caro, isti spiritus. Quid est hoc? Qualis dignitatio, fratres mei! Erigite animum ad speranda et capienda potiora. Nolite vos addicere cupiditatibus saecularibus. Pretio empti estis: propter vos Verbum caro factum est: propter vos qui erat Filius Dei, factus est filius hominis; ut qui eratis filii hominum, efficeremini filii Dei. Quid erat ille, quid factus est? Quid were you, quid facti are you? Erat ille Filius Dei. Quid factus is this? Filius hominis. Eratis vos filii hominum. What are you facti? Filii Dei. Communicavit nobiscum mala nostra, nobis daturas bona sua. Sed ille ipso quo factus est filius hominis, dist a nobis. Nos filii hominum per concupiscentiam carnis: ille filius hominis per fidem virginis. Mater cuiuslibet hominis concubuit et concepit: unusquisque autem natus est de homine patre suo, et de homine matre sua. Christus autem natus est de Spiritu sancto et Maria virgine. Accessit ad nos, sed a se non multum recessit; immo a se quod Deus est nunquam recessit: sed addidit quod erat naturae nostrae. Accessit enim ad id quod non erat, non amisit quod erat. Factus est filius hominis: sed non cessavit esse Filius Dei. Per hoc Mediator in medio. What is it, in the middle? Nec sursum, nec deorsum, Quomodo nec sursum, nec deorsum?
Topic: Jesus and Nathanael (Jn 1,48-51). Location: Unknown. Date: Unknown.

1. What our Lord Jesus Christ says to Nathanael, if we look closely, is not for him alone, because under the fig tree the Lord saw, and there is no doubt about it, all of humanity. The fig tree in this passage, you see, meant sin. It doesn't mean it in everyone, but it does in this place, as I said, because of the congruence that can be seen in the fact that, as you know, the first man covered himself with fig leaves when he sinned. Embarrassed, in fact, by their crime, they covered with these leaves the members that God had given them and which they had just made shameful. There is no shame in divine work; But that blush had been preceded by a cause: sin. De Nec sursum, quia caro: nec deorsum, quia non peccator. Sed tamen in quantum Deus, semper sursum. Nec enim sic venit ad nos, ut dimitteret Patrem. A nobis ivit, et non nos dimisit: ad nos veniet, et illum non dimittet.
DE VERBIS EVANGELII IOANNIS: «CUM ESSES SUB FICU, VIDI TE», ETC., CHAP. 1.48-51

CAPUT I.—1. Nathanael sub ficu, genus humanum sub peccato.—Quod dictum audivimus a Domino Iesvi Christo Nathanaeli, si bene intellegamus, non ad ipsum pertinet solum. Ipse quippe Dominus Iesus sub ficu vidit omne genus humanum. Isto enim loco intellegítur per arborem fici significasse peccatum. Non ubique hoc significat, sed hoc loco, ut dixi, ea scilicet significandi congruentía, qua nostis primum hominem, quando peccavit, foliis ficulneis Fuisse subtectum (cf. Gen 3,7). His foliis enim Pudenda texerunt, quando de peccato suo erubuerunt: et quae Deus illis membra, ipsi sibi Pudenda fecerunt. Non enim erubescendum est de opere Dei: sed confusionem praecessit causa peccati. Yeah

not having preceded iniquity, nakedness would never blush. They were naked and were not ashamed, since they had not yet given cause to blush. To what end did I say all this? So that we see in the fig tree the symbol of sin. What does it mean, therefore: When you were under the fig tree, I saw you? I saw you when you were under sin. And, Nathanael returning to what had happened the day before, he remembered having been under a fig tree, where Christ was not. He was not with bodily presence; With spiritual presence, where is it not? Knowing, then, that he had been alone under the fig tree, where the Lord Christ was not, in telling him he said to him: When you were under the fig tree, I saw you, he discovered divinity in him and exclaimed: You are the King of Israel. 2. The Lord says to him: Because I told you that I saw you under the fig tree, do you wonder? greater things you must see. What are these greater things? You will see heaven open, and the angels of God ascend and descend upon the Son of Man. Let us remember the episode recorded in one of the holy books: Genesis. As Jacob was preparing to sleep in a certain place, he placed a stone as a headboard; and in his dreams he saw a ladder reaching from earth to heaven, and the Lord leaning on it; The angels went up and down there. This is what Jacob saw. A man's dream would not be narrated in Scripture if some mystery were not figured in it and if in that vision there were not for the understanding the announcement of some event non praecessisset iniquitas, nunquam erubesceret nuditas. Nudi enim erant, et non confundebantur. Non enim com[681]miserant unde confunderentur. Hoc autem dixi, quare? Ut per ficum intellegamus significatum esse peccatum. Quid est ergo, Cum esses sub jicu, vidi te? (1.48). Cum esses sub peccato, vidi te. Et ad rem gestam quidem respiciens,_ rememberatus est Nathanael se gone sub ficu, ubi non erat Christus. Non ibi autem erat praesentia corporali: scientia vero spíritaali ubi non est? Et quoniam sciebat se solum Fuisse sub ficu, ubi Dominus Christus non erat: quando dixit ei, Cum esses sub arbore fici, vidi te; et agnovit in illo divinitatem, et excíamavit, Tu es rex Israel (ib., 49). CAPUT II.—2. Somnium Jacob figura Fuit.—Dominus ait, Quia dixi ubi, Vidi te cum esses sub arbore ficu, inde miraris; maiora horum videbis. What sunt is this major? Et dixit: Videbitis caelum apertum, et Angelos Dei ascendants et descendants super Vilium hominis^ ​​(ib., 50. 51).

Recolamus veterem historiam conscriptam in libro sancto, id est, in Genesi. Quando Iacob in loco obdormivit, lapidem ad caput posit; et in somnis vidit scalam a terra pertingentem usque ad caelum: et Dominus incumbebat super eam; Angelí autem ascendebant et descendebant per eam. Hoc vidit Iacob. Somnium hominis non scriberetur, nisi magnum in illo aliquod figuraretur mysterium, et magnum aliquid prophetatum in

important. So much so that Jacob, understanding the meaning of the vision, fixed the stone there and sprinkled oil on it. This suggests the idea of ​​chrism, and chrism, the anointing of Christ, the Anointed One. He, in effect, is the Stone rejected by the builders, which became the head of the corner. Stone of which he himself said: Whoever stumbles against this stone will be broken into pieces, and whoever it falls on will be crushed to dust. He stumbled against the Stone on the ground, and it will come from above when it comes from above to judge the living and the dead. Woe to the Jews, for having stumbled upon Christ when He was a poor boulder! This man, he said, does not come from God, because he breaks the Sabbath. If you are the Son of God, get off the cross. Senseless! You laugh to see the Stone on the ground! But you laugh because you are blind, and, because you are blind, you stumble; and because you stumble, you shatter; and, now shattered by that boulder, the day will come when it will fall on you to reduce you to dust. So did Jacob anoint the stone to make it an idol? No; to turn it into a symbol. But let us come to Nathanael, since the Lord Jesus wanted to expose us to Jacob's vision. 3. Those studied in the school of Christ know how Jacob and Israel are the same: two names of a single man. The first name Jacob received at birth, and it means supplanter. When those two twins were born, the first was their brother Esau, and the younger's hand was seen on the foot illa visione intellegeretur. Denique ipse Iacob quia intellexit quid viderit, posit ibi lapidem, et perfudit oleo (Gen 28,11-18). Nam agnoscitis chrisma: agnoscite et Christum. Ipse est enim lapis, quem reprobaverunt aedificantes; ipse factus est in caput anguli (Ps 117,22). Ipse est lapis, de quo ipse dixit: Quicumque offenderit in lapidem illum, conquassabitur: super quem vero venerit lapis Ule, conteret eum (Mt 21,44). Offenditur in íacentem: veniet autem super eum, cum venerit de alto iudicare vivos et mortuos. Vae Iudaeis, quia cum iaceret humiliter Christus, offenderunt in eum. Non est, dicunt, homo iste a Deo, qui solvit sabbatum (lo 9,16). If Filius Dei is, descend from the cross (Mt 27:40). Insane, icet lapis, et ideo rides. Sed cum rides, caecus es: cum caecus es, offendis: cum offendis, conquassaris: cum quassatus fueris illo moda iacente, postea veniente desuper contereris. Ergo unxit lapidem Iacob. Numquid idolum fecit? Significavit, non adoravit.

Modo ergo audite, Nathanaelem istum attendite, per cuius occasionem Dominus Iesus exposee nobis voluit visionem Iacob. CAPUT III.—3. De duplici nomine et de lucta Iacob.—Nostis qui in schola Christi erudíti estis, Iacob ipsum esse et Israel. Duo sunt nomina: nam homo unus Fuit. Primum nomen Iacob, when natus est; accepit, quod interpretatur Supplantator. Quando autem illi gemini nati sunt, prior natus est frater Esau, et inventa est manus illius minoris in pede maioris. Tenebat pedem fratri suo praecedenti nascendo, postea et

of the eldest, as if holding by the foot the brother who was born before him; then he followed him. The act of grabbing his brother's plant gave rise to him being called Jacob, that is, supplanter. Some time later, returning from Mesopotamia, an angel fought with him on the road. Is there any proportion between the strength of an angel and that of a man? Therefore there is an enigma here; Therefore there is a mystery here; Therefore there is a prophecy here; then there is a figure here; Then let's see how to understand it. Observe, in fact, how they fight. They fight, and Jacob beats the angel, he grabs him; The man held back the defeated angel; He held him down, yes. And he said to him: I will not leave you unless you bless me. In this blessing of the victor, the defeated was represented by the Anointed One. Thus, that angel, personification of the Lord Jesus, says to Jacob: You will no longer be called Jacob; Your name will be Israel, which means he who sees God. Immediately it touched the nerve of his thigh, that is, in the "palm of the haunch" or buttock, and it withered, and Jacob became lame. And he was defeated! The defeated man was so powerful that, touching his buttock, he made him limp. Then he allowed himself to be defeated because he had the power to strip away his strength and the power to recover it. The defeated will not be angry, because the Crucified - of whom he was a type - will not be angry; But he blessed him, saying, Your name shall not be Jacob, but Israel. Then the supplanter became the one who sees God. It hit, as I already said, the nerve in his thigh and made him give up. Look at Jacob to the people of the Jews,

the thousands who went before and behind the Lord's horse, who, mixed among the apostles, worshiped the Lord and cried: Hosanna to the Son of David! Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord! See there the blessed Jacob. The lame remains in the Jews of today; because the buttock or width of the thigh means the multitude of his descendants, of whom a psalm speaks, where the faith of the Gentiles is predicted with these words: A strange people was my vassal, and as soon as they heard about me, they obeyed me; I was not with them, and I was heard; I was with these, and I was killed... A town that I did not know served me; At the first news of my arrival he obeyed me. Because faith comes from hearing preaching, and preaching from the word of Christ. The psalm continues: Strange children lied to me; refers to the Jews. The strange children lied to me; Other people's children grew old and lame from their paths. With my finger I have shown you the blessed Jacob and the lame Jacob 1. 4. But, in this regard, we must not pass over in silence a point, enough, in itself, to produce unrest in any of you; namely: why, after the name of the grandfather of this Jacob had changed, Abraham, who was previously called Abraham, and God changed his name, saying to him: You shall not be called Abraham, but Abraham, he has not since then been called Abraham again. Search the Scriptures, and you will see how, before receiving another

ipse secutas est. Et proptet hoc factum, quia plantara tenuit fratri suo appellatus est lacob (Gen 25,25), id est, Supplantator. Postea vero cum rediret de Mesopotamia, luctatus est cum [682] eo angelus in via. Quae virtus compare potest angelí et hominis? Ergo mysterium est, ergo sacramentum est, ergo prophetia est, ergo figura est; ergo intellegamus. Videte enim etiam luctaminis modum. Dum luctatur, praevaluit angelo lacob. Great significance. Et cum praevaluisset angelo homo, tenuit illum; tamen ipse homo eum, quem vicerat, tenuit. Et ait illi: Non te dimitto, nisi henedixeris mihi. Quando victor a victo benedicebatur, Christus figurabatur, Ángelus ergo ille, qui intellegitur Dominus Iesus, ait ad lacob: Iam non vocaberis lacob, sed erit nomen tuum Israel: quod interpretatur, Videns Deum. Deinde tetigit nervum femoris eius, id est latitudinem lacob femoris, et aruit ei: et factus est claudus lacob (Gen 32,24-32). Ipse est ille victus. Tantum potuit ille victus, ut et femur tangeret, et claudum faceret. Ergo volens victus est. Potestatem enim habuit Pondi virtutem suam, et potestatem habuit assumendi eam (lo 10,18). Non irascitur victus, quia non irascitur crucifixus. Nam et benedixit eum, they say, Non vocaberis lacob, sed Israel. Tune supplantator factus est videns Deum. Et tetigit, sicut dixi, femur eius, et fecit eum claudicare. Serves in lacob populum Iudaeorum, illa miHia sequentium

et praecedentium iumentum Domini, qui iuncti Apostolis adorabant Dominum, et clamabant, Hosanna filio David; benedictus qui come in nomine Domini (Mt 21,9). Ecce lacob benedictus. Iam claudus rernansit in eis, qui modo Iudaei sunt. Latitudo enim femoris, significat multitudi. nem generis. De quibus Psalmus, cum Gentes credituras prophetasset say: Populus quem non cognovi, servivit mihi, in auditu auris oboedil vit mihi (Ps 17,45). Non ibi Fui, et auditus sum: hic Fui, et occisus sum. Populus quem non cognovi, servivit mihi, in auditoru auris oboedivit mihi. Igitur fides ex auditu, auditus autem per verbum Christi (Rom lo 17). Et sequitur: Filii alieni mentiti sunt mihi: de Iudaeis. Filii alien} mentiti sunt mihi, filii alieni inveteraverunt, et claudicaverunt a semitis suis (ib., 46). Assignavi vobis lacob, et benedictum et claudum. CAPUT IV.—4. Abraham cur primum nomen suum cum posteriorg non retinet, lacob vero e contra.—Verum ex hac occasione non est praetereundum, quod potest fortasse sua sponte vestrum aliquem cotn. I will move: quid sibi vult, quod cum mutatum esset nomen Abrahae avi huius lacob (nam et ipse prius Abram vocabatur, et Deus mutavit illi nomen, et dixit, Non vocaberis Abram, sed Abraham (Gen 17,5) ex illo non est vocatus Abram. Quaerit in Scripturis, et videbitis superius antequam acciperet aliud nomen, non est vocatus nisi Abram: posteaquaír, The subject is much discussed by Augustine, who always gives the same interpretation. See sermons 5,6-8; 229 F,2 (= GUELF. 10);

name, his name was none other than Abraham, and after receiving it his name was none other than Abraham. Jacob, when he received another name, heard the same words: You shall not be called Jacob; you will be called Israel. Search the Scriptures, and you will see that they were always called one and the other: Jacob and Israel. And this is because the significance of Abraham's name was to receive fulfillment in this century. This name means, in effect, that he was to become the father of many peoples here, while the name of Israel refers to the future century, where we will see God. The people of God, the Christian people, are, currently, Jacob and Israel; Jacob in reality, Israel in hope. As Jacob supplanted his brother, the lesser people supplanted the greater; Have we not supplanted the Jews? We have supplanted them in the sense that they were supplanted because of us. If they had not been blinded, Christ would not have been crucified; Had Christ not been crucified, his precious blood would not have been shed; If that blood had not been shed, the earth would not have been rescued. And since their blindness was to our advantage, the older brother was supplanted by the younger, and the younger was called supplanter. How long, however, will it be? 5. The time will come, in the last days of the world, when all Israel will believe; It will not be those currently alive, but their children, alive then. These now will go their ways to their destinations and will pass into perpetual damnation; accepit, non est vocatus nisi Abraham. Iste autem Iacob, quando accepit aliud nomen, eadem verba audivit, Non vocaberis lacob, sed vocaberis Israel. Quaerite Scripturas, et videte quia utrumque semper vocatus est, et Iacob et Israel. Accepto alio nomine Abram, non aliud est vocatus nisi Abra [685] ham: accepto alio nomine Iacob, et Iacob vocatus est, et Israel. Nomen Abrahae in hoc saeculo explicandum Fuit: hic est enim factus pater tumbarum gentium, unde nomen accepit. Nomen autem Israel ad alterum saeculum pertinet, ubi videbimus Deum. Populus ergo Dei, populus Christianus, in hoc tempore et Iacob est et Israel; Jacob in re, Israel in spe. Supplantator enim fratris dicitur populus minor populi maioris. Numquid us supplantavimus Iudaeos? Sed supplantatores dicimur illorum, quia nostri causa sunt supplantati.

Nisi excaecati essent, Christus non crucifigeretur: si Christus non crucifigeretur sanguis Ule pretiosus non funderetur: si sanguis ille non funderetur, orbis terrarum non redimeretur. Quia ergo nobis profuit caecitas illorum, ideo a minore fratre maior supplantatus est, et appellatus est minor Supplantator. Sed quamdiu hoc? CAPUT V.—5. Israeli in fine credenti viewed Dei promissa.—Veníet tempus, veniet finís saeculi, et credet totus Israel: non illi qui moda sunt, sed filii ipsorum qui tune erunt. Nam moda isti per via suas ambulantes ibunt ad loca sua, transibunt ad damnationem perpetúan!.

But, when all the Jews form a single people, what we sing will be realized: I will be satisfied when your glory appears, when the promise that now is only a promise of seeing face to face becomes reality. Now we see him in reflection, in an enigma and only partially; but when, equally purified, resurrected and crowned, they put on their immortal form and perpetual incorruption, both peoples will see God face to face; There will be no more Jacob, but Israel forever; In the eyes of the Lord they will then appear like this holy Nathanael, who personifies them, and he will say to them: See there the genuine Israelite, in whom there is no deceit. See there the genuine Israelite. These words should bring Israel to your mind, and by association with Israel they should remind you of that dream where you saw the ladder from earth to heaven, God leaning on it and the angels descending and ascending. Jacob saw this dream. It was after this dream that it was called Israel, that is, when it came from Mesopotamia shortly after and during the journey. If, consequently, this Jacob, to whom the name Israel was imposed, saw the ladder and, in turn, Nathanael was a true Israelite without any artifice, do you not already understand why the Lord said to him: Greater things you must see, and why Jacob's dream was brought to his memory when he saw him marvel at those words: I saw you when you were under the fig tree? Well, to whom was the Lord saying this? To a man who had just called a true Israelite and without hypocrisy. It is valid, therefore, as much as telling him: «You will see fulfilled in you the dream of the one whose name I have given you; do not be amazed When autem factus fuerit unus totus populus, fiet illud quod canimus: Satiabor, dum manifestabitur gloria tua (Ps 16,15). Dum venerit promissio, quae nobis promittitur, ut videamus facie ad faciem. Modo videmus per speculum in aenigmate et ex parte: quando autem uterque populus iam purgatus, iam resuscitatus, iam coronatus, iam in immortalem formam et in incorruptionem perpetuam commutatus, videbit Deum facie ad faciem, et iam non erit Iacob, sed solus erit Israel; tune eum in persona huius sancti Nathanael videbit Dominus, et dicet: Ecce veré Israelita, in quo dolus non est (lo 1,47). When you hear, Ecce I will see Israelite; yeniat tibi inmentem Israel: cum venerit tibi inmentem Israel, veniat tibi inmentem somnium illius, in quo somnio scalam vidit a terra usque ad caelum, Dominum superincumbentem, Angelos Dei ascendants et descendants. Hoc somnium Iacob vidit.

Post hoc autem appellatus est Israel: id est, post paulum veniens de Mesopotamia et agens iter. First, however, the afflictions of this life must pass, where he who accompanies us to whom we say: Help us in tribulation. This life for the discreet is nothing but uninterrupted tribulation. The soul has two executioners who torture it not at the same time, but alternately: fear and pain. When your things are going well, you fear; When your things go wrong, you suffer. Who is not deceived by the prosperity of this century and who is not broken by adversity? We must take, therefore, while the hay lasts, the safest path: the Word—the Word—of God. The prophet having said: All flesh is like grass, and all its glory is like the flower of hay; The grass withers, the flower withers, as if we asked him: "What hope is left for the hay, what duration is left for the flower of the hay?" He added: But the Word of the Lord remains eternally. And that Word of God, how am I to hear it? The Word of the Lord became flesh and lived among us. That Word of God is telling you: "Do not reject my promises, for I did not reject your hay." Now, what the Word of the Lord did for us so that, clinging to him, we would not pass away like the flower of the hay; that which he did for us: the Word became flesh, taking flesh without changing into flesh, remaining and assuming: remaining what already was and assuming what was not; This, I say, that he did for us, is also figured in that pool.

CAPOT III. — 3. Piscinae probaticae significatio. Humilitas Christi per superbiam non respuende.—Dico Breviter: aqua illa, Iudaicus populus erat; quinqué porticus, Lex. Et ego, inquit, crediturus sum Deum in carne, Deum natum ex femina, Deum crucifixum, flagellatum, mortuum, vulneratum, sepultum? Absit ut hoc credam de Deo; indignum est. [688] Cor loquatur, non cervix. Superbo videtur indigna Domini humilitas, ideo a talibus longe fit sanitas. Noli te extollere: if you see sanari, descend. That is why the sick lay in the porches, but they were not cured there. Is this not what the Apostle said: If a law capable of giving life had been given? Therefore these porches, which represent the law, could not heal the sick. Someone will say: "Then what was it given for?" The apostle Paul himself is right: Vero the Scripture enclosed everything under the dominion of sin, so that the blessing of the promise could be granted to believers by virtue of faith in Christ. They were sick, they considered themselves healthy; But, receiving a law that they could not comply with, they realized their illness and requested the doctor's intervention; They wanted to be healed, because they knew they were sick; and they would not have known it except seeing it was impossible for them to fulfill the law. The man considered himself innocent, and boasting of a fictitious innocence aggravated his illness. The law, therefore, was enacted to tame pride and make it manifest; not to heal the sick, but to convince the proud. Let your charity pay close attention to this: the law was not given to heal the sick, but to know them. And thus, those sick of the Gospel would have been able to keep their illnesses more secret within their homes if there were not those porticos; But there were some, and in them everyone could see them, although the porticos did not cure them. Since violations of the law made man even more guilty, the usefulness of the law consisted in bringing sins to the surface, with the sight of which the sinner could curb his pride and ask for help from divine mercy. to the Apostle: The law was crossed to increase crime; but where sin grew, grace abounded all the more. What does it mean: The law was crossed to increase crime? The same thing from another place: Because where there is no law, there is no transgression either. Before the law a man may be called a sinner, not a transgressor; but, once the law is promulgated, if he violates it, he becomes guilty not only of sin, but of transgression as well. Since the transgression was added to the sin, the crime increased. When crime abounds, human pride ends by submitting and blessing God and telling him: I am sick; and repeat those words from another psalm, which come only from a humble breast: I said: "Have mercy on me, Lord; heal my soul, because I have sinned against you. Let the sick soul say this, at least convinced of having transgressed the law; convicted, but not cured by the law. And listen to Paul himself demonstrate to you how, even though the law is good in itself, it is not it that frees you from sin, but the grace of Christ. Because the law may well prohibit and command; but to prepare the healing medicine for the disease that prevents man from fulfilling the law, she cannot do that; That is done by the grace of Christ. The Apostle therefore says: I delight in the law of God according to the inner man; In other words: I already see that what the law rebukes is evil, and what it commands is good. Why, then, was that sick person not cured? Let us consider his words: I have no one, he said, who, when the water is moved, puts me in the pool; When I arrive, another has already come down. 4. The Jews were rioting. «How is this! “Why does he do these things on the Sabbath?” And, above all, as a result of the words: My Father is still working, and that is why I also work. They were scandalized by this because they gave an entirely carnal meaning to God's rest, the seventh day, from all activity. This rest is spoken of in Genesis; It is a magnificently written and deeply thought out passage. But the Jews imagined that, if God had rested on the seventh day, it was because he was tired from working; and that, if he had blessed this day, it was because he had recovered from his fatigue that day. The very fools did not understand that, if God had done everything with a single word, He could not get tired. Tell me where you have read how God could have gotten tired of saying: Let it be done, for this is how what he did was done. Would a man today get tired of doing things the way God made them? He said: Let there be light, and there was light; let the firmament be made, and it was made. Did he get tired of not having been obeyed when he said it? Scripture briefly answers this elsewhere: He spoke, and the things were; He commanded, and things were created. Whoever acts like this, what job does he have? But if you don't have any work, how do you rest? In that Sabbath rest after God had ceased to work, our rest was symbolized; because, after the six ages of the world have passed, rest will come, and these six ages are like six days. The first day goes from Adam to Noah; the second passed

I entered the flood and Abraham; the third, from Abraham to David; the fourth, from David to the Babylonian captivity; the fifth, from the deportation to Babylon until the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ. Now the sixth day is passing. We are, therefore, in the sixth age, on the sixth day 2. Consequence: since on the sixth day man was made in the image of God, let us reform ourselves in the image of God. It was that which God then made the formation; this, our reform; that was the creation; this, the repair. After the day where we now are, after this age, will come the rest promised to the saints, prefigured in the days of Genesis. Because, to tell the truth, God, after having produced his creatures, no longer does anything new in the world, where his works will only revolve around themselves and transform, because nothing was added to them from the point at which they received being. However, if the one who made the world did not govern it, what had been done would be undone; He has, therefore, to take control of his actions. And since nothing was added to creation, it is said that he rested from all his works; But because he does not cease to govern what he did, the Lord said well: My Father is still working. May your charity attend: it is said that he rested because he finished; He concluded his works and did not add anything afterwards. He governs what he did, therefore he does not cease to work. But with the ease with which he did it, he governed with that same ease. Do not go, brothers, to imagine that, not having worked at birth,

Deus ab omnibus operibus suis (Gen 2,2). Scriptum est enim in Genesi, et optime scriptum est, et rationabile quare scriptum est. lili autem putantes quasi Deum fatiguetum post omnia requie [692] visse seventh die, et ideo benedixisse eum, quia in eo a lassitudine refectus est, non intellegebant stulti, quia qui verbo fecit omnia, fedari non potuit. Legant, et dicant mihi quomodo posset fatigueri Deus dices: Fiat; et factum est. Hodie si sic faciat homo, quomodo fecit Deus, quis fatiguetur? Dixit: Fiat lux; et facía est lux. item, Fiat firmamentum; et factum est (Gen 1,3,6,7): aut si dixit, et factum non est, fatiguetus est. Quadragenarius numerus in June Moysi, Eliae et Christi. Quadragesima before Pascha. Quinquaginta dies post Pascha.—Redeamus ergo ad rem. Perfectio iustitiae quadragenario number demonstratur. Quid est quadragenarium numerum implere? Continere se ab amore huius saeculi. Continentia a rebus temporalibus, ne perniciose amentar, quasi ieiunare est ab isto saeculo. Ideo Dominus quadraginta diebus ieiunavit (cf. ib., 4,2), et Moyses (cf. Ex 34,28), et Elias (cf. 3 Reg 19,8). Qui ergo dedit

forty days, could he not fast eighty or a hundred? Why did he not want to fast more than what was permitted to his servants except because there was a mystery in this number 40: because that number meant that we should fast or abstain from the eastern century? Which is as good as saying what the Apostle says: The world is crucified for me and I for the world. Whoever does this fulfills the number 40. But, in short, what does the example of the Lord teach us? Moses, Elijah and Christ having fasted, then the law, the prophets and the Gospel teach the same thing. The only teaching of all the Scriptures is that you abstain from the world and turn your love to God. This type of fast is figured in the law by the fast of Moses for forty days; in the prophets, by that of Elijah for forty days, and in the Gospel, by the fasting of the Lord for forty days as well. This also explains why the Lord showed himself on the Mount of Transfiguration between Moses and Elijah. The law and the prophets, in fact, bear witness to the Gospel. But why does the number 40 mean the perfection of justice? In a psalm it is read: O God, I will sing to you a new song and I will sing psalms with the ten-stringed psaltery; This psalter symbolizes the ten precepts of the law, which the Lord did not come to repeal, but to perfect. Now this law is spread throughout the entire earth, which, as is well known, has four extremes: east and west, south and north,

as the Scripture says. Hence also that that container or tablecloth where all the species of animals were found in an image, and was shown in vision to Peter, while a voice told him: Kill and eat (to make us understand that all peoples had to receive the faith and be incorporated into the guild of the Church, as what we eat is incorporated into our body), was lowered from heaven by means of four ropes, an emblem of the four parts of the world, demonstrating that everyone had to believe. Then the number 40 means the abstinence of the century. This renunciation is the fullness of the law; The fullness of the law is charity. Hence we fast forty days before Easter, because the forty days before Easter are the image or figure of our current laborious life, where we fulfill the law by dint of sacrifices, bitterness and restraint. Beyond Easter, that is, while we celebrate the days of the Lord's resurrection, which means our own resurrection, celebrate it for fifty days; because, adding the denarius of the reward to the forty, the number 50 is obtained. -—And why does the denarius mean reward? —Haven't you read that the laborers hired to work in the vineyard, both those of the first hour, those of the sixth hour, and those of the last hour, received only one denarius? Therefore, when our righteousness is added to its reward, we will be in the number 50. Let us not faint in this forty-year anniversary, so that we may rejoice in that fiftieth anniversary. 10. Who fulfills the law without charity? Ask the Apostle: The fullness of the law is charity. The entire law, in fact, is encrypted in a single word, that of Scripture: You shall love your neighbor as yourself. But the precept of charity is twofold: You will love your Lord God with all your heart, with all your soul, with all your mind. Here is the great precept. The other is similar to this: "You shall love your neighbor as yourself." The entire law and the prophets are contained in these two commandments. Without this double love it is impossible to fulfill the law. Failure to comply with the law is a disease. That's why the man in the pool was sick; He had been there for thirty-eight years, two to go. What does missing two mean? He did not fulfill the two commandments mentioned. What does it matter to fulfill the others, if these are not fulfilled? Are you thirty-eight? It is of no use to you if both are missing. 1. It is often asked how it is that God finished doing all his works on the sixth day and rested on the seventh day, that is, on Saturday, as it is written in the book of Genesis, where the holy Scriptures begin, saying the Son of God, by whom all things were made: My Father is working until now; I also work 1. With this he refuted the Jews, who blamed him for having said to a paralyzed man on the Sabbath: Get up, take up your mat and walk. Is the Son contrary to the Word of the Father, being the same Word of the Father? It is necessary for us to understand this so as not to resemble the Jews, who understood the Sabbath so carnally that they imagined God to be idle since the Saturday on which he rested. And if they did not believe this, perhaps they believed that it worked on creatures for six days, resting on Saturdays and having fun on holidays, like children on vacation. This

The point is resolved by saying that God completed and perfected the creation of his works in six days, and on Saturday he rested or stopped, not from governing the creatures, but from creating them. These masses of the world, or let's say the sky and the earth, if they are not governed by him, they fall apart. And he rules the world without work, not like the one who carried the stretcher. And, if it is well understood, God works and rests at the same time, since everyone who works without work rests in the same work. If you ask me if God is doing nothing, I tell you: "Would we live if He did nothing?" And if you ask me again if God has rest, I will tell you again: "And how can he give it to us, if he does not have the same thing that he must give?" Therefore, he has rest and works right now. You can't do that, but he is God and you are not. The time had come for the shadows to pass and the day to dawn, as described in the Song of Songs: Until the day dawns and the shadows dissipate. 2. When Jesus ordered the sick man healed by him to take the stretcher, he dispelled the ancient shadows. The time had already come to fulfill what the Apostle said: Let no one, therefore, condemn you on account of food or drink, or on holidays, or new moons, or Saturdays, all things that were a shadow of those to come. Those observances of the Jews that God had imposed on them were a shadow of the future and what was to come Christ began to make present with his arrival; what was expected had come; What it meant was already seen by the eyes.

Topic: Faith and intelligence; the vision of the Word (Jn 5,19). Location: Unknown. Date: Around 417.

1. The hidden depths of the divine kingdom demanded his belief before leading us to his intelligence; Faith, in fact, is the step of intellection, and intellection is the reward of faith. A prophet says it openly to all those who, as it should be the other way around, rush into the search for intelligence without giving anything for belief. It says: If you do not believe, you will not understand. Because faith also has a kind of light of its own in the Scriptures, in prophecy, in the Gospel, in the writings of the apostles. All these readings that are now given to us are lamps in the darkness and support while the day comes. The apostle Peter says: And we have something even more firm, namely, the prophetic word; which you do very well to attend to, like a lamp that shines in a dark place, until the day shines and the morning star rises in your hearts.

The Son cannot do anything by himself, except what he sees the Father do. Here the error of the Arians6 arises: one rises to fall, because one does not humble oneself to rise. What impression have these words made on you? You have heard how the Son cannot do anything on his own, except what he sees the Father do, and you deduce that the Son is inferior to the Father. Yeah; I know well that you deduce from this the inferiority of the Son; I know, I know; that is your impression; believes, however, that it is not minor; believe it as long as you cannot see it; That's what I told you recently. You tell me: "How can I believe, if the words of the Word itself say the opposite?" He says: The Son cannot do anything by himself, except what he sees the Father do. Pay close attention to what follows: For all the things that the Father does, the Son also does. He did not say: "Such as those," but: those same ones. (Muttering in the audience.) Don't make noise among yourselves; Keep your charity composure for a few moments. Here we need serenity of spirit, a faith full of piety, veneration, the presence of God and not to look at me, poor tray, but at the one who puts the bread on this tray. For a carnal understanding, better still, for a carnal discourse, there is something like two architects, the Father and the Son: the Father, who acts on his own, and the Son, who acts when he sees his Father. What shall I say? Two artisans: father and son, for example. The father made a closet that his son would not be able to make if he did not see the father doing it; but, studying the piece of furniture made by the father, he manages to build another one, not the same one. I leave for a little later the words that follow in the evangelical text, and I ask the Arian now: Is this how I have sensitized him, as you understand it? Did the Father do something, and when the Son saw the Father do it, did he become something similar? That's what the words that made such an impact on you sound like. Because it does not say: "The Son cannot do anything of himself, except what he hears the Father commands him," but: The Son cannot do anything of himself, except what he sees the Father do; which you understand like this: the Father did something, the Son took care to see how he did it, to do it himself; something, however, different, but equal to that done by the Father. But what the Father did, by whose hands did he do it? If not through the Son, if not through the Word, you incur blasphemies against the Gospel, according to which all things were made through him. Therefore, the same thing that the Father had already done, he had done by the hands of the Word; and, if he had done it by the hands of the Word, he did it by the hands of the Son. Who is that other person who pays attention to the work of the Father in order to do something similar? You do not usually say that the Father has two sons; His Only Begotten is one and only; only in divinity, not only in inheritance for its goodness alone. The Father made them joint heirs with his Son; not generated, like him, from his own substance, but made, thanks to him, from his adoptive family. Because we were called

to the adoption of children, as Holy Scripture attests. 10. What do you say then, Arian? The Only One says in person, the only Son of God himself says in the Gospel, the Word himself tells us, we hear him himself say: The Son cannot do anything by himself, except what he sees the Father do. —Then what the Son did, he did it because he had seen the Father do it. —However, the Father does nothing except by the hands of the Son... I see that you are embarrassed, heretic; Certainly you get upset; but this discomfort, like that caused by hellebore, will be healthy for you. You no longer know yourself; It seems to me that you would give away your opinion and carnal way of seeing things. Put your carnal eyes behind your back and lift the sight of your heart, if you have any, to the contemplation of the divine. Those words that are in your ears are, indeed, human words on the lips of a man; In the Gospel you hear the words of an evangelist, that is, a man speaking to another man; but they are words that speak to you about the Word of God, so that by hearing the human you may rise to the knowledge of the divine. The divine Master was the one who placed this concern in you, to instruct you, and has planted this question, to awaken your attention. The Son cannot do anything by himself, except what he sees the Father do. Logically, he should have added: "Whatever things the Father does, the Son does just as they do"; But he did not say that, but: All things that the Father does, these same things the Son also does. The Father does not do some things and the Son does others, because everything the Father does, he does through the hands of the Son.

He resurrected Lazarus the Son: perhaps this resurrection was not also the work of the Father? The Son gave sight to a blind man: did not the Father also enlighten him? Yeah; the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit. It is a trinity of people; but its actions are unique, its sovereignty is unique, its eternity is unique, its coeternity is unique, and the actions of the Trinity are the same. The Father does not create some men, the Son others, and the Holy Spirit others; It is one man himself whom the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit create; The Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit are but one and the same Creator. 11. The plurality of people appears here; but you must recognize oneness of divinity. Because there is a plurality of people, it has been said: Let us make man in our image and likeness. He does not say: «I am going to make man; "Look carefully at what I do, so that you can, in your turn, do something like that." Let us make, in plural, our image, also in plural. Where to find the singularity of divinity? Continue reading: And God made man... It is said: Let us make man, and it is not said: "The gods made man." The unity is seen, therefore, where it was said: God made man. 12. What remains, then, from the crude Arian interpretation? Be ashamed, hide, be done with it; speak to us the Word of God. The pious, the believers, those of us who, because we are imbued with faith, have acquired some right, however weak, to intellection, let us now turn our faces to the Word, source of light, and let us say to Him in unison: Lord, the things that the Father does, those same things You do, because whatever the Father does, you do.

body saw what was before it, although nothing was hidden from its divinity. Forget, then, forget a little the condition of servant and think of that of God, in which he already existed prior to the creation of the world, and for which he was equal to the Father. Accept and recognize this equality, of which the Apostle told you: Who, despite his divine condition, did not consider being equal to God a stolen prey. Look at him, if you can, in this light so that you can see what his seeing is. In the beginning the Word already existed. The Word, how does it see? Does the Word have eyes? Are there these eyes of ours in him? I do not mean carnal eyes, but those eyes of pious hearts, of which it has been said: Blessed are the pure in heart, for they will see God. 14. That Christ that you contemplate is, at the same time, man and God; what it shows you is humanity, what it reserves for you is divinity. And see how he shows you humanity and reserves divinity for you: He who loves me, says, keep my commandments; Whoever loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will also love him. And, as if answering this question: "What will you give to him who loves you?", he adds: And I will show myself to him as I am. What does this mean, brothers? Well, weren't the same people he was promising to reveal himself to already be seeing him? Who do I tell? Who saw him and who did not see him? To an apostle who wanted to see the Father to be satisfied: Show us the Father, and it is enough for us, the Savior says: As long as I have been with you, and you have not yet known me? Whoever sees me, also sees my Father.

When he said this to him, he is before the eyes of the servant, in the condition of a servant, keeping his divine condition for the already deified eyes. You pretend to see the Father; look at me, because now you see me and you don't see me; You see what I took on for you, you don't see what I reserved for you. Observe the commandments, purify your eyes, because whoever loves me keeps my precepts, and I will love him. As if to say: "It is to the keeper of my commandments that I will reveal myself as I am." 15. If, therefore, we cannot, brothers, see what the seeing of the Word is, where are we going? Are we not, perhaps, demanding a vision out of time? Why expect to be shown what we are not yet able to see? When, therefore, we are told about the gaze, about the seeing of the Word, we are told about something that we long for, but cannot yet make our own. If you saw the seeing of the Word, perhaps that same seeing of the Word would be seeing the Word itself; because the Word is not one thing and the seeing of the Word is another; otherwise, he would be of a mixed and complicated nature, double and compound; but the Word is simple, of ineffable simplicity. It is not like man, where man is one thing and man's seeing is another. Doesn't it sometimes happen that man's seeing goes out and man remains? This is what I was referring to when I said I was going to say something that not everyone could understand, and I still pray to God that someone understood it. My brothers, what is asked of us is to recognize, at least, that this seeing of the Word surpasses our intellectual capacity; weak capacity, which we have to apply

Theme: The resurrection of the dead and retribution (Jn 5:25-29). Location: Unknown. Date: Between 410 and 420. 1. Our hope, brothers, is not limited to this time, nor to this world, nor to the happiness with which men who forget God blind themselves. The first thing that a Christian soul must know and defend is that we have not come to Christianity for the enjoyment of the goods here, but for another not well known, which God has already promised us, but of which men cannot yet get an idea. Of which, in fact, he has said: What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor heart of man desired, this God has prepared for those who love him. Of a good so magnificent, beautiful and ineffable, no man has been able, consequently, to give a notion; but he has the divine promise in his favor. Man now, blind in heart as he is, is incapable of conceiving such a promise, nor is there any way to make clear what the man himself to whom such a promise is made will be tomorrow. When the Lord said these words, He closed them like this: These will go to eternal combustion, but the righteous to eternal life. This is the eternal life that we are promised. 2. For the same reason that 'men have love for this

life of the earth, they were promised life, and for the same reason that they are afraid of dying, they were promised eternal life. —What do you love? -Live. —Well, you will have it. —What do you fear? -Die. —Well, you won't suffer it. It seems that it should be enough for human weakness to be told: "You will have eternal life." Because of what is happening here, man's understanding could get an idea of ​​what is in store for us in the future. However, what a great disproportion! He lives, he does not want to die; hence the love of endless life, always wanting to live, never wanting to die. With all this, those who have to go to the torturous penalties of hell must want to die, and they will not be able to. Therefore, the excellence of life does not lie in living long or in living always; The great thing is to live happily 2. Let us love eternal life. How much it is worth working for life without end, we can infer from seeing the love of men for the present, temporary and ending life, and how they fight for it; Well, when there is fear of death, they exhaust their capacities, not to eliminate, but to postpone death. How man works when death comes upon him, fleeing, hiding, giving everything he has to evade it; getting tired, suffering torture and discomfort, bringing doctors and doing, in short, everything within his power! And see how, by dint of sacrifices and spending what he has, he can manage to live a little longer; live forever, that cannot be done. Yes, well, with so much effort,

The testimony of the Son and John
Topic: The testimony of the Son and John (Jn 5:31-35). Location: Unknown. Date: Between 412 and 416.

1. We have just heard some words of the holy gospel, and it is possible that someone has missed what the Lord Jesus said: If I bear witness of myself, my testimony is not true. Must not the testimony of the Truth be true? Is it not he who said: I am the way, the truth and the life? Who should be believed, if not the Truth? Obviously, those who do not take the side of believing the Truth only want to believe falsehood. To discover the true meaning of these words, it is necessary to understand them as responding to what their interlocutors thought: If I bear testimony of myself, my testimony is not true. He well knew his testimony about himself to be true; but, in attention to the weak, the unbelievers, the unintelligent, the Sun resorted to the candles; The tenderness of his eyes could not bear the brilliance of the Sun.

Testimonium Christi, etiam de se ipso quam verum sit.—Audivimus verba sancti Evangelii: et hoc potest aliquem permovere, quod ait Dominus Iesus, Si ego testimonium perhibeo de me, [714] testimonium meura non est verum (lo 5,31). Quomodo ergo non est verum testimonium veritatis? Nonne ipse est qui dixit: Ego sum via, et sales, et vita? (14.6). Cui ergo credendum est, si veritati non est credendum? Profecto enim non vult credere nisi falsitati, qui non eligit credere veritati. Dictum est ergo hoc secundum ipsos, ut sic intellegas, et ex his verbis hunc sensum concipias: Si ego testimonium perhibeo de me, testimonium meum non est verum, id est, sicut putatis. lile enim noverat verum esse de se testimonium suum: sed propter infirmos, propter incredulos, propter non intellegentes, sol luzerns quaerebat. They thought within themselves: If we speak of men, the people, who have John as their prophet, will stone us; and if we say of heaven, he will say to us: "How then did you not believe it?" Because John bore witness to Christ. The heart was in a fist, because of the issue that they themselves had raised; Caught in their own snares, they responded: We don't know. What other voice could have come out of that darkness? The noble thing is to say when a man does not know something: "I don't know"; But when, knowing it, he says, "I do not know," he testifies against himself. They knew very well that the baptism of John and the excellence of the Precursor were from heaven, but they did not want to come to terms with the one to whom John had testified. Are not the martyrs, perchance, witnesses of Christ, who bear witness to the Truth? And, looking at it carefully, that testimony that the martyrs give to Christ is a testimony given by him to himself; In fact, he lives within the martyrs so that they may bear witness to the Truth. Listen to one of the martyrs, the apostle Paul himself: Are you looking for proof that it is Christ who speaks in me? Then, when John bears witness, Christ, who dwells in John, bears witness to himself; and whether Peter bears witness, whether Paul bears witness to Christ, whether the apostles, or Stephen, who dwells in all of them bears witness to himself. He is God without them; They without him, what are they? 4. It has been said of him: Going up on high, he took captivity with him, and distributed gifts to men. What does captivity take prisoner mean? He defeated death. What does it mean, I say, he led captivity captive? The devil sought his death, and the devil himself was held captive by the death of Christ. He climbed to the top. Do we know of something higher than the sky? Clearly and in the sight of his disciples he ascended to heaven; so we know, so we believe and so we confess. He distributed gifts to men. What gifts? The Holy Spirit. Now,

Well, whoever gives such a gift, what will it be? Admirable goodness of God, who gives us a gift equal to himself!; His gift is the Holy Spirit; and the Father, and the Son, and the Holy Spirit are one God: the Trinity. And what good did the Holy Spirit bring us? Listen to the Apostle: The love of God, he says, has been poured into our hearts. Where from, oh beggar, did that love of God poured into your heart come to you? How could this divine love be poured into the heart of man? We have, said the Apostle, the treasure is in clay vessels. To what end in clay vessels? To highlight the strength of God. Having, finally, said: The love of God has been poured out in our hearts, and, in order that no one should attribute to himself the love of God, 2 he added: By the Holy Spirit, who was given to us. Therefore, for you to love God, it is necessary that God dwell in you, that his love comes to you from him and returns from you to him; or be it, that you receive his motion, put his fire in you, enlighten you and raise up his love. 5. Because there is struggle in our body itself; our life is a combat, and the combat is a danger; and we can only do so through the mercy of those who love us. What a struggle this is ours, you heard it when the Apostle was read. Because the whole law, he says, has its fulfillment in a single word, in that "you shall love your neighbor as yourself." This love comes to us from the Holy Spirit. You will love your neighbor

Iesus, Nec ego dicam vobis in qua potestate ista jacio (Luke 20:2-8). Et confusi sunt, et impletum est, Paravi luzernam Christo meo; inimicos eius induam confusione. CAPUT II.—3. In martyribus Christus sibi ipse perhibet testimonium. Martyres norme testes sunt Christi, et testimonium perhibent veritati? Sed si diligentius cogitemus, quando illi martyres perhibent testimonium, ipse sibi perhibet testimonium. Ipse enim habitat in martyribus, ut perhibeant testimonium veritati. Audi unum ex martyribus, ipsum apostolum Paulum: Numquid experimentum vultis accipere eius qui in me loquitur Christus (2 Cor 12,3)? Dum perhibet ergo testimonium Ioannes, Christus sibi perhibet testimonium, qui habitat in Ioanne. Perhibeat testimonium Petrus, perhibeat Paulus, perhibeant ceteri Apostoli, perhibeat Stephanus; ipse sibi perhibet testimonium, qui habitat in omni[715]bus. Ipse enim sine illis Deus est; illi sine illo quid sunt? 4. Caritas ex Spiritu sancto.—De ipso dictum est, Ascendit in altum, captivavit captivitatem, dedit dona hominibus (Ps 67,19; Eph 4,8). What is it, captivavit captivitatem? Vicit mortem. What is it, captivavit captivitatem? Mortem procuravit diabolus, et ipse diabolus de morte Christi est captivatus. Ascendit in altum. Quid altius cáelo novimus?
Such, in fact, is the original meaning of the Greek word martyr.

Evidenter et ante oculos discipulorum suorum ascendit in caelum (Act 1,9). Hoc scímus, hoc credimus, hoc fatemur. Dedit donates hominibus. What donut? Spiritum sanctum. Qui such dat donum, qualis ipse est? Magna est enim mercy Dei: donum dat aequale sibi; quia donum eius Spiritus sanctus est, et unus Deus tota Trinitas, Pater, et Filius, et Spiritus sanctus. Quid nobis praestitit Spiritus sanctus? Apostolum audi: Caritas Dei, inquit, diffusa est in cordibus nostris. Unde tibi, o mendice, caritas Dei diffusa est in corde tuo? Quid, aut in quo caritas Dei diffusa est in corde humano? Habemus, inquit, thesaurum istum in vasis fictilibus. Quare in vasis fictilibus? Ut eminentia virtutis sit Dei (2 Cor 4,7). Denique cum dixisset, Caritas Dei diffusa est in cordibus nostris; ne putaret quisque a se sibi esse quod diligit Deum, continuo addidit, per Spiritum sanctum qui datus est nobis (Rom 5,5). Ut ergo ames Deum, habitet in te Deus, et amet se de te; Id est, ad amorem suum moveat te, accendat te, illuminet te, excitet te. CAPUT III.—5. Lucia animae et carnis. Subdenda anima Deo, animae caro.—Lucta est enim in isto corpore: quamdiu vivimus, pugnamus; quamdiu pugnamus, periclitamur: sed in his omnibus superamus, per eum qui dilexit nos (cf. ib. 8,37). Pugnam nostram, moda cum Apostolus legeretur, audistis: Omnis, inquit, Lex in uno sermone impletur, in eo quod est, Diliges proximum tuum sicut te ipsum (Gal 5:14). This dilectio of Spiritu sancto est. Diliges proximum tuum sicut te ipsum. Prius

as yourself. First examine if you already know how to love yourself; When this is, I will let you love your neighbor as yourself. But if you still don't know how to love yourself, be careful not to deceive your neighbor as you are deceiving yourself. If you love evil, you do not love yourself; witness the psalm: Vero he who loves iniquity hates his soul. And if you hate your soul, what does it profit you to love your flesh? If you live according to the flesh, you will die; But if with the spirit you put to death the tricks of the flesh, you will live. Explain to us, Apostle, what spirit you are referring to. Because man also has a specific spirit, typical of his nature, and thanks to it he is a man; Spirit and body are the two constituents of the human being. And of that spirit of man it has been said: No one knows the innermost being of man except the spirit of man that is in him. I see, then, that man has, by necessity of his own essence, a spirit, and I hear you say: If with the spirit you put to death the tricks of the flesh, you will live. Now I ask: With what spirit: with mine or with God's? Those your words fill me with indecision. When, in fact, one speaks of the spirit, this means sometimes the spirit of man, other times the spirit of vermin, since it is written that all flesh that had the spirit of life in it died in the flood. Therefore the spirit of man is called the same as that of beasts. And sometimes the wind is even called spirit, as recorded in a psalm: Fire, hail, snow, frost, the spirit of the storm. Since the term spirit means so many things, with what spirit did you say,

Oh Apostle, are the works of the flesh to be mortified? With mine? With God's? Hear what follows and you will understand; the words that come after dissipate the difficulty. When he had said: If with the spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live, he immediately added: For all those who are led by the Holy Spirit are children of God. You act if you let yourself be carried away, and you act well if you are led by the good Spirit. Consequently, in the words: If with the spirit you put to death the sinisters of the flesh, you will live, one was left doubting which spirit they were referring to; but in those that come after them, do you not see the Lawgiver? Do you not recognize the Redeemer? Because it was your Redeemer who gave you the Spirit with which you are to mortify the sinisters of the flesh. All those led by the Spirit of God, those are children of God. They are not children of God if they are not led by the Spirit of God; but, if they are led by the Spirit of God, they fight, because they have a sovereign reinforcement in him. God, in fact, is not a bystander when we fight, as the people are before the gladiators. The people can declare themselves for a hunting athlete, but they cannot intervene in the combat. It is God himself who has just put these words before us through the mouth of the reader, after having communicated them to us through the ministry of the Savior; Now listen to some reflections, brief in number, although weighty. 2. It is, without a doubt, easy to apply all this to the Jews; It is to be feared, however, that, thinking too much about them, we turn our eyes away from ourselves. Because, although the Lord speaks before his disciples, it is certain that what he said to them, he also said to posterity. What he said: See that I am with you until the end of the ages does not refer only to them, but to the Christians who would be thereafter until the end of the world. Therefore speaking to them, he says: Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees. They then thought he was telling them for not having stocked up on bread; They did not understand that the words: Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees, mean the same as "beware of the doctrine of the Pharisees." And what was the doctrine of the Pharisees except that which you heard recently? 'You seek glory from one another and receive it from one another, and you do not seek the glory of the one God. The apostle Paul says this about them: I attest to them that they have a zeal for God, but misunderstood. He says they have zeal for God; I recognize it, I know it very well, I was with them and I was one of them. They have zeal for God, but misunderstood. What does it mean, oh Apostle?

that "having misunderstood zeal"? Explain to us what kind of understanding you recommend and you are sorry they do not have it and you want it to be in us. Put it below, where he clarified what had been dark for us. What does it mean: They have zeal for God, but misunderstood? Because, not knowing the justice of God and preferring to maintain their own, they did not surrender to the justice of God. Ignoring, therefore, the justice of God and insisting on maintaining one's own, that is, expecting glory from one another and not seeking the glory of the only God, is the leaven of the Pharisees, from which they command one to beware lest we be told: Why do you say to me: "Lord, Lord," and do not do what I say? 3. Let us, therefore, leave a little to the Jews, to whom the Lord was then speaking. They are not here nor are they willing to listen to us. They hate the Gospel; When the Lord was alive, they obtained false testimonies to kill him, and, even though he was dead, they bought more testimonies against him with money. When we say to them: "Believe in Jesus," they answer: "Are we going to believe in a dead man?" When we add that he was resurrected, they respond: “No way! "His disciples took him from the tomb." The Jewish buyer loves falsehood and despises the truth of the Lord Redeemer. What you say, O Jew, your elders bought it with money, and the fruit of their purchase has been bequeathed to you. You lie about who bought it for you, not who bought a lie for you.
