Finally, the Church can also say, in conclusion: If you believed Moses, you would also believe me, since he wrote about me; because I—the Church—am the body of him of whom Moses wrote; Moses also wrote about the Church. Moses, furthermore, has written of the Church itself; In fact, these words refer to her: In your descendants all nations will be blessed. Moses wrote this in the first of his books; Therefore, if you believed Moses, you would also believe Christ; but, despising the words of Moses, you must necessarily despise those of Christ. There they have, he says, Moses and the prophets; listen to them No, father Abraham; But if any of the dead go there, they will hear him. To which he said: "If you do not listen to Moses and the prophets, you are not to believe a risen man from the dead who comes." This was told to the Jews; but it has no value against heretics. He had risen from the dead who said: It was necessary that Christ should suffer and rise from the dead on the third day. —I believe this, says the heretic. —Do you believe it? —I believe it. "Then why don't you believe what follows?" If you believe that it was necessary for Christ to suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, which was said from the head, also believe what

Apostolus: futidata est Ecclesia, [724] manet usque nunc; et uberius manet, multiply manet, tenet quod accepit ab Apostólo, Si quis annuntiaverit vobis praeter quam quod accepistis, anathema sit (Gal 1,9). Quid ergo? What do you say? Mundus non sum? Ibi baptizaras, mundus non sum? Etiam is not. Quare? Quia ego ibi non fue. Sed qui ubique est, ibi Fuit. Qui ubique est, ibi Fuit, in cuius nomen credidi. Tu nescio unde veniens, immo non veniens, sed volens ut ego ad te veniam, hic positus dicis mihi: Non es recte baptizatus, quia ego ibi non Fui. Vide quis ibi Fuit. What dictum is Ioanni? Super quem videris Spiritum descendentem quasi columbam, hic est qui baptizat (lo 1,33). Ipsum habes quaerentem te: immo quia mihi ab ipso baptizato invidisti, ipsum perdidisti. CAPOT VII.—8. Quae sit Catholicorum, quae Donatistarum doctrina. Intellegite ergo, fratres mei, vocem nosttam et illorum, et videte quid eligatis. Nos hoc dicimus: Simus sancti, Deus scit; simus iniqui, et hoc magis ipse scit: vos ín nobis spem non ponatis, qualescumque simus. Si boni sumus, facite quod scriptum est: Imitatores mei estote, sicut et ego Christi (1 Cor 4:16). Si autem mali sumus, nec sic deserti estis, nec sic sine consilio remansistis: audite dtcentem, Quae dicunt, facite; quae autem faciunt, faceré nolite (Mt 23,3). lili autem contra: Nisi boni fuerimus,

peristis. Ecce est alius qui veniet in nomine suo. Ergo vita mea ex te pendebit, et salus mea ex te religabitur? Itane oblitus sum fundamentum meum? Nonne petra erat Christus? (cf. 1 Cor 10:4). Nonne qui aedificat super petram, ipsum non deicit ventus, pluvia, illuminate? (cf. Mt 7:25). Come ergo mecum, si vis, super petram, et noli mihi esse velle pro petra. 9. Donatistae nec Moysi, nec Christo credunt vel resurgenti. Donatistae in Christum iniurii.—Dicat ergo et novissimum illud Ecclesia, Si crederetis Moysi, crederetis et mihi; de me enim Ule scripsit: quia corpus sum eius, de quo scripsit. Et de Ecclesia Moyses scripsit. Nam Moysi verba dixi, In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes (Gen 22:18). Moyses hoc in primo libro scripsit. Si crederetis Moysi, crederetis et Christo. Quia Moysi verba contemnitis, necesse est ut Christi verba contemnatis. Habent ibi, inquit, Moysen et Prophetas, audiant illos. Non, father Abraham; sed si quis a mortuis venerit, ipsum audient. Et ille: Si Moysen et Prophetas non audiunt, nec si quis a mortuis resurrexerit, credent (Luke 16,29-31). Hoc de Iudaeis dictum est: ergo non dictum de haereticis? CAPUT VIII.—A mortuis resurrexerat qui dicebat, Oportebat Christum pati, et resurgere a mortuis tertia die. Hoc credo. Creed, question. Do you believe? Quare non credis quod sequitur? Quia credis, Oportebat Christum pati, et resurgere a mortuis tertia die; hoc dictum est de capite: crede et quod

comes next about the Church: And that penitence for the remission of sins would be preached in her name for all nations. Why accept what is said about the head and disbelieve what is said about the body? What did the Church do to you to want, in a way, to decapitate it? You want to remove its head from the Church, and believe in the head, and ignore the body, as if it were a body without a soul. In vain you flatter the head as a devoted servant; Whoever tries to decapitate, tries to kill the head and the body. They are ashamed to deny Christ, and they are not ashamed to deny the words of Christ. Neither we nor you saw Christ with our eyes. The Jews saw him, and killed him. We did not see it, and we believe; His words are with us. Compare yourselves to the Jews: they despised him hanging on the tree, you despise him sitting in heaven; Despite their claims, the title of Christ remained; You see, with your arms crossed, that the baptism of Christ is erased. But, brothers, what recourse do we have if it is not to also pray for these arrogant, for these inflated ones, who go so far back in this way? Let us say to God for them: Let them know that your name is Lord and that not men, but you alone are Most High over all life. Returned to the Lord, etc. sequitur de Ecclesia, Praedicari in nomine eius paenitentiam et remissionem peccatorum per omnes gentes. [725] Quare credis de capite, et non credis de corpore? Quid tibi fecit Ecclesia, ut eam velis quodam moda decollare? Tollere vis Ecclesiae caput, et capiti credere, corpus relinquere, quasi exanime corpus. Sine causa capiti, quasi famulus devotus blandiris. Qui decollare vult, et caput et corpus conatur occidere. Erubescunt deniale Christum, et non erubescunt deniale verba Christi. Christum nec nos vidimus oculis, nec vos. Iudaei viderunt, et occiderunt. Nos non vidimus, et credimus: verba ipsius nobiscum sunt. Compare your ludaeis: illi contempserunt pendentem in ligno, vos contemnitis sedentem in cáelo: illis suggerentibus stetit titulus Christi, vobis stantibus deletur Baptismus Christi. Sed quid restat, fratres, nisi oremus et pro superbis, oremus et pro elatis, qui se sic extollunt? Dicamus pro illis Deo, Cognoscant quia tibi nomen Dominus: et non homines, sed tu solus altissimus super omnem terram (Ps 82,19). Conversi ad Dominum, etc.
Topic: The multiplication of the loaves (Jn 6:5-15). Location: Unknown. Date: After 400.

1. It is a great miracle, dearly beloved, to satisfy five thousand men with five loaves and two fish, and still have enough left for twelve baskets. Great miracle, by faith; but the fact is not so admirable if we think of the maker. Who multiplied the loaves between the hands of the distributors, does he not multiply the seeds that germinate in the earth and fill the barns with grains? But since this portent is renewed every year, no one is surprised; But the reason for not admiring it is not its insignificance, but rather its frequency of repetition. 1. In doing these things, the Lord spoke to the understandings, not so much with words as through his works. The five loaves symbolize the five books of the law of Moses; because the old law is, with respect to the Gospel, what barley is to wheat. There are in these books - of the law - deep mysteries concerning Christ, which is why he said: If you believed Moses, you would believe me also, since he has written about me. But just as in the barley the core is under the chaff, so is Christ veiled.
DE VERBIS EVANGELII IOANNIS, UBI NARRATUR MIRACULUM DE QUINQUÉ PANIBUS ET DUOBUS PISCIBUS. CHAP. 6.5-14

1. Miraculi meaning.—Miraculum grande factum est, dilectissimi, ut de quinqué panibus et duobus piscibus saturarentur quinqué hominum millia, et residua fragmentrum implerent duodecim cophinos. Grande miraculum: sed non multum mirabimur factum, si attendamus facientem. lile multiplicavit in manibus frangentium quinqué panes, qui in terra germinantia multiplicat semina, ut grana pauca mittantur et horrea repleantur. Be quia illud omni anno facit, nemo miratur. Admirationem tollit non facti vilitas, sed assiduitas. Dominus autem quando ista faciebat, non solum per verba, sed etiam per ipsa miracula intellegentibus loquebatur. Quinqué breads signifiant quinqué books Legis Moysi. Lex vetus hordeum est ad evangelicum triticum. Magna in illis libris de Christo mysteria continentur. Unde ait ipse: Si crederetis Moysi, crederetis et mihi: de me enim Ule scripsit (lo 5,46). Sed quomodo in hordeo medulla sub palea latet; sic in velamento mysteriorum Legis latet Christus. Ut
See note 4 to sermon 126.

in the mysteries of the law; and as the mysteries of the law are unfolded by exposition, so the loaves grew by breaking them. This same presentation that I have been making is breaking bread. The five thousand men mean the people subject to the five books of the law; The twelve baskets are the twelve apostles, who, in turn, were filled with the recesses of the same law; The two fish are either the two commandments of the love of God and neighbor, or the two peoples: that of circumcision and that of the foreskin - Jew and Gentile - or the two sacred functions of the empire and the priesthood. Exposing these mysteries is like breaking bread; understanding them is nourishing. 2. Let us return to the maker of these things. He is the bread that came down from heaven; a bread, however, that repairs without diminishing; It can be submerged, it cannot be consumed. This bread was figured in the manna; whence it was said: He gave them bread from heaven; Man ate the bread of angels. Who but Christ is the bread of heaven? But that man might eat the bread of angels, the Lord of angels became man. If this had not been done, we would not have their meat; and, if we did not have his meat, we would not eat the bread of the altar. And since we have been given such a valuable pledge, let us run to take possession of our inheritance. Let us long, my brothers, to live with Christ, since we have his death as a pledge. How can someone who has suffered our evils not give us his goods? In this country, in this perverse century, what abounds but being born, working, suffering and pañis mysteria illa exponuntur, et dilatantur; sic et panes illi crescebant, quando frangebantur. Et hoc quod vobis exposui, panem vobis fregi. Quinqué millia hominum significant plebem sub quinqué libris Legis constitutam. Duodecim cophini sunt duodecim Apostoli, qui et ipsi de fragmentis Legis impleti sunt. Duo pisces sunt, aut duo praecepta dilectionis Dei et proximi, aut duo populi ex circumcisione et praeputio, aut duae illae sacrae personae regís et sacerdotis. Haec cum exponuntur, franguntur; cum intelleguntur, manducantur. 2. Christus pañis factus incarnatione. Mercator Chri\126]stus. Redemptor noster, quomodo.—Convertamur ad eum qui ista fecit. Ipse est pañis, qui de cáelo descendit (lo 6,41): sed pañis qui reficit, et non deficit; pañis qui sumi potest, consumí non potest. Ipsum panem etiam manna significat. Unde dictum est: Yanem caeli dedit illis, panem Angelorum manducavit homo (Ps 77, 24 et 25). Quis est pañis caeli, nisi Christus?

Sed ut panem Angelorum manducaret homo, Dominus Angelorum factus est homo. Si enim hoc non factus esset, carnem ipsius non haberemus: si carnem ipsius non haberemus, panem altaris non manducaremus. Festinemus ad hereditatem, quia magnum inde pignus accepimus. Ftatres mei, desideremus vitam Christi, quia tenemus pignus mortem Christi. Quomodo nobis non dabit bona sua, qui passus est mala nostra? In terris istis, in isto saeculo maligna quid abundat, nisi nasci, laborare et mori? Human debaters, convince me, si liar: at-
The multiplication of the loaves

die? Examine human things, and deny me if I lie. See if men are here for any other purpose than to be born, suffer and die. Such are the products of our country; that is what abounds. To provide himself with such merchandise the divine Merchant descended from heaven; And because every merchant gives and receives: he gives what he has and receives what he does not have, he gives the purchase money and receives what he bought, Christ also gave and received. But what did he receive? What abounds among us: being born, suffering and dying. And what did he give? Reborn and resurrected and forever reign. Oh good Merchant, buy from us! But what do I say buy us, if rather we should thank you for having bought us? And at what price! At the price of your blood that we drink... Yes; you give us the price... The gospel we read is our instrument 2. We are your servants, we are your creatures, because you made us and redeemed us. A slave can buy anyone from him; what it cannot do is create it; the Lord, on the other hand, created and redeemed his servants. Through creation he gave them existence; through redemption he gave them independence. We had come into the hands of the prince of this century, the seducer and enslaver of Adam, the beginning and origin of our slavery; but the Redeemer came, and the seducer was defeated. And what did the Redeemer do to the enslaver? To rescue us he made the cross a noose, where he put his blood as bait; blood that the enemy could have shed and did not deserve to drink. And because he shed the blood of someone who owed him nothing, he was forced to return the tendite omnes nomines, utrum ad aliud sint in hoc saeculo, quam nasci, laborare et mori. Haec sunt mercimonia regionis nostrae, ist hic abundant. Ad such merces Mercator ille descendit. Et quoniam omnis mercator dat et accipit; dat quod habet, et accipit quod non habet; quando aliquid comparat, dat pecuniam, et accipit quod emit: etiam Christus in ista mercatura dedit et accepit. Sed quid accepit? Quod hic abundat, nasci, laborare et mori. Et quid dedit? Renasci, resurgere et in aeternum regnare. O bone Mercator, eme nos. Quid dicam, eme nos, cum gratias agere debenamus, quia emisti nos? Pretium nostrum erogas nobis, sanguinem tuum bibimus; erogas ergo nobis pretium nostrum. Et Evangelium legimus, instrumentum nostrum. Servi tui sumus, creature tua sumus: fecisti nos, redemisti nos. Emere potest quisque servum suum, creare non potest: Dominus autem setvos suos et creavit et redemit: creavit ut essent; redeem, ne semper captivi essent.

Incidimus enim in principem huius saeculi, qui seduxit Adam et servum fecit, et coepit nos tanquam vernaculars possidere. Sed venit Redemptor, et victus est deceptor. Et quid fecit Redemptor noster captivatori nostro? Ad pretium nostrum tetendit muscipulam cruze suam: posit ibi quasi escam sanguinem suum. Ule autem potuit sanguinem istum fundere, non meruit bibere. Et in eo quod fudit sanguinem non debitoris, iussus est reddere debitares; fudit

that they should; For having shed the blood of the Innocent, he was forced to get rid of the guilty. The Savior, in fact, shed his blood to erase our sins, and thus the letter of obligation that held us to the devil was erased by the blood of the Redeemer. For we were not subject to him except by the bonds of our sins. They were the chains of our captivity. And he came and chained the strong man with his passion and entered his house, that is, into the hearts where he dwelt, and took away his vessels. He had filled them with his bitterness, and even gave it to our Redeemer to drink with the gall; But, by snatching away the vessels that the devil had filled and making them his own, our Lord poured out the bitterness and filled them with sweetness. 3. Let us love him, because he is sweet. Taste and see how sweet the Lord is. It is to be feared; but you have to love him even more. He is man and God: one Christ, God and man at the same time; and since he is a man, he is a soul and a body, but not two people. In Christ there are, indeed, two substances: God and man; more people only one; and thus, notwithstanding the incarnation, God is a trinity, not a quaternity. Is it possible, therefore, that God does not have mercy on us, when he became man for us? He did so much—for us—that he is even more astonishing than his promises, and his works should move us to believe in what he promised. We would hardly believe what he did if we had not seen it. Where do we see it? In the

towns that have their law, in the crowds that follow them. Thus the promise he made to Abraham when he was told: In your descendants all nations will be blessed has been fulfilled. If he looked at himself, when would he have believed it? He was a man, and alone, and old, and his wife was sterile and of such advanced age that, even without the defect of sterility, conception would be impossible. There was no basis at all on which to support hope: however, looking at the person who made the promise, he believed it, even without leading the way. Here, then, is fulfilled before us what was the object of their faith; We believe, consequently, what we do not see because of what we are seeing. He begat Isaac: we have not seen him; Isaac begat Jacob: which we also did not see; He fathered twelve children; which we have not seen either, and his twelve sons begat the people of Israel; that now we are seeing... Well, I have already begun to say what we are seeing, I continue... Of the people of Israel, the Virgin Mary was born, who gave birth to Christ, and it is evident how in Christ all nations are blessed. Is there anything truer? Is there anything more true? Is there anything more obvious? You who came out of gentility with me, desire with me the future life. If God already fulfilled in this century what he had promised to do in the descendants of Abraham, how could he not fulfill his eternal promises to those he made of Abraham's descendants? The Apostle says it: If you are Christians, then you are descendants of Abraham. They are words of the Apostle.

sanguinem innocentis, iussus est recedere a nocentibus. lile quippe sanguinem suum ad hoc fudit, ut peccata nostra deleret. Unde ergo Ule nos tenebat, deletum est sanguine Redemptoris. Non enim tenebat nos nisi vinculis peccatorum nostrotum. Istae erant catenae captivorum._ Venit ille, alligavit fortem vinculis passionis suae: intravit in dornum eíus, id est, in corda eorum ubi ipse habitbat, et vasa eius arripuit (cf. Mt 12,29). We sumus vasa. This impleverat ille amartitudine sua. Hanc amartitudinem etiam our Redemptori in felle propinavit. Impleverat ergo nos ille tanquam vasa sua: Dominus autem noster arripiens vasa eius [727] et sua faciens, fudit amaritudinem, implevit dulcedine. 3. Amandus Christus. Ex eo quod Deus fecit, credibile fit quod promisit.—Amemus ergo eum, quia dulcis est. Enjoy yourself, et videte quia suavis est Dominus (Ps 33,9). Timendus est, sed plus amandus est. Homo et Deus est: unus Christus homo et Deus est; quomodo unus homo, anima et corpus: non autem Deus et homo duae personae. In Quisto duae sunt quidem substantiae, Deus et homo: sed una persona, ut Trinitas maneat, non accesonte homine quaternitas fiat. Quomodo ergo fieri potest ut nostri non misereatur Deus, propter quos homo factus est Deus? Multum est quod fecit: mirabilius est quod fecit, quam quod promisit; et ex eo quod fecit, debenmus credere quod promisit. Hoc enim quod fecit, vix crederemus, nisi et videremus. Ubi videomus? In populis cre-

dentibus, in multitudine ad eum adducta. Quia impletum est, quod promissum est Abrahae: et ex his quae videmus, credimus quae non videmus. Unus homo fuet Abraham, et dictum est illi, In semine tuo benedicentur omnes gentes (Gen 12:3). If ad se attenderet, when will it be believed? Unus homo erat, et iam senex erat, et uxorem sterilem habebat, et aetate iam ita progressam, ut concipere non posset, etiamsi sterilis non Fuisset. Non erat prorsus unde aliquid speraretur. Sed promittentem attendebat, et credebat quod non videbat. Ecce ille quod credit, we see. Ergo ex his quae videmus, debenmus credere quae non videmus. Genuit Isaac, non vidimus: et Isaac genuit Iacob, et hoc non vidimus: et Iacob genuit duodecim filios, et ipsos non vidimus: et duodecim filii eius genuerunt populum Israel; magnum populum videmus. Iam coepi et dicere quae videmus. De populo Israel nata est virgo María, et peperit Christum; et ecce in Christo benedicuntur omnes gentes. Quid verius? quid certius? quid apertius? Desiderate mecum futurum saeculum, qui congregati estis ex Gentibus. In hoc saeculo implevit Deus promissum suum de semine Abrahae. Quomodo ergo non dabit nobis aeterna promissa sua, quos fecit esse semen Abrahae? Hoc enim dicit Apostolus: Si autem vos Christi, Apostoli verba sunt, ergo Abrahae semen estis (Gal 3,29).

4. We have begun to be a great thing; no one thinks little of it. We were nothing, we are already something. We have said to the Lord: Remember that we are dust; but from dust he made man; He gave life to this dust, and in the person of Christ our Lord he elevated this dust to the heavenly kingdoms. From here, in fact, he took his flesh; from here he took his land, to raise it to heaven who made the earth and the sky. Suppose, then, that we are told today for the first time about two things that have not yet been realized and we are asked which thing is more surprising: that God has become man or that man has become God. £ Which is greater wonder? Which one is more difficult? What has Christ promised us? What we have not yet seen: to be his men, to reign with him and not to die forever and ever. We are made to believe that a man, coming from nothing, arrives at immortal life is a harsh thing. And yet this is what we believe when the dust of the world, which blinds the eyes of faith, has been shaken off from our hearts. We are told to believe this: that after death we will go with these bodies, victims of death, to life where we do not die. Admirable thing indeed; still, however, it is surpassed by God dying once. Between men receiving life from the hand of God and God receiving death from the hand of men, doesn't the latter seem more incredible? Then, if this is a fact, we create what is to be. Will God not give us the most credible, if the most incredible was done? 4. Quod praestitit Christus, mirabilius est quatn quod promittit.— Magnum aliquid coepimus esse; nemo se contemnat: nihil Fuimus; sed aliquid sumus. Diximus Domino, Memento quia pulvis sumus (Ps 102,14): sed ille de pulvere hominem fecit, et pulveri vitam dedit, et in Quisto Domino nostro iam ipsum pulverem ad caeli regna perduxit. Quia hinc accepit carnem, hinc accepit terram, et terram levavit in caelum, qui fecit terram et caelum. Si ergo duae res novae adhuc non factae proposerentur nobis, et quaereretur a nobis, Quid est mirabilius, ut qui Deus est fiat homo, aut qui homo est fiat homo Dei? What is mirabilius, what is difficilius? Quid nobis promisit Christus? Quod nondum videmus: hoc est, ut simus homines ipsius, et regnemus cum illo, et non moria[728]mur in aeternum. Quasi hoc difficult creditur, ut homo natus perveniat ad eam vitam, ubi nunquam moriatur. Hoc est quod excusso corde credimus, excusso dico a mundi pulvere, ne ipse pulvis claudat nobis oculos fidei.

Hoc est quod iubemur credere, quia cum mortui fuerimus, etiam cum corporíbus mortuis in vita erimus, ubi nunquam moriamur. Mirabile hoc est: sed mirabilius est quod fecit Christus. Quid est enim incredibilius, ut vivat semper homo, aut ut aliquando moriatur Deus? Accipere homines vitam a Deo credibilius est? accipere Deum mortem ab hominibus, puto quia incredibilius est. Et iam factum est: credamus et quod futurum est. Si factum est quod est incredibilius, non

God can make men angels, since he makes men from an earthly and horrible seed. What will we be? Angeles. What were we? It's embarrassing to remember it; But it is worth thinking about it, although I blush to mention it. What were we like? Where did God make men? What were we before being totally? Nothing, And when we were in the womb, what were we? Imagining it is enough. Throw out of the understanding the matter from which you came and bring it to what you are now. You live, but the grasses and trees also live; you feel, but animals also feel. You are men, and in this you have an advantage over animals; and you are of a higher order than animals, because you have notion of the great good things that God has given us. You live, you feel, you understand, you are men. What other benefit can compare to this? That of being Christians. If we had not received this gift, of what benefit would it be for us to be men? We are Christians, then; We belong to Christ. There the world rages against us; He will not be able to break us, because we belong to Christ. And if he caresses us, he will not be able to seduce us: we belong to Christ! 5. We have found a great protector, brothers. You know how wide men get with their protectors. The private of a powerful man is threatened, and responds: "Long live so-and-so, my lord, and you can do nothing to me." How much louder and with more reason can we say: "Long live our Head, and you can do nothing to me!" » Because our protector is our Head. On the other hand, whoever relies on any protector is his client; we are nothing but nobis dabit quod est credibilius? Potens est enim Deus Angelos homines faceré, qui semina terrena et horribilia homines fecit. Quid erimus? Angeli. Quid Fuimus! I could remember: cogorconsidere, et erubesco dicere. What was fuemus? Unde Deus homines fecit? Quid fuemus antequam omnino essemus? Nihil eramus. Quando in ventribus matrum eramus, quid eramus? Sufficit quod recolitis. Tollite encouragement ab eo unde facti estis, et cogitate quod estis. Vivitis: sed vivunt et herbae et arbores. Sentitis: sentiunt et pécora. Homines estis: pécora transistis, superiors pecoribus estis; quia intelligitis quanta praestitit nobis. Vivitis, sentitis, intellegitis, homines estis. Is this autem benefit quid compari potest? Christiani estis. Hoc enim si non acceperimus, quid nobis prodesset quia homines essemus? Christiani ergo sumus, ad Christum pertinemus. Saeviat mundus, non nos frangit; quia ad Christum pertinemus.

Blandiatur mundus, non nos seducit; ad Christum pertinemus. 5. Christianorum sub patrono Christo securitas.—Magnum patronum invenimus, fratres. Nostis quia tendunt se homines de patronis suis. Minanti alicui, respondert clients maioris: Except capite domini mei illius, nihil mihi facis. Quanto fortius et certius nos dicimus: Salvo capite nostro, nihil nobis facis? Quoniam patronus noster caput est nostrurn,

members of our protector. Leaning on him, no one will be able to separate us, whatever evils befall us in this world, because everything that happens is nothing, and through the path of evils we will reach the goods that do not pass away. CAPUT I.—1. Ad regenerationis gratiam invitationntur Catechumeni.— Sicut audivimus, cum sanctum Evangelium legeretur, Dominus Iesus Christus exhortatus est promissione vitae aeternae ad manducandum carnem suam et bibendum sanguinem suum. Qui audistis haec, nondum omnes intellexistis. Qui enim baptizati et fideles estis, quid dixerit, nostis. Who autem Inter vos adhuc Catechumeni, vel Audientes vocantur, potuerunt esse cum legeretur audientes, numquid et intellegentes? Ergo sermo noster ad utrosque dirigitur. Qui iam manducant carnem Domini, et bibunt sanguinem eius, cogitent quid manducent, et quid bibant: ne, sicut dicit Apostolus, iudicium sibi [735] manducent et bibant (1 Cor The catechumens were divided into hearing and competent. While the former were those who had determined to be baptized one day, the latter were those who at the beginning of Lent gave their name to be baptized on the night of the next Easter. See complementary note 64: The catechumenate: vol. VII p.766. The catechumens, as is known, could only attend the liturgy of the word, after which they were dismissed and only the faithful, that is, those already baptized, remained in the temple for the continuation of the Eucharistic sacrifice, which in this way became something hidden and unknown to them. In their presence they spoke only of Baptism and not of the Eucharist, which has received the name "discipline of the arcane." 140,19,48. The Saint, in fact, usually addresses the topic with phrases like this: "The baptized know..."

banquet, to which they are invited. These days, the magistrates distribute provisions; Christ does it daily; His table is the one that stands in the center of the church. For what reason, catechumens, do you not come to the banquet of the table that you have in sight? 3 Perhaps right now, while the gospel was being read, you said within yourselves: What do the words mean: My flesh is true food and my blood is true drink? How do you eat the flesh and how do you drink the blood of the Lord? Do we understand what he says? Who closed the door on you so you can ignore it? It is veiled; but, if you wish, it will be revealed to you. Make the profession and you will have the question resolved. The faithful already understand what the Lord said; You, however, call yourself a catechumen, you call yourself a listener, and you are deaf. You have the ears of the body open, for you hear the words that were spoken; but your heart's ears are still closed, because you do not understand what has been said. I don't argue; I plainly state the truth. Easter is there; register for baptism. If the festivity does not move you to it, be moved by curiosity to know what he said: He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood remains in me and I in him. To know the same as me, what that means, knock, and it will be opened to you. And as I say to you: "Knock, and it will be opened to you," so I knock so that you will open to me; I call to your heart making my words sound in your ears. 11,29). Qui autem nondum manducant, et nondum bibunt, ad such epulas inviting festinent. Per istos dies magistri pascunt, Christus quotidie pascit, mensa ipsius est illa in medio constituta. Quid causae est, o Audientes, ut mensam videatis, et ad epulas non accessatís? Et forte moda cum Evangelium legeretur, dixistis in cordibus vestrís: Putamus quid est quod dicit, Caro mea veré esca est, et sanguis meus veré potas est? (6.56). Quomodo manducatur caro Domini, et bibitur sanguis Domini? Putamus quid dicit? Quis contra te clausit, ut hoc nescias? Velatum est: sed si voleris, erit revelatum. Access ad professionem, et solvisti quaestíonem. Quod enim dixit Dominus Iesus, iam fideles noverunt. Tu autem Catechumenus diceris, diceris Audiens, et surdus es. Aures enim corporis patents habes, quia verba quae dicta sunt audis: sed aures cordis adhuc clausas habes, quia quod díctum est non íntellegis. I dispute, I don't argue. Ecce Pascha est, da nomen ad Baptismum.

Si no te excitat festivitas, ducat ipsa curiositas: ut scias quid dictum sit, Qui manducat carnem meam, et bibit sanguinem meum, in me manet, et ego in íllo (ib., 57). Ut scias mecum quid dictum sit, pulsate, et aperietur tibi. Et ut tibi dico, Pulsa, et aperietur tibi: ita et ego pulse, aperi mihi. Auribus personans, ad pectus pulse. Augustine insists that his listeners decide once and for all to be baptized and thus be able to participate in the Eucharist. A long-term catechumenate was very common, which allowed one to live more peacefully while awaiting the total forgiveness that baptism provides.

2. If the catechumens, my brothers, must be exhorted not to delay coming to the immense grace of regeneration, how much greater care will we not display in arranging the faithful to take advantage of what they attain, and thus not eat or drink these delicacies to their own condemnation? So as not to eat or drink to your irreparable harm, live well; Exhort them to this, not by word, but by your customs, so that those who have not yet received baptism may hasten to follow you; but so that they do not die by imitating you. Married people, keep the conjugal faith towards your wives 4 and give them what you demand of them. You demand chastity from your wife; Give him an example, not advice. You are the guide, watch where you are going; You must go where she can follow you without danger; Even more: you must walk where you want your wife to walk. Ask for strength from the weaker sex; you both have the lust of the flesh; The strongest be first to defeat it. However, it is painful to say that many men are advantaged by women. They keep chastity, and they do not want to keep it; and in that same failure to keep it they pin their dignity as men, as if the strength of sex consisted of being more easily defeated by the enemy. This is a fight, a combat, a contest. The man is stronger than the woman; the man is the head of the woman; and the woman fights and wins, and you succumb to the adversary! You have a wife and yet you come to the Lord's table and eat the flesh of Christ and drink his blood; if you are to marry, reserve it for your wives. Just as you want them to come to you, they must find you. What young man does not want to take a chaste woman? And if he must accept a maiden, who does not want her intact? You look for it intact, be yourself intact; You want it pure, don't be impure. This is not possible for her and impossible for you; and if it is impossible for you, it is also impossible for her. But she can be pure; then his example tells you that it is not impossible. She can do it because God governs her. You would be more glorious to do like her. Why more glorious? Because the vigilance of her parents guards her, the very blush of her fragile sex restrains her, and, in short, she fears the laws that you do not fear 5. Therefore, if you did it, you would be more glorious, because, if you do it, it is out of fear of God. She has much to fear outside of God, you only fear God, although the one you fear is greater than all. And it is to be feared in public and in private. Salts? He sees you. Are you coming in? He sees you. Does the candle light? He sees you. Is it turned off? He sees you; and he sees you when you enter your room and when you are alone in your heart. Fear, fear him who does not lose sight of you, and at least be chaste through fear; or, if you want to sin, find where I do not see you and do your will there. 3. Those of you who have taken a vow of purity 0, punish more

severely the body and do not give it free rein even to what is permitted; in such a way that you abstain not only from illicit union, but also from lawful glances. Whatever your sex, men and women remember to live the life of angels on earth. Angels do not marry or take wives, and such will we be after we are resurrected. How much better you begin to be before death than men will be after the resurrection! Be faithful to your state, because God keeps special honors for you. The resurrection of the dead has been compared to the stars of heaven. One star in heaven is distinguished from another in brightness, according to the Apostle; so will also be the resurrection of the dead. Therefore, virginity, marital chastity and holy widowhood will not shine equally. They will shine differently, but they will all be there. Nor is the splendor identical, but the sky will be common. 4. Topic: The Eucharist (Jn 6:58). Location: Unknown. Date: Unknown. 1. What words have you heard from the mouth of the Lord inviting us? Who invited? Who did you invite and what did you prepare? The Lord invited his servants, and prepared them as food for himself. Who will dare to eat his Lord? Yet he says: He who eats me lives for me. When you eat Christ, you eat life. Nor is it put to death to be eaten, but it gives life to the dead. When it is eaten it gives strength, but it does not diminish. Therefore, brothers, let us not be afraid to eat this bread for fear that it will run out and we will not find anything to eat later. Let Christ be eaten; eaten he lives, since dead he rose again. We don't even break it into pieces when we eat it. Nec ideo magistri vestri sumus, quia de loco superiore loquimur vobis: sed magister est [743] omnium qui habitat in ómnibus nobis. Ipse moda in Gospel nobis omnibus loquebatur, et dicebat nobis, quod etiam ego dico vobis: dicit autem ille de nobis, et nobis et vobis, Si manseritis in verbo meo, non utique in meo, qui moda loquor; sed in eius, qui moda ex Gospel loquebatur: Si manseritis in verbo meo, inquit, veré discipuli mei estis (lo 8,31). Ad discipulum parum est accessé, sed manere. Ñon ergo ait, Si audieritís verbum meum; aut, Si accesseritis ad verbum meum; aut, Si laudaveritis verbum meum: sed videte quid dixerit, Si manseritis in verbo meo, veré discipuli mei estis; et cognoscetis veritatem, et vertías liberabit vos (ib., 31-32). 5. But if the flesh of Christ was not the flesh of sin, but was like the flesh of sin, how could he condemn sin in the flesh through sin itself? An image is ordinarily given the name of what it represents. A real, true man is called a man; But you show a man painted on a wall, and you ask what that painting is, and the answer is: "A man." Therefore, the Apostle called sin the flesh that had likeness to sinful flesh, so that it might be a sacrifice for sin. 4 The same Apostle says in another place: He made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us. To him who knew no sin... Who knew no sin except he who said: See, the prince of the world is coming, and he will find nothing in me? He made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us; God made Christ himself, the one who ignored sin, to be sin for us. What does this mean, brothers? If it were said: "God made sin against him"; or, "He caused him to have sin," would seem intolerable; How then do we tolerate it being said: He made him sin? Is Christ sin himself? Those who have knowledge of the Old Testament Scriptures understand this language. In fact, not once, but several times, many times, the name of sin is given to the sacrifices for sins. For example, a goat, a ram, anything in short, was offered for sin; the very victim offered for sin was called sin. In resolution: the very victim that was offered for sin was called sin. And so the sacrifice was called a sin CAPUT IV.—5. Peccata, sacrificia pro peccatis.—Si [745] ergo similarity erat carnis peccatí, non caro peccati; quomodo, Ut de peccato damnaret peccatum in carne? Location: Unknown. Date: In 417 or 418.

1. The Lord Jesus, as we heard when the gospel was read to us, opened the eyes of a man blind from birth. If we consider, brothers, the penal inheritance with which we all come into the world, everyone is blind. If Christ came to enlighten us, it was because the devil managed to blind us. He, who seduced the first duodecim, sed omnes qui manemus in verbo eius, veré discipuli eius sumus. Et cognoscemus veritatem, et veritas libe[746]rabit nos: id est, Christus Filius Dei, qui dixit, Ego sum veritas (lo 14,6). Liberos nos faciet; hoc est, liberabit nos, non a barbaris, sed a diabolo; non a corporis captivitate, sed ab animae iniquitate. Solus est qui sic liberat. Nemo se liberum dicat, ne servus remaneat. Non remanebit in servitute anima nostra, quia quotidie dimittuntur debita nostra.

FROM VEEBIS EVANGELII IOANNIS: "EGO VENI, UT FACIAM OPERA EIUS QUI MISIT ME." AGAINST ARIANS. ET DE EO QUOD AIT ILLUMINATUS ILLE QUI ERAT CAECUS NATUS: «SCIMUS QUIA PECCATORES ÜEUS NON EXAUDIT.» CHAP. 9

CAPOT I. — 1. Caecitas omnium hominum a nativitate.—Dominus Iesus, sicut audivimus cum sanctum Evangelíum legeretur, aperuit oculos homini qui caecus erat natus. Fratres, si attendamus hereditariam poenam nostram, totus mundus caecus est. Ideo venit Christus illuminator, quia diabolus fuet excaecator. Omnes caecos nasci fecit, qui primum homi-
Healing of the blind man

man, is the author of the blindness in which everyone is born. Run, then, to the Illuminator; run, create, receive the mud mixed with your saliva. Wash your face in the pool of Siloam. The evangelist was careful to warn us of the meaning of Siloam, which, he says, is interpreted "sent." And who is the one sent except the one who told us right now in the reading: I have come to do the works of him who sent me? See there the pool of Siloam; wash your face, be baptized so that you may be enlightened and see whom you did not see before. 2. And the first thing is to open your eyes to see the meaning of the words I have come to do the works of him who sent me. Here, in fact, the Arian already lets his voice be heard. —There you see it, he says; The works of Christ were not his works, but those of the Father, who sent him. —I would never say that about having my eyes in their place; if in that one, let's say, that has been sent, as in Siloam, he had washed his face. What do you say? —It's not me; He said it himself. "So what did he say?" —I have come to do the works of the one who sent me. —Then they are not your own works? -No. —Then why does that Siloam, that Messenger, that Son, that Only One, say that you think you are a degenerate?... What do his words mean: All the things that the Father has are mine? You say that he did other people's works, because he said: To do the works of him who sent me. I say, speaking in your own way, that the things of the Father were foreign. By virtue of what do you try to impose on me that the words of Christ: I have come to do his works, mean that these works are not mine, but those of him who sent me? nem decepit. Currant ad illuminatorem, currant, credant, accipiant lutum de saliva factum. Saliva quasi Verbum est, terra caro est. Lavent faciem in Piscina Siloae. Pertinuit autem ad Evangelistam exposee nobis quid significat Siloa, et ait, Quod interpretatur missus (lo 9,7). Quis est ipse missus, nisi qui dixit in ipsa lectione, Ego, inquit, veni, ut faciam opera eius qui me misit? (ibid. 4). Ecce Siloa; wash yourself face, baptizamini, ut illuminemini, et videatis qui ante non videbatis. 2. Locus ab Arianis calumnióse usurpatus.—Ecce primum ad hoc, quod dictum est, oculos aperite: Ego, inquit, veni ut faciam opera eius qui me misit. Iam hic existedit Arianus, et dicit: Ecce videtis quia Christus non fecit opera sua, sed Patris qui eum misit. Nunquam hoc diceret, si videret, hoc est, si in ipso qui missus est, tanquam in Siloa, faciem clavaret. Quid ergo you say? Ecce, inquit, ipse dixit.

Quid dixit? Veni, ut faciam opera eius qui me misit. Non ergo sua? Nom. Et quid est quod ait ipse Siloa, ipse missus, ipse Filius, ipse Unicus that you want to esse degenerem? Quid est quod ait, Omnia quae habet Pater, mea sunt? (ibid. 16,15). You say quia opera aliena faciebat; quia dixit, Faciam opera eius qui me misit. Ego dico quia Pater res alienas habebat; secundum cor tuum loquor. Unde mihi vis praescribere quia dixit Christus, Veni, ut faciam opera eius, quasi non mea, sed eius qui misit me?

3. I conjure you, Lord Christ, to resolve this issue, to put an end to this opposition. All the things that the Father has are mine, you say. So are they yours and not the Father's? Because Christ does not say: "All things that the Father has he gave to me"; although, if he had said it, he would have expressed his equality with him. The cumbersome thing is what he really said: All the things that the Father has are mine. Understanding it this way: All things that the Father has are from the Son; all things that the Son has are from the Father. See, in fact, how it is expressed elsewhere: All my things are yours and yours are mine. Matter, then, concluded as regards the things that the Father has; keep it in harmony, do not come at us with tricks. As for the works of the Father, the Son says that they are also his works. His, then, are those that are the Father's, to whom he said: All that is mine is yours and all that is yours is mine. Does it not follow, therefore, that my works are yours and that yours are mine? Everything the Father does, he said it himself, the Lord said it, the Only Begotten said it, the Son said it, the Truth said it... What did he say? Whatever the Father does, the Son does equally. Magnificent expression, transcendental truth, stupendous equality! All the things that the Father does, the Son also does. Was it not enough to say: "All the things that the Father does, the Son also does"? No, it is not enough; that's why he added: likewise. Why did you add the same? Because some blunt understandings that go around with their eyes closed tend to say: “The Father works by commanding, the Son works by obeying; then CAPUT II.—3. Opera Patris et Filii eadem.—Interrogo te, Domine Christe, solve quaestionem, fini contentionem. Omnia, inquit, quae habet Pater, mea sunt. Ergo Patris non sunt, si tua sunt? Non enim ait, Omnia quae habet Pater, dedit mihi: quamvis si et hoc dixisset, aequalitatem ostendisset. Sed molestum est quod dixit, Omnia quae habet Pater, mea [747] sunt. If you understand: Omnia quae habet Pater, Filii sunt; omnia quae habet Filius, Patris sunt. Audi illum alio loco: Omnia mea tua sunt, et tua mea sunt (lo 17,10). Finita est quaestio, de his quae habet Pater et Filius: concordes habent, tu noli litigare. Opera Patris quae dicit opera sua; Quia et tua mea sunt: ​​quia illius Patris dicit opera, cui dixit, Omnia mea tua sunt, et tua mea sunt. Ergo opera mea tua sunt, et opera tua mea sunt.

Quaecumque enim Pater facit: ipse dixit, Dominus dixit, Unigenitus dixit, Filius dixit, Veritas dixit, Quid dixit? Quaecumque Pater facit, haec et Filius facit similiter (ib., 5,10). Magna expressio, magna veritas, magna aequalitas. Omnia quae Pater facit, haec facit et Filius. Sufficeret, Omnia quae Pater facit, haec facit et Filius. Non-sufficit; addo, similiter. Quare addo, similiter? Quia solent dicere non intellegentes, et nondum apertis oculis ambulantes, solent dicere: Pater

unequally. But if they do it equally, as this one does, that one does it, and what that one does, that one does the same. 4. However, the Arian says: "The Father commands the Son to do." Your carnal idea; but, without judging the truth, I agree to it. Alright; The Father commands and the Son obeys; But is it not because he commands and obeys that he is not the Son of his own nature? Give me two men, father and son; one as much as the other: whoever rules is a man; who obeys, man; He who commands and he who obeys, are they not of the same nature? Has he who rules not engendered the son of his own substance? Has he who obeys lost his nature by obeying? Take, therefore, provisionally as two men the Father, who commands, and the Son, who obeys; without forgetting, however, that they are both God. There is, however, a difference: that the two men are two different men; but the Father and the Son do not both form but one God, which is an entirely divine wonder. If, then, now you want me to attribute obedience to the Son, you must admit with me the identity of his nature and that of the Father. The Father has generated a being, which is himself; that if the Father begot something other than what he himself is, he did not beget a true Son. The Father says to the Son: From the womb, before the star, I begot you. What does before the star mean? The times are signified by the star. Then before the times, before everything that is said before, before everything that does not have to be fecit iubendo, Filius obsequendo; ergo dissimiliter. Si autem similiter, quomodo ille, sic ille: sic quae ille, haec iste. CAPUT III.—4. Filius Dei consubstantialis et coaeternus Patri.— Sed iubet Pater, inquit, ut faciat Filius. Carnaliter quidem sapis, sed sine praeiudicio veritatis, cedo tibi. Ecce Pater iubet, Filius obsequitut: numquid ideo non est eius naturae Filius, quia ille iubet, ille obsequitur? Da mihi duos homines, patrem et filium: homines sunt duo; qui iubet, homo est; Qui obsequitur, homo est: qui iubet et qui obsequitur, unam habent eamdemque naturam. Numquid ille qui iubet, non de natura sua genuit filium? Numquid ille qui obsequitur, obsequendo naturam perdidit? Accipie ergo interim, quomodo accipis duos homines, Patrem iubentem, Filium obsequentem, tamen Deum et Deum. Sed simul isti duo sunt homines, simul ille unus Deus: hoc est divinum miraculum. Interim si vis ut tecum agnoscam obsequium, prius mecum agnosce naturam.

Hoc genuit Pater, quod ipse est. Si aliud genuit Pater, quam quod est ipse, non verum genuit Filium: Pater dicit ad Filium Ex uterus ante luciferum genui te (Ps 109,3). What is it, ante luciferum? Per luciferum significantur tempora. Ergo ante tempora, ante omne quod ante dicitur; ante omne

The Gospel does not say: "In the beginning I made the Word," as it was said: In the beginning God made heaven and earth; or “In the beginning the Word was born,” or “In the beginning God begat the Word.” What does it say then? It existed, it existed. Do you hear? It existed! Believe. In the beginning there was the Word, and the Word was in God, and the Word was God. Each repetition of the word this: existed, pushes away any idea of ​​time, because it always existed. Therefore, since God always existed and was always with his Son, and since, furthermore, he can beget outside of time, it is he who said to his Son: From the womb, before the star, I begot you. What does it mean about the belly? Does God have a belly? Are we going to think that God has a bodily organization? Not even by dream! Why then did he say from the womb except to signify that he begot him from his own substance? Therefore, if he came from the womb, he was the same as the one who begot him; because, if the Son were of any other nature than that of his Father, he would not be a Son, but a true monster. 5. imperfect? Of course! Hear what follows: And in your book they will all be written. But perhaps, brothers, the spiritual ones pray and are heard because they are not sinners.
