Hoc non diceret si hanc in corde suo luzm uideret. Si enim peccatores deus non exaudisset, confusus de temple ille publicanus descenderet. Descendit autem iustificatus magis quam ille pharisaeus. Unde autem descendit iste iustificatus? Quia fecit quod ait scriptura: Peccatum meum cognovi et iniquitatem meam non operui. Dixi: Proloquar adversum me delictum meum domino meo et tu dimisisti iniquitatem cordis mei (Ps 31,5). Certe ergo peccatores deus non exaudit? Hoc ergo credite quod iam illuminati credunt: exaudit deus peccatores. Etením quod ait dominus in iudicium se uenisse in hunc mundum ut qui non vident [793] videant et qui vident caeci fiant

(lo 9,39), multos non intellegentes potest mouere. Saluator enim Christus uenit. In quodam loco et ait: Non enim venit filius hominis ut et iudicet mundum sed ut salvetur mundus per ipsum (lo 3,17). Si ergo propterea uenit ut saluos faciat, acceptabile est quod ait uenisse se ut qui non vident videant. Illud autem durum est ut qui vident caeci fiant. Si intellegamus non est durum sed purum. Ut autem intellegatis quam ueraciter dictum sit, referte oculos ad eos ipsos duos who prayed in temple. Pharisaeus uidebat, publicanus caecus erat. (188) Quid est: uidebat? Videntem se putabat; de uisione sua, hoc est de iustitia, gloriabatur. Ule autem caecus erat quia peccata sua confitebatur. Iactauit ille merita sua, confessus est iste peccata sua. Descendit iustificatus (Luke 18:14) publicanus magis quam ille pharisaeus, quia Christus uenit in mundum ut qui non vident videant et qui vident caeci fiant. Ideo eum dixissent pharisaei qui tune audiebant dicentem: Numquid et nos caeci sumus? (lo 9,40) utique illi similes weret qui ascenderat in templum et dicebat deo: Gratias ago tibi quoniam non sum sicut ceteri homines, iniusti, adulteri, raptores (Luke 18,11), tamquam diceret: gratias tibi ago quia non sum caecus, sed uideo, sicut et ceteri homines de genere ipsius publicani. Quid illi dixerunt: Numquid et nos caeci sumus? Et dominus ad illos: Si caeci essetis non haberetis peccatum. Nunc autem quia dicitis: videmus,
The healing of the man born blind

you," but it remains. In fact, sin already existed. Because the fact of not confessing it, it does not disappear, but remains. Let the blind run, then, to Christ to be enlightened. Christ is truly light in the world, even in the midst of terrible men. Divine miracles have been performed, and no one has performed miracles since the beginning of the human race except him to whom the Scripture says: He alone works wonders. Why was it said: The only one who works wonders, except because, when he wants to do them, he does not need any man? On the other hand, man, when he does them, has need of God. He is the only one who works wonders. Because? Because the Son is God in the Trinity with the Father and the Holy Spirit, certainly one God, the only one who works wonders. Christ's disciples also did wonderful works, but none alone. What wonderful works did they also do? As it is written in the Acts of the Apostles, the sick wanted to touch the hem of their clothes, and by touching them they were cured; The sick lying in their beds wanted his shadow to touch them as he passed by. What wonders they did, but none of them alone! Listen to your Lord: without me you can do nothing. Therefore, dearly beloved, let us love the patriarch as a patriarch, the prophet as a prophet, the apostle as an apostle, the martyr as a martyr; to God, however, above all things, and let us presume that he alone, without a doubt, will save us. The prayers of the saints can help us, peccatum vestrum manet (lo 9,41). Non dixit: peccatum accessit, sed: manet. Etat enim. Cum enim non confitemini, non tollitur, sed manet. Currant ergo ad Christum caed ut illuminentur. Lumen enim Christus in mundo, et inter nomines pessimos. Diuina miracula facta sunt, ñeque quisquam fecit miracula ab initio generis humani nisi ille cuí dicit scriptura: qui facit mirabilia solus (Ps 71,18). Quare dictum est: qui facit mirabilia solus, nisi quia quando ipse uult faceré, non indiget nomine? Quando autem facit homo, indiget deo. Fecit miracula solus. Quare? Quia deus in trinitate est fflius cum patre et spiritu sancto, utique unus deus qui facit mirabilia solus. Discipuli autem Christi fecerunt mirabilia et ipsi, sed nemo solus. Qualia mirabilia fecerunt et ipsi? Sicut scriptum est in Actibus apostolorum: aegri concupiscebant fimbrias eorum tangere, et tangentes sanabantur; uolebant aegroti ut umbra transeuntium tangerentur iacentes.

Qualia mirabilia fecerunt, et nemo illorum solus! [794] Audi dominum ipsorum: Sine me nihil potestis faceré (lo 15.5). Ergo carissimi patriarcham sicut patriarcham, prophetam sicut prophetam, apostolum sicut apostolum, martyrem sicut martyrem, deum tamen super omnia diligamus et ab ipso only us future greetings sine dubio praesumamus. Adiuuare nos possunt orationes sanctorum bene de deo

who enjoy merits as a gift from God, without any prior merit of their own, since the merits of any saint are gifts from God. God works in light and darkness, in visible things and in hearts. He works wonders in his temple when he works them in holy men. In fact, all the saints are inflamed together by the fire of charity and constitute a single temple for God; They are a single temple, each one in particular and all together. You have heeded what was said to holy Elijah: Go to Zarephath of Sidon; there I have sent a widow woman to feed you. There was, indeed, a great hunger, but it was not a big deal for God to feed his servant and servant without human help. Why then was he sent to that woman? Why didn't the raven already bring him God's food? The raven did so without obtaining personal benefit, since, although it fed the prophet by the will of God, it did not mean that it would ever reign with Christ. It was sent to the widow for the widow's sake, not Elijah's; not because she did not find food somewhere else, but so that, by feeding that righteous man, she would merit before God. He arrived, then, and found her collecting firewood. He questions her and begs her for food. She answers that she had nothing to make bread with; He told her that he only had enough for her and her children and that they would die when they consumed it. Still, what did he say at death's door? I'm going to pick up two pieces of wood. When he picked up the two pieces of wood he was looking for the cross. Perhaps he should have denied meritorum, nullo tamen praecedente fructu meritorum suorum, quoniam merita cuiusque sancti dona sunt dei. Deus qui (189) operatur in aperto, operatur in occulto, operatur in uisibilibus, operatur in cordibus. Ipse in temple suo facit mirabilia sua quando facit in hominibus sanctis. Omnes enim sancti simul caritatis igne conflantur et unum templum deo faciunt, et singuli templum sunt et omnes simul unum templum. Animaduertistis quid dixerit sancto Heliae: Vade in Sarepta Sydoniae, ibi mandavi mulieri viduae ut pascat te (1 Reg 17,9). Famis enim erat magna sed non erat magnum et sine cuiusquam hominis ministry pascere ministrum seruum suum. Quid enim ad illam mulierem adhuc missus est et non ei coruus nourishes dei afferebat? Be nullo fructu suo coruus. Non enim, quia nutu dei prophetam pascebat, ideo coruus quandocumque cum Christo erat regnaturus.

Missus est ad uiduam bono uiduae non Heliae, non quod ille aliunde alimentum non inueniret, sed ut illa sibi apud deum, pascendo iustum, meritum comparaet. Venit ergo et inuenit eam colligentem ligna. Interrogat et poscit alimentum. Illa respondit se non habere unde faceret panem, tantum enim se habere dixit quod ipsi soli sufficeret et filiis suis, quod cum consumpsissent, morerentür. Tamen ante mortem quid ait: Colligo duo ligna (ib., 12). When duo ligna colligebat, cruze quaerebat. Numquid autem poscentem

food to the man of God who asked for it? Where is what the Lord had said to Elijah: I have commanded a widow woman to feed you? If he already had the mandate, he should have also recognized who he was coming from and said to him: “Come, Lord; Eat, because the Lord has already commanded me, regarding you, to offer you hospitality and to give you what I do not have to have for you. This was not what he told him, but what you heard: I only have to consume myself with my children and die. But he replied: Go away; Make the bread and bring me first. This is what the Lord said: until he gives rain to the land, neither the flour nor the oil will rise. All the assets of that widowed woman consisted of a little flour and a little oil. However, any possession, no matter how rich, did not admit of comparison with the small centerboard that hung from a pole; Whatever that great possession was, at that moment it was thirsty, while that centerpiece did not diminish. She believed him instantly, went and did it, and took in the man of God to feed him. This is what the Lord had said: I have commanded. What does it mean: I have commanded? I have prepared the will for you to believe. Let us give thanks to his mercy, since the Lord prepares the will. hominem dei alimentum debuit excusare? Ubi est quod dixerat dominus ad Heliam: Mandavi mulieri viduae ut pascat te? Iam si mandatum habebat agnoscere debuit uenientem et dicere: Domine, ueni, manduca, iam enim dominus mihi mandauit de te ut hospitium tibi praeparem et ex eo quod non habeo porrigam (190) ut habeam tibi. Non hoc dicit, sed audistis quid dixerit: Tantum habeo quod sola cum filiis /neis consumam, et moriar (ib.). Et ille: Vade, fac panificium et affer mihi prius. Hoc enim dicebat dominus, quia quousque det pluviam in tena, nec fariña illa, nec oleum deficit (ib., 13.14). Totum patrimonium mulieris uiduae modica fariña erat et modicum oleum. [795] Sed non comparatur quilibet opulentas fundus urceo modico penden ti in palo: quicumque enim esset ille magnus fundus illo tempere sitiebat, urceus autem ille non deficiebat. Illa continuo credidit, iuit et fecit, hominem dei alendum suscepit. Hoc est quod dixerat dominus: Mandavi. Quid est: mandavi? Voluntatem ad fidem paraui. Gratias eius misericordiae quoniam praeparatur voluntas a domino (Prov 8:35, sec. LXX).

Topic: The healing of the man blind from birth (Jn 9,1-41). Location: Unknown. Date: Unknown. The works that Christ the Lord did then in bodies, He now does in hearts'; Although it is true that it in no way ceases to carry them out in bodies, what it does in hearts is much greater. In fact, if it is a great thing to see the light of heaven, how much more so is it to see the light of God! For precisely this, to see the light that is God, the eyes of the heart are healed, opened and purified. God, says the Scripture, is light and in him there is no darkness; and the Lord in the Gospel: Blessed are the pure in heart, because they will see God. Therefore, those of us who are surprised and amazed that this blind man sees, let us beg, with whatever strength the Lord grants us, the healing and purification of our hearts. The goodness of customs proves that hearts have already been purified. Well, what is the point of seeing ourselves purified from sins in the sacred fountain 2, if we immediately stain ourselves with terrible customs?

[PLS 2,795] (RB 50 [1938] 190) (lo 9) Opera domini Christi quae tune fecit in corporibus, moda facit in cordibus, quamquam in multis etiam corporibus faceré omnino non cesset, sed plus est quod in cordibus facit. Si enim magnum est uidere lumen caeli, quanto maius est uidere lumen dei! Ad hoc enim oculi cordis sanantur, ad hoc aperiuntur, ad hoc mundantur, ut uideant luzem, quod est deus. Deus enim lux est, ait scriptura, et tenebrae in eo non sunt ullae (1 lo 1,5), et dominus in euangelio: Beati mundo corde quia ipsi deum videbunt (Mt 5,8). Qui ergo caecum istum uidentem miramur, cordibus nostris sanandis atque mundandis, ipso donor quantum ualemus, instemus. Mores sint boni, et corda mundata sunt. Quid enim prodest a peccatis in sacro fonte mundari et continuo pessimis moribus inquinan?
See sermon 88,3. The baptismal font.

The very order of this action of the Lord by which he granted sight to the blind man invites us to consider something great and important. In fact, Jesus Christ the Lord could—who is there who would deny him that power?—touch the eyes of the blind man without saliva or mud and restore or, better yet, cause him sight. I could have done it. Why do I talk about having touched him with my hands? What could I not have done with a single word if I had commanded it? What can't the Word do with the word? Not just any word, but this: In the beginning there was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God. This Word, which in the beginning was God together with God, became flesh to dwell among us. Then the Word walked clothed in flesh 3. While the flesh was visible, the Word was hidden. But previously, many prophets, as her messengers in her spirit and truth, had predicted that this Word was going to come in the flesh. Many were those who came first proclaiming: “Behold, he will come; "He will come in whom the forgiveness of sins will take place." “Behold, it will come”: they said this in multiple ways, with multiple figures, with the multiplicity of symbolic sacrifices and with so many mysteries still covered with a veil. Nothing could be heard other than: "Behold, he will come." Once arrived, the bridegroom's friend immediately said from the water: Behold the lamb of God, behold he who takes away the sin of the world; the one whose coming had been promised; the one of whom Moses wrote, of whom the law and the Ordo ipse operis huius dominici quod illuminatus est caecus alíquid (191) bear witness magnum et necessarium ammonet intueri. Poterat enim dominus Iesus Christus—et quis est qui dicat: non poterat?— tangere oculos eius sine sputo et luto, et continuo illi reddere uel potius illi faceré aspectum. Poterat hoc. Quid dicam: manus si tetigisset? Quid ille non posset uerbo si iussisset? Quid uerbo non potest uerbum, non qualecumque uerbum, sed quod in principle erat verbum et verbum erat apuá deum et deus erat verbum (lo 1,1). Hoc uerbum in principle deus apud deum caro factum est (ib., 2.14) ut habitaret in nobis. Ambulabat ergo uerbum carne uestitum. Et caro patebat, uerbum latebat. Sed hoc uerbum in [796] carne uenturum multi ante prophetae tamquam praecones eius in spiritu eius et ueritate ante praedixerunt. Multi ante uenerunt dicentes: Ecce ueniet, et talis ueniet in quo fuga est remissio peccatorum.

Ecce ueniet multis modís, multis figuris, multis sacrificorum typis, multis mysteriorum uelamentis. Nihil aliud sonabat quam: ecce ueniet. Qui posteaquam uenit, continuo amicus sponsi de aqua: Ecce agnus dei, ecce qui tollit peccatum mundi (lo 1,29); qui promittebatur esse uenturus, de quo scripsit Moyses, cuius lex et prophetae sunt testes, propter quem By this Augustine does not mean that the union between human and divine nature in Jesus was as external as clothing is to man,
The healing of the man born blind

prophets, by whom the built temple was to be consecrated; he whose blood is figured in the victims of the priests: Behold the Lamb of God, behold he who takes away the sin of the world. Thus, then, the Lord, in curing this man blind from birth, in whom the human race was represented, also blind from birth, maintained a precise order. He spit on the ground, making mud, and the Lord anointed his eyes with saliva. The earth means the prophets; It began with the earth because, what else are prophets but earth? Being, in fact, men originating from the earth, they received the spirit of the Lord and anointed the people of God. Through prophecy, they saw it, but they did not yet possess it. Consider now where he was sent to wash his face. To the pool of Siloam. What does Siloam mean? Fortunately, the evangelist did not silence it: it is translated "sent." Who was sent but he of whom it was said, Behold the Lamb of God? In it the face is washed, and the one who had been anointed gains sight, because in Christ the Lord all prophecy came true. He who does not know Christ walks only anointed. And, if perhaps he considers him a prophet, he behaves like a Jew. Why do you consider him only a prophet? Go to Siloam to see and know the one whose saliva you carry. The order that was followed in this man's eyes was also maintained in his heart. Pay attention to the question that the Jews asked him: What sanctificandum aedificatum est templum, cuius sanguis figuratus est in uictimis sacerdotum, ecce agnus dei, ecce qui tollit peccata mundi. Seruauit ergo et dominus in isto curando caeco nato, in quo figurabatur genus humanum caecum natum, in hoc ergo nomine illuminando seruauit ordinem. Spuit in terra et lutum fecit, et inunxit oculos eius saliua dominus. Terra prophetas significat, haec enim praemissa est terra quia prophetae quid nisi terra? Homines uidelicet de terra acceperunt spiritum domini et inunxerunt populum dei. Prophetia uidebant sed nondum tenebant. Sed uide quo est missus ut faciem lauaret. Ad Piscinam Syloa. Where is Syloa? Bene quod non tacuit euangelista: quod interpretatur (192) missus. Quis est missus, nisi de quo dictum est: Ecce agnus dei? In ipso lauatur facies et qui fuet inunctus uidet, quia in domino Christo Completa est omnis prophetia. Qui non cognoscit Christum inunctus ambulat. Et si forte prophetam legit, iudaeus est. Quid legis prophetam?

Vade ad Syloam ut uideas eum et cognoscas cuius saliuam portas. Ordo autem iste qui praecessit in oculis hominis huius, etiam in eius corde, seruatus est. Attendite quemadmodum interrogauerunt eum iudaei. What do you say about homine isto?
Sermon CXXXVI C The Healing of the Man Born Blind

you say about that man? I say, he replied, that he is a project. He had not yet washed the face of his heart in Siloam. His eyes were open, but his heart was still anointed. After having washed his face, he responded as best he could, like someone who is anointed and does not yet see. It appeared to be evidently anointed in his heart, at the same time as the opening of the eyes of his flesh. When he still did not see, being anointed, he said something; namely: We know that God does not hear sinners. If this were true, the publican would beat his chest in vain. But let us forgive this statement to those who, being still anointed, did not see. God also listens to sinners. They are the wards 4, the humble, the poor, and it is written: Judge in favor of the ward and the needy; Do justice to the humble and the poor. Humble and poor was he who did not dare to raise his eyes to heaven. Therefore he beat his chest, saying: Be merciful to me, for I am a sinner. And he went home justified. Why does he say: Be merciful to me, for I am a sinner? There is no doubt that God listens to sinners. Who is the pupil but the one still small in faith? But the little boy, the child, the ward, once he has grown up and begins to enter youth, he ceases to be a ward and is called an adult. And, when he reaches the age of twenty-five, such a designation fits him perfectly. What should I say, brothers? If we consider the greatness of the holy angels, is it not true that we men who are on earth are pupils? But (9:17). I say, inquít, quia propheta est (ib.). Nondum lauerat faciem cordis in Syloa. Oculi quidem iam patebant, sed cor inunctum erat. Quando faciem lauerat, responderit ut potuit, ut inunctus nondum uidens. Defendit unctionem suam, hoc est cordis sui, oculorum autem corporis iam apertionem. Dixit etiam aliquid ut inunctus nondum uidens: Scimus quia peecatores deus non exaudit (ib., 31). Hoc si uerum esset, sine causa publicanus ille pectus tunderet. Sed adhuc inuncto nondum uidenti hoc ignoscamus. Nam et peccatores exaudit deus. Ipsi sunt enim pupilii humiles pauperes: ludicate, inquit, [797] pupillo et egeno, humilem et pauperem iustificate (Ps 81,3). Humilis et pauper erat qui oculos in caelum leuare non audebat. Percussit pectus suum dices: Domine, propitius esto mihi peccatori. Et descendit iustificatm in domum suam (Luke 18:13-14). Crux: propitius this mihi pecatori? Certe peccatores exaudit deus. Quid est pupillus, nisi in fide adhuc paruulus?

Pupus, pupulus, pupíllus quando iam creuerit et pubesceré ceperit, non est pupillus, sed iam (193) adultus dicitur. Cum ad annos uero uiginti quinqué peruenerit, iam legitimus nuncupatur. Quid dicamus, fratres? Siconsiderus magnitudeinem sanctorum angelorum, nonne nomines in terra positi pupilii sumus? Sed dicit aliquis: Quomodo? Pupilii sumus non carnaliter, carnaliter The pupillus is one who ceases to be under the power of the father, whether due to the death of the latter or the emancipation of the former; but always still a child.

someone will say: "How?" We are pupils not according to the flesh, since in that sense only those whose father has died are pupils; a ward according to the spirit is one whose father is hidden. We will stop being pupils when we see our father. Let us consider, then, the blind man, with his eyes already open, but not yet anointed on his heart, at the moment when he washes his face. The Jews, angry, defeated and convicted and full of fury against the blind man who already saw, threw him outside. When they threw him out, then he entered precisely where the Jews present in the house of God could not throw him out. So, having been cast out, he found the Lord in the temple, who said to him: Do you believe in the Son of God? In fact, the one who had given him bodily vision, although he still had to illuminate his heart, knew him. It is now that he washes the face of his heart, when he comes to Siloam, because it is now that he believes in him as the only begotten sent. He answered him: Who is he, Lord, that I believe in him?, as if he were still anointed and did not yet see. And the Lord: You have seen him; The one who is talking to you, that is it. Listening to this is, in truth, equivalent to washing your face. So, finally, he, having just washed his face and already seeing, said: I believe, Lord; and, falling down, he worshiped him. enim pupillus est cuius pater mortuus est; spiritaliter pupillus, cuius pater oceultus est. Tune pupilii non erimus quando patrem nostrum uiderimus. Ergo iste iam patentibus oculis, corde tamen adhuc inunctus, quando lauit faciem inueniemus. Irati iudaei, uicti atque conuicti, et caeci irascentes uidenti, miserunt eum joras (lo 9,34). Quando foras miserunt eum, tune ingressus est unde eum non possent foras mittere iudaei positi in domo dei. Ergo foras missus inuenit dominum in Templo et ait üli — utique cognoscebatur a quo illuminatus erat corpore, restabat corde. Modo lauat faciem cordis sui, moda uenit ad Syloam, quia moda intellegit unigenitum missum — Tu credis, inquit, in filium dei? Et ille: Quis est, domine, ut credam in eum (ib., 35-36), quasi inunctus nondum uidens. Et dominus: Et vidisti eum et qui loquitur tecum ipse est (ib., 37). Haec uerba audire hoc est faciem lauare. Denique ille moda Iota iam facie, uidens corde: Credo, inquit, domine, et prostratus adoravit eum (ib., 38).
Topic: The good shepherd (Jn 10:1-15). Location: Unknown. Date: Unknown.

1. Your faith does not ignore, dear ones, and we know that you have learned from the Master, who trains us from heaven and in whom you have placed your hope, how our Lord Jesus Christ, who already suffered for us and rose again, is the Head of the Church, and the Church is His Body; and that the health of this Body is the union of its members and the bond of charity. If charity catches a cold, illness occurs, even if one belongs to the Body of Christ. It is true, however, that he who has exalted our Head can heal his members, always on condition of not taking impiety to the point of having to amputate them, but of remaining attached to the Body until health is achieved. Because, as long as any member remains in the organic unity, there remains the hope of saving him; Once amputated, there is no remedy to heal it. Since he, then, is the Head of the Church and the Church is his Body, the total Christ is the combination of the Head and the Body. He has already risen - therefore, we already have the Head in heaven, where he advocates for us. That's ours
IN EVANGELII IOANNIS CAPUT 10,1-16. DE PASTORE, ET MERCENARIO, ET FÜRE

CAPUT I.—1. Sanitas membrorum in unitate et caritate.—Nonignot fides vestra, carissimi, et íta vos didicisse novimus, maestro Magistro de cáelo, in quo spem vestram posuistís, quia Dominus noster lesus Christus, qui iam pro nobís passus est et resurrexit, caput est Ecclesiae, et est corpus eius Ecclesia, et in eius Corpore unitas membrorum et compago caritatis, tanquam sanitas exsistit. Quicumque autem in caritate friguerit, ínfirmatur in corpore Christi. Sed potens est ille, qui iam exaltavit caput nostrum, etiam infirma membra sanare: dum tamen non nimia impietate praecidantur, sed haereant corpori doñee sanentur. Quidquid enim adhuc haeret corpori, non desperatae sanitatis est: quod autem praecisum fuerit, nec curari, nec sanari potest. Cum ergo sit ille caput Ecclesiae, et sit corpus eius Ecclesia, totus Christus et caput et corpus est. Resurrexit iam ille. Caput ergo habemus in cáelo. Caput nostrum

Head without sin and without death is already propitiating God for our sins, so that we too, resurrected at last and transformed, may follow the Head to heavenly glory. Where the head goes, in fact, the other members go too. Being, then, his members, let us not lose, while we are here, the hope of following our Head. 2. Consider, brothers, where the love of our Head reaches. Although already in heaven, he continues to suffer here while the Church suffers. Here Christ hungers, here he thirsts, and is naked, and is homeless, and is sick and imprisoned. Whatever his Body suffers, he himself has said that he suffers; and at the end, turning his Body to the right and placing those who now tread on him on the left, he will say to those on the right hand: Come, blessed of my Father, to receive the kingdom that has been prepared for you since the beginning of the world. And why this? Because I was hungry, and you gave me food; and he continues there, as if he had received the favor in person. And this is so extreme that, not understanding it, those on the right have to respond, saying: When, Lord, did we see you hungry, homeless or imprisoned? He will say to them: What you did to one of my little ones, you did to me. In this way, in our body the head is on top, the feet are on the ground; However, when in some crowding and squeezing of people someone steps on you, doesn't your head say: "You're stepping on me"? Nobody has stepped on your head interpellat pro nobis. Caput nostrum sine peccato et sine morte, iam propitiat Deum pro peccatis nostris: ut et nos in fine resurgentes, et immutati in gloriam caelestem, sequamur caput nostrum. Quo enim caput, et cetera membra. Sed dum hic sumus, membra sumus; ne desperemus, quia secuturi sumus caput nostrum. [755] CAPUT II.—2. Unitas Christi et membrorum.—Videte enim, fratres, dilectionem ipsius capitis nostri. Iam in cáelo est, et hic laborat, quamdiu hic laborat Ecclesia. Hic Christus esurit, hic sitit, nudus est, hospes est, infirmatur, in carcere est. Quidquid enim hic patitur corpus eius, se dixit pati: et in fine segregans ipsum corpus suum ad dexteram, et reliquos a quibus moda conculcatur segregans ad sinistram, dicturus est his qui sunt ad dexteram: Venite, benedicti Patris mei, percipite regnum quod vobis paratum est ab origine mundi. Quibus meritis?

Esurivi enim, et dedistis mihi manducare; et cetera sic exsequitur, tanquam ipse accepisset: usque adeo ut illi non intellegentes responder ct dicant, Domine, quando te vidimus esurientem, hospitem, et in carcere? Et dicit eis: Cum uni ex minimis meis fecistis, mihi fecistis. Sic etiam in nostro corpore caput sursum est, pedes in terra sunt: ​​tamen in aliqua constipatione et coartatione hominum, quando tibi aliquis pedem calcat, nonne dicit caput: Calcas me? Nec caput tuum, nec linguam

nor the tongue; They are up and safe; nothing bad has happened to them; But, because unity reigns from head to toe, the fruit of the connection that charity produces, the tongue does not ignore it, but rather says: "You are treading on me." In this way, Christ, the Head whom no one steps on, said: I was hungry, and you gave me food. How did it end? Then they will go to eternal fire, and the righteous to eternal life. 3. In the words just heard the Lord presents himself to us, at the same time, as shepherd and door. He has both things there: I am the door and I am the shepherd. It is a door in relation to the Head; He is a shepherd in relation to the Body. In fact, to Peter, the only one on whom the Church is organized, 2 he says: Peter, do you love me? He answered, "Lord, I love you." Feed my sheep. And, having said to him three times: Peter, do you love me?, Peter became sad at the third question, as if he who had seen the intimacy of the denier did not now also see the faith of the confessor. I had always known him; He had known him even at the time when Peter did not know himself. He did not know himself when he said: I will be at your side until I die. How little did he know the seriousness of his weakness! In no other way are the sick frequently unaware of what is happening to them, and the doctor knows it; He who has it does not know it, and he knows it tuam quisquam calcavit: sursum est, in tuto est, nihil ei mali contigit; et tamen quia per conexionem caritatis unítas est a capite usque ad pedes, non se inde lingua separavit, sed dixit: Calcas me; cum eam nemo cpntigerit. Quomodo ergo lingua, quam nemo contigit, dicit: Calcas me; sic Christus caput, quod nemo calcat, dixit, Esurivi, et dedistis mihi manducare. Et illis qui hoc non fecerunt, say: Esurivi, et non dedistis mihi manducare. Et quomodo conclusit? Sic: Ibunt Mi in ambustionem aeternam, iusti autem in vitam aeternam (Mt 26,31-46). CAPUT III.—3. lanua Christus. Petrus infirmus sibi ipsi ignotus.— Cum ergo Domínus nunc loqueretur, dixit se esse pastorem, dixit se esse et ianuam. Utrumque ibi habes: et, Ego sum ianua; et, Ego sum pastor (lo 10,11.9, etc.). Ianua is in capite, pastor in corpore. Dicit enim Petro, in quo uno format Ecclesiam: Petre, do you love me? Respondit: Master, master. Ride oves meas. Et tertio: Petre, do you love me? Contristatus est Petrus, quod eum tertio interrogavit (lo 21,15-17): quasi ille qui vidit conscientiam negatoris, non videret fidem confitentis. Noverat illum semper, noverat illum et quando se Petrus ipse non noverat.

Tune enim se non noverat, quando dixit, Tecum ero usque ad mortem: et quam esset infirmus, nesciebat. Quomodo plerumque revera et infirmis contingit, ut aegrotus nesciat quid in illo agatur, medicus autem sciat: cum Ule aegritudinem ipsam patiatur, medicus non patiatur. Magis dicit medicus quid agatur in altero, quam ille qui aegrotat quid agatur in se ipso. Another commentary on this evangelical text can be seen in Treatises on the Gospel of Saint John 45. See complementary note 4: Saint Augustine and Mt 16,18 vol. X p.884.

who doesn't have it. At that time, the sick person was Peter, and the Lord was the doctor. That one claimed to have strength, when in reality he didn't; but the Lord, feeling his pulse, said that he had to deny him three times. And it happened to the letter as the Doctor had predicted, not as the patient boastfully announced. If, then, the Savior asked him after the resurrection, it was not because he was unaware of the great sincerity of the affection that Peter had for him, but so that a triple confession of love could erase the triple denial of fear 3. 4. Then the Lord asking Peter if he loves him: Peter, do you love me? What was Peter to do for the benefit of the Lord, already resurrected and about to ascend to heaven to sit at the right hand of the Father? It was, then, like saying to him: “What you will give me, what you will do for me if you love me, is to feed my sheep; "It is to enter through the door and not jump through the other side." You heard when the gospel was read: Whoever enters through the door, he is the shepherd; But he who goes up from another side is a thief and a robber, and his intention is to separate them, scatter them and carry off the sheep. Who comes through the door? Who enters through Christ. And who is this? Who imitates the passion of Christ, who knows the humility of Christ; And since God became man for us, let man recognize that he is not God, but a mere man. Who, in effect, wants to pretend to be God, being nothing more than Petrus ergo tune infirmus, Dominus autem medicus. This dicebat se habere vires, qui non habebat: ille autem tangens venam cordis eius, dicebat quod ter eum esset negaturus. Et ita factum est quomodo praedixit medicus, non quomodo praesumpsit aegrotus (cf. Le 22,33.34. 55-61). Ergo post resurrectionem suam Dominus interrogavit eum, non nesciens quo ille animo confiteretur amorem Christi, [756] sed ut trina confessione amoris, deleret trinam negationem timoris. CAPUT IV.—4. Quid a Petro demanded. Intrare per ianuam in ovile.— Ergo hoc Dominus demanded Petro, Petre, do you love me? quasi, Quid mihi dabis, quid mihi praestabis, quia do you love me? Quid erat praestaturus Petrus resurgenti Domino, et eunti in caelum, atque sedenti ad dexteram Patris? Quasi diceret, Hoc mihi dabis, hoc mihi praestabis, si amas me, ut pascas oves meas: per ianuam intres, non per aliam partem ascendas.

Audistis, cum Evangelium legeretur, Qui intrat per ianuam, pastor est: qui autem ex alia parte ascendit, fur est et latro; et dissipare quaerit, et spargere, et tollere (lo 10,2.1.10). Quis est qui intrat per ianuam? Qui intrat per Christum. Who are you? Qui imitatur passionem Christi, qui cognoscit humilitatem Christi: et cum Deus factus sit homo pro nobis, cognoscat se homo non esse Deum, sed hominem. Qui enim vult Deus videri, cum sit homo, non imitatur illum, qui cum Deus esset, ' This association is frequent in the Saint. See, among others, sermons 138,4; 147.3; 253.1; 295.4; 299.7, etc. On the other hand, it is not the only one: SAN JERÓNIMO, Cartas Ti,4.

man, certainly does not imitate him who, being God, became man. You are not told: "Be less than what you are," but: "Know what you are." Know yourself weak, know yourself a man, know yourself a sinner, know yourself to be God who justifies, know yourself stained. Lay bare in confession the stain of your heart, and you will belong to the flock of Christ; The confession of sins will make the Doctor want to heal you. The patient who says: "I have nothing" does not worry about the doctor. Had not the Pharisee and the publican gone up to the temple? The first boasted of being healthy, the second showed the Doctor his sores; The first said: Oh God, I thank you, because I am not like this publican. He took his neighbor's foot to climb up; where, if the publican had been healthy, the Pharisee would have looked askance at him, because he would have had no one to blame. But how did that one-faced man get to the temple? He was certainly not healthy; But since he said he was healthy, he did not come down cured. On the contrary, the other, looking at the ground, without daring to raise it to heaven, wounded his chest, saying: Oh God! Be merciful to me, my sinner. And what did the Lord say? I truly tell you that this justified man came down from the temple and not the Pharisee. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled and he who humbles himself will be exalted. Then those who rise up want to climb into the sheepfold from another side than through the door; Those who humble themselves enter the fold through the door. Hence this one enters and the other goes up. To climb, as you see, is to seek heights; who homo factus is. Tibí autem non dicitur, Esto aliquid minus quam es: sed, Cognosce quod es. Cognosce te infirmum, cognosce te hominem, cognosce te peccatorem; cognosce quia ille iustificat, cognosce quia maculosus es. Appareat in confessione tua macula cordis tui, et pertinebis ad gregem Christi. Quia confessio peccatorum invitationt medicum sanaturum: quomodo in aegritudine qui dicit, Sanus sum, non quaerit medicum. Numquid non ad templum ascenderat Pharisaeus ille et Publicanus? Lile de sua sanitate gloriabatur, iste vulnera sua medico ostendebat. Dicebat enim ille: Deus, gratias ago tibí, quia non sum sicut Publicanus iste. Gloriabatur super alterum. Ergo si Publicanus ille sanus esset, invideret illi Pharisaeus; quia non haberet super quem extolleretur. Quomodo ergo venerat, qui sic invidebat? Non erat utique sanus: et cum se sanum diceret, non descendit curatus.

Ule autem ad terram oculos deiciens, et non audens in caelum tollere, percutiebat pectus suum, they say: Deus, propitius esto mihi peccatori. Et quid dicit Dominus? Amen dico vobis, quia descendit iustificatus de temple (lo 10,16-17) Publicanus, magis quam Pharisaeus: quia omnis qui se exaltat, humiliabitur; et qui se humiliat, exaltahitur (Luke 18:10-14). Qui ergo se exaltant, per alteram partem volunt ascendé ad ovile: qui autem se humiliant, per ianuam intrant ad ovile. Ideo de illo dixit, intrat: de illo, ascendit. Who ascended,

rises does not enter, but falls; But whoever stoops to enter through the door, he does not fall, but is a shepherd. 5. The Lord speaks in this gospel about three types of people, who we must study: the shepherd, the mercenary and the thief; and I understand that, when it was read to us, you noticed the characteristics with which he designated the shepherd, those of the mercenary and those of the thief. He said of the shepherd that he gave his life for his sheep and entered through the door; of the robber or thief, who came up on another side; of the mercenary stated that, seeing the wolf or the thief, he flees, because he has no love for the sheep: he is a mercenary, not a true shepherd. This one enters through the door, because he is a shepherd; the thief climbs another way, because he is a thief; The mercenary, seeing those who try to take the sheep, fears and escapes, because he is a mercenary, because he does not care about the sheep: in the end he is a mercenary. If we found these three people, your holiness would have found who to love, who to tolerate and who to avoid. The shepherd must be loved, the mercenary tolerated, the thief avoided. There are men in the Church who, according to what the Apostle says, announce the Gospel for convenience, seeking from men their own growth, now in money, now in honors, now in human praise 4. Seeking at all costs videtis, qui alta petít, non intrat, sed cadit. Ille autem qui se submíttit, ut per ianuam intret, non cadit, sed pastor est. CAPUT V.—5. Three personae ad ovile venientes: shepherd, fur, mercenarius. Diligendus est pastor, mercenarius tolerandus, cavendus latro.—Sed tres personas dixit Dominus, et deben mus illas investigare in Gospel; pastoris, mercenarii et furis. Cum legeretur, puto quod animadvertistis, designavit pastorem, designavit mercenarius, designavit furem. Pastorem dixit animam suam poné pro ovibus et intrare per ianuam. Furem dixit et latronem ascendé per alliam [757] partem. Mercenarium dixit, lupum vel etiam furem si videat, fugere; quia non est illi cura de ovibus: mercenarius est enim, non pastor. Ule intrat per ianuam, quia pastor est; ille ascendit per alliam partem, quia fur est: ille videns eos qui volunt tollere oves, timet et fugit, quia mercenarius est, quia non est illi cura de ovibus; mercenarius is enim. If we invenerímus three of these persons, invenit Sanctitas vestra et quos diligatis, et quos toleretis, et quos caveatis. Diligendus is pastor, tolerandus is mercenarius, cavendus is latro.

Sunt homines in Ecclesia, de quibus dicit Apostolus, qui ex occasione evangelizant, quaerentes ab hominibus commoda sua (Phil 1 21), sive pecuniaria, sive honorum vel laudis humanoe. Quomodolibet * We must not forget that Augustine was already speaking in post-Constantinian times, in which the clergy was considered a special class, entitled to the honor owed to the other magistrates and high officials of the empire, and enjoyed many privileges. Later laws had to put obstacles in this career of the cleric to prevent the introduction of those who sought only those privileges. This is how Augustine's phrase is understood: "I know how much men love the clergy" (sermon 355,6).

their personal advantages, they do not look, when preaching, both to the health of those to whom they preach and to their particular emoluments. But whoever hears the doctrine that heals someone who is not healthy, if he believes in it without placing hope in it, the preacher will lose, but the believer will gain. 6. There you have the Lord saying of the Pharisees: Sit on the seat of Moses. The Lord was not referring only to them, nor was it his intention to send those who believed in him to the schools of the Jews, so that they could learn there the way of the kingdom of heaven. Well, what! Had he not come to form his Church and separate from the rest of the nation, like grain from chaff, the Israelites who believed and hoped well and loved well, to make circumcision a wall, to which another wall was to join, that of Gentiles, and he himself be the cornerstone where these two walls of different directions would meet? Did not the Lord say of these two peoples, destined to merge into one: I also have other sheep that are not of this sheepfold, of the fold of the Jews; and it is necessary that I bring them, and they will hear my voice, and there will be one flock and one shepherd? That is why there were two boats from which he called his disciples. It was also an emblem of the two peoples to have cast the nets where such an abundance and number of fish came out that the nets were one finger's breadth away from breaking: And they filled, he says, the two boats. There were two boats, but they meant one Church

unique, unified in Christ, made of two peoples coming in different directions. The same thing was meant by the two women, Leah and Rachel, wives of one man, Jacob. These two peoples, finally, are represented in the two blind men sitting on the side of the road, to whom the Lord restored their sight. And, if you look carefully at the Scriptures, you will still find many other places where these two Churches are meant, which are not two, but one; because such was the mission of the Cornerstone: to make two peoples a single people; and that of the Shepherd was nothing more than making two flocks into one flock. So, since the Lord had to train his Church and have his own school, independent of the Jews, as we are now seeing, should he order the believers in him to go to the Jews so that they could learn from them? But under the name of Pharisees and scribes he gave us to understand that there would be some in the Church who would say and not do, as he designated himself in the person of Moses. Moses, in effect, was a figure of Jesus Christ; and if, when speaking to the people, his face was veiled, it was to signify that the Jews, while in the law they sought carnal joys and delights and an earthly kingdom, would have before their eyes a veil that would not allow them to see Christ in the Scriptures. With the veil removed after the Lord's passion, the secrets of the temple were revealed. Because of that, when the Lord was hanging on the cross, the veil of the sanctuary was torn from top to bottom, and the apostle Paul says: When you pass to Christ the veil will be taken away. Who,

volentes accipere muñera evangelizant, et non tam salutem eius quaerunt cui annuntiant, quam commodum suum. lile autem qui audit salutem ab eo qui non habet salutem si ei crediderit quem Ule annuntiat, ñeque in illo spem posuerit, per quem illi annuntiatur salus: qui annuntiat, habebit detrimentum; cui annuntiatur, habebit lucrum. CAPUT VI.—6. Dictum Christi in Pharisaeos, spectare et ad malo de Ecclesia pastors. Ecclesia una ex Iudaeis et Gentibus.—Habes Dominum dicentem de Pharisaeis, Cathedram Moysi sedent (Mt 23.2). Non eos solos significat Dominus: quasi vero eos qui crederent in Christum, ad Iudaeorum scholam mitteret, ut ibi discerent quemadmodum iter sit ad regnum caelorum. Nonne ideo Dominus venit, ut institueret Ecclesiam, ipsosque Iudaeos bene credentes et bene sperantes et bene diligentes segregaret tanquam frumenta a paleis, et faceret unum parietem circumcisionis, cui coniungeretur alius paries ex praeputio Gentium, quibus duobus parietibus de diverse venientibus esset ipse lapis angularis? Nonne ergo idem Dominus de duabus istis plebibus in uno futuris dixit: Habeo et alias oves, quae non sunt ex hoc ovili? Loquebatur autem Iudaeis: Oportet me, inquit, et eas adducere, ut sit unus grex, et unus pastor (lo 10,16-17). Ideo duae naves erant, unde vocaverat discipulus. Duas ipsas plebes significant, quando miserunt retía, et levaverunt tantam vim et tantum numerum piscium, ita ut penis retia rumperentur: Et oneraverunt, inquit, duas naves (cf. Lk 5,2-7). Duae significant ships

unam Ecclesiam, sed de duabus plebibus factam, coniunctam in Christo, quamvis de diverse venientem. Hoc significant etiam duae uxores, habentes unum virum _Iacob, Lia et Rachel (cf. Gen 29). Has duas significant etiam duo caeci, qui sedebant iuxta viam, quos Dominus iliurninavit (cf. Mt 20:30-34). Et_ si advertatis Scripturas, in multis locis invenietis significari duas Ecclesias, quae non sunt duae, sed una. Ad hoc enim valet lapis angularis, ut ex duabus faciat unam. Ad hoc valet ille pastor, ut de duobus gregibus faciat unum. Ergo Dominus docturus Ecclesiam, et habiturus scholam 1758] suam praeter Iudaeos, sicut moda videmus, numquid credentes in se, ad Iudaeos missurus erat, ut discerent? Sed nomine Pharisaeorum et Scribarum significavit quosdam in Ecclesia sua futures, qui dicerent, et non facerent: se autem figuraverat in persona Moysi. Etenim personam eius gerebat Moyses, et velum ante se ideo ponebat, quando loquebatur populo; quia quamdiu illi in Lege carnalibus gaudiis et voluptatibus dediti erant, et regnum terrenum quaerebant, velamen positum erat contra faciem eorum, ne viderent Christum in Scripturis. Áblato enim velamine, posteaquam passus est Dominus, visa sunt secreta templi. Ideo cum in cruz penderet, scissum est velum templi a summo usque deorsum (cf. Mt 27:51): et aperte dicit apostolus Paulus, Cum autem transieris ad Christum, auferetur velamen. Qui autem

However, do not pass on to Christ, even if you read Moses, you will have the veil drawn over your heart, in the Apostle's phrase. Trying, then, to announce that there would be this kind of doctors in his Church, what did the Lord say? In Moses' chair sit scribes and Pharisees; Do what they say and don't do what they do. 7. There are evil clerics who, hearing this sentence, spoken for them, try to distort its meaning. I myself have seen how some labored in corrupting this passage; And, if they could, wouldn't they erase him from the Gospel? But, not being able to eliminate him, they try to adulterate him; but the grace and mercy of the Lord are with us, and does not allow them to achieve it, because he walled all his words with his truth and weighed them, in such a way that, if any unfaithful reader or interpreter wanted to amputate or add something, the judicious man would only have to read the previous or the following to restore to the Scripture what was cut and find the meaning that was intended to be falsified. And what do you think those referred to by the phrase say: What they say, do it? Because there is no doubt what is said to the laity. Well, when a layman wants to live well, what does he say to himself when he sees a bad clergyman? The Lord has said: Do what they say, but do not do what they do. My obligation is to walk in the way of the Lord and not follow his customs. I will hear not his words, but those of God. Let me follow God and let him follow his desires. Because, if I am going to defend myself before non transierit ad Christum, quamvis legat Moysen, velamen positum est super cor eius, sicut dicit Apostolus (cf. 2 Cor 3,16.15). Cum ergo praefiguraret quosdam such futures Dominus in Ecclesia sua, quid ait? Scribae et Pharisaei cathedram Moysi sedent: quae dicunt, jacite; sed quae faciunt, faceré nolite (Mt 23,2). CAPUT VIL—7. Clerici malí pervertere nitentes Evangelium, dum exemplo suo laicos ad peccatum trahunt.—Quando illud audiunt clerici mali quod in ipsos dicitur, volunt pervertere. Nana audi quosdam pervertere velle istam sententiam. Numquid non, si illis liceret, non delerent illam of Gospel? Quia vero delere illam non possunt, pervertere illam quaerunt.

Sed adest Domini gratia et mercy, nec sinit eos faceré; quia circumsepsit veritate sua omnes sententias suas, et libravit; ut quisquís inde aliquid praecidere voluerit, aut inducere male legendo vel interpretando, ille qui cor habet, quod praecisum est de Scriptura iungat Scripturae, et legat superiora vel inferiora, et inveniet sensum quem volebat ille mal interpreta!. Ouid ergo putatis dicere istos de quibus dicitur, Quae dicunt, jacite? Quia revera laicis dicitur. Laicus enim qui vult bene vivere, cum attenderit clericum malum, quid sibi dicit? Dominus dixit, Quae dicunt, jacite; quae jaciunt, {acere nolite. Ambulem viam Domini, non sequar istius mores. Audiam ab illo, non verbo ipsius, sed Dei. Sequar Deum, sequatur ille cupiditatem suam. Quia si voluero apud Deum sic I will defend myself, ut dicam, Domine, vidi male vivostem illum

God saying: "Lord, I have lived badly because such a clergyman lived badly", will he not perhaps say to me: "Bad servant, have you not heard it said: What they tell you, do it; what they do, do not do it? And the bad layman, the unfaithful, the one who does not belong to the flock of Christ, the one who does not belong to the wheat of Christ, the one who, like chaff, is tolerated on the threshing floor, what is said when he begins to reproach the word of God? «Go away!, stop the nonsense. The bishops themselves, the clerics themselves, do not do it, and you demand that I do it? This person is not looking for a lawyer for a bad trial, but rather a partner in torture. Surely, in fact, on the day of judgment, that evil man whom he liked to imitate will not protect him; For just as the devil seduces none of the seduced to reign with him, but to have companions in condemnation, so all those who follow in the footsteps of the wicked do not seek help to ascend to heaven, but company in the flames of hell. 8. How, I say, do those clergymen of bad living manage to falsify this thought when they are told: «The Lord has said well: Do what they say; don't do what they do"? «And very well said, they respond. You have been commanded to do what we tell you and not to do what we do. Because we offer the sacrifice, and it is not lawful for you. See where these mercenary rogues turn (if they were shepherds, they wouldn't say that). Now, to close their mouths, all you have to do is see the sequence of the Lord's words: They sit, he says, on the seat of Moses; do what they say, do not do clericum tuum, et ideo male vixi: nonne mihi dictus est, Serve nequam, non a me audieras, Quae dicunt, jacite; quae autem jaciunt, faceré nolite? Malus autem laicus, infidelis, non pertinens ad gregem Christi, non pertinens ad frumentum Christi, qui tanquam palea in zona toleratur, quid sibi dicit, quando coeperit illum arguere verbum Dei? Exi: quid mihi loqueris? Ipsi episcopi, ipsi clerici non illud faciunt, et me cogis ut faciam? Quaerit sibi non patronum ad causam malam, sed comitem ad poenam. Nam never eum ille defensurus est in die iudicii, quemcumque malum voluerit imitari. Quomodo enim dia [759] bolus omnes quos seducit, non seducit cum quibus regnet, sed cum quibus damnetur: sic omnes qui sequuntur malo, committees sibi ad gehennam quaerunt, non patrocinia ad regnum caelorum. CAPUT VIII.'—8.

Perversa interpretatio Evangelü.—Quomodo ergo pervertunt isti hanc sententiam, quando illis dicitur male vivostibus, Mérito dictum est a Domino, Quae dicunt, jacite; quae jaciunt, faceré nolite? Recte dictum est, inquiunt. Dictum est enim vobis, ut quae dicimus, faciatis; quae autem nos facimus, vos non faciatis. We enim offerimus sacrificium, vobis non licet. Videte versutias hominum: quid dicam? mercenariorum. Nam si pastors essent, ista non dicerent. Ideo Dominus ut os illis clauderet, secutus est, et dixit, Cathedram Moysi

what they do, because they say, and do not do. What is to be inferred from here, brothers? If the Lord spoke of offering the sacrifice, would He have said: They say, and do not do? Because they make the sacrifice, they offer the sacrifice to God. What is it that they say and don't do? Hear what comes next: They tie heavy and unbearable burdens and throw them on the necks of the men; They don't even want to move them with a finger. This description and example are a clear reproach. One thing clearly stands out in the attempts to adulterate this passage: that they do not target any other target in the Church than that of their personal conveniences and that they have never read the Gospel, because, if they knew this page, they would never dare to say what they say. 9. You are going to see more clearly how in the Church we have individuals of this type, so that no one comes telling us: «He only said it about the Pharisees; He did not say it except from the scribes; "He only said it about the Jews, because the Church does not have people like that." Who are those of whom the Lord said: Not everyone who says to me, “Lord, Lord,” will enter the kingdom of heaven? Then, since capital punishments carried with them the confiscation of the property of the condemned, the word meant any punishment of this nature, especially exile, and those who were exiled were called outlaws. Historically, Sulla's proscriptions are famous, the name given to the black lists of citizens that appeared posted in the Forum, and, without further legality, those included in them were condemned to death and their property confiscated. For this procedure Cicero lost his life. See J. GUILLEN. XJrbs Rama. Life and customs of the Romans (Salamanca 1978) II 104-105.

De spinis me iubes uvam When Augustine preached this sermon it must have already been customary, judging by his words, for priests to also preach. It must be remembered in this regard that, as soon as he was ordained a priest, his bishop Valerius allowed him to preach against the usage and custom of the churches of Africa, according to Saint Possidius (Life of Augustine 5). It was the beginning of a new way of proceeding, and a little later Augustine congratulated Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, for also accepting it: "Our mouths have been filled with joy and our tongues have been filled with exultation by announcing to us the holy thought that you have put into execution with the help of the Lord who inspired it in you. We are referring... especially to the ministry of the word of the priests who now speak to the people in your presence. Through his tongue charity cries out in the hearts of men more than their voice in your ears..." (letter 41,1). We must not forget that the practice was not rare in the East.

We speak from experience, because this has happened to us before; otherwise we wouldn't believe it. Many ask us for bad advice: that we authorize them to lie, to deceive cunningly, thinking to give us pleasure in it. But I do not think I will displease the Lord if I assure you, in the name of Christ, that no one, for such things, has found in me assent to his will; because, with the permission of the one who called us to the episcopate, I am not a mercenary, without a pastor, although I say what the Apostle says: What matters the least to me is being judged by you or by some human court; But I don't judge myself either; For even though my conscience accuses me of nothing, that does not mean I am justified; The one who judges me is the Lord. In other words: My conscience is not good because you praise Me. Why praise what is not seen? Praise him who sees everything, and let him correct me if he sees something offensive to his eyes. Because we don't consider ourselves completely healthy either, we rather beat our chest and say to God: "Be merciful to me, so that I may not sin." I believe I can say, however, that, as I am in his presence, I seek nothing apart from your salvation; that we often lament the sins of our brothers, these sins that repel us and torment our souls; and that sometimes we call them to order; or rather, we do not stop correcting them. Witnesses are those who remember the times they have been corrected by me 10.

Topic: The good shepherd (Jn 10:11-16). Place: Carthage. Date: Between 411 and 412.

1. We have just heard the Lord Jesus commending to us the duties of the good shepherd, from which it follows, Evangelii quid aliud dicit servo? cum diceret, Domine, sciebam te molestum sive durum hominem, quia metis ubi non seminasti, et colligis ubi non sparsisti; et timens abii, et abscondi talentum tuum in tena: ecce habes quod tuum est. Et ille: Serve, inquit, nequam et piger, magis quia me sciebas molestum et durum esse, puté ubi non seminavi, el colligere ubi non sparsi, ipsa avaritia mea debuit te docere quia lucrum quaero de pecunia mea. Oportuit te ergo ut dares pecuniam meam nummulariis et ego veniens cum usuris exegissem quod meum est (Luke 19:20-23). Numquid dixit, Dares et demandings? We ergo, fratres, damus; come what I demand. Pray, ut paratos us inveniat.

CAPUT I. — 1. Bonus pastor cur commendatus in singulari.—Audivimus Dominum Iesum commendantem nobis boni pastoris officium. In qua commendatione admonuit us utique, ut intellegi datur, esse bonds

as it is plain, the existence of good shepherds. In order, however, to warn us against the false idea that he refers to the guild of shepherds, he says: I am the good shepherd. And the reason for being so is explained immediately: The good shepherd gives his life for his sheep. On the other hand, the hireling, who is not a shepherd, sees the wolf coming and flees, because he does not take care of the sheep: because he is a hireling. Therefore the good shepherd is Christ. And Peter, isn't he a good shepherd? Did he not also give his life for the sheep? And Paul? And the other apostles? And the blessed martyred bishops who succeeded them? What can we even say about San Cipriano? Were they not all good shepherds, and not hired servants, of whom it is said: I assure you, they have already received their reward? Yeah; all these were good shepherds; not only for having shed his blood, but for having shed it in defense of the sheep; They did not pour it out of vanity, but out of charity. 2. Because there are also heretics 2 who, having, perhaps, suffered some discomfort due to their iniquities and errors, proudly display the name of martyrs, to steal more easily hidden under this brilliant pallium, since they are wolves. To know how to classify them, listen to a good shepherd, the apostle Paul, say how not always when they suffer until they give their bodies to the flames should they think that they gave their lives for the sheep and not against the sheep. Yes, I, he says, speaking shepherds' tongues. Et tamen ne intellegeretur perverso moda multitudo pastorum: Ego sum, inquit, pastor bonus. And where he sits pastor bonus, consequently ostendit: Pastor, inquit, bonus animam suam ponit pro ovibus. Mercenarius autem, et qui non est pastor, videt lupum venientem, et fugit: quoniam non est el cura de ovibus; mercenarius is enim (lo 10,1112.13). Pastor ergo bonus Christus. Quid Petrus? Nonne bonus shepherd? nonne et ipse animam pro ovibus posit? Quid Paulus? Quid ceteri Apostoli? Quid eorum tempora consequentes beati episcopi martyres? Quid etiam sanctus iste Cyprianus? Nonne omnes pastors boni; non mercenarii, de quibus dicitur, Amen dico vobis, perceperunt mercedem suam (Mt 6,2)? Omnes ergo isti pastores boni, non solum quia sanguinem fuderunt, [764] sed quia pro ovibus fuderunt. Non enim fuderunt elatione, sed caritate. CAPOT II.—2.

Martyrium sine caritate nihil prodest.—Nam et apud haereticos, qui propter iniquitates et errors suos aliquid molestarum perpessi fuerint, nomine martyrii se iactant, ut hoc pallio dealbati facilius furentur, quia lupi sunt. Si autem scire vultis in quo numero habendi sunt, pastorem bonum Paulum apostolum audite: quoniam non omnes qui corpora sua in passione etiam ignibus tradunt, aestimandi sunt sanguinem fudisse pro ovibus, sed potius contra oves. Why, if not, did that Peter, whose chest had your eyes as witnesses, become sad when you asked him again and again - so that he could erase with a triple confession of love the triple sin of his denials 4 -; why, I say, he became truly sad, interrogated insistently by someone who knew the truth of what he was asking and had given him the love that he protested; Why, stunned, did he burst into those words: Lord, you, who know everything, do you also know that I love you? Why, then, do you speak to these good shepherds of a single good shepherd, if not to thus recommend unity to them? The Lord is going in person to explain this to you more clearly through our ministry, reminding your charity of the same place in the Gospel. Listen to him. To tell you so emphatically: I am the good shepherd, was to say to you: Everyone else, everyone responded. Non est ergo bonus, qui amat tantum bonum? Unde illa responsio ex intimis prolata visceribus? Unde ille Petrus testes oculos tuos habens in corde suo, contristatus quod eum non solum semel, sed iterum et tertio interrogasti, ut trina confessione amoris, deleret trinum peccatum negationis; unde ergo contristatus, quod saepe interrogatus esset ab eo qui sciret quod interrogabat, et donaverat quod auditebat; unde contristatus, talia verba retulit: Domine, tu seis omnia, ipse nosti quoniam do I love you? (cf. 21:15-17). Itane ille talia confitens, immo profitens lieretur? Veraciter ergo respondedit amorem tuum, et de intimo corde protulit amantis vocem. Tu autem dixisti: Bonus homo de bono thesauro coráis sui proferí bona (Mt 12,35). Ergo et pastor, et bonus pastor: nihil quidem ad potestatem ac bonitotem pastoris pastorum; sed tamen etiam ipse et shepherd, et bonus: et ceteri such shepherds boni. CAPUT V.—5.

Et exponit apertius ipse Dominus per ministerium nostrum, ex ipso Gospel commemorans Caritatem vestram, et dices, Audite quid commendavi, Ego sum pastor bonus, dixi: quia omnes ceteri, omnes pastores boni membra mea sunt. good shepherds, they are my members, because there is but one head and one body: one Christ. There is, therefore, only one body, a single flock, formed by the Shepherd of the shepherds, under the staff of the supreme Shepherd. Doesn't the Apostle teach that? For just as the body, being one, has many members, and all the members of the body, though many, are one body, so also is Christ. Therefore, if Christ is also like this and if he has all the good shepherds incorporated into him, it is right that he only speaks of one when he says: I am the good shepherd. I, the only one; all the others form a single unit with me. He who feeds outside of me feeds against me; Whoever does not collect with me, scatters. Hear him now recommend unity even more vehemently. I have, he says, other sheep that are not from this sheepfold. This sheepfold, in fact, to which he spoke, was of Israelites according to the flesh; But there were other Israelites according to faith, who were still outside among the Gentiles, already predestined, not yet gathered together. He, who had predestined them, knew them; He knew them, who had come to redeem them by the outpouring of his blood. They didn't see him, but he saw them; They had not yet believed in him, and he already knew them. I have, he says, other sheep that are not from this sheepfold, since they do not belong to the carnal lineage of Israel; They will not, however, be left out of the fold; It is necessary to bring them to me, so that it may be one flock and one shepherd. 6. The word sodales, in fact, means commensals, to eat together: like a group of edales1. This reproach from the psalm is addressed to them: If my enemy had spoken evil of me, I would certainly have endured it. And if he who hated me had spoken of me insolently, perhaps I would have hidden myself from him; but you, who share my soul with me, my guide and my confidant, who together with me ate sweet delicacies..., in the house of God we walked together. Why do the Donatists now rise up in rebellion against the house of God, the Catholic Church, if not because they came from among us, but were not ours? Make sure, then, O Beloved of my soul, that I do not come to find these your guests, similar to those of Samson, unfaithful to their friend, because they were going to bribe his wife. Then, so as not to appear among them as an unknown and anonymous person, I, the one who has his fervent, brilliant doctrine. Dexteram tuam notam fac mihi, et erudites corde in sapientia (Ps 89,12). The good Shepherd, the most beautiful of the sons of men, now responds to his Beloved, whom he made the most beautiful of the daughters of men. Listen, then, and be warned, so as not to incur his threats, and love what he warns. What does he answer? How much softness, but also how much severity along with his caresses! He rebukes her, but in order to retain and preserve her. If you do not know yourself, oh the most beautiful of women!... Well, although there are others who are beautified by the gifts of the Bridegroom, they are, in the end, heresies; They are beautiful by their attire, they are not beautiful by nature; beautiful on the outside: they shine on the outside, because they boast of the name of justice; On the other hand, all the beauty of the king's daughter is internal. If, well, you don't know yourself; If you do not know yourself as the only one, then you are found in the whole world, and you are chaste, and you should not allow yourself to be corrupted by the perverse language of unworthy diners; if you do not know yourself and do not know that you have been espoused to me to present yourself to Christ as a pure virgin; If you do not walk well with me and do not fear that clumsy doctrines will corrupt your thoughts, as the serpent seduced Eve with cunning; If you don't know yourself, I say, by these characters, stituta. Theme: The unity of the Father and the Son (Jn 10:30). Location: Unknown. Date: Between 416 and 418.

1. The Lord God, Jesus Christ, the only Son of God, born of God the Father without any mother and born of a virgin mother without a man father, have heard what he said: I and the Father are one. Accept this and believe it, so that you deserve to understand it, for faith must precede intelligence, so that intelligence may be the prize of faith 1, as a prophet expressly said: If you do not believe, you will not understand. It is to faith, therefore, where preaching is directed when it simply exposes the mysteries and it is to intelligence where the discussion, which subtleties, looks. And so, to begin by imbuing your souls with faith, we preach to you Christ, the Only Son of God the Father. Why is it called Unique? The Father of this only Son has many children by grace. All saints, in truth, are children of God by grace; but only Jesus Christ is by nature.
FROM VERBIS EVANGELII IOANNIS “EGO ET PATER UNUM SUMUS.” CHAP. 10.30

Sic accipite hoc, sic credite, ut mercamini intellegere. Fides enim debent praecedere intellectum, ut sit intellectus (idei praemium. Propheta enim apertissime dixit, Nisi credideritis, non intellegetis (Is 7,9, sec. LXX). Quod ergo simpliciter praedicatur, creilcndum est: quod subtiliter disputatur, intellegendum est. Children by grace are not of the nature of the Father, and that is why no saint dared to say like this One: I and the Father are one and the same. Is not the Father also our Father? And if it is not our Father, how do we say when we pray: Our Father, who art in heaven? Yeah; We are also his children; but he made us children by his will, not because he begot us from his nature. Christ, then, being of the same nature as the Father, spoke truth when he said: I and the Father are one. What does the same thing mean? We are of one and the same nature. Is there time to look for age differences? If among us it is the father before the son, it is because they are both temporary. And one grows while the other ages. But, I have already said, it is not in point of nature that the father is older than the son, but in age. Do you want to see it? Wait; let the son grow, and he will be equal to his father. For the little son it is enough to grow to reach the height of his father. According to you, the Son of God is so inferior to his Father that he cannot grow or reach the greatness of his Father. Therefore the Son of Man is of a condition that surpasses that of the Son of God. As? Because a son of man grows to become equal to his father, while Christ, according to you, is born inferior to his Father to always be inferior to him, without even the hope of equaling him over time. And you say this because they are different in nature. But why do you say this if not because you do not believe that they are Son and Father of the same substance? Confess, at least, the identity of substance and tell it inferior later. Notice the men: here is a man. What substance is yours? He is a man. And the son he fathers? Man too, although smaller. Different age, identical nature. You also say: The Son is of the same nature as the Father, but inferior to him. Say it, take a step forward; say that they are of the same substance, although inferior to him, and you will come to see in him—Son—his equal. It is not a little progress,

indeed; It is not a diminished approximation, to come to confess the same, to confess the same substance, although less. But the Son, you say, is not of the same substance as the Father, that is, one is gold and the other is silver; which is like saying that a man has begotten a horse, because one is the substance of the man and another is that of the horse. Therefore, if the Son is of another substance than his Father, the Father has generated a monster. When the creature, e.g., the woman, gives birth to a non-human being, we say that she gave birth to a monster. In order not to be a monster, what is born must be just like the one who engendered it: the man must produce a man, the horse a horse, the dove a dove, the bird a bird. 4. Father, a man with hair on his chest, and you are a chicken. This one to whom such is said, is degenerated due to ailment; by nature, equal to his father. What does this mean?
