What are you looking at the speck in your brother's eye, and not seeing the beam in your own? And the soul, which walks outside of itself, is brought back to itself. And just as she had distanced herself from herself, she had distanced herself from her Lord. This soul, in fact, had looked at itself, and came out pleased with the examination, thereby falling in love with its independence. She walked away from him without staying within herself; feel impelled to go out of yourself, go out of yourself and rush towards the exterior. Love the world, love the temporal, love the earthly. Loving oneself, with contempt for those who made it, would mean decaying, becoming less; as far as there is from a thing made to the one who made it'*. Therefore God must be loved in such a way that we even forget ourselves, if that were possible. How is this conversion to be carried out? The soul forgot itself, but for love of the world; forget yourself now, but to love the architect of the world. Pushed outside of herself, in a certain way she lost herself; and since he doesn't even see his facts, he justifies his excesses. Floating adrift, she displays her arrogance, her frivolities, her honors, her jobs, her riches, and all vanity contributes to making her infatuated. But rebuke comes, correction comes, he makes it come to him, he is displeased with himself, he confesses his ugliness, he desires beauty, and the dissipated returns to God in shame. 4. Does he pray against her or pray for her who says: Cover his face with ignominy? Fills, he says, his face with ignominy,

and they will seek your name, O Lord! Was it, then, abhorrence to wish to cover their faces with shame? If you are longing for them to seek the name of the Lord, doesn't He love you extremely? But is there only love or only hatred here, or is there hatred and love at the same time? Yes, yes; hates and loves. He hates what is yours, he loves you. What does it mean: “He hates what is yours, he loves you”? Hate what you made, love what God made. Yours, what are they but sins? And you, what are you but what God made? You disdain what you were made, you love what you made; You love your works outside of yourself, you despise the work of God within yourself. It is not strange that you go outside, it is not strange that you slip, it is not strange that you distance yourself from yourself, it is not strange that you are called a spirit that goes and does not return. Hear, hear him who calls you saying: Return to me, and I will return to you. God is not removed nor brought back; He is not moved when he corrects nor is there any change in him when he rebukes. If he is far from you, it is because you distanced yourself from him. It was you who fell from him, it was not he who hid from you. Now, therefore, hear him say to you: Return to me, and I will return to you. In other words: "This turning I to you is nothing but you turning to me." God, in fact, pursues those who turn their backs on Him and illuminates the faces of those who turn their faces to Him. Oh fugitive, where will you flee from God? 2 Where will you flee, fleeing from whom no space circumscribes and is absent from nowhere? Who gives freedom to the converted, does he take revenge for the one who has fled? Fugitive, is your judge; Return to him and you will find him a father.

ierat, sic a domino suo. Se enim respexerat, sibique placuerat, suaeque potestatis amatrix facta fuet. Recessit ab illo, et non (697) remansit in se: ideo et a se pellitur, et a se excluditur, et in exteriora prolabitur. Amat mundum, amat temporalia, amat terrena. Quae si se ipsam amaret, neglecto a quo facta est, iam minus esset, iam deficeret, amando quod minus est: minus est enim ipsa quam deus; et longe minus, tantaque minus, quanto minus est res facta quam factor. Ergo amandus est deus: ita ut pro amore eius, si fieri potest, nos ipsos obliviscamur. Quis ergo est iste transitus? Oblita est anima se ipsam, sed amando mundum: nunc obliviscatur se, sed amando artificem mundi. Press [728] ergo a se, quodam moda, perdidit se; et quia nec facta sua novit videre, iustificat iniquitates suas. Effertur et superbit in petulantia, in luxuria, in honoribus, in potestatibus, in divitiis, in potentia vanitatis. Arguitur, corripitur, ostenditur sibi, displicet sibi: confitetur foeditatem, desiderat pulcnritudinem; et quae ibat effusa, redit confused. 4. Contra illam videtur orare, qui dicit, Imple facies eorum ignominia. Imple, inquit, jactes eorum ignominia, et quaerent nomen tuum, domine (Ps 82,17). Oderat eos, quorum facies impleri ignominia cupiebat?'

Vide quemadmodum amet eos, quos vult quaerere nomen domini. Amat tantum, an odit tantum? An et hate, et amat? Immo et odit, et amat. Odit tua, amat te. Quid est, odit tua, amat te? Odit quod fecisti, amat quod deus fecit. Quae sunt enim tua, nisi peccata? Et quis es tu, nisi quod fecit deus? Neglegis quod factus es, diligis quod fecisti: amas extra te opera tua, neglegis in te opus dei. Merit is, merit laberis, merit et a te ipso pergis; merit audis: spiritus ambulans et non rever tens (Ps 77,39). Audi potius vocantem et dicentem: convertimini ad me, et convertar ad vos (Zach 1,3). Non enim deus avertitur et convertitur: manens corripit, incommutabilis corripit. Aversus est, quia tu te avertisti; tu ab illo fecisti casum, non ipse a te fecit occasum. Ergo audi dicentem tibi: convertimini ad me, et convertar ad vos. Hoc est enim, quod convertor (698) ad vos, quia convertimini ad me. Fugientis dorsa petsequitur faciem redeuntis illuminat. Quo enim fugies, a deo fugiens? Quo fugies' fugiens ab illo, qui nullo loco continetur, et nusquam absens est; qul conversum liberat, punit aversum? Quem habes iudicem fugiens, hunc patrem habeto rediens.
'* Note the Platonic language of this description,
The thought is frequent. See sermon 341 A,3 (= MAI 22); Enarrations to Psalms 67,2; 74.9; 94.2; 138,10-11; Commentary on the Letter of Saint John to the Parthians 6,3.

5. Swollen by pride, this same swelling hindered him from returning through the narrowness. Who, in fact, made the way for us, cries: Enter through the narrow gate. He tries to enter, but the swelling prevents him; and the more the swelling prevents him from doing so, the more harmful his efforts become. Because, for a bloated person, narrowness is a torment, which contributes to making him more bloated; And if it still increases in volume, how can it enter? So it has to deflate. As? Taking the medicine of humility; let him drink this bitter but healthy potion, the potion of humiliation. Why try to shrink? The masses do not allow it; not big, but swollen. Because magnitude or corpulence is an indication of solidity, swelling is inflation. Therefore, whoever is swollen, do not consider himself great; deflate yourself to be of authentic and solid greatness. Do not covet these things here; Do not boast about the pomp of these fleeting and corruptible things; hear the voice of him who said: Enter through the narrow gate; and also: I am the way. As if the timid person asked him: "Where am I going to enter?", he answers: "I am the way, enter through me." To enter through this door you have to walk this path; because if he said: I am the way, he also said: I am the door. What do you worry about where to return, where to return and where to enter? So that you do not go astray, he made all this for you: a way and an entrance. In two words he says it: Be humble, be meek. 5. Tumuerat autem superbia, et ipso tumore per angustum rediré non poterat. Clamat ille, qui factus est via: intrate per angustam portam (Mt 7,13). Conatur ingredi, prevented tumor; et both magis perniciose conatur, quanto magis impedit tumour. Tumidum enim vexat anguish; vexatus autem amplius tumebit. Amplius tumens, when intrabit? Ergo detumescat, si cupit ingredi. Unde autem detumescat? Accipiat humilitatis medicamentum. Bibat against tumorem poculum amarum, healthy thirst: bibat poculum humilitatis. What is artat? Non sinit moles, non magna, sed túmida: magnitudeo enim soliditatem habet, tumor infla[729]tionem. Non sibi magnus tumidus video: detumescat, ut magnus sit, ut certus et solidus. Non ista desideret: non de ista pompa rerum labentium corruptibiliumque glorietur. Audiat eum ipsum qui dixit: intrate per angustam portam; dicentem: ego sum via. Quasi enim quaereret tumidus, Qua intrabo? ego sum, inquit, via.

Per me intra: non nisi per me ambules, ut intres per ianuam. Nam sicut dixi ego sum via, ita ego sum ianua (lo 10.7). Quid quaeris qua redeas, que redeas, qua intres? Ne alicubi erres, ipse tibi omnia factus est. Breviter ergo dicit: humilis this, mitis this. Áudiamus hoc apertissime dicentem, ut videoamus qua sit via, quae sit via, quo sit via. What do you see coming? Certe forte avaritia omnia vis possidere. Omnia mihi tradita sunt a Paire meo (Mt 11:27), inquit,
"I am the way, the truth and the life"

But let him tell us with the utmost clarity, so that you can see with your eyes where the path goes, what the path is and where the path goes. Where do you want to go? You are, quite possibly, an ambitious person who would want everything for himself. Well... The Father put all things in my hands. You will perhaps say: «Good; He put them in Christ's hands, but not in mine..." Listen to what the Apostle says; Listen, as I told you a while ago; Do not despair break the wings of your spirit; Hear how you were loved when you were not lovable; Hear how you were loved when you were clumsy and ugly; before, in short, there was something worthy of love in you. You were loved first so that you would become worthy of being loved. Well, Christ, says the Apostle, died for the benefit of the wicked. Did the wicked deserve to be loved? Please tell me what the wicked deserved. —Damnation, you answer. —Well, with all that, Christ died for the wicked. There you see what he did for you when he was wicked; what do you reserve for the pious? What was done for the wicked? For the wicked Christ died. You, who wanted to possess everything, there is a way to find everything; Do not seek it through the path of greed, seek it through the path of piety. If you go that way, you will possess it, because you will possess the Maker of all things, and, possessing him, everything with him will be yours. 6. These ideas that I present to you are not deductions from reasoning. Listen to the Apostle's own words: He who did not forgive his own Son, but gave him up for all of us, how could he not also give us all things with him? Obviously! Oh miser, there you have all the things. Finally, Fortasse dicturus is: Christo sunt tradita: numquid mihi? Audi apostolum dicentem: audi, ut dixi iam dudum, ne desperatione frangaris: audi quomodo amatus es non amandus, audi quomodo amatus es turpis, foedus, antequam esset ín te quod amari dignum esset. Amatus is prius, ut dignus fires qui amareris. Etenim Christus, sicut ait apostolus, pro impiis mortuus est (Rom 5,6). An forte impius amari merebatur? (699) Quaero quid merebatur impius. Damnari, you respond. Christus tamen pro impiis mortuus est. Ecce quid tibi praestitum est impio: iam pío quid servatur? Quid praestitum est impio? Christus pro impiis mortuus est. Desiderabas autem omnia possidere. Noli per avaritiam: per pietatem hoc quaere; si enim ita quaesieris, possidebis. Tenebis enim eum per quem facta sunt omnia, et eum ipso omnia possidebis. 6. Non haec nos quasi ratiocinando dicimus.

Ipsum audi apostolum dicentem: qui filio proprio non pepercit, sed pro nobis ómnibus tradidit illum; quomodo non et eum illo omnia nobis donavit? (Rom 8:32). Avare, ecce habes omnia. Omnia quae amas ut impedaris a Christo contemne, the ipsum dyes in quo possis omnia possidere. Ipse ergo medicus nihil tali indigens medication, tamen ut exhortaretur aegrotum, bibit quod

Therefore, if you find no hindrance, disarm everything you love and take possession of Christ, in whom you can be master of everything. The physician, who was absolutely in need of such a remedy, nevertheless took, to cheer up the patient, what he did not need; It was a mode of language to overcome the resistance of the sick and revive the depressed. The chalice, he says, that I must drink; I, in whom this potion has nothing to heal, because there is none, I am going to drink it, with all this, so that you, who need to drink it, do not back down and drink it. See now, brothers, if humanity, taking such excellent medicine, should continue to be sick. God has already humbled himself, and man is still proud! Listen and learn. All things, he says, the Father put into my hands. If, then, you desire everything, you will have everything with me; If you desire the Father, you will have it through me, you will have it in me. What good is it for me, you say, to have everything, if I don't have him? You say well. If, then, you want to have him too, listen to what follows. For, having said, The Father has put all things into my hands, as if exhorting and saying, "Come to me if you would have all things," and you said, "I do not desire all things, but him who made all things," he goes on and says, "No one knows the Son except the Father, and no one knows the Father except the Son." Don't lose heart, listen to the rest: And whoever the Son wants to reveal it to. To whoever wants, he says. —Maybe I don't want to. —I would not have come to you humble if I did not want you to know him as exalted. Perhaps here you will also say: "Even if I know him, I would like to know the Father." Do you want to know the Father? Hears Felipe's voice; opus non erat, tamquam alloquens recusantem, et trepidum erigens, bibit prior. Calicem, inquit, quem ego bibiturus sum (Mt 20:22). Qui in me non habeo quod ab illo chalice sanetur, bibiturus sum tamen, ne tu dedigneris, cui opus est ut bibas. Iam videte, fratres, si amplius debent aegrotare genus humanum accepts so much medicine. Iam humilis deus, et adhuc [730] superbus homo. Audiat, disc. Omnia, inquit, mihi tradita sunt a Patre meo. If you desire omnia, mecum habebis. If you wish Patrem, per me habebis, in me habebis. Utquid habebo omnia, you say, si illum non habuero? Straight you say. Si et ipsum vis habere, audi quod sequitur.

Cum enim díxisset, omnia mihi tradita sunt a Patre meo, tamquam exhortans et dices, Veni ad me, si vis omnia possidere, et ne tu díceres, Nolo omnia, sed eum voló qui fecit omnia, sequitur et dicit: nemo novit filium nisi Pater, et nemo novit Patrem nisi filius. Noli desperare, audi cetera: et cui voluerit Filius revealre (Mt 11,27). Cui voluerit, inquit: mihi forte nolit? Non vendeet ad te humilis, si (700) tibí nollet innotescere excelsus. Forte et hic dicis: Etiam si ipse mihi innotescat, Patrem velim discere. Patrem vis nosse? Audi vocem Philippi; prior nuntiavit hanc vocem, et optime, ut decebat: sitiebat enim beatitudinem, et ubique eam quaerens, ubique sitiens remanebat; nusquam inveniebat unde satiaretur. Ait domino sitiens: dominate, ostende nobis Patrem, et sufficit nobis
"I am the way, the truth and the life"

He was the first to speak about this, and very well, as was right. Thirsty for happiness, he looked for it everywhere; But his thirst was not quenched in any of them, he found nowhere to dampen his ardor. And with this thirst he says to the Lord: Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us. What does "enough for us" mean? There will be rest, and nothing more to search. The Lord: I have been with you for so long and you still haven't met me? Felipe, who sees me, also sees the Father. Consequence: for the Son to be manifested, it is necessary not to find the Son inferior to his Father, or these words say nothing: I and the Father are one and the same. Now he who is one with the Father emptied himself for you, taking the form of a servant. He annihilated himself, taking the form of a slave, when, away from him, he gave you that; for when you return to him, he kept you: I and the Father are one. 7. See how openly he said this: Whoever keeps my commandments, that one loves me; He who loves me will be loved by my Father, and I will love him. Here he leaves us in suspense, as if insinuating that he plans to give us something, since he loves us. It's like if a man tells you: "I love you"; You immediately think about what it will give you, what good it will bring you, what it will give you, how it will be useful to you. Therefore the Lord says: And I will love him. You ask what he will give you? Hear the following: I will manifest my very being to him. What does this mean, brothers? You are seeing where charity takes away. We will see something, and that something is the Word of God; that something is the God who is in God, by whom all things were made. We are told of an award, and the award is this. (14.8). Quid est, sufficit nobis? Ibi requiescens, amplius non requiram. Et dominus: tanta tempore vobiscum sum, et non cognovistis me? Philippe, qui me videt, videt et Patrem (ib., 9). Hoc ergo opus est, ut ostendat se Filius. Non enim minorem Patre inventurus is Filium, aut frustra dixit, Ego et Pater unum sumus (lo 10,30). Sed qui in se unum cum Patre, propter te tamen semetipsum exinanivit formam servi accipiens (Phil 2,7). Quod semetipsum exinanivit formam servi accipiens, donavit hoc tibi averso a se; I convert autem ad se servavit tibí Ego et Pater unum sumus. 1. Et vide quam aperte hoc dicat. Qui diligit me, mandata mea custodit; qui autem diligit me, diligetur a Patre meo, et ego diligam eum (lo 14,21). Suspendit nos, quasi quid daturus, quia diligit nos.

Quomodo si tibi homo dicat, Diligo te, non attendis nisi tibi donet, quid tibi praestet, quid prosit, in quo sit utilis. Ait ergo dominus: et ego diligam eum. Quaere quid tibi daturus sit. Audi quod sequitur: et ostcndam ei me ipsum (ib.). Quid est hoc, brothers? Videtis quo rapiat ílamma caritatis Visuri sumus aliquid: et ipsum aliquid, Verbum dei est; ct ipsum aliquid, deus apud deum, per quem facta sunt omnia. Munus

How exuberant and how foolish is the rejoicing of men! The tumultuous agglomeration of those who gather around the high-sounding claims of propaganda, which urges them with its appeals and childish displays to go and see, boils everywhere. See, what? Go where? Where the soul goes, already corrupted, to return even more corrupted and unworthy of the embraces of its legitimate Spouse. There he runs. Now, Christ, in turn, promises a spectacle to the eyes in the future: I will love him and show him not the depths of the abysses, not the secrets of the earth, not the variety of plants, not the multitude of animal species, not, in short, the number of the stars, not the rotation of the stars, not the measurements of times. Why see that? You would have seen it, and you certainly would not have seen great things. I did these things. I will manifest my own being to him. 8. Someone will perhaps say: "And when, when will this be revealed to us?" Dilating it is not denying it. And why do you delay it? To expand the capacity of the soul. Something great, my brothers, must give us; what do I say big? Very great, if one can call it that. See how many goods he grants to the wicked and how many favors to the unworthy. These too? Also, because it makes the sun rise for the good and the bad. See how creatures serve the wicked, so as to focus on natural gifts. They have health, they have integrity of senses, they have a spirit that animates the earthly limbs, they enjoy this air, they enjoy the light, they have a rational soul that elevates them above the enuntiatur, munus proponitur. Quanta hominum, et quam vana laetitia! Fervet undique tumultus concursantium, indicate [73 ljtium sibi quasi magnum aliquid, excitantium se hortatione et nugatoriis blandimentis iré, videre. What will I go? quid videre? Quo corrupta anima pergat, redeatque corruptior, et indigna amplexu tam legitimi viri sui. IUuc itur, illuc curritur. And propose futurem quandam visionem, futurem expectationem Christus. Dicit enim: diligam eum, et ostendam ei — non quod feci, non sinum abyssorum, non secreta terrarum, non varietates herbarum, non multitudinem generum animalium, non postremo numerum siderum, non conversiones astrorum, non dimensions temporum. Ut quid (701) enim haec vis videre? Quae si videres, certe magna non essent. Ego feci haec. Ostendam me ipsum illi. 8. Sed quando istud erit, dicit aliquis, quando ostendet? Differt, non aufert. Et in differendo quid agit? Desiderio dilatat sinum animae.

Magnum quiddam daturus est, fratres; et quid dico vel magnum? Si vel hoc dícendum est. Videte quanta dat impiis, et quanta donat indignis. Quare et ipsis? Quia facit solem suum oriri super bonds et malo (Mt 545). Vide quemadmodum serviat creatura blasphemis: ipsa naturalia dona circumspice. Habent salutem, habent integritatem sensuum, habent spiritum membra terrena vegetantem, habent perfunctionem aeris huius, visionem lucis, rationabilem mentem, qua ceteris animantibus excellen-
"I am the way, the truth and the life"

animals; an opulence, let's say, available to the rich and the poor, the good and the bad. Everyone eats, everyone is illuminated by this sun, everyone lives as if at the expense of the public treasury. And everything comes from the Lord. Is it not possible to think, brothers, that he keeps something better for his own, that he prepares something better for the faithful, so that those who now believe without seeing it can see it? To believe before seeing is to deserve future vision. So the procrastination of goods develops your capacity, increases by desire, prepares you to receive the promise you so long for. 9. Something has already been given to us; He has given us his Spirit as a pledge. What does “he has given us as a pledge” mean? This giving us his Spirit comes to mean this: "See if I will give you something, because from now on I give you what will light the flame of charity so that the sweetness pushes you to satiety." Taste and see how gentle the Lord is. From what you now drink you will be satisfied. They will be satisfied with the abundance of your house, he says; and continues: Because in you is the source of life, and in your light we will see the light. Are the sources of life and light different things? This is said in many ways; but, no matter how you say it, it is always ineffable. So, let us encourage ourselves and let the flame of desire burn within us. Dilating it is not taking it away. Let us advance towards that sublime goal: there we will find our fill, there the source of life; That source of life that came to be clothed in our flesh is the magnet of our desires. Unworthy, he gave away his death; worthy, he saves us his life. 10. But, brothers, we were saying, la tumestiores sunt. Haec omnia divitibus, pauperibus, bonis, malis tanquam divitiae communes iacent. Aluntur omnes, illustrantur ista luz omnes, tanquam de publico vivunt. Dat haec omnia. Hinc, fratres, cogitare non debenmus quid servet suis, quid praeparet fidelibus, ut videant non videntes et credentes? Credere antequam videas, meritum estfuturae visionis. Exercetur ergo capacitas tua dilatione bonorum; ut aucta desiderio, sis idoneus capere quod promittit, et quod desideras. 9. Nam aliquid iam dedit: dedit enim pignus Spiritum suum. What is it, pignus dedit? Tamquam say: Ecce quia dabo aliquid, inde nunc do quod te erigat, quod inflamed caritatem, quod gustatum rapiat ad satietatem. Enjoy yourself et videte quam suavis est dominus (Ps 33,9). Unde gustastis, inde satiabimini. Inebriabuntur, inquit, ab ubertate domus tuae, et reliqua. Quoniam apud te est fons vitae, et in lumine tuo videbimus lumen (Ps 35,9-10).

Numquid alliud fons vitae, et alliud lumen? Multis modis dicitur, quod quidquid dictum fuerit non dicetur. Ergo crigamur, [732] inflammemur, inardescamus, desideremus. Et si differimur, non auferimur. Teneamus tantum viam: ibi erit satietas nostra, ibi crit fons vitae. Venit ipse fons vitae, indutus est carne, fecit ut desideremus. Praestitit indignis mortem suam, servat dignis vitam suam. JO, Sed quia; ut diximuSj fratres, tumore superbiae non redibamus,
"I am the way, the truth and the life"

The sin of pride prevented our return to God; That is why he gave death to the unworthy; He became humble to exalt the comeback. He did it to reduce the swelling you were suffering from. Swollen, the two disciples wanted to enter and, using their mother - they did not dare - they went to beg her. Their very blush could already warn them of the unreasonable nature of what they were asking for. Not daring, therefore, directly, they made their old mother speak to the Lord, as if she deserved it because of her age. They desired the kingdom where one enters only through the narrow gate; But they, still swollen by the greed for honor, the more they wanted to enter, the more harm they did to themselves. The Lord diminishes them by giving them the bitter drink of which I have just spoken; swelling remedy 3. You said: «I can't; You force me to enter through the narrowness, and I cannot enter through the narrow." Come to me, he says, all you sick and burdened. Your burden is your swelling. Come to me, all you sick and burdened, and I will give you relief. Put my yoke around your necks and learn from me.

tools and animals of the earth, and created the fish, and placed the stars in the sky, and separated the day from the night, and established the firmament itself, and placed the light on one side and the darkness on the other; That is the same one who says: Learn from me. Will he tell us, by chance, to do these kinds of wonders that he did? Who will be capable? That's a thing from God. Fear not, he says; I'm not going to put such a weight on your shoulders. Learn from me what I did for you. Learn from me, he says; not to give being to creatures, as I gave it to them; I don't even tell you, learn from me to do what I gave some the power to do; but not to all, but to those whom I pleased: to raise the dead, to restore sight to the blind, to open the ears of the deaf; No, that is not important enough for me to show you. Full of satisfaction and joy the disciples returned, saying: Look: in your name, even the demons themselves have submitted to us. The Lord said to them: Do not rejoice so much because the demons submit to you; Rejoice, yes, that your names are written in heaven. He gave to those who pleased to expel demons and to whom he pleased he gave to raise the dead; But miracles like these were also performed before the incarnation of the Lord: some dead people were brought back to life, lepers were cleansed of their leprosy; it is written. But even those miracles, who did them except he who, if after David was Christ man, before Abraham was Christ God? Don was his all that; He did it by the hands of men, although he did not invest all of them with such power.

11. The Master of the angels cries, the Word of God cries, food of all intelligences that is not diminished, food that remakes and is always the same; He cries out therefore, saying: Learn from me. Let the people listen to those who say: Learn from me! And answer him: What will we learn from you? Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart. Because, if I distribute all my goods to the poor and give my body to the flames, without charity, it brings me no benefit. I exhort, therefore, your charity to that charity; but I would not exhort you to charity if you did not have some charity. I exhort you, then, to the fullness of what is already in principle; I urge you to perfection of what you have begun. And I beg you to pray for me, so that what I advise you may be perfected in me. We are all imperfect; We will reach perfection, where all things are perfect. The apostle Paul says: Brothers, I do not yet realize that I have achieved it. Help, what you heard is your death sentence. You who hear such and presume of yourself, do not bring out your innocence to me. Your innocence! How can you boast of being innocent? You may well say: "I did not steal anything from anyone." Well, I believe you; Perhaps I am an eyewitness to this: yes, you have not stolen anything from anyone; but you have heard: You shall not covet. —I don't get close to someone else's wife. —Well, I believe you, I see it; but you have heard it said: You shall not covet. Why do you look around you and not turn your eyes inside yourself? Look closely inside yourself, and you will find another law in your members. Take a good look inside yourself, don't go outside of yourself. Descend into your intimacy, and you will find in your members a law in conflict with the law of your reason, and that has you tied as a captive to the law of sin, which is in your members. Not without cause is the sweetness of God hidden from you; because the law holds you captive, which is in your members; law in conflict with the law of your reason. And the sweetness that is hidden from you is the sweetness that angels drink; sweetness that you cannot drink or taste while you live in captivity. You would not even know lust if the law did not say: You shall not covet. Such, then, you heard and feared; and you wanted to fight, but you could not triumph. But, on the occasion of the precept—concupiscence irritated by the prohibition of the law—sin gave rise to death. Without a doubt, you will recognize in these words the language of the Apostle: On the occasion of the precept, he committed all lust into sin. What did you boast about in your pride? There you have it; With your own weapons the enemy has defeated you. You wanted a law to entrench yourself in, and there you see how the enemy

He found a loophole in the law through which to attack you. Taking the occasion from the precept, sin made the precept an ambush, says the Apostle, where it gave me death. Isn't this what I said before: "With your own weapons the enemy defeated you"? He hears the same Apostle continue in his reasoning: Therefore the law is holy, and the commandment is holy, and just, and good. Now answer the Manichaeans, rebukers of the law; quote to them this passage from the Apostle: Therefore the law is holy, the commandment is holy, and just, and good. Then, did the good become death for me? Not that! But sin, so that it might be shown to be sin, brought death to me through a good thing. And why all this? Because you only had fear instead of love for what you received. You feared punishment instead of loving justice; and those who fear punishment would want, if possible, to do their own thing without fear of any punishment. God forbids adultery; You, however, who coveted another's wife, do not go to her, you do nothing, although the opportunity is good, and you have time, there is where and there is no witness. With all that, you don't do it, why? Because you fear punishment. —No one will know. —Shouldn't God know? Yes, yes; and because God must know what you do, you don't do it. But the one you fear is the threatening God, not the legislator God. Why don't you do it? Because if you do, you will be sent to eternal fire. You fear fire. If you loved chastity, you would not do it even if you had to go absolutely unpunished. If God told you: «Do it if you want; I will not condemn you;

You heard how the Lord praises those who believe without having seen above those who believe because they have seen and have even been able to touch. What would have happened if the Lord had risen without the scars? Or could his flesh not have been resurrected without traces of the wounds remaining on it? Topic: "Simon Peter, do you love me?" (Jn 21,15-17). Location: Unknown. Date: In 409-410. 1. The events and words recorded in today's gospel took place and were said to have resurrected the Lord. In it we see our Lord Jesus Christ asking Peter if he loved him. Therefore, the Lord asks the slave, the Master the disciple, the Creator the man, the Redeemer the redeemed, the Firmness the wavering, the one who knows everything in advance the one who ignores everything, and in asking he teaches; because there was nothing in Peter's soul unknown to the Lord, who read in his heart. Ask him once, and he answers; but it is not enough; ask him a second time, and no different from the first, and the answer is identical. The question is repeated three times, Petri amorem. Ter negaverat timor, ter confessus es amor. Trinitas negationis, desertio veritatis: trinitas confessionis, testimonium dilectionis.

They were the ones who predicted the future, based on the mamen of the prodigies that occurred, such as monstrous or exceptional births, or even normal atmospheric phenomena: lightning, interpreted according to their frequency and the section of the sky in which they took place; and, above all, examining IHN viscera of animals, particularly birds: their dimensions, shape and color, special PII of the liver. Virgines oleum non jerentes.—Propone ergo hominem eleemosynam facientem, sic ut omnino nesciat aliquis, si fieri potest, nec ille cui datur; ut eius etiam oculos vitans ponat potius quod inveniat, quam porrigat quod accipiat. Iste utique incurrit in illam sententiam, et non facit quod Dominus ait: Luceant opera vestra coram hominibus, ut videant bona jacta vestra (Mt 5,16). Nemo videt facta eius bona, non invitation ad imitandum. Erunt ceteri steriles, quantum in ipso est, dum putant a nemine fieri quod praecepit Deus, si hoc nomines agant, ut non videantur bona opera eorum: cum maior mercy in eum fiat, cui proponitur bonae imitationis exemplum, quam cui porrigitur reficiendi corporis alimentum. Propone alterum eleemosynas suas apud populum ventilantem atque iactantem, nihil aliud in eis quam velle laudari: luzant opera eius coram hominibus. Omnium lampades luzbant: sed aliae non habebant secum unde illam pascerent luzm, et ab eis quae habebant ita distinguishbantur, ut illae stultae, illae sapientes dicerentur (cf. Mt 25,1-13). Quid est ergo, ferré oleum secum, nisi habere conscientiam placendi Deo de bonis operibus, et non ibi finem gaudii sui seguiré, si homines laudent, qui conscientiam videre non possunt? Quia facit enim, potest videre homo: quo autem animo faciat, Deus videt. CAPUT XII.—13. Conciliantur loca in speciemcontrare.—Proponamus ergo aliquem praeceptum utrumque servantem, utrique oboedientem. Porrigit panem esurienti, et porrigit coram illis quos vult faceré imitatores suos; imitatus etiam Apostolum dicentem: Imitatores mei estofe, sicut et ego Christi (1 Cor 4,16, et 11,1). Porrigit ergo pauperi panem, manifestus in opere, devotus in corde. Utrum laudem suam ibi quaerat, an gloriam Dei nullus hominum videt, nullus hominum iudicat: sed tamen illi qui studio benévolo ad imitandum parati sunt, quod bonum fieri vident, etiam pío animo fieri credunt; et laudant Deum, cuius praecepto et dono talia fieri vident. Apparet ergo opus eius, ut videant homines, et glorificent Patrem qui in caelis est: ipse autem effectus eius
Vision of Peter and Sermon on the Mount

Focus on the Father who is in heaven; Instead, it depends on his heart that his alms is hidden and that the Father, who sees in what is hidden, rewards him. This man observed the proper manner: he did not despise any precept, but fulfilled both. In fact, he refrained from practicing his justice before men, that is, with the aim of being praised by them, when he wanted his good deed not to be praised, but to God. Since such a desire is within one's own conscience, that almsgiving was done secretly, so that it might reward him from whom nothing is hidden. Who, when acting, can show his heart to men, to show them with what intention he does it? 14. Those words, brothers, were said by the Lord with quite premeditation. Pay attention to them: Beware of performing your justice before men, to be seen, he says, by them. If the sentence concludes with the words to be seen by them, it is reprehensible and an object of guilt to want to do good only for the praise of men, without seeking anything else. Whoever, therefore, works only to be seen by men, finds in this phrase the reprobation of God. On the other hand, where he orders that our good works be seen, he does not conclude the phrase with the sole indication that man be seen and praised, but rather he moves on to the glory of God, as the term to which the intention of the one who works must reach. Let your works shine before men, he said, so that they may see your good works;

but this is not what you should look for. What then? He continues saying: and glorify your Father who is in heaven. If you seek the glory of God, do not fear being seen by men. Even then your alms is hidden; Only he whose glory you seek knows that you seek it. This is why the apostle Paul says, after having been put down as a persecutor of the Gospel and raised up as a preacher: He was unknown to the churches of Christ in Judea. They had only heard that "he who previously persecuted us now announces the faith that he then destroyed"; and in me, he said, they glorified God. He did not rejoice in being known as a man who had received, but rather in being praised by God who had given it to him. He himself said: If I still pleased men, I would not be a servant of Christ. And, notwithstanding this, he says in another place: Just as I also please everyone in everything. It's a similar case. But what does it add? Not seeking, he said, my benefit, but that of many so that they may be saved. This is equivalent to what he said in the other place: And in me they glorified God, which also corresponds to what the Lord says: That they may glorify your Father, who is in heaven. In fact, they are saved when they glorify in the works they see men doing the one from whom they themselves received them. 15. Two questions still remain; If, on the one hand, I fear being burdensome to those who are already tired, on the other I fear disappointing those who are still hungry. I remember what has already been resolved and what remains to be resolved. There is still

in corde est, ut sit eleemosyna eius in abscondito, et Pater qui videt in abscondito, reddat ei. Servavit iste modum quena debuit, nullius praecepti contemptor, sed utriusque perfectionr. Cavit enim ne ièret iustitia eius coram hominibus, id est, ne ibi haberes finem, ut ab hominibus laudaretur, quando non se ipsum, [805] sed Deum volunt in opere suo bono laudari. Ea vero voluntas quia intus est in ipsa conscientia, facta est eleemosyna illa in abscondito, ut ille retribuat, cui nihit absconditur. Quis enim potest cor suum hominibus demonstrare cum facit, ut ostendat qua intentione animi faciat? CAPUT XIII.—14. Sensus legitimas utriusque loci ex ipsís Christi verbis eruitur.—Nam et ipsa verba, fratres, satis perpense a Domino dicta sunt. Attendite quomodo dicat: Cávete faceré iustitiam vestram coram hominibus, ut videamíni, inquit, ab eis (Mt 6,1). Si ibi posuit finem, ubi dixit, ut videoamini ab eis; Iste finis est reprehensibilis atque culpabílis, usque ad hominum laudem velle benefacere, nihil amplius inde quaerere. Quisquis ergo ideo tantum facit, ut videoatur ab hominibus, reprehenditur a Domino in ista sententia. Illic vero ubi iubet videri bona facta nostra, non ibi finem posuit, ut tantummodo nomines hominem videant, et hominem laudent: sed transit ad gloriara Dei, ut usque ad illam perducatur operantis intentio. Luceant, inquit, opera vestra coram hominibus, ut videant bona facta vestra: sed non hoc tumbas quaerere.

Quid ergo? Addit et dicit: et glorificent, inquit, Patrem vestrum qui in caelis est (Mt 5,16). Hoc si quaeris, ut glorificetur Deus, noli timere ne videaris ab hominibus. Etiam sic intus est eleemosyna tua in abscondito; ubi solus ille cuius gloriam quaeris, te videt hoc quaerere. Unde apostolus Paulus posteaquam Evangelii persecutor prostratus est, et erectas est praedicator, dicit: Eram autem ignotus facie Ecclesiis ludaeae, quae erant n Christo. Tantum autem audientes weret, quia qui aliquando nos persequebatur, nunc evangelizat fidem quam aliquando vastabat; et in me, inquit, magnificabant Deum. Non gaudebat quia homo qui acceperat, cognoscebatur; sed quia Deus qui dederat, laudabatur. Ipse enim dixit: Si adhuc hominibus placerem, Christi servus non essem (Gal 1 22.23.24.10). Et tamen alio loco dicit: Sicut et ego omnibus per omnia placeo. Et ist similis quaestio est. Sed quid adiungit? Non quaerens, inquit, quod mihi prodest, sed quod multis, ut salvi fiant (1 Cor 10:33). Hoc est, quod illo loco ait, Et in me magnificabant Deum: quod etiam Dominus dicit, Ut glorificent Patrem vestrum qui in caelis est. Tune enim salvi fiunt, cum in operibus quae fieri per nomines vident, eum glorificant a quo haec homines acceperunt. CAPUT XIV.—15. Quaestio tertia, from Gospel, ut sinistra nesciat o pus dexterae.—Restant duae quaestiones: sed vereor ne oneri sim iam fastidientibus, item timeo ne fraudm adhuc esurientes. Memini tamen

to find out what it means: Let your left hand not know what your right hand does and, regarding the love of enemies, to know why the ancients seem to have been given license to hate enemies, while we are commanded to love them. What should I do? If I address both questions with a few words, I run the risk of not being understood as I should; If I do it more calmly, I fear burdening you with the weight of the sermon rather than elevating you with the fruit of my exposition. In any case, if your understanding is less than sufficient, consider me still indebted to a more extensive explanation at another time. But it is not advisable now to leave things without saying a word about them. The left means the carnal desire of the soul, and the right, spiritual charity. If, then, when someone gives alms, he mixes the desire for temporal comforts, in order to obtain any of these through that work, he mixes the knowledge of the left with the works of the right. If, on the contrary, it helps man out of charity alone and with a pure conscience before God, without having its eyes fixed on anything else, except to please the one who commands it, the left does not know what the right is doing. 16. More difficult is the question about love for the enemy; It cannot be settled with a few words. However, as you listen, pray for me and perhaps the Lord God will quickly grant us what we think is difficult. We live from a single barn, since we form a single family. What quid solverim, et quid debenam. Restat enim videre quid sit: Nesciat sinistra tua quid faciat dextera tua (Mt 6,3); et de dilectione inímici, cur antiquis videbatur data lícentia ut odissent inimicos, quorum nobis imperatur dilectio. Sed quid fació? Si breviter de his dísseram, fortassis non ita ut oportet intellegar: si diutius, timeo ne plus gravem vos onere sermonis, quam fructu expositionis sublevem. Be certain if minus quam satis est, intellexeritis; adhuc me tenere debitorem, [806] ut alio tempore ista plenius disserantur. Tamen nunc non oportet ea sic relinqui, ut omnino nihil inde dicatur. Sinistra is animi cupiditas carnalis, dextera is animi caritas spiritualis. Si ergo cum quisque facit eleemosynam, miscet cupiditatem temporalium commodorum, ut in opere illo aliquid tale conquírat; miscet sinistrae conscientiam operíbus dexterae.

Si autem simplici caritate etpura coram Deo conscientia homini subvenit, nihil aliud intuens, nisi ut illi placeat qui haec iubet, nescit sinistra quid facit dextera. CAPUT XV.—16. Quaestio quarta, de inimici dilectione et odio.— De dilectione autem inimici difficilior est quaestio, nec ea brevitate solvi potest. Sed cum auditis, orate pro nobis; et forte Dominus Deus cyto dabit quod putamus esse difficile. Ex uno enim hórreo vivimus; quia in a sumus family. Quod ergo nos putamus esse valde intus in abdito,
Vision of Peter and Sermon on the Mount

We think that it is hidden at the bottom, perhaps the one who promised it to us puts it at the door so that he can easily give it to those who ask for it. Christ himself, the Lord, loved his enemies, for, hanging on the cross, he said: Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do. Esteban followed his example; When they were stoning him he said: Lord, do not accuse them of this crime. The servant imitated the Lord, so that no servant would be lazy thinking that what was done could only be done by the Lord. If it seems too much for us to imitate the Lord, let us imitate our fellow servant. We have all, in fact, been called to the same grace; Why then was it said to the ancients: You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy? Because perhaps they were also told the truth, although we, when the time came, were told more clearly through the presence of the one who knew what and to whom something had to be hidden or revealed. If we have an enemy that we are never commanded to love, it is the devil: You will love your neighbor, that is, man, and you will hate your enemy, that is, the devil. But since it is common for there to be enmities between men themselves, in the minds of those who, through their unbelief, give way to the devil and become vessels for him, it may also be the case that man abandons his malice and converts to the Lord; Therefore, even while he behaves cruelly, while he persecutes, one must love him, one must pray for him and one must do good to him. In this way you fulfill the first precept of loving man, your neighbor, forte ipse qui promittit ponit in limine, ut facillime dari possit petentibus. Dilexit inimicos ipse Dominus Christus: pendens enim in intersection ait, Pater, ignosce Hits quia nesciunt quid faciunt (Luke 23,34). Secutus est eius exemplum Stephanus, cum lapides in eum iacerentur, et ait: Domine, ne statuas Mis hoc delictum (Act 7,59). Dominum imitatus est servus, ut nemo servorum sit piger, et putet hoc esse factum quod a solo Domino fieri poterat. Si ergo multum est ad nos imitari Dominum, imitatemur conservum. Ad eamdem quippe gratiam vocati omnes sumus. Quare ergo antiquis dictum est: Diliges proximum tuum, et oderis inimicum tuum? (Mt 5,43). Quia fortassis et ipsis verum dictum est; sed nobis apertius pro temporum distributione, per eius praesentiam qui videbat quid quibus vel tegendum esset vel aperiendum. Si enim habemus inimicum, quem nunquam diligere iubemur; est autem diabolus: Diliges proximum tuum, hominem; et oderis inimicum tuum, diabolum.

Sed quia in ipsis hominibus saepe existunt inimicitiae, in animis eorum qui per infidelitatem dant locum diabolo, et eius vasa fiunt, ut operetur in filiis diffidentiae; potest autem fieri ut relinquat homo malitiam suam, et convertatur ad Dominum; et dum adhuc saevit, dum adhuc persequitur, diligendus est, et orandum pro illo, et bene illi faciendum: ita et primum praeceptum implebis, ut diligas proximum tuum hominem, et oderis in}-

and to hate the devil, your enemy, and the second: to love men, your enemies, and pray for those who persecute you. 17. Unless you think that the Christians did not pray at that time for Saul, the persecutor of the Christians themselves. Perhaps the voice of the martyr Stephen was heard so that he would convert. In fact, he was among their persecutors and kept the clothes of those who stoned him. He himself, writing to Timothy, also says: First of all, I ask you that petitions, prayers, supplications, and thanksgivings be made for all men, for kings and for all those constituted in dignity, so that we may lead a serene and peaceful life. He therefore ordered to pray for the kings when they persecuted the Churches. But those whom they then persecuted while praying for them, they now defend after having been heard for their benefit. 18. Do you also want to fulfill that precept given to the ancients? Love your neighbor, that is, every man. We are all born from the first two parents and, consequently, we are all neighbors. Clearly the Lord Jesus Christ himself, who commanded to love one's enemies, declared that all the law and the prophets were enclosed in these two precepts: You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and with all your soul, and with all your mind, and you shall love your neighbor as yourself. It prescribes nothing about love for the enemy. So is there anything that is not included in those two premicum tuum diabolutn; et secundum, ut diligas inimicos tuos homines, et ores pro eis qui te persequuntur (cf. ibid., 44). CAPUT XVI. 17. Orandum pro persequentibus.—Nisi forte putas non orasse Christianos illo tempore pro Saulo persecutor Christianorum. Fortassis ad eius conversionem vox illa Stephani martyris exaudita est. In illo enim persecutorum eius numero Fuit, et lapidantium ropa servavit (cf. Acts 7,57). idem etíam ad Timotheum scribns ait: Obsecro primum omnium jieri deprecationes, adhorationes, interpellationes, gratiarum actiones, pro ómnibus hominibus, pro regibus et ómnibus qui in sublimitate sunt, ut quietam et tranquillam vitarn agamus (1 Tim 2, [807] 1,2). Iubebat ergo orari pro regibus: et tune reges persequebantur Ecclesias. Sed quas tune pro se orantes persequebantur, nunc pro se exauditas defendunt. CAPUT XVII.—18. Proximi nomine inimicus etiam diligendus praecipitur.—Vis ergo et illud antiquorum custodire praeceptum? Dilige proximum tuum, hoc est omnem hominem.

Ex duobus enim primis parentibus omnes nati, omnes utique proximi sumus. Certe enim ipse Dominus Iesus Christus qui diligi praecipit inimicos, in duobus illis praeceptis totam Legem et Prophetas penderé testatus est: Diliges Dominum Deum tuum ex toto corde tuo, et ex tota anima tua, et ex tota mente tua; et, Diliges proximum tuum tanquam te ipsum (Mt 22,37-40). Nihil ibi praecepit de dilectione inimici. Non ergo totum haec duo praecepta continent?

concepts? In no way. Well, when it says: You will love your neighbor, all men are included there, even if they are enemies, because thinking about spiritual proximity you do not know what that man who temporarily seems like an enemy to you is in the presence of God. Since God's patience leads him to penitence, perhaps he will come to know and follow the one who leads him. If God himself, despite knowing who must remain in their sins and who, abandoning justice, must inevitably fall into iniquity, makes his sun rise on the good and the evil and lets the rain fall on the just and the unjust, patiently inviting them to penitence so that those who despise his goodness ultimately experience his severity, how much it is not appropriate for man to be eager to relent, lest, not knowing how it should be in the future, paying attention only to the present enmity, hate him with whom he is to reign in eternal happiness! Therefore, fulfill the first precept: Love your neighbor, that is, every man, and hate your enemy, that is, the devil. Also fulfill the second: Love your enemies, but men; Pray for those who persecute you, but for men; Do good to those who hate you, but to men. 19. If your enemy is hungry, feed him; If he is thirsty, give him a drink; By doing this you will heap burning coals on his head. A problem arises here too. How, in fact, does one love the one whom one wants to see burn Absit. Quia cum dicit, Diliges proximum tuum, ibi sunt omnes homines, etiamsi fuerint inimici: quia etiam secundum spiritualem propinquitatem nescis quid tibi sit in praescientia Dei homo, qui tibi ad tempus videtur inimicus. Quia enim patientia Dei ad paenitentiam eum adducit, fortassis cognoscet et sequetur ducentem. Si enim Deus ipse qui novit qui sint in peccatis perseveraturi, qui relicturi iustitiam et irrevocabiliter ad iniquitatem lapsuri, tamen facit solem suum oriri super bonds et malo, et pluit super iustos, et íniustos, invitations utique ad paenitentiam per patientiam, ut qui neglexerint eius bonitotem, experiantur in fine severitatem; quanta sollicitudine plaquebilem oportet esse hominem, ne forte nesciens qualis futurus sit, cum praesentes eius inimicitias attenderit, oderit eum cum quo in aeterna congratulate yourself regnabit? Imple ergo praeceptum primum: Dilige proximum tuum, omnem hominem; et oderis inimicum tuum, diabolum. Imple et secundum.

Dilige inimicos tuos, sed homines: ora pro eis qui te persequuntur, sed pro hominibus: bene fac eis qui te oderunt, sed hominibus (cf. Mt 5:44). CAPUT XVIII.—19. Expltcatur Apostoli locus, de carbonibus congerendis super caput inimici. Si esurierit inimicus tuus, ciba illum; si sitit, potum da illi: hoc enim faciens, carbones ignis congeres super caput eius (Rom 12:20).—Et hic quaestio est. Quomodo enim quisque diligit, quem

in the middle of coals? If it is understood well, there is no room for controversy, since it speaks of those devouring coals that are applied to man against the malicious tongue. When one does good to his enemy and, without being overcome by his evil, overcomes evil with good, most of the time he will regret his enmity and will be angry with himself for having harmed such a good man. The true ustion is penitence, which, as if they were burning coals, consumes their enmity and evil.

sower of words, but also harvester of customs. Thus, we, although so small and unable to compare ourselves with his excellence, sow the words of God in the divine field, which is your heart, at the same time that we hope for an abundant harvest in your customs. However, we urge you to pay greater attention to that content of the same reading that invites us to speak to you, in case, with the help of the Lord, our God, we say something that can hardly be understood by everyone without our explanation and that, once understood, should not be despised by anyone. 2. He spoke in Athens. The Athenians enjoyed great fame among other peoples in regard to any type of literature and thought. It was the homeland of the great philosophers. From it the different currents of ideas had spread throughout the rest of Greece and the other countries on earth. There the Apostle spoke announcing Christ crucified, a scandal for the Jews and madness for the Gentiles; On the other hand, for those called, Jews and Greeks, Christ, the Power and Wisdom of God. You yourselves may think how dangerous it was to announce this in the midst of proud and learned people. In fact, after finishing his speech, listening to his announcement of the resurrection of the dead, the central point of the Christian faith, some mocked him, and others, on the other hand, said: We will hear from you again on this matter. But there were those who believed, among whom Dionysius the Areopagite, one of the magistrates of Athens, is mentioned - for Areopagus is the name given
motto: Paul in Athens (Acts 17,17-34). Place: Carthage. Date: In 413.

1. In reading the Acts of the Apostles, your charity noticed, together with me, how Paul addressed the Athenians and how those who mocked the preaching of the truth called him sower of words. Although it came from mocking mouths, such a designation should not be rejected by believers. He was, in effect, vult arderé carbonibus? Sed si intellegatur, nulla contentio est. De illis enim vastatoribus carbonibus dicítur, qui dantur homini adversus linguam subdolam (Ps 119,3.4). Cum enim quisque benefecerit inimico, et non victus malo eius, vicerit in bono malum; plerumque illum inimicitiarum suarum paenitebit, et irascetur sibi, quod tam bonum hominem laeserit. Ipsa vero ustio, paenitentia est, qua tanquam carbones ignis inimicitias eius malitiasque consumit.
DE VERBIS ACTUUM APOSTOLORUM: "QUIDAM AUTEM EPICUREI ET STOICI PHILOSOPHI DISSEREBANT CUM EO", ETC., 17,18-34

[808] CAPUT I.—1. Paulus apud Athenienses praedicans.—Advertit nobiscum Caritas vestra, cum legeretur líber Actuum Apostolorum, Paulum locutum esse Atheniensibus, et ab eis qui praedicationem veritatis irridebant, dictum Fuisse verborum seminatorem. Dictum est quidem ab irridentibus, sed non respuendum est a credentibus. Erat enim revera ille

seminator verborum, sed messor morum. Et nos licet tantilli et nequáquam illius excellentiae comparandi, in agro Dei, quod est cor vestrum, verba Dei seminamus, et uberem messem de vestris moribus exspectamus. Verumtamen unde admonemur loqui Caritati vestrae, quod ipsa lectione continetur, hortamur attentius advertatis, si quomodo adiuvante Domino Deo nostro dicimus aliquid, quod nec facile, nisi dicatur, ab ómnibus possit intellegi; ñeque cum intellectum fuerit, debeat ab ullo contemni. 2. Vides Christianorum.—Apud Athenas Ioquebatur. Athenians in omni literature atque doctrina per alios popules magna fame pollebant. Ipsa erat patria magnorum philosophorum. Inde se per ceteras Graeciae atque alias orbis terras varia et multiple doctrina diffuderat. Ibi Apostolus Ioquebatur, ibi annuntiabat Christum crucifixum: ludaeis quidem scandalum, Gentibus autem stultitiam; ipsis vero vocatis ludaeis et Graecis Christum Dei Virtutem et Dei sapientiam (1 Cor 1:23-24). Hoc annuntiare Inter superbos et learned quanti perículí fuerit, vestrum est cogitare. Denique sermone finito, audita illi resurrectione mortuorum, quae praecipua fides est Christianorum, alii irridebant; dicebant autem alii: Audiemus te de hoc iterum (ib., 32). Nec defuerunt qui crediderunt, atque in eis nominatur quidam Dionysius Areopagites, id est Atheniensium principalis (Areopagos enim Atheniensium curia vocabatur); et mu-

to the curia of that city—, to a certain noble woman and to others. That is, as a consequence of the Apostle's word, the crowd was divided into three groups that we can present in this order worth noting: those who mocked, those who doubted, and those who believed. As we heard, it was written: Some scoffed, others said: "We will hear you again about it"; These were the ones who doubted. Others finally believed. Between those who mocked and those who believed, there are those who doubted in the middle. He who mocks, falls; He who believes, stands; whoever doubts, fluctuates. We will hear from you again about it, they said; It is not known whether they will fall on the side of the mockers or the believers. Did that sower of words work in vain? If he had feared the mockers, he would not have reached the believers, in the same way that if that sower of whom the Lord speaks in the Gospel - this was Paul in effect - had feared to throw the seed because of the possibility that it would fall on the road, or among the brambles or on stony ground, the seed would never have been able to reach the good soil. Let us also sow, let us scatter the seed: you prepare the hearts, bear fruit. 3. If your charity remembers well, in the reading we also heard that certain Epicurean and Stoic philosophers dialogued with the Apostle. Without a doubt, many of you do not know who each other are or were, it is

to say, what they thought, what they placed the truth in and what they sought with their philosophizing; but, since we speak in Carthage, many know it. Let them help us tell it to you. What I think needs to be said is certainly relevant. Listen to us, both those who don't know it and those who know it. Those who do not know it, educate yourselves; Those who know him, be encouraged. Know the ones, recognize the others. 4. First of all, listen in general terms to the common desire of all philosophers, within which five divisions were established, each differentiated by its particular opinions. Without distinction, all philosophers, with their study, their research, their dialogues and their lives, wanted nothing more than to achieve a happy life. This was the only cause of their philosophizing, and I think they also have this in common with us. If I asked you why you believed in Christ, why you became Christians, truly every man would answer me: "Thinking about a happy life." But the question is this: where to find that one thing that everyone agrees on. This is where the divisions come from, because wanting a happy life, wanting it, desiring it, waiting for it and seeking it is, I think, common to all men. Therefore it seems to me that I fell short in saying that this desire is common to philosophers and Christians; I should have said rather to all men, absolutely all, good and bad. In fact, whoever is good is good enough to be happy; and whoever is bad would not be if he did not hope to be happy

lier quaedam nobilis, et alii. Facta est ergo loquente Apostólo tripartita illa multitudo, per quosdam gradus mira distinctione disposita; irridentium, dubitantium, credentium. Quidam enim, ut scriptum esse audivimus, irridebant, quidam dicebant, Audiemus te de hoc iterum (ib.); isti doubters weret; aliqui crediderunt. inter irridentes et credentes, medii sunt doubtantes. Qui irridet, cadit; qui credit, stat; qui doubt, fluctuat. Audiemus te de hoc iterum, inquiunt: incertum an casuri essent cum irridentibus, an staturi cum credentibus. CAPUT II.—Numquid tamen inaniter laboravit seminator ille verborum? lile vero si formidaret irridentes, non perveniret ad credentes: quomodo seminator ille evangelicus, quem commemorat Dominus (nam utique hoc erat Paulus), si trepidaret mittere semina, ne aliud caderet in via, aliud Inter spinas, aliud in loca petrosa; nunquam semen posset etiam ad terram optimal pervenire. Et nos seminemus, spargamus: corda praeparate, fructum date. [809] 3. Epicurei et Stoici cum Apostólo conferentes.—Hoc quoque, si meminit Caritas vestra, cum legeretur audivimus, quod quídam ex philosophis Epicureis et Stoicis conferebant cum Apostólo. dispensation of divine providence that acts through men without their realizing it, which, being so many philosophical sects existing in Athens, only the Stoics and Epicureans entered into discussion with Paul. I say it bluntly: the unlearned believe me, the learned judge me. I am not going to dare lie to the unlearned with the learned as judges, especially considering that I am talking about something about which both the unlearned and the learned can judge truthfully. My first statement is this: man consists of body and soul. I am not asking you to believe this, but I am asking you to judge it. I am not afraid that anyone will judge me badly regarding that statement; no one known. Man, therefore, no one doubts, consists of soul and body. This substance, this reality, this person called man, seeks a happy life. You also know this; I do not urge you to believe it, but I urge you to recognize it. I am talking about man, that is, about this not insignificant reality, which is superior to all beasts, all birds and all fish and any being that bears flesh and is not human; man, then, which consists of soul and body, but not of any soul, since the beast also consists of soul and body; Man, therefore, who consists of a rational soul and a mortal body, seeks a happy life. Tota igitur quaestio est, quid faciat beatam vitam. Constituite nunc ante oculos vestros Epicureans, Stoics, et Apostolum: quod etiam sic dicere potui, Epicureans, Stoics, Christianos. Interrogemus prius Epicureans, quae res faciat vitam beatam. Respondent: Voluptas corporis. Hic iam credatis peto, quia iudices habeo. Respondent: Voluptas corporis. Quid dicitis, Stoici, quae res facit vitam beatam? Respondent: Virtus animi. Intendat mecum Caritas vestra, Christiani sumus, inter philosophos disceptamus.

Videte quare illae tantum duae sectae procuratae sunt cum Apostolo collaturae. Nihil est in homine, quod ad eius substantiam pertineat atque naturam, praeter corpus et animam. Horum duorum in uno, hoc est in corpore, Epicurei posuerunt beatam The moral ideal of the Stoics is linked to their conception of God and the world. The universe is an intelligent whole and man is a part of it that especially participates in this intelligence or logos. According to this, the ideal consists of living in accordance with oneself, with the inner logos or, in other words, living in accordance with nature. It is the logos that dominates and regulates man's behavior; From here comes an essentially intellectual morality, in which knowledge occupies a predominant place. Morality is the rejection of passion and the triumph of reason, through adherence to the logos, universal reason and law of the world.

De anima quid Epicurei sentiunt. Christiani quidam moribus epicurei.—Ecce sunt, conferunt cum Apostólo; aliquidne plus habeat Apostolus; an vero uni harum duarum sectae necessario consentiré debenet, ut etiam ipse causam beatae vitae, aut in corpore, aut in animaponeret. Nunquam poneet Paulus in corpore: hoc enim magnum non est; cum ipsi minime ponant causam beatitudeinis in corpore, qui melius sentiunt de corpore. Et quod est gravius et detestabilius, prius dicuht animam post mortem dissolved quam corpus. «Adhuc», inquiunt, «post efflatum spiritum manente cadavere, et integris membrorum lineamentis aliquan2 The Epicureans were materialists. For them, the soul is composed of very subtle material elements or atoms, similar to those of breath or heat, two things that the soul resembles, but which it surpasses through another even more subtle part, which maintains the compound in unity for the duration of life only.

It should not surprise us, then, that they have placed the highest good, that is, the cause of happiness in the body, which they considered superior to the soul. Would the Apostle do this? Far be it from him to put the highest good in the body! The highest good being the cause of happiness, the Apostle was grieved that certain Christians accepted the opinion of the Epicureans, more typical of swine than of men. 3 Among such were those who corrupted good customs with their perverse gossip, saying: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we will die. That the Epicureans dialogued with the Apostle means that there are also Epicurean Christians. What else are those who say day after day: Let us eat and drink, tomorrow we will die? Where does this phrase lead: «There is nothing after death; "Our life is nothing more than the passage of a shadow"? Among other perversely thought things, they said to themselves: Let us make ourselves wreaths of roses, before they wither; There is no meadow through which our lust does not pass; Let us leave signs of our joy everywhere, because this is our part and our lot. 7. If we harshly rebuke this way of thinking, if we offer even greater resistance to these desires, they will add the following: Let us oppress the righteous who is poor. And yet, even when placed in this place, we are not afraid to say: "No tum durantibus, anima tnox ut exierit, veluti fumus vento diverberata dissolvitur." Non ergo miremur quod summum bomim, id est, beatitudeinis causam in corpore posuerunt, quod se melius quam animam habere senserunt. Numquid hoc faceret Apostolus? Absit ut poneet in corpore summum bonum. Summum enim bonum est causa beatitudinis: immo vero doluit Apostolus, quosdam e numero Christianorum elegisse sententiam Epicureorum, non hominum, sed porcorum. Ex hoc enim numero etant illi corrumpentes mores bonds colloquiis malis, et dicentes: Manducemus et bibamus; you were enim moriemur (1 Cor 15:32). Epicurei contulerunt cum Paulo apostólo: sunt et Christiani epicurei. Quid enim sunt aliud dicentes quotidie: Manducemus et bibamus; were you enim moriemur? Quo pertinet, Nihil erit post mortem, umbrae enim transitas est vita nostra. Dixerunt enim apud se cogitantes non recte inter cetera: Coronemus nos rosis, antequam marcescant: nullum pratum sit quod non pertranseat luxuria nostra, ubique relinquamus signa laetitiae, quoniam haec est pars nostra, et haec est sors (Sap 2,8-9).

be epicureans. Think, yes, of what such people say, although speaking perversely: Tomorrow we will die; but our death will not be total; after death what follows death remains. Whoever dies will be accompanied by either life or punishment. Let no one say: "Who is there that has returned from there to here?" That rich man, dressed in purple, wanted to return, but it was too late, and he was not allowed. Burned with thirst, he asked for a drop of water who looked with disdain at a poor hungry man. Let no one, therefore, say: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we will die. If you want to say: Tomorrow we will die, I do not forbid it, but change what precedes it. The Epicureans, in fact, thinking that they do not have to live after death and as lacking anything else except what delights the flesh, say: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we will die. But Christians, who are to live after death, indeed, who are to live happily, should not say: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we will die. Keep this last: Tomorrow we will die, but put before it: "Let us fast and pray, for tomorrow we will die." I add one more thing - I add a third thing so as not to overlook what must be considered above all, namely, that with your fasting the hunger of the poor is satisfied or that, if you cannot fast, you feed him whose satiety procures the forgiveness of your sins. So say; Christians: "Let us fast, pray and donate, because tomorrow we will die." And in case you only want to mention two things, I prefer that you say: "Let us donate and pray", rather than quidem illud, quod dictum est ab his non recte loquentibus: Cras enim moriemur (1 Cor 15,32); sed non omni moda moriemur; manet enim post mortem quod sequitur mortem. Comes morentii aut vita erit, aut poena. Nemo dicat: Quis huc inde reversus est? Dives ille purpuratus sero rediré voluit, et permitti non potuít. Stillam sitiens inquisivit, qui esurientem pauperem fastidivit (cf. Lk 16:19-24). Nemo ergo dicat: Manducemus et bibamus, cras enim moriemur (1 Cor 15:32). Si vultis dicere, Cras enim moriemur: I do not prohibit; be aliud before dicite. Epicurei quippe velut non victuri post mortem, quasi aliud nihil habentes nísi quod delectat carnem, dicunt: Manducemus et bibamus; cras enim moriemur. Christiani vero post mortem victuri, et felicitos [812] potius victuri post mortem, non dicant: Manducemus el bibamus; cras enim moriemur: sed tenete quod dicitur: Cras enim moriemur; et dicite: Ieiunemus et oremus; cras enim moriemur.

"Let's fast and not donate." Far be it from the Apostle to place the highest good of man, that is, the cause of happiness, in the body! 8. But perhaps the dispute with the Stoics is not meaningless. To those who ask them what they put the happy life in, that is, what the happy life brings to the name, look what they answer: "It is not bodily pleasure, but the virtue of the soul." What did the Apostle say about this? Did you give your approval? If he gave it, let's give it too. But he did not approve it, because the Scripture rejects those who trust in its virtue. The Epicurean, by placing the highest good of man in the body, places his hope in himself. But although the Stoic places the highest good of man in the soul, that is, in the most excellent part of man, he also places his hope in himself. Both Stoic and Epicurean are names. Cursed is everyone who puts his hope in man. What to say then? With the three of them before our eyes—the Epicurean, the Stoic, and the Christian—let us question each one separately. "Tell us, Epicurean, what makes a man happy." Answer: "Bodily pleasure." "You tell us, Stoick." •—"The virtue of the soul." "You speak, Christian." —«The gift of God». 9. Therefore, brothers, as before our eyes, the Epicureans and the Stoics disputed with the Apostle, and by their dispute they taught us what we should reject and what to choose. The virtue of the soul is a thing worthy of praise; both prudence that discerns good and evil and justice that distributes to each one what is his, or temperance that restrains passions or

strength that calmly endures discomfort. A great thing worthy of praise; Praise her, Stoic, as much as you can, but tell me: "Where does it come from?" It is not the virtue of your soul that makes you happy, but rather the one who gave it to you, who inspired you to want and gave you power 4. Apostolus in corpore poneet summum bonum hominis, id est, beatitudeinis causam. CAPUT VII.—8. Stoicorum opinio Apostólo non probata.—Sed cum Stoicis non indecens fortasse luctamen est. Ecce enim intertoganti ubi ponant efficiens beatae vitae, id est, quod facit in homine beatam vitam; responder, non corporis voluptatem, sed animi esse virtutem. Quid Apostolus? Annuit? Si annuit, annuamus. Sed non annuit: revocat enim Scriptura eos qui confidunt in virtute sua (cf. Ps 48,7). Epicureus itaque in corpore ponens summum hominis bonum, in se spem ponit. Sed enim Stoicus in animoponers summum hominis bonum, in re quidem meliori hominis posuit; sed etiam ipse in se spem posit. Homo est autem et Epicureus et Stoicus. Maledictus igitur omnis qui spem suam ponit in homine (cf. Ier 17,5). Quid ergo? Iam constitutis ante oculos nostros tribus, Epicurean, Stoic, Christian, interrogemus singulos. Dec, Epicuree, quae res faciat beatum. Answer: Voluptas corporis. Dec, Stoice. Virtus animi. Dec, Christiane. Donum Dei. CAPUT VIII.—9. Scio quia fortassis irrisurus es me, et eris in eis de quibus scriptum est quia Paulum irrídebant. If your way is, ego semino, seminator enim verborum sum pro modulo meo. Quod fuet convicium tuum, officium est meum. Ego semino: cadít in te quod semino, tanquam in terram duram. Ego non sum piger; et invenio terram bonam. Quid tibi faciam? You don't mock the rock; recognize the cross in the rod and Christ in the fountain, and, if you feel thirsty, drink virtue. Fill yourself at the source; you will perhaps belch thanksgiving; What you have that comes from him you will no longer attribute to yourself, but belching you will exclaim: I will love you, Lord, my virtue. You will no longer say: "The virtue of my soul makes me happy"; You will not be among those who, knowing God, did not honor him as God or give thanks to him, but became foolish in their thoughts and their foolish hearts were darkened. Thinking they were wise, they became fools. What is believing to be wise, but to have everything of oneself, to be self-sufficient? They became fools; just fools. False wisdom is true foolishness. You will be, however, among those of whom it is said: Lord, they will walk in the light of your face and in your name they will exult all day long and will be exalted in your righteousness, because you are the glory of their virtue. You sought virtue; say: Lord, my virtue. You were looking for a happy life; say: Happy is the man whom you instruct, Lord. Happy are the people, not those who possess bodily pleasure; not he who possesses the virtue of the soul, but happy is the people of whom the Lord is their God. This is the homeland of happiness that everyone desires, but that not everyone seeks rightly. Let us not invent the path to such a homeland in our hearts or embark on false paths: the path even came from there. 10. What does the happy man want, what does he want but not to be deceived, not to die, not to feel pain? And what are you looking for? feel

hungrier and eat more? Why, if it is better not to feel hungry? Only he who lives eternally without fear and without any deception is happy. The soul, in fact, hates to be deceived. How great the soul's spontaneous hatred of being deceived can be gleaned from the fact that those who, with their minds disturbed, laugh, are the object of tears for the healthy, despite the fact that man prefers laughing to crying. Faced with the dilemma between laughing and crying, who is there who answers anything other than this: "I want to laugh"? In the same way, when faced with being deceived and having the truth, every man responds that he wants to have the truth. The choice falls on laughing and having the truth; between laughter and crying, choose laughter; between deception and truth, possessing the truth. But the force of truth is so invincible that man prefers to cry with a healthy mind rather than laugh with a disturbed one. There, in that homeland, truth will reign, with no room for deception and error. The truth will also exist, but not crying. There will also be authentic laughter and enjoyment of the truth, since life will be there. If pain existed, there would be no life, since eternal and imperishable torment cannot be called life. That is why the Lord did not want to call life what the wicked must have, although they must live in fire an endless life so that the punishment is also endless: Their worm will not die and their fire will not be extinguished. He did not want to call this life, but rather the one that is happy and eternal. Hence, when that rich man asked the Lord, What good thing must I do to obtain eternal life?

Nothing else calls life but the happy one. For the wicked will also have it eternal, but not happy, since it will be full of torments. So he asks: Lord, what good must I do to obtain eternal life? The Lord responds by indicating the commandments. And he replies: "I have fulfilled all that." But when he answered him referring to the commandments, what did he say? If you want to get to life. He did not talk to her about the happy life, since the unhappy one should not even be called life. Therefore, life, which is worthy of being called by this name, is nothing more than the happy one. And it will not be happy if it is not eternal. This truth and this life is what they want, what we all want. But where does one go to such great possession, such great happiness? Philosophers invented ways of error. Some said: "This way"; others: "Not here, but there." The way was hidden from them because God resists the proud. It would be hidden from us too if it had not come to us. For this reason the Lord said: I am the way. Lazy wayfarer! Since you did not want to come to the road, the road came to you. You were looking for where to go: I am the way. You were looking for where to go: I am the truth and the life. You will not go astray if you go to him for him. This is the doctrine of Christians, which is in no way to be compared, but is to be incomparably preferred to the doctrines of the philosophers, to the filth of the Epicureans and the arrogance of the Stoics 5. quidem vitam aeternam non nominabat, nisi beatam. Nam habebunt impii aeternam, sed non beatam vitam, quia cruciatibus plenam. Ergo ille ait: Domine, quid boni faciam, ut vitam aeternam consequar? Respondit illi Dominus de mandatis. Ait ille, Haec omnia feci. Sed quando responder de mandatis, quid ait? Si vis come ad vitam (ib., 19,16.17). Non ei dixit beatam; quia misera nec vita diceda est. Non ei dixit aeternam; quia ubi mortis timor est, nec vita diceda est. Ergo vita, quae hoc nomine dignita est, ut vita dicatur, non est nisi beata; et beata non est, nisi aeterna. Hanc volunt omnes, hanc volumus omnes, veritatem et vitam: sed ad tam magnam possessionem, ad tam grandem felicitatem qua itur? Instruxerunt sibi vias erroris philosophi; alii dixerunt: Hac; there: Non hac, sed hac. Latuit eos via, quia Deus superbis resistit (cf. 4,6). Lateret et nos, nisi venisset ad nos. Ideo Dominus: Ego, inquit, sum via.

Piger viator, vinore nolebas ad viam; ad te venit via. Quaerebas qua ires: Ego sum via. Quaerebas quo ires: Ego sum veritas et vita (lo 14,6). Non errabis quando is ad illum, per illum. Haec est doctrina Christianorum, non plañe conferenda, sed incomparabiliter praeferenda doctrinis philosophorum, immunditiae Epicureorum, superbiae Stoicorum.
Augustine considers the Stoics arrogant to identify with God; see n.l.

Theme: The struggle between the spirit and the flesh (Rom 7,15-25). Place: Carthage. Date: In 418 or 419. 1. How many times this text, taken from the letter of the apostle Paul, is read, we must fear that, if misunderstood, it provides an opportunity to sin for those who are looking for it. In fact, men, prone to sin, barely contain themselves before it. As soon as they hear the Apostle who says: I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I detest, they do evil and pretending that they dislike doing so, they consider themselves similar to the Apostle who said: I do not do the good that I want, but the evil that I do not want. From time to time this text is read and it necessarily leads us to the dispute to prevent men, by misinterpreting it, from turning what is healthy food into poison.
