CAPUT II.—Vox ergo triumphi nondum est: sed quiafutura est, Docet te idem apostolus, they say: Oportet corruptibile hoc induere incorruptionem, et mortale hoc induere immortalitatem. Cum autem corruptibile hoc induerit incorruptionem, et mortale hoc induerit immortalitatem: ibi est vox triumphi: tune fiet sermo qui scriptus est, Absorpta est mors in victoriam. Dicant triumphantes: Ubi est, mors, contentio tua (1 Cor 15,53-55). Dicemus ergo; quandoque dicemus; et ipsum quandoque non erit longe.

Non enim tantum remanet de saeculo, quantum iam exemptum est. Hoc igitur tune dicemus. Augustine divides the history of the world into six stages, the last of which begins with the coming of Jesus Christ. Hence he logically considers the time remaining until the end of time much shorter than the time that has already passed. See supplementary note 22: The ages of the world v.VII p.751.

If some of you understood it, you undoubtedly experienced how difficult it is. We have proposed, with the help of God's mercy, to expose with our words this reading and this text of the Apostle's letter that is uncomfortable and dark, but salutary for those who understand it. We feel indebted to your charity and we see you demanding our debt. As we pray so that you can receive it, pray you too so that we can explain it to you. Let our prayer be in agreement, and in this way God will make you good listeners and us faithful payers of the debt. 2. When we lived in the flesh, says the Apostle, the passions of sins that exist through the law acted in our members until they produced fruits of death. It gives the impression—and here appears the first great danger for those who do not understand—that the Apostle recriminates and accuses the law of God. There will be no shortage of people who will tell me: Far be it from the mind of any Christian! Who, except a madman, would dare to suspect such a thing of the Apostle? And yet, my brethren, the misunderstanding of these words supplied the leaven of foolishness to the fury of the Manichaeans. They affirm, in effect, that the law was given by Moses, not by God, and they insist that it contradicts the Gospel. When arguing with them, they try to convince Catholics with these testimonies of the Apostle Paul that they do not understand—how can I say?—that they do not understand, or better yet, that they do not care about it. It is not too much to ask whoever is interested, after hearing the slander in the mouth of the heretic, to at least examine

the context of the reading in the codex'. And if he does this, he will immediately find there with which to refute the charlatan adversary and with which to defeat the rebels and enemies of the law. Even if he is slow to understand the words of the Apostle, he will clearly see the praise of the law of God proclaimed there. 3. See his words first and pay attention. When we were in the flesh, he says, the passions of sins that exist through the law acted in our members. The Manichean now raises his neck, raises his horns, charges and attacks. Behold, he says: the passions of sins that exist by the law. How can the law be good by which the passions of sins exist in us and act in our members until they produce fruits of death? Read, continue a little further, listen to everything patiently, even if you don't understand it. But I did not know sin except through the law, for I was unaware of lust until the law said: You shall have no wicked desires. At some time I lived without the law; but with the arrival of the precept, sin revived. I am dead and it has come to pass in me that the precept given for life—what is more related to life than: You shall have no perverse desires?—was the cause of death in me, since sin, taking the opportunity of the precept, deceived me and through it caused my death. He terrified lust, but did not quench it; It terrified her, but did not repress her; It produced fear of punishment, but not love of justice. Therefore, he said, the law is indeed holy, and the precept holy, just, and good. Has what is good become death for me? No way. Death is not the law, but sin. But sin, in order for sin to appear - to say dead is equivalent to saying hidden - through a good thing, death worked in me, so that, with the prevarication added, I became exceedingly sinful or sinful through the precept. If there were no precept, transgression would not be added to the sin. In another place the same Apostle clearly says: Where there is no law, there is no transgression either. What to say? You will have no perverse desires. The man heard the law, and recognized the sin; declared war, and found captivity. But perhaps another man, you will say, not the Apostle. What shall we say then, my brothers? Did the Apostle not have in his flesh any concupiscence contrary to his will, to which he denied consent when it made itself present, tickled, incited, solicited, inflamed and tempted? I say to your charity that if we believe that the Apostle absolutely lacked any concupiscence to resist, we have a very high opinion of him. I wish it were so! What is best for us is not to envy the apostles, but to imitate them. However, dearly beloved, I hear the confession of the Apostle himself, that he has not yet reached a perfection in his justice as great as we believe to be that of the angels, whom we hope to equal if we reach the desired goal. What else does the Lord promise us in the resurrection, when he says: In the resurrection of the dead they will not take husband or wife, for they will not begin to die, but they will be equal to the angels of God?

4. Then someone will say: "How do you know that the apostle Paul did not yet possess the perfection of the angels?" I do no insult to the Apostle; I believe in no one but himself; I am not looking for any other witnesses. I neither listen to the suspicious nor pay attention to those who praise excessively. Tell me, Holy Apostle, about yourself, without leaving any doubt that you are talking about yourself. Regarding these your words: I do not do what I want, but what I hate, there are no shortage of those who say that in you you personify who knows who else who is tired, depressed, defeated and captive. And before he had said: Not that he has already achieved it or that he is perfect. There are still those who contradict him, saying that the Apostle said this because he had not yet reached immortality, not because he was far from the perfection of justice. That is, he possessed the justice of angels, but not their immortality. This is what they claim; that clear. You just said: "He equaled the angels in justice, but not in immortality. Therefore he already possessed the perfection of justice, but, pursuing the definitive palm, he sought immortality.

Non enim invidere nos oportet Apostolis, sed Apostólos imitari. Verumtamen, carissimi, audio ipsum Apostolum confitentem, nondum eum ad tantam perfectionem iustitiae pervenisse, quantam in Angelis esse credimus: quorum Angelorum aequalitatem speramus, si ad hoc quod volumus perveniamus. Quid enim aliud nobis Dominus promittít ín resurrectione, ubi ait: In resurrectione mortuorum ñeque cloudnt, ñeque uxores ducent; non enim incipient mori, sed erunt aequales Angelis Dei? (Mt 22,30; Le 20,35.36).

4. Apostolum loqui de propria sua imperfectione.—Dicit ergo aliquis: Et tu unde six quia Paulus apostolus angeli iustitiam et perfectionem nondum habebat? Non facio iniuriam Apostólo, non credo nisi Apostólo, alium testem non quaero; suspicantem non audio, nimium laudantem non curo. Dec mihi, heal Apostle, de te ipso, ubi nenio dubitat quia de te ipso loqueris. Nam ubi dixisti: Non quod flew ago; sed quod odi, illud fació (Rom 7,15), existunt qui dicant, quod alium in te nescio quem transfiguraveris laborantem, deficient, victum, captivum. Tu mihi dic de te, ubi [835] nemo dubitat quia loqueris de te. Fratres, ait Apostolus, ego me ipsum non arbitror apprehendisse. Et quid facis? Vnum autem, quae retro oblitus, in ea quae ante sunt extentus, secundum intentionem, ait, non secundum perfectionem; secundum intentionem sequor ad palmam supernae vocationis Dei in Christo Iesu. Supra iam dixerat: Non quia iam acceperim, aut iam perfectus sim (Phil 3,12-14). Adhuc contradicitur et dicitur: Dicebat ista Apostolus, quia nondum pervenerat ad immortalitatem; non quia nondum pervenerat ad iustitiae perfectionem. Iam ergo tan iustus erat quam sunt Angeli, sed nondum immortalis sicut sunt Angeli. Sic, inquiunt, sic est prorsus. Dixisti mode: Tam erat iustus quam sunt Angeli, sed nondum immortalis sicut sunt Angeli. Ergo perfectionem iustitiae iam tenebat, sed sequendo palmam supernam, immortalitatem quaerebat.

5. Show us, Holy Apostle, another clearer place, where you confess your weakness, not where you seek immortality. Murmurs and objections are also heard against this text. I seem to be hearing the thoughts of some, in which they say to me: “It is true; I know what you're going to tell me. He confesses his weakness, but weakness of the flesh, not of the mind; weakness of the body, not of the soul; and it is in the soul, not in the body, that full justice is found. Indeed, who does not know that without a doubt the Apostle was fragile and mortal in his body? These are his words: We carry this treasure in clay vessels. Why do you take care of the clay glass? Tell us about the treasure and see if it lacked anything, if there is anything that could be added to the gold of justice. Let's listen to him himself so as not to appear insulting. It goes like this: And so that I do not become conceited with the magnitude of my revelations. Here you have, then, the Apostle who fears the precipice of pride at the same time that he proclaims the greatness of his revelations. So that you know that the Apostle who wanted to save others still needed personal healing; So that you may know this, if you hold his honor in high esteem, listen to what remedy the doctor applies to the tumor; listen, not to me, but to him. Listen to his confession to recognize him as a teacher. Listen: And so that I do not become conceited with the magnitude of my revelations. I can now ask the apostle Paul: So as not to become conceited, holy Apostle? Do you still have to be wary of pride? Does CAPUT IV.—5. still exist? Infirmitatem animi sui confitetur Apostolus.—Dic nobis, sanete Apostóle, alium aliquem manifestiorem locum, non ubi quaeris immortalitatem, sed ubi confiteris infirmitatem. Et hic iam whispering, iam contradicitur. Videor mihi audire quorumdam cogitationes, et hic dicitur mihi: verum est, novi quid dicturus es: confitetur infirmitatem, sed carnis, non mentís; confitetur infirmitatem, sed corporis, non animi: in animo autem est perfection iustítia, non in corpore. Nam quisignot utique Apostolum in corpore Fuisse Fragilem, Corpore Fuisse Mortalem, sicut dicit: Habemus thesaurum istum in vasis fictilibus? (2 Cor 4:7). Quid tibi ergo cum vase fictili? Of thesauro aliquid loquere. Si aliquid minus habuit, si erat quod ei ad aurum iustitiae posset addi, inveniamus. Ipsum audiamus, ne iniuriosi existimemur. Et ne magnitudeine revelationum mearum, Apostolus dicit: In magnitudeine revelationum mearum ne exfoliar (2 Cor 12,7).

Nempe hic agnoscitis Apostolum habentem magnitudeinem revelationum, et timentem elationis praecipitium. Ut ergo noveris quia et ipse Apostolus, qui volebat alios safes faceré, adhuc curabatur: ut noveris quia et ipse adhuc curabatur; si magnipendis ipsius honorem, audi quid medícus ei apposuerit ad tumorem; audi non me, ipsum audi. Audi confitentem, ut felt teacherm. Audi; Et ne magnitudeine revelationum mearum exfoliate. Ecce iam possum dicere apostólo Paulo: Ne extollaris, sanete Apostóle? You will not extollaris,

the fear that you will become conceited? Do you still have to find medicine against this disease? 6. What do you tell me? Hear also what I am; don't climb too high; fear rather. Listen to how the lamb enters where the ram is in such danger. So that I do not become conceited, he said, with the magnitude of my revelations, the thorn of the flesh, the angel of Satan, has been given to me to buffet me. What would not be the feared tumor, if the plaster applied was so sharp! Tell me now that his justice was equal to that of the angels. Does the holy angel also receive in heaven, so that he does not become conceited, the sting, angel of satan, that slaps him? Such suspicion about the holy angels should not even cross your minds. We are men; let us recognize the apostles as men, although saints. They are select vessels, but still fragile, that are still pilgrims in the flesh, without having achieved triumph in the heavenly homeland. He himself prayed to the Lord three times to remove this sting and was not heard regarding his will, because he was not heard regarding his health. Perhaps, therefore, when he says: We know that the law is spiritual, I, on the other hand, am carnal, he does not speak nonsense. 7. Is the Apostle then carnal who said to others: You who are spiritual, instruct him in the spirit of sweetness? He speaks to others as spiritual and he is carnal? But what did he say to the spiritualists themselves, who have not yet adhuc cavendum est? Tu ne extollaris, adhuc timendum est? Tu ne extollaris, adhuc huic infirmitati medicine quaerenda est? CAPUT V.—6. Tumoris epithema Apostólo datum.—Quid mihi, inquit, say you? And your audi quid sim; et noli altum sapere, sed time. Audi quomodo brevis agnus ingrediatur, ubi aries sic periclitatur. Ne magnitudeine, inquit, revelationum mearum exfoliate, datus est mihi stimulus carnis meae, angelus satanae, qui me colaphizet (ib.). Qualem tumorem timuit, qui mordacissimum epithema accepit? Iam ergo moda it said quia tanta in illo erat iustitia, quanta est in Angelis sanctis. An forte et angelus sanctus in cáelo, ne extollatur, accipit stimulum angelum satanae, a quo colaphize[836]tur? Absit hoc de sanctis Angelis suspicari. Homines sumus, Apostólos sanctos homines agnoscamus; vasa elect, sed adhuc fragility; adhuc in hac carne pilgrims, nondum in caelesti patria triumphantes. Ergo quoniam Dominum ter rogavit, ut ab illo iste stimulus auferretur; nec auditus est ad voluntatem, quia exauditus est ad sanitatem (cf.

2 Cor 12,7-9); forte non indecenter ipse loquitur, ubi dicit, Scimus autem quia Lex spiritualis est; ego autem carnalis sum (Rom 7:14). 7. Sanctus quisque in hac vita carnalis et spiritualis.—Ergo carnalis Apostolus, qui alus dicebat: Vos qui spirituales estis, instruite huiusmodi in spiritu lenitatis? alios tanquam spirituales alloquitur, et ipse carnalis (jst? Sed quid dixit et ipsis spiritualibus, quia nondum erant in perfec-

found in the celestial and angelic perfection, that they had not yet reached the security of that homeland, but lived in the restlessness of this pilgrimage? What did he tell them? It is true that he called them spiritual: You, he said, who are spiritual, train him in the spirit of sweetness, also taking care for yourselves, so as not to be tempted. Notice this: He feared that the one whom he previously called spiritual would suffer the weakness of temptation. From which it follows that the spiritual can be tempted, if not in the mind, then in the flesh. It is spiritual because it lives according to the spirit; but as regards its mortal part it is still carnal. It is spiritual and carnal at the same time. Spiritual: With my mind I serve the law of God; carnal: with the flesh, however, to the law of sin. Therefore, is oneself carnal and spiritual? Certainly; As long as you live here, that's how it is. 8. Do not be surprised, you, whoever you are, who give in and consent to carnal desires, which either consider them good to satisfy your passion or, although you consider them bad, you give in and consent to them, follow them where they lead you and carry out their perverse suggestions: you are completely carnal. You, and whoever you are like, are completely carnal. On the other hand, if you have perverse desires, something prohibited by the law when it says: You will not have perverse desires and you nevertheless fulfill the other precept of the law: Do not follow your lusts, as far as the mind is concerned, you are spiritual; and as for the flesh, carnal. One thing is, in fact, tione caelesti et angelica, nondum erant in illius patriae securitate, sed in huius peregrinationis sollicitudine versabantur? quid eis dixit? Certe spirituales eos vocavit: Vos, inquit, qui spirituales estis, instruite buiusmodi in spiritu lenitatis, intendens te ipsum, ne et tu tenteris (Gal 6,1). Ecce, quem spiritualem iam appellavit, timuit illi tentationis fragilitatem, unde posset tentari spiritualis, etsi non ex mente, utique ex carne. Spiritualis enim, quia secundum spiritum vivit; adhuc autem ex parte mortalí carnalis: idem spiritualis, idemque carnalis. Ecce spiritualis: Servian mind tegi Dei. Ecce carnalis: carne autem legi peccati (Rom 7:25). idem ergo ipse et spiritualis et carnalis? idem plane, quamdiu hic vivit, sic est. CAPUT VI.—8.

Quis totus carnalis, quis ex parte vel totas spiritualis.—Noli mirari, quisquís es, quicumque carnalibus concupiscentíis cedis atque consentís, qui eas vel bonas putas ad explendam libidinis saturitatem, vel certe sic iam vines malas, ut eis tamen cendo consentías, et quo ducunt sequaris, et ea quae mala perpetres suggerunt; totus carnalis, it is. You, your quisquís talis es, totus carnalis es. Si autem concupiscis quidem, quod Lex vetat, cum dicit: Non concupisces (Ex 20,17); servas tamen aliud quod item Lex iubet, Post concupiscentias tuas non eas (Eccli 18,30): mente spiritualis es, carne carnalis. Aliud est enim, non con-

not having bad desires, and another not to go after them. The first corresponds without a doubt to the perfect; The second is typical of those who fight, of those who fight and get tired. If there is ardor in the fight, why distrust victory? When will victory come? When death is absorbed into victory. Then you will see the cry of the one who triumphs, not the sweat of the one who fights. What is that future triumphant cry, when this corruptible body puts on incorruption and this mortal puts on immortality? You see the victory; listen to their shout of joy and expect the same triumph. Then what is written will be fulfilled: Death has been absorbed into victory. Where is your strife, oh death? Where is your sting, O death? Where? Note that it existed, but no longer exists. Where is your strife, oh death? This is: I don't do what I want; Here it is: We know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal. If, then, the Apostle says that about himself; If he says—I speak conditionally—if he says of himself: We know that the law is spiritual, but I am carnal, clearly he is spiritual in the mind and carnal in the body. When, then, will it be totally spiritual? When it is fulfilled: An animal body is sown and a spiritual body will be resurrected. Therefore now, while the heat of strife exists, I do not do what I will; I am partly spiritual and partly carnal. Spiritual at the top, carnal at the bottom. I still struggle; I have not yet won and I value not being defeated. I don't do what I want, but what I hate. What are you doing? Have bad cupids; aliud, post concupiscentias suas non iré Non concupiscere, omnino perfectí est; post concupiscentias suas non iré, pugnantis est, luctantis est, labóranos est. Ubi fervet struggle, quare despair victory? When was victory? When absorbebitur mors in victoriam. Tunr enim vox erit triumphantis, non sudor pugnantis. How future is this triumphantis, cum corruptibile hoc induerit incorruptionem, et moríale hoc induerit immortalitatem? Vides victorem, audí exsultantem, exspecta triumphantem. Tune fiet sermo qui scriptus est, Absorpta est mors in victoriam. Ubi est, mors, contentio tua? ubi est, mors, aculeus tuus? (1 Cor 15:53-55). Ubi is there? Ecce erat, et non est. Ubi est, mors, contentio tua? Ecce mortis contentio: Non quod flew ago (Rom 7:15). Ecce mortis contentio: Scimus quia lex spiritualis est; ego autem carnalis sum.

Si ergo Apostolus de se ipso dicit; If I say, I do not confirm: if Apostolus dicit, Scimus quia lex spiritualis est, ego autem carnalis sum (ib., 7,14): [837] mente enim spiritualis, corpore carnalis: quando totus spiritualis? Cum, Seminatur corpus animale, resurget corpus spirituale (1 Cor 15:44). Modo ergo quando fervet mortis contentio, non quod voló ago: ex parte spiritualis, ex parte carnalis; ex parte meliore spiritualis, ex parte inferióte carnalis. Adhuc confligo, nondum vici: magnum mihi est non vinci. No» quod flew, hoc ago; quod odi, illud jacio (Rom 7:15). What do you say? Concupiscus. Etsi concupiscentiae non con-

wishes. Although I do not consent and do not go after them, I certainly have them and, without a doubt, even in that part, I am myself. 9. It is not that my self is only in the mind and another different person in the flesh. What if not? Therefore, myself: I in the mind and I in the flesh. There are not two contrary natures 4, but one man consisting of two parts, as one is the God who made man. Therefore, I myself serve the law of God with my mind, and with my flesh the law of sin. With my mind I do not consent to the law of sin; rather, I would like that law not to exist in my members. I wouldn't want to, but it exists: I don't do what I want; Since I have perverse desires, without wanting to have them, I do not do what I want, but what I hate. What do I hate? Having perverse desires. I hate having them, and yet I suffer them in the flesh, though not in the mind. I do what I hate. 10. Well, if I do what I do not want, I acknowledge that the law is good. How is that understood? You would recognize the goodness of the law if you did what it commands. If you do what she forbids, how do you recognize her? It is true: If I do what I do not want, I recognize that the law is good. In what way? The law commands not to have perverse desires. What do I want? Not having them. Wanting what the law wants, I recognize that it is good. If saying: You will not have perverse desires, I would like to have them, I did not feel it, etsi post concupiscentias meas non eo; tamen adhuc concupisco: et utique etiam in ipsa parte ego sum. CAPUT VII.—9. Idem carnalis simul et spiritualis.—Non enim ego in mente, et alius in carne. Be quid? Igitur ipse ego: quia ego in mente, ego in carne. Non enim duae naturae contrae, sed ex utraque unus homo: quia unus Deus, a quo factus est homo. Igitur ipse ego, ego ipse, mind servio legi Dei, carne autem legi peccati (Rom 7:25). Mente non consentio legi peccati: sed tamen nollem esse in membris meis lex ulla peccati. Quia ergo nollem, et tamen est; non quod flew ago: quia concupisco, et nolo, non quod flew ago; sed quod odi, illud jacio (ib., 7,15). What did I hate? Concupiscere. Odi concupiscere, et tamen ago illud carne, non mente: Quod odi, illud jacio. 10. Consentiens cum lege.-—Si autem quod nolo, illud jacio; consentio legi, quoniam bona est. Quid est hoc: Si quod nolo, illud fació; consentio Legi, quoniam bona est? (ib., 7,16). Consentires legi, si quod vellet faceres: facis quod lex odit, quomodo consentís legi?

Prorsus, Si quod nolo, hoc jacio; consentio legi, quoniam bona est. What's up? Quia iubet lex: Non concupisces (Rom 7,7; Ex 20,17). Why did ego fly? non concupiscere? Volendo quod vult lex, consentio legi, quoniam bona est. Si diceret lex, Non concupisces, et ego vellem concupiscere; non con4
Against the Manichaeans.
The law of the spirit and the flesh of sin

I would recognize it as good and I would find myself completely separated from it by the perversity of the will. If the law says: You will not have perverse desires, I want to have them, I do not give my approval. What are we left with? What do you say, oh law!? You will have no perverse desires. I don't want to have them, I don't want to; What you don't want, I don't want either; That's why I approve of you, because what you don't want, I don't want either. My weakness does not fulfill the law, but my will praises it. Therefore, if I do what I do not want, my approval of the law comes not from the fact that I do what I do not want, but from the fact that I do not want what it does not want. Having bad desires, even without consenting to them, is already acting. Let no one look to the Apostle for an example of sin and become that. I don't do what I want. What does the law say? You will have no perverse desires. I don't want to have them and yet I have them. I have them, even if I don't give them my consent or go after them. I offer resistance, I turn away my mind, I deny it weapons, I restrain my limbs, and yet, what I do not want occurs in me. What the law does not want, I do not want either; I do not want what she does not want, and, consequently, I approve of her. 11. It is I myself who is in the flesh and in the mind, but my self is more in the mind than in the flesh. Since I am in the mind, I am in the ruling part, for the mind is the one that governs and the flesh is the governed. And my self is more in the part through which I govern than in the other in which I am governed. My self is, therefore, more in my mind: Now, however, I no longer do that. What does it mean now, Sentrem legi, et omnino ab illa voluntatis perversitate divetsus existencerem. They say te enim lege: Non concupisces, et ego vellem concupiscere; non consentio legi Dei. What way? quid say, or lex? Non concupisces. Et ego nolo concupiscere, et ego nolo; quod non vis, nolo: ideo consentio, quia quod non vis, nolo. Non implet legem infirmitas mea; sed Legem laudat voluntas mea. Ergo si quod nolo, hoc ago; ideo consentio legi, quia nolo quod non vult, non quia ago quod nolo. Ipsum enim agere concupiscere est, non concupiscentiae consentiré: ne aliquis iam in Apostólo peccandi sibi quaerat exemplum, et det malum exemplum. Non quod flew ago. Quid enim lex dicit? Non concupisces. Et ego nolo concupiscere, et tamen concupisco; quamvis concupiscentiae meae assensum non praebeam, quamvis post eam non eam. I resist enim, I averto mentem, I denied weapon, I have membra; et tamen fit in me quod nolo.

Quod non vult lex, nolo cum lege; quod non vult, nolo: ergo consentio legi. CAPUT VIII.—11. Ignorare peccatum.—Sed quia ego sum in carne, ego sum in mente; sed magis ego sum in mente, quam in carne. Quia enim ego sum in mente, ego sum in regente: mens enim regit, caro regitur: et magis sum ego in eo quo regó, quam in eo in quo regor. Quia ergo magis ego in mente: Nunc autem iam non ego operor illud.

instead? Now, however, I who was previously sold to sin, once redeemed, having already received the grace of the Savior, so that with my mind I delight in the law of God, it is not I who do that, but the sin that dwells in me. I know that it does not dwell in me. Repeat in me; listen to what follows: this is, in my flesh, good. I don't lack the will. I know. What do you know? That good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh. Before you had said: I don't know what I do. If you ignore it, how do you know? As soon as you say I don't know it as much as I know it; I don't know how that is to be understood. Or is this way of understanding correct, namely: when he says: I don't know what I do, the verb I don't know is equivalent to I don't approve of it, I don't accept it, I don't like it, I don't consent to it, I don't praise it? In fact, Christ will not ignore those to whom he will say: I do not know you. I also understand it this other way: I don't know what I do, because I don't know what I don't do. It is not I who do that, but the sin that dwells in me. I do not know it, because I do not do it, as an example of what is said of the Lord: To him who did not know sin. What does it mean: didn't know? So he didn't know what he was reproaching and punishing? If, then, he punished without knowing, he punished unjustly. But since his punishment is just, it follows that he knew what he was punishing. And yet he did not know sin, that is, he had not committed sin. I don't know what I'm doing; I don't do what I want, but what I hate. If I do what I do not want, I recognize that the law is good. Now, however, having received the grace, I do not do it; free is the

mind, but captivates the flesh. It is not I who do it, but the sin that dwells in me. I know, in fact, that good does not dwell in me, that is, in my flesh. 12. I do not lack the will to do good, but I do lack doing it perfectly. There is no lack of wanting, but there is a lack of doing it with perfection. It does not speak of doing, but of doing with perfection. It does not indicate that you do nothing, because concupiscence rebels and you do not give your consent; You like someone else's woman and you don't agree, you withdraw your thoughts and enter the court of your mind. You see the external noise of concupiscence and you issue the sentence against it, purifying your conscience. «I don't want to, you say; I don't." Consider that you like him; However: «I don't do it; I have something to delight in.” Indeed, I delight in the law of God according to the inner man. Why these disturbances in your flesh? Why do you tempestuously suggest to me foolish, temporary, fleeting, vain and harmful pleasures? Why, like a parrot, do you keep telling me those things? The unjust told me their pleasures. This concupiscence also comes from there. He presents me with pleasures, but not according to your law, Lord. Indeed, I delight in the law of God, not because of my merits, but because of the grace of God. You, concupiscence, stir up the flesh, but you do not subject the mind to your empire. I will wait on the Lord and will not fear what the flesh will do to me. Not someone else's, not mine either. Does the person who does all this do nothing? What he does is much and great, but still

iam gratia, non ego operator illud; liberate this menu, expensive captiva. Non ego operor illud, sed id quod in me habitat peccatum. Scio enim quia non habitat in me, hoc est in carne mea, bonum (Rom 7:15-18). CAPUT IX.—12. Perficere legem in hac vita sanctis non conceditur.—• Velle enim adiacet mihi, perficere autem bonum non adiacet (Rom 7:18). Adiacet velle, perficere non adiacet. Non dixit: faceré; thirst, perficere. Non enim nihil facis. Rebellat concupiscentia, et non consentís; delectat uxor aliena, et non annuis, mentem avertis, in secretarium mentis intras. Vides foris strepentem concupiscentiam, profers adversus eam sentenliam, mundans conscientiam. Nolo, inquis, non facio. Puta quia delectat, non fació, habeo cui condelecter. Condelector enim legi Dei secundum interiorem hominem (ib., 7,22). Quid you de carne tumultuaris? 1. The reading of the holy Apostle ended yesterday with these words: Therefore, I myself serve the law of God with my mind; with the flesh, however, to the law of sin. With them he showed what he had wanted to say in the previous ones: It is no longer I who do it, but the sin that lives in me, that is, I did it not with the mind by denying consent, but with the flesh, through concupiscence. He designates this with the name of sin, because from it—from the lust that resides in the flesh—all sins have their origin. Any sin, whether of word, deed or thought, has no other origin than evil desire and illicit pleasure. Those of you who were present the day before yesterday 7 heard how the noise, the fire and the smoke terrified the people who stood at a distance and how, on the contrary, the Holy Spirit came, the very finger of God, fifty days after the shadow of the Passover, and rested in tongues like fire on each of those present. But this time he did not instill fear, but love, so that we would not be servants, but children. He who does good for fear of punishment does not yet love God, he is not yet counted among the children. Still, I hope he at least fears punishment! Do good; do it at least for fear of punishment, if you still cannot do it for love of justice. The mistress will arrive, and then the slave will leave, because perfect charity expels fear. But you received the spirit of adoption as sons, by which we cry: Abba, Father! Let the heart cry out: Our Father, who art in heaven. Why didn't he just say Father? What do the two names mean: Abba, Father? If you ask what Abba means, you will be answered: Father. Abba is the Hebrew name for father. Why did the Apostle want to put both? Because he saw the cornerstone that the builders rejected and which later became the head of the corner. It is not called a cornerstone without reason, since it unites two walls that come from different directions. On the one hand, circumcision; on the other, the foreskin, and the distance between them is identical to that which separates them from the angle; at the same time, the respective closeness to the angle indicates the reciprocal closeness. Their union occurs at the angle. He is our peace, he who made the two things one. Therefore, on the one hand, circumcision; on the other, the foreskin, but there is the union of the walls, that is, the glory of the angle. You have received the spirit of adoption as sons by which we cry: Abba, Father! 16. What will be the reality, if the guarantee is such? We should not talk about a guarantee, but about a deposit. in what is seen, but in what is not seen. What is seen is temporary; what is not seen, eternal. Because we hope for what is not seen and we wait for it with patience, we are precisely told in the psalm: Wait in the Lord, act manfully; Let your heart be comforted and wait for the Lord. The promises of the world always deceive; never, however, those of God. What the world promises seems to be delivered here, that is, on this earth where one must die and where we are now; On the other hand, what God promises will be given to us in the land of the living; This is the reason why many get tired of waiting for the truthful, without being ashamed to love the fallacious. Of them the Scripture says: Woe to those who lost their temper and walked in perverse ways! They are the children of eternal death, who do not stop insulting those who behave manfully and wait on God, comforted in their hearts; Full of boasting, they present to them their temporary pleasures, which for a time sweeten their jaws, although later they must find them more bitter than gall. They tell us: «Where is what is promised to you after this life? Who has returned from the other world to tell you the truth of what you believe? Look at us, happy for having been satisfied with pleasures; see that we wait for something visible; You, on the other hand, torment yourselves with the tortures of temperance, believing what you do not see. Next they add the words mentioned by the Apostle: Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we will die. But observe what we must be on guard against, according to his admonition:

Bad words, he said, corrupt good customs. Be sober in the right measure and do not sin. 2. Beware, therefore, brothers, that your customs are corrupted by such charlatanism, that hope is extinguished, that patience is weakened, and that you are led into paths of perversion. Even more: keep with humility and meekness in the right paths that the Lord teaches you, to which the psalm refers: He will guide the humble in judgment and teach the meek his ways. Unless he is humble and meek, no one can perpetually preserve patience in the midst of the fatigues of this world, without which the hope of the future life cannot be preserved. He is meek and humble who does not offer resistance to the will of God, whose yoke is light and whose burden is light, but only for those who believe in him, place their hope in him and love him. In this way, humility and meekness will not only lead you to love his consolations, but also to endure his punishments, like good children. That means waiting patiently for what you do not yet see. Work and walk like this. You walk in Christ who said: I am the way. Learn how to walk in him, not only in his word, but also in his example. The Father did not spare his own Son, but gave him up for us all. He did not resist, but wanted it equally, since the will of the Father and the Son is one in accordance with the equality of the divine form, possessing which, he did not consider being equal to God an object of plunder. We have just heard the blessed Paul who exhorted and strengthened us with these words: If God is for us, who can be against us? Who he is in favor of God showed it above when he said: Those whom he predestined, he called; Those whom he called he justified, and those whom he justified he glorified. What will we say to this? If God is with us, who can be against us? God's favor toward us is manifested in that he predestined us, called us, justified us, and glorified us. If God is with us, who can be against us? He predestined us before we existed; He called us when we were far from him; He justified us when we were sinners and glorified us when we were mortal. If God is with us, who can be against us? Whoever wants to wage war on those predestined, called, justified and glorified by God, prepare and think if you will be able to fight against God. When we heard: If God is with us, who can be against us?, we understood that only he who conquers God will be able to make us
DE VERBIS APOSTOLI, ROM 8,30-31: «Quos AUTEM PRAEDESTINAVIT, ILLOS ET VOCAVIT; QUOS AUTEM VOCAVIT, ILLOS ET IUSTIFICAVIT”, ETC. «SI DEUS PRO NOBIS, QUIS CONTRA NOS?» AGAINST PELAGIANS

CAPUT I.—1. Praedestinatis nemo nocere valet.—Apostolum beatum audivimus exhortantem et confirmantem nos, cum diceret nobis: Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? Pro quibus autem sit Deus, superius ostendit, ubi ait: quos autem praedestinavit, illos et vocavit; quos autem vocavit, illos et iustificavit; quos autem iustificavit, illos et glorificavit. Quid ergo dicemus ad haec? If Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? (Rom 8:32-31). Deus pro nobis, ut praedestinaret nos; Deus pro nobis, ut vocatet nos; Deus pro nobis, ut iustificadoret nos; Deus pro nobis, ut gloriñcaret nos. If Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? Praedestinavit, antequam essemus; vocavit, cum aversi essemus; iustificavit, cum peccatores essemus; glorificavit, cum mortals essemus. If Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? Praedestinatis a [863] Deo, vocatis, iustificatis, glorificatis, qui vult adversan, paret se, si potest bellare adversus Deum. Ubi enim audimus: Si Deus pro nobis, quis contra nos? nisi qui Deum vincit, non laedit

damage. And who can defeat the Almighty? Whoever wants to fight against him will harm himself. Christ said nothing else from heaven to Paul when he was still Saul: It is not good for you to kick against the sting. Get angry and damage as much as you can; Whoever kicks against the sting, does he not harm himself? 2. Of these four extraordinary things mentioned by the Apostle and which refer to those who have the favor of God, that is, predestination, vocation, justification and glorification, we must consider which we already have and which we still await. Thinking of what we already possess, let us praise the giving God, and thinking of what we do not yet have, let us consider Him as a debtor. In effect, he has become a debtor, not receiving anything from us, but promising what he pleased. It is one thing to say to a man: "You are indebted to me for what I gave you" and another thing to say: "You owe me what you promised me." When you say the first, the benefit came from you, but lent, not donated; In the second case, although you gave nothing, you have the right to demand. The goodness of the one who promised will give it to you, so that faith does not turn into evil, since he who deceives is evil. Can we perhaps say to God: "Give me back what I gave you"? What have we given to God, if everything we are and have that is good we received from him? Nothing, therefore, we have given him. In this sense, we cannot consider God as a debtor, especially since the Apostle tells us: Who knows?

What was the Lord's thought or who was his advisor? Or who gave it to him before so that he has to give it back? The only right we have to demand something from our Lord is to say to him: "Keep what you promised, since we did what you ordered, although this is also your work, since you helped those who were struggling." 3. Let no one, therefore, say: "God called me because I worshiped him." How would you have worshiped him if he had not preceded his call? If God called you because you worshiped him, then you went ahead to give him something for which he repays you. Do not these words of the Apostle destroy your argument?: Who gave him before so that he has to give back? But note that, when you were called, at least you already existed. Predestination is prior to existence. What did you give to God when you didn't even exist to be able to give it to him? What did God do when he predestined someone who did not exist? What does the Apostle say?: He calls things that are not, in the same way as those that are. If you already existed, you would not be the object of predestination; If you had not gone away, you would not have been called; If you were not impious, there would be no justification, and if you were not earthly and abject, glorification would be unnecessary. Who gave him before so that he has to give back? From him and through him and in him all things exist. What do we compensate him with? To him the glory. Let us give thanks to God and not be ungrateful, because when we did not exist he predestined us, because he called us far away and because being sinners he justified us.

Deus nobis debitar factus ex promissis.—In his autem quattuor rebus, quas commendavit Apostolus insignes, quae pertinent ad eos pro quibus est Deus, id est, praedestinatione, vocatione, iustificatione, glorificatione; in his ergo quattuor rebusconsiderare debenmus quid iam habeamus, et quid adhuc exspectemus. In his enim quae iam habemus, laudemus Deum largitorem: in his quae nondum habemus, teneamus debítorem. Debitor enim factus est, non aliquid a nobis accipiendo, sed quod ei placuit promittendo. Aliter enim dicimus homini: You must mihi quia dedi tibi; et aliter dicimus: You must mihi, quia promisisti mihi. When you say: You must mihi, quia dedi tibi, a te processit beneficium, sed mutualum, non donatum. Quando autem dicis: You must mihi, quia promisisti mihi, tu nihil dedistí, et tamen demandis. Bonitas enim eius qui promisit, dabit, ne in malitiam fides convertatur. Qui enim fallit, malus est, Deo autem numquid dicimus: Redde mihi, quia dedi tibi? Quid dedimus Deo, quando totum quod sumus, et quod habemus boni, ab illo habemus? Nihil ergo ei dedimus. This is not burned modum

voce exigamus debitorem Deum, máxime dicente nobis Apostólo: Quis enim cognovit sensum Domini?, aut quis consiliarius eius Fuit?, aut quis prior dedit Mi, et retribuetur ei? (Rom 11,34,35). Illo ergo moda possumus demandinge Dominum nostrum, ut dicamus: Redde quod promisisti, quia fecimus quod iussisti: et hoc tu fecisti, quia laborantes iuvisti. CAPOT III.—3. Vocati et praedestinati sumus gratis.—Nemo ergo dicat: Ideo me vocavit Deus, quia colui Deum. Quomodo coluisses, si vocatus non Fuisses? Si propterea te vocavit Deus, quia coluisti Deum: ergo prior dedisti, et retribuit tibi. Nonne istam tibi vocem Apostolus tollit, cum dicit: Aut quis prior dedit Mi, et retribuetur ei? Be ecce when vocatus es, vel iam eras. Quomodo praedestinareris, nisi when you were not? Quid Deo dedisti, when qui aliquid dares, weren't you? Quid ergo fecit Deus, quando praedestinavit qui non erat? Quod ait Apostolus: Qui vocat ea quae non sunt, tanquam ea quae sunt (ib., 4,17)._ Si iam esses, non praedestinareris; nisi aversus esses, non vocareris; nisi impius esses, non iustificadoreris, nisi terrenus et abiectus esses, non glorificadoreris. Quis ergo prior dedit Mi, et retribuetur ei? Quoniam ex ipso, et per ipsum, et in ipso sunt omnia. Quid ergo reddi[864]mus? Ipsi glory (Rom 11,36). Quia non eramus, quando sumus praedestinati; quia aversi eramus, quando sumus vocati; quia peccatores eramus, quando sumus iustificati: agamus Deo gratías, ne remaneamus ingrati.

4. We had set out to consider what we have already achieved of those four things and what we still hope to achieve. Even before we existed, we were already predestined. We were called when we became Christians. We certainly already have this. Are we justified yet? What does it mean to be justified? Do we dare say that we also have this? Will there be any of us who dare to say that it is fair? I think that saying that he is righteous is equivalent to saying that he is not a sinner. If you dare to say this, John comes to your attention: If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth does not dwell in us. What are we left with? Do we lack justice at all? Or do we have something, but not fullness? Let's investigate this. If we have part and lack another part, increase what we have and what we do not have will be filled. A man has been baptized, all his sins have been forgiven; as far as they are concerned it is justified, we cannot deny it. However, the fight against the flesh, against the world and the devil remains. He who fights, sometimes wounds and sometimes is wounded; He can win and he can perish; We are waiting to see how it comes out of the sand. For if we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves and the truth does not dwell in us. Likewise, if we say that we lack justice at all, we deny the gifts of God. If we lack justice at all, we also lack faith, and if we have no faith, we are not even Christians. If we have faith, some justice

we possess, do you want to know the measure of that something? The righteous live by faith; The just, I say, lives by faith, since he believes what he does not see. 5. The fathers, the holy rams, the leaders who were the apostles announced what they not only saw with their eyes, but also touched with their hands. Notwithstanding this, the Lord, reserving for us the gift of faith, to one of his disciples who had touched and handled him, who had sought and found the truth with his fingers and exclaimed: My Lord and my God, said these words: You have believed because you have seen. And with his gaze fixed on us who were coming behind, he continued: Blessed are those who believed without having seen. We have neither seen nor heard, and yet we have believed. We are called blessed, and do we lack all justice? The Lord came in the flesh to the Jews and they put Him to death; Without coming to us, we accepted him: The people whom I did not know served me and obeyed me just by hearing. These being us, do we lack all justice? Certainly not. Let's be grateful so we don't lose what we have and acquire what we don't have. Therefore, this third thing is also found in us. We have been justified, but justice grows as we progress. I am going to tell you and discuss with you in a certain way how this growth occurs, so that each one of you, now justified, that is, having obtained the forgiveness of sins through the bath of regeneration and received the Holy Spirit, and progressing from day to day, sees where he is, advances,

CAPUT IV.—4. Iustificati utrum iam simus. Luda hic in iustificatis manens.—Proposueramus autem considere de his quattuor rebus quid iam consecuti fuerimus, quid adhuc adipiscendum exspectemus. Praedestinati ertim iam sumus et antequam essemus. Vocati sumus, quando christiani facti sumus. Iam ergo et hoc habemus. Iustificati, what? Quid est, iustificati? Audemus dicere, iam hoc tertium habere nos? Et erit quisquam nostrum qui audeat dicere: Iustus sum? Puto enim hoc esse, Iustus sum, quod est, peccator non sum. Si audes hoc dicere, occurrit tibi Ioannes: Si dixerimus quia peccatum non habemus, nos ipsos decipimus, et veritas in nobis non est (1 lo 1,8). Quid ergo? Nihil habemus of iustitia? An habemus, sed non totum habemus? Hoc ergo quaeramus. Si enim aliquid habemus, et aliquid non habemus; crescat quod habemus, et implebitur quod non habemus. Ecce enim baptizad sunt nomines, omnia illis peccata dimissa sunt, iustificati sunt a peccatis; I will deny non possumus: restat tamen lucta cum carne, restat lucta cum mundo, restat lucta cum diabolo. Qui autem luctatur, aliquando ferit, aliquando percutitur; aliquando vincit, aliquando perimitur: quomodo de stadio exeat attenditur. Nam si dixerimus quia peccatum non habemus, _ nos ipsos decipimus, et veritas in nobis non est (ib.). item, si dixerimus quia iustitiae nihil habemus, adversum Dei dona mentimur. Si enim iustitiae nihil habemus, nec fidem habemus: si fidem non habemus, chris-

tiani non sumus. Si autem fidem habemus, iam aliquid habemus iustitiae. Ipsum aliquid, vis nosse quantum sit? Iustus ex fide vivit (Hab 2,3; Rom 1,17): iustus, inquam, ex fide vivit; quia credit quod non videt. CAPUT V.—5. Iustificatio aliqua veré per fidem.—Patres, arietes sancti, duces Apostoli, quando annuntiaverunt, non solum viderunt oculis, sed etiam manibus_ tractaverunt: et tamen Dominus servans nobis donum fidei, carem discipulorum suorum tractanti, palpanti, veritatem digitis inquirenti et invenienti, exclamant: Dominus meus et Deus meus; ait ipse Dominus et Deus: Quia vidisti, credidisti. And our future intuens: Beati, inquit, qui non viderunt et crediderunt (lo 20,28.29). Non vidimus, audimus.et credidimus. Beati praedicti sumus, et de iustitia nihil habemus? Venit Dominus carnaliter ad Iudaeos, et occisus est: non venit ad nos, et acceptus est. Populus quem non cognovi, servivit mihi, in obauditu auris oboedivit mihi (Ps 17,45). Nos sumus, et de iustitia nihil habemus? Omnino habemus. Grati simus ex eo quod habemus: ut addatur quod non habemus, et non perdamus quod habemus. Ergo et hoc tertium iam agitur in nobis. Iustificati sumus: sed ipsa iustitia, cum proficimus, crescit. Et quomodo crescit dicam, et vobiscum quodammo conferam; ut unus [865] quisque vestrum iam in ipsa iustificatione constitutus, accepta scilicet remissione peccatorum per lavacrum regenerationis, accepto Spiritu sancto, proficiens de die in diem, videat ubi sit, ac-

progress and grow until reaching consummation, not understood as an end, but as perfection. 6. Man begins with faith. What is proper to faith? Believe. But even this faith must be distinguished from that of unclean spirits. What is proper to faith? Believe. But here is what the apostle James says: The demons also believe and tremble. If you only have faith and live without hope or lack love, think: The demons also believe, and tremble. What is so great about saying that Christ is God? Peter said it and heard: Blessed are you, Simon, son of Jonah; But the demons also said it and heard: Be silent. Peter was called blessed because it was not revealed to you by flesh and blood, but by my Father who is in heaven. The demons, however, heard: Be silent. They say the same thing as Peter and are rejected. They say the same thing, but the Lord looks at the root, not the flower. That is why he says in the letter to the Hebrews: So that no bitter root when it sprouts causes discomfort and many become contaminated by it. First of all, then, distinguish your faith from that of demons. As? The demons said it with fear; Peter, with love: Add, therefore, hope to faith. And what hope is there that does not arise from a certain goodness of conscience? Add love to the same hope. According to the Apostle, we have an excellent way: I show you an excellent way: Although I speak in the tongues of men and angels, if I do not have charity, I am like sounding brass or a clanging cymbal. This is how he lists the other assets,

confirming that without charity they are useless. Therefore, let the three remain: faith, hope and charity; but the greatest of all is charity. Pursue charity; Discern your faith, then. You are part of the group of the predestined, the called and the justified. The apostle Paul says: Neither circumcision nor the foreskin is worth anything; only the je has value. Say something else, oh Apostle! adds something and distinguishes: The demons also believe, and tremble; add and distinguish, for demons also believe what they hate, and tremble. Distinguish, O Apostle, mark the limits of my faith and separate my cause from that of unholy people. Without a doubt, it distinguishes, separates and delimits it: Faith, he says, that works out of love. 7. Let each one of you, my brothers, look inside, judge yourself and examine your works, your good works; See what you do for love, no. waiting for some temporal retribution, but for the promise and face of God. Nothing God promised you is worth anything apart from himself. God would satisfy me with nothing, except with the promise of himself. What is the whole earth? What the immensity of the sea? What all the sky? What are all the stars, the sun, the moon? What the army of angels? I thirst for the creator of all these things; I hunger and thirst for him and to him I say: In you is the source of life, and, in turn, he tells me: I am the bread that came down from heaven. Caritas.—Incipit homo a fide: quid pertinet ad fidem? Credere. Sed adhuc ista fides discernatur ab immundis spiritibus. Ad fidem quid pertinet? Credere. Sed ait apostolus Iacobus: Et daemones credunt, et contremiscunt (Iac 2,19). Si tantum credis, et sine spe vivis, vel dilectionem non habes: Et daemones credunt, et contremiscunt. Quid magnum est, if you say Christum Filium Dei? Hoc dixit Petrus, et audivit: Beatus es Simón Bar lona: hoc dixerunt daemones, et audierunt: Obmutescite. lile beatus, dicitur ei: Quia non revelavit tibi caro et sanguis, sed Pater meus qui in caelis est (Mt 16,17). lili autem audiunt: Obmutescite (Mark 1,23): et hoc ipsum dicunt, et repelluntur. Una vox est: sed Dominus radicem interrogat, non florem. Unde dicitur ad Hebraeos: Ne qua radix amaritudinis sursum germinans molestet, et per illam contaminantur multi (Hebr 12,15). Prius ergo discerne fidem tuam a fide daemonis. Where do you discern? Daemones hoc dixerunt timendo, Petrus amando. Adde ergo fideí spem. Et quae spes est, nisi de aliqua conscientiae bonitote? Speique ipsi adde caritatem. Desuper eminentem viam habemus, dicente Apostólo: Supereminentem viam vobis demonstro: Si linguis hominum loquar et Angelorum, caritatem autem non habeam,

factus sum velut aeramentum sonans, aut cymbalum tinniens: et cetera enarrat bona, et sine caritate nihil prodesse confirmat. Maneant ergo haec, fides, spes, caritas: maior autem horum caritas (cf. 1 Cor 12:31; 13). Sectamini caritatem. Discernite ergo fidem vestram. Iam estis de praedestinatis, vocatis, iustificatis. Paulus Apostolus dicit: Ñeque circumcisio aliquid valet, ñeque praeputium; be faithful. Dic adhuc, Apostóle, adde, discern; quia, Et daemones credunt et contremiscunt (Iac 2,19): ergo adde et discerne, daemones enim credunt, et contremiscunt quod oderunt. Distinguish, Apostle, et circumeide fidem meam, et discerne causam meam de gente non sancta (c£. Ps 42,1). Plan distinguishit, discernit, circumeidit. Omnium istorum Creatorem site: ipsum esurio, ipsum site, ipsi dico: Quoniam apud te est fons vitae (Ps 35,10). Qui mihi dicit: Ego sum pañis qui de cáelo descendí (lo 6,41). Esuriat et sitiat pere-

hunger and thirst for you, so that it may be satisfied with your presence. The world smiles at many things, beautiful, resistant and varied, but the one who made them is more beautiful, more resistant, more resplendent, softer. I will be satisfied when your glory is revealed. If faith that works through charity exists in you, you belong to the group of those predestined, called and justified. So let it grow in you. Faith that works through charity cannot exist without hope. At the end, will faith exist there? Will we still be told: "Believe"? Certainly not. We will see him and contemplate him. Dearly beloved, we are children of God and what we will be has not yet been revealed. Since it has not yet manifested, faith is necessary. We are children of God, predestined children, called, justified; We are children of God and what we will be has not yet been revealed. Therefore, for now, faith is needed until what we will be is revealed. We know that when he appears, we will be like him. By virtue of faith? No. Because we will see him as he is. 8. What to say about hope? Will it exist there? It will cease to exist when the expected reality becomes present. Hope is also necessary during the pilgrimage; It is she who comforts us along the way. The traveler who gets tired on the road, endures the fatigue because he hopes to reach the goal. Take away his hope of arriving, and his strength will instantly be broken. Therefore, hope in the present time is also part of the justice of our peregrigrinatio mea, ut satietur praesentia mea. Arridet mundus multis rebus, pulchris, fortibus, variis: pulchrior est ille qui fecit, fortior et clarior ille qui fecit, suavior ille est qui fecit. Fides enim quae per dilectionem operatur; sine spe esse non potest. Cum autem venerimus, iam erit ibi fides? dicetur nobis, Crede? Don't utique. Videbimus eum, contemplabimur eum. Dilectissimi, filii Dei sumus, et nondum apparuit quod erimus. Quia nondum apparuit, ideo fides Filii Dei sumus, praedestinati, vocati, iustificati: filii Dei sumus, et nondum apparuit quod erimus. Mode ergo fides, antequam appareat quod erimus. Scimus quod cum apparuerit, similes ei erimus. Numquid quia credimus? No. Quare ergo? Quoniam videbimus eum sicuti est (1 lo 3,2). CAPUT VIII.—8.

Spes, in hac peregrinatione sólatium.—Quid spes? erit ibi? Spes iam non erit, quando erit res. Etenim ipsa spes peregrinationi necessaria est, ipsa est quae consolatur in via. Viator enim quando laborat ambulando, ideo laborem tolerat, quia pervenire sperat. Tolle illi spem perveniendi, continuo franguntur vires ambulandi. Ergo et spes quae hic est, ad iustitíam pertinet peregrinationis nostrae. Ipsum Aposto

nation. Listen to the Apostle himself: While we wait for adoption, we still groan within ourselves. Where there are groans, one cannot speak of that happiness of which the Scripture says: The fatigue and tears have passed. Therefore, he says, we still groan within ourselves, while we wait for the adoption, the redemption of our body. We still moan, why? We have been saved in hope. The hope that is seen is not hope. If someone sees something, how can they expect it? If, on the other hand, we wait for what we do not see, through patience we wait for it. For this patience the martyrs were crowned; They desired what they did not see and despised suffering. Founded on this hope they said: Who will separate us from the love of Christ? The tribulation? The anguish? The chase? Hunger? The nudity? The sword? Because for you... Where is the for who? Because for you we go to death every day. For you. And where is it: Blessed are those who did not see and believed? Look where it is: it is in you, because your own faith is in you. Or does the Apostle deceive us when he says that Christ dwells in our hearts through faith? Now dwell by faith, then by vision; by faith while we are on the way, while our pilgrimage lasts. While we are in the body, we wander away from the Lord; We walk in faith, not in vision. 9. If this is faith, what will be the vision? Listen to it: God will be all in all: What is all? so my moans. In the homeland there will be no place for prayer, but only for praise. Why not stop prayer? Because nothing will be missing. What is an object of faith here will be an object of vision there; what is hoped for here will be possessed there; What is asked for here is received there. However, in this life there is a certain perfection, achieved by the holy martyrs. This is due to the ecclesiastical custom, known to the faithful, of mentioning the name of the martyrs before the altar of God, and not to pray for them, but for the remaining deceased of whom mention is made. It is an insult to pray for a martyr, to whose prayers we must entrust ourselves. He fought against sin until he shed his blood. To some, still imperfect, but undoubtedly partially justified, the Apostle says in the letter to the Hebrews: You have not yet resisted to the point of shedding blood in your fight against sin. If they had not yet shed blood, it is because others had done so. Who went so far as to shed their blood? The holy martyrs, to whom the reading of the holy apostle James referred. My brothers, consider your greatest joy to endure the various trials. This is said to those already perfect, who, in turn, can say: Try me, Lord, and tempt me. Knowing, he says, that tribulation produces patience and patience produces perfect work. 2. Justice must therefore be loved, but in this love of justice there are different degrees, according to the progress of each one.

The first is not to put anything that pleases before justice. This is the first degree. What have I said? May justice be the most delighting among all that delights you; It is not that you do not like other things, but that justice pleases you more. There are certain things that naturally delight our weakness, as food and drink do to the hungry and thirsty; how we delight in this light that expands from the sky once the sun has risen, or that which comes from the stars and the moon or that which is lit on the earth with torches that dissipate the darkness from the eyes; We are delighted by a sweet voice and a soft song, and the good smell; Anything that is related to any pleasure of the flesh also delights our touch. Of these things that delight our bodily senses, some are lawful. As I said, the great spectacles of nature cause delight to the eyes, but also the spectacles of theaters. The first is legal, the second illegal. The sacred psalm sung softly, but also the songs of the actors, cause delight to the ear. The first is legal, the second illegal. The flowers and aromas, creatures of God, cause delight to the sense of smell, but also the incense on the altars of demons. That is legal, this is illegal. Not forbidden food causes delight to the taste, but also the sacrificial banquets.

An answer that would not be true if it did not give you a certain delight, since you only love what delights. Delight yourself in the Lord, says the Scripture. The Lord is justice. You should not represent God as a statue. God is like the invisible things, and in us the best is the invisible. Faith is better than flesh, than gold, than silver, money, fields; better than family and wealth, although these things are seen and, on the other hand, faith is not. What, then, will we think that God is more similar to, the visible or the invisible? to the precious or the vile? I am going to talk about the most vile things. Suppose you have two servants, one with a deformed body and the other full of beauty, but while the deformed one is faithful, the other is unfaithful. Tell me which of the two you love more and I will prove that you love more what is not seen. Or was it that by loving the faithful, although deformed, servant more than the beautiful, but unfaithful, servant, you made a mistake and put the ugly before the beautiful? It is beautiful, I do not deny it, because if I denied it I would be an insult to the Creator. The tempter approaches and says to you: “If you do not bear false testimony in my favor, I will take your gold; If, however, you say it, I will give you even more. Both delights fight within you; Now I ask which one you put ahead, which one is preferable to you: gold or truth; gold or false testimony. Does one thing shine and not the other? In true testimony what is sought is truth and fidelity. Does gold shine, but not fidelity? Be ashamed, have eyes. Give to your Lord what you loved in your servant. Recently, when I asked you about your two servants, one deformed, but faithful, and the other beautiful, but unfaithful, you indicated which one you loved more; you responded fairly, putting before it what should be put before it. Return now to yourself, for it is you we are dealing with. No doubt you loved the faithful servant. Does not your Lord deserve to have a faithful servant in you? What did you promise your faithful servant? If you loved him very much, the supreme prize of freedom. What is so extraordinary about that promise made to your servant? It is freedom, yes, but temporary. Do we not often see many servants who need nothing, while others who are free have to beg? To whom you promised freedom you demanded fidelity, and are you not faithful to those who promise you eternity?

6. It would be too long to review all the senses, but you can apply what I said about the eyes to the rest. Put the delight of the mind before the delight of the flesh. Illicit pleasures undoubtedly delight your flesh; Let your mind delight in invisible, beautiful, chaste, holy justice, full of harmony and sweetness, so as not to submit to it out of fear. If you submit out of fear, it does not yet delight you. You must avoid sin, not for fear of punishment, but for love of justice. That is why the Apostle says: I speak to you in a human way, in consideration of the weakness of your flesh. As before you gave your members to the service of impurity and iniquity to work iniquity, now lend your members to the service of justice with a view to sanctification. What does it mean: I speak to you in a human way? I tell you what you can bear. When you lent your members to iniquity to commit foolishness, did you do so moved by fear, or invited by pleasure? What do you answer? We all respond, because even those of you who live well now, perhaps once lived poorly. When you committed sin, you delighted in it. What led you to sin: fear or the sweetness of it? You will answer: sweetness. It is gentleness that leads to sin, and is it going to be fear that pushes you towards justice? Examine yourselves, probe your interior. Even if he who threatens takes our gold, justice is softer and more resplendent. Glory in the Lord
Theme: Glory in the Lord (1 Cor 1:31). Place: Carthage. Date: Probably in 397.

1. The Apostle's recommendation is clear: Whoever glories, let him glory in the Lord; in the Lord to whom we have sung: Deliver me through your righteousness and save me. This is boasting in the Lord: glorying in his righteousness, not your own. Divine justice that was hidden from those who boast of their own. This vice was especially evident in the Jews, who rejected the New Testament and anchored themselves in the old man. In vain they had read and sung what was written in their codices: Deliver me for your justice. Ignoring God's justice and wanting to establish their own, they did not submit to God's. Let no one, even if he is just, boast of his justice. To him who did this it was said: What do you have that you have not received? Therefore, whoever boasts, let him boast in the Lord. What is that science that they lack, even though they have zeal for God?... Do you want to hear what science they lack? Pay attention to what follows: Ignoring God's justice, they wanted to maintain their own and did not submit to God's. Therefore, if you have zeal for God and want to have it according to science, belonging to the new alliance, to which the Jews could not belong because their zeal for God was not according to science, recognize that justice is from God and do not want to attribute it to yourself, if you have any. If you live righteously, if you fulfill the commandments of God, do not put it to your credit, because this is what it means to want to maintain one's own righteousness. The condition to possess what you have received is to recognize from whom you have received it. You have nothing that you have not received. Theme: Fornication, healthy fear, the strength of love (1 Cor 6:9-19). Location: Unknown. Date: Unknown.

1. In the reading we hear how the Apostle corrected and repressed human passions. He himself said: Do you not know that your bodies are members of Christ? Am I going to take the members of Christ to make them members of a prostitute? Be no way. He clearly said that our bodies are members of Christ, since Christ is our head in that he became man for us. He is the head of which it was said: He Himself is the Savior of our body. His body is the Church. Therefore, if our Lord Jesus Christ had only taken the human soul, only its members would be our souls; But since he also took the body, by virtue of which he is head for us who consist of soul and body, for this very reason our bodies are also his members. Consequently, if someone desiring to commit fornication degrades himself and despises himself in his own body, at least he does not despise himself.

Tota exaggeratio calamitatis est, quia Following the Christianization of the empire that followed the conversion of Constantine, bishops frequently became officials of the State, with judicial powers. Augustine had become the judge of the city (see also sermon 167,4; Commentary on Psalm 25,2,13), an office that displeased him extremely (Caria 48,1), and not only because of the many hours he spent on such a task, since, according to Possidius, his biographer, sometimes the audience lasted until mealtime and other times he had to spend the entire day fasting for that reason (Life 19; also Letter 139,3). He cannot put to death your flesh in any other way than by causing the departure of the soul by which your flesh lives. In fact, your flesh lives thanks to the presence of the soul, and as long as the soul is present in your flesh, it will necessarily live. Whoever seeks your death, what he wants is to cast out of your flesh the life for which your flesh lives. Do you think there is no other life for your soul to live for? Your soul is a certain life, thanks to which your flesh lives. Don't you believe that there is another life through which your own soul lives or that, as your flesh has a life, the soul through which your flesh lives, your own soul, has a life of its own? Don't you think that just as when the flesh dies the soul, its life, expires, so when the soul dies, some of its life expires? Let us find, then, what this life is, not that of your body, which is your soul, but the life of the life of your body, the life of your soul. Once found, I think that more than this death by which you fear that the soul will be thrown out of your flesh, you must fear that other, so that the life that nourishes it will not be thrown out of your soul. 3. What was said referred specifically to bodily fornication. It must be said, because in Holy Scripture not only is this specific fornication mentioned and recriminated, but also another more generic one. Let's try with God's help to say something reasonable about it. This fornication, in a general sense, appears clearly in the psalm that says: For behold, those who turn away from you will perish; you lost everyone who fornicates away from you. And then, to show how one can evade and flee from this generic fornication, he added: For me it is good to adhere to God. From this it can be easily seen that the generic fornication of the human soul is that by which someone, instead of adhering to God, adheres to the world. Therefore the blessed apostle John says: If anyone loves the world, the love of the Father does not reside in him. In turn, the apostle James: Adulterers, do you not know that the friendship of this world is the enemy of God? With a few words it was defined that he who loves the world cannot possess the love of God, and that he who wants to be a friend of the world is an enemy of God. This is also referred to by what the Lord says in the Gospel: No one can serve two masters, for either he hates one and loves the other, or he suffers one and despises the other. And he concludes: You cannot serve God and money. This, then, as I already said, is fornication in the general sense of the soul, which encompasses in itself absolutely everything, and which contains

It consists in adhering to the world and not to God. And so we can also understand, applied to this fornication, the words of the Apostle: Any sin that a man commits remains outside the body; but whoever commits fornication sins against his own body. In fact, if the human soul does not fornicate, that is, it adheres to God and not to the world, man could incur any other sins, completely unrelated to carnal concupiscence, due to the very fragility of the mortal condition or due to ignorance, or due to negligence, forgetfulness or lack of intelligence, referring to this in the words: Any sin that man commits remains outside the body, since no sin can be found here as a result of bodily or temporal concupiscence; rightly, then, it may be said that any such sins are external to the body. But if a worldly man, adhering to the world, turns away from God, committing fornication away from God himself, he sins against his own body, since the human spirit is drawn to any temporal and carnal goods by bodily lust, by the sensitivity and prudence of the flesh, and is dissipated by serving the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever. 4. It is outside the evil that is all bodily and temporal concupiscence. For only through the evil of carnal lust in the broad sense does the soul fortify itself against God in any kind of sin. In this case, the soul, as if bound and imprisoned by bodily and temporal desires and delights, sins against its own body, always putting itself at the service of its concupiscence; it leans towards the world and moves away from God, which is what it means, as has already been said: The beginning of man's pride is apostasy from God. To guard against this evil of fornication in the generic sense, the blessed John exhorts us with these words: Do not love the world or what is in it, because what is in the world is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes and worldly ambition, which do not come from the Father, but from the world. Thus, then, this love of the world that encompasses in itself all worldly concupiscence is generic fornication, or in the broad sense, by which one sins against one's own body, due to the fact that the human spirit, helpless and abandoned from the Creator of all, incessantly serves all bodily desires and pleasures, visible and temporal. corpus esse; id est, extra corporeae et temporalis omnis concupiscentíae malum, alienum esse, extra corpus, ut saepe dictum est, esse. And the Apostle, indicating that one has greater love for the eyes than for the other members, to show oneself loved by the Church of God, says: I bear witness in your favor that, if it had been possible, you would have put out your eyes and given them to me. There is, therefore, nothing in the body more sublime and more respected than the eyes and there is perhaps nothing more in the extremity of the body than the little toe of the foot. Even if this is the case, however, it is advisable that there are fingers in the body and that they are healthy, before they become an eye covered in slime due to some condition, since health, common to all members, is more precious than the functions of each one of them. So you see that in the Church a man has some small gift and, yet, he has charity; perhaps you will see in the same Church another more eminent, with a greater gift, who, however, has no charity. Be quid commune in omnibus. Officia diverse sunt, sanitas una est. Hoc est ergo in membris Christi caritas, quod est in membris corporis sanitas. Meliori loco positus est oculus, in eminenti, et tanquam ad consilium in arce constitutus, unde prospiciat, unde videat, unde ostendat: honor magnus in oculis, et loco, et sensu ardentiore, et agilítate, et vi quadam, quam cetera membra non habent. Proinde plerumque homines per oculos suos iurant, quam per quodlibet alterum membrum. Nemo alicui dixit: Sic te diligo quomodo aures meas; et est aurium sensus oculis suppar et proximus. What is ceteris dicam? Every day I say homines: Sic te diligo tanquam oculos meos.

Et apostolus significans maiorem in oculis haberi dilectionem, quam in ceteris membris, cum se dilectum ab ecclesia dei diceret, ait: Testimonium enim vobis perhibeo, quia, si fieri posset, oculos vestros eruissetis, et dedissetis mihi (Gal 4,15). Nihil ergo in corpore sublimius oculis et honoratius; et nihil in corpore extremius fortasse, quam digitus minimus pedis. Cum ita sint, expedit tamen in corpore digitum esse, et sanum esse, quam oculum esse, et in perturbatíone lippire: sanitas enim, quae communis est ómnibus membris, pretiosior est officiis singulorum. Ita vides in ecclesia hominem parvum aliquod donum habentem, et tamen habentem caritatem: alterum eminentem forte in

the first the furthest finger, and the second the eye; The one who was able to obtain health, that is the one who contributes the most to the body as a whole. Finally, any member that becomes sick in it is a nuisance to the entire body, and, in truth, all the members contribute their collaboration so that the one who is sick heals and most of the time it heals. But if it has not healed and the rot generated indicates the impossibility of this, the good of all is considered in such a way that it is separated from the unity of the body. 7. Suppose I don't know which Donato was an eye in the body; suppose that was it; We do not know what it was, but suppose it was what it is said to have been; What good did such excellent honor and glory do to him? He could not enjoy health, because he had no charity. Furthermore, such are so rotten that they must necessarily be amputated; and when they say that they have others with them, these are worms of rot: they are worms amputated from the body, incapable of admitting health. In fact, as long as a member is capable of health insofar as it is not separated from the body, health flows from the other healthy members and flows to the place of the wound; But once the limb where the wound is located has been amputated, health can no longer find where and from where to get there. For this reason they are also compared to pruned branches, the apostolic reading showing agreement with that of the Gospel. In order not to move from here, the Lord strongly recommended nothing else to us but charity: ecclesia aliquo maiore dono, [104] et tamen non habentem caritatem. lile sit extremus digitus, ule sit oculus: ille magis pertinet ad corporis compaginem, qui potuit obtinere sanitatem. Denique molestum est corpori cetero, quicquid aegrotatit in corpore; et datur quidem ab ómnibus membris opera, ut sanetur quod aegrotum est, et plerumque sanatur. Si autem sanatum non fuerit, et tantam putredinem conceperit quae sanari non possit, ita consulitur omnibus membris, ut de corporis compage praecidatur. 7. Fuerit ergo nescio quis Donatus quasi oculus in corpore, fuerit ita; non scimus qualis fuerit, sed prorsus talis fuerit qualis dicitur; quid illi profuit excellentia honoris et gloriae? Tenere non potuit sanitatem, quia non habuit caritatem. Denique ita isti putrefacti sunt, ut necessario praeciderentur; et quod se habere aliquos dicunt, vermes putredinis sunt: ​​praecisi vermes sunt, nec sanitatem possunt admitiere.

Etenim tandiu membrum admittit sanitatem, quandiu est de corpore non praecisum: de ceteris enim sanis manat sanitas ad vulneris locum; cum autem fuerit praecisum membrum ubi vulnus est, qua et unde ad illud sanitas veniat, non invenitur. Ideo et sarmentis praecisis comparantur, et concurrit cum apostolica lectione evangélica lectio. Et ibi enim dominus, ut maneamus in illo, non nobis máxime commendavit nisi
