Antequam iudicaret, bonus iudex erat,_cui dixisti: Non sum haereticus, audi me. Sed iudicavit proconsul, inquit, secundum leges imperatorum, non secundum leges evangelii. Ita fecerit, secundum leges imperatorum proconsul iudicaverit: si ergo male contra te iudicant imperatores, quare a proconsule ad eorum iudicium provocasti? Iam werent leges imperatorum contra te, an nondum weret? Si nondum erant, non secundum ipsas proconsul judicavit; Yes, this Crispinus was a Donatist bishop of the city of Calama, where, on the Catholic side, Saint Posidius, Augustine's friend and biographer, was from. As a result of the abuses of a clergyman of his and the same name against the aforementioned Posidius, he was taken to court, which sentenced him to pay the fine that was imposed on him for having been declared a heretic. He appealed to the proconsul, rejecting the accusation of heresy. After several meetings between the two bishops of the Calama city, Crispinus was condemned as a heretic, although he did not have to pay the fine thanks to the intercession of the Catholic bishop. Not happy with the sentence, he finally appealed to the emperor, who sentenced him as the previous judges had done. Once again he was free to pay the fine imposed thanks to the intercession of the Catholic bishops, especially Augustine. See Life 12, written by Saint Posidius, and Against Cresconius, Donatist grammarian III 47,50-51.

The report written by the proconsul Anulinus to the emperor Constantine is preserved, in which it is recorded that men from Majorinus' side appeared before him carrying with them the libels of accusation against Caecilian and asking him to send them to the emperor, and that he did what they asked. In the same letter the emperor writes that he passed them the document that had been sent to him by Anulinus; From that letter it is not possible to know what documents these are, but they are known from Anulino's relationship, which today is found in public domain codices. He was better than you, because you transferred him to the emperor, and he, to the bishops. The matter was sentenced in a court of bishops, they being the first to accuse. They, dissatisfied with the ecclesiastical ruling, began to murmur, and appeared before the emperor again, requesting an imperial court after the episcopal ruling. They con-

another ecclesiastical court at Arles 6 yielded, and they themselves appealed to the emperor in person from this same judgment. Overcome by his impertinence, he wanted to take the matter into his own hands and meet him in person. He took him, met him, and declared Caecilian absolutely innocent, and from this moment the laws of the emperors against them began. What's strange about it? Do you dare to reject the sentence of the one from whom you requested it? Why did you want to take the trial to its jurisdiction? You had the Church in Africa; Didn't you have it all over the world too? But how to go to the place from which they had already separated? They were no longer united to the Church, but to the emperor, before whom the trial was held. That is why he, in his meekness, wanted the bishops to judge, and then he gave in to their wishes until he became judge himself. From then come the laws contrary to you; see if not against you. First of all, you yourselves were responsible: you were the first accusers, you were the ones who, lastly, appealed, and you were the ones who did not stop murmuring. "Have I been defeated, he said, with the Gospel in my hand?" You were defeated in that court that you yourself chose. 9. "But we do not reject the sentence of the Gospel." Certainly, even if he did not say it, we would read it, we would bring it out, we would manifest it. Read the Gospel: let's see where the Lord Jesus Christ says the Church is. Let's listen to him, let him tell us where the Church is. If he says that his Church is in Africa, let us all run to Donato's party; If it says that it is in the entire globe of the earth, the amputated limbs return to the body: the breaking of the branches is not such that they cannot be grafted again. You have the apostle Paul who states: But you say, "The branches have been broken off, that I may be grafted in." Well, they broke away through unbelief, and you, on the other hand, remain in faith. Do not be conceited, but fear, for if God did not spare the natural branches, he will not forgive you either. The Jews had been broken off like natural branches and the Gentiles were grafted in, like a wild olive tree on the olive tree. Through these branches and this olive tree, grafted, we all participate in the olive tree. But, as the Apostle had threatened the branches of the olive tree that were becoming proud, with their pride they became such that they also deserved to be cut off for their pride, just like the natural branches broken off previously. But what does the Apostle say? They too will be grafted unless they remain in unfaithfulness; You too will be broken off if you do not continue in the faith. Let no one, therefore, be proud of being in the vine, nor let anyone despair of being outside of it. If you become arrogant while in the vine, be careful not to be cut; If you are outside the vine, do not lose hope, dare to be grafted. But they are not to be grafted with their own hands, for the Apostle says: God is able to graft them in again. Do not say: "And how can a thing separated, a branch broken off, be grafted again?" with

You rightly say that it is not possible, if you have your eye on human possibilities, but not if you consider divine majesty. What to say then? Can a farmer do what has already been done by the Lord? He took an olive tree and grafted it to the olive tree, and the olive tree grafted on the olive tree did not produce bitter berries, but olives. Do this now someone else, graft the wild olive tree into the olive tree, and you will see that the wild olive tree produces nothing but berries. God showed his power, not in grafting the olive tree into the olive tree, but the olive tree into the olive tree and in making the olive tree partake of the softness of the olive tree, so that, stripped of bitterness, it was clothed in softness; and will it not have the power to graft itself through humility to you who had broken off through pride? «Your exhortation is good, you say; But first show me that I have been broken off, lest you must exhort yourself to come to me instead of exhorting me to be grafted into you.” I dare to say: "Listen to me" and yet I am afraid to say: "Listen to me"; I fear he despises man. Furthermore, I urge you to despise man, for if you despised man you would not belong to Donato's party. Donato was, indeed, a man. Therefore, if we speak our own words, let us be despised, but if we repeat the Lord's words, let us listen to him, who is neither listened to nor freely despised: listening to him leads to reward, and not listening to him leads to punishment. Let's listen to him; Let him be the one who speaks to us.

resurrection he manifested himself to his disciples, he revealed his scars to them, he was willing to be touched and not just to be seen. Are you in communion with all peoples? Are you in communion with that Church that has spread to all peoples, beginning with Jerusalem? In us, however, the presence of majesty walks if it finds the breadth of charity. Exhorting us to this, the Apostle says: Enlarge yourselves, so as not to join forces with the unbelievers. If we expand, God walks in us; but the fact that we enlarge ourselves is the work of God himself. Has it been because he is spiritual that he has ended this life, which in its entirety is a temptation on earth? Therefore, very appropriately and rightly, he was told: Keep an eye on yourself, lest you also be tempted. And after having given the warning to them, that is, to the spiritual ones, he then wrote that more general phrase: Bear each other's burdens, and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ. What does it mean for some to carry the burdens of others? Let the carnal man bear the burden of another carnal man, and the spiritual man bear the burden of another spiritual man. Bear each other's sins, that is, do not ignore each other's sins. If evil desires devour you, commit iniquities daily to satisfy them and seek those who praise you. Believe me, you will find nothing but flatterers or seducers. In what sense flatterers or seducers? I must explain my words. Those are flatterers who know that you do wrong and yet praise you; On the other hand, those who praise you when you do wrong, thinking that what you do is good, are not flatterers, since they praise from the heart, but they are seducers, because by repeating their praise they seduce you to do evil and do not let you breathe. In effect, you leave after empty applause, you think that what you do is good, you lose your property, you empty your house and leave

Naked your children. Those praises made you foolish: you run, you move your hands, you receive favors, you put them at the door; you plant your house and collect winds. "How, you ask, are these my seducers if they praise me from the heart?" They are your seducers because before, from error, they seduced themselves. Or is it that someone who seduces himself is going to make an effort to put stairs next to you with an intention other than to seduce you? Therefore the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and he who works wickedly is blessed. Beware of those who praise you in this way and avoid those who bless you in this way. Furthermore, do good. "But, you say, if I do it, I will displease so-and-so." —"Displease him and please God, for if you displease him by pleasing God, you will have the glory in yourself and not in another." But the bad despoil the good, and the lovers of this world curse those who despise it, they insult them, they are on the hunt for something to reproach them; to such a point that, if something bad is said about them, they immediately believe it, and if something good is proclaimed, they do not want to believe it, and your heart is disturbed to the point of fainting in good works because no one has appeared to praise you, flatter you or seduce you, and the testimony of your conscience is not enough for you, in the theater of your interior, before the presence of God. "Why are you troubled, I beseech you, why are you troubled?" "Because there are many bad things they say about me." —«Do you have to say this? You would not be disturbed in the ship of your heart if Christ were not asleep in it.

Carry each other's burdens

Theme: Bearing each other's burdens (Gal 6:2-5). Location: Hippo. Date: In the year 411. 1. Through the Apostle's mouth, the truth exhorts us all to mutually carry our burdens, and in the same invitation he showed us the fruit that we will obtain from this by adding: And thus you will fulfill the law of Christ, a law that we will not fulfill unless we mutually carry our burdens. I will endeavor to show you with the help of the Lord what these burdens are and how they are to be borne, since we must all, to the best of our ability, try to fulfill the law of Christ. Do not forget to demand from me what I have set out to show you, and when I have fulfilled it, do not bother me again. What I have proposed to show, feeling helped by the Lord and by your prayers, my intention is this: what are the burdens that the Lord commands us to carry mutually and how it should be done. If we fulfill it, what he put the fruit into will automatically be realized, namely: the fulfillment of the law of Christ.
DE VERBIS APOSTOLI, GAL 6,2-5: «INVICEM ONERA VESTRA BEAR YOURSELF»; ET OF ISTIS: “UNUSQUISQUE ONUS SUUM PORTABIT”. AGAINST DONATISTAS, PAULO POST HABITAM CARTHAGINE COLLATIONEM PRONUNTIATUS

CAPUT I.—1. Lex Christi a portantibus invicem onera sua impletur. Omnes nos per Apostolum admonet veritas, ut invicem onera nostra portemus: et in eo ipso quo nos admonet, ut invicem onera nostra portemus, quo fructu id faciamus ostendit, adiungens et dices: Et sic adimplebitis legem Christi (Gal 6:2): quae non implebitur, nisi invicem onera nostra portemus. Quae sint onera ista, et quemadmodum portanda sint, [896] quoniam quidem omnes pro nostris viribus conari debenmus implere legem Christi, adiuvante Domino conabor ostendere. Quod me demonstraturum esse proposui, mementote ut exigatis: et cum reddidero, non petatis. Hoc me demonstraturum esse proposui, adiuvante Domino intentionem meam et pro me orationes vestras, quae sint onera quae invicem nos iubet ut portemus Apostolus, et quemadmodum portanda sint. Hoc si fecerimus, illud ubi fructum posit, sua sponte consequetur, ut impleamus legem Christi.

2. Someone will say: "The Apostle did not speak here with excessive clarity, and you intend to explain what these burdens are and how they are to be carried?" There is a point there that forces us to distinguish charges from charges. In the same text you read you find this: But each one will carry his own burden. The following has already occurred to your sensitivity: If each one has to carry his own burden, how does it say: Carry each other's burdens? Therefore, we must distinguish burdens from burdens so that the Apostle does not seem to contradict himself. Both things: that each one has to carry his own burden and the warning and invitation to mutually carry ours, he did not write on different occasions, nor in different letters, or in the same one, but one thing before and another much later, but in the same place, so that the words are one next to the other. 3. There are burdens in which each one carries his own, without sharing it or leaving it to another, and there are others in which you can just say to your brother: "I'll help you carry it" or "I'll carry it in your place." If, then, it is necessary to distinguish, understanding is not easy. Contradicting those who thought that man can be contaminated by the sins of others, the Apostle responds: Each one must carry his own burden. Furthermore, against those who because of this may be tempted by laziness, so that, having acquired the security that they are not contaminated by the sins of others, they do not worry about correcting anyone, he says: Bear each other's burdens. I have said it 2. Onera distinctionnda.—Dicit aliquis: Obscure enim apostolus locutus est, ut tu coneris exposere quae sint ista onera, vel quemadmodum invicem sustinenda? Est illic quaestio, quae nos cogit onera distinguishe. Et in ipso quippe capitulo lectionis habes ibi positum: Unusquisque autem proprium onus portabit (ib., 5). Iam ergo occurrit sensibus vestris, Si unusquisque onus proprium portabit, quomodo dicit, Invicem onera vestra pórtate? (ibid., 2). Nisi quia onera distinctionda sunt, ne sibi contra loqui putetur Apostolus. Non enim longe, non enim in alia Epistle non enim in hac ipsa longe superius aut inferius; sed in eo ipso loco, ita ut sibi sint eadem verba contigua, utrumque posuit, et quia unusquisque proprium onus portabit, et quod admonuit et hortatus est, ut invicem onera nostra portemus. CAPUT II.—3.

Onerum duo genera.—Alia ergo sunt onera, in quibus unusquisque proprium portat, nec portat cum alio alter, nec proicit in alterum; et alia sunt onera, in quibus recte dicis fratri, Porto tecum, aut Porto pro te. Si ergo distinctione opus est, non est facilis intellectus. Contra eos ergo quí putabant posse hominem contaminan peccatis alienis, responder Apostolus: Unusquisque onus proprium portabit. item, contra eos quibus per hoc possit neglegentia subintrare, ut quasi securi facti quod non contaminarentur peccatis alienis, neminem curarent corrigere: Invicem onera vestra pórtate. briefly, and briefly I have made the distinction, and I believe without preventing the truth from being manifest. In fact, you have heard few words, and you understood it immediately. I have not seen your hearts, but I have the voices of the heart as witnesses. Now, with the certainty that you have understood, let us talk a little more carefully, not with a view to further understanding, but to recommend what has already been understood. 4. The orator who addresses the entire world, from the kind of tribune of his exalted authority, exclaims: «Listen, human race; Listen, children of Adam; Hey, race that toils in vain; I see your sweat, see my gift. The one who cries out is Christ, the teacher, the Son

only one of God, the only true, authentic one; the truth shouts: Learn from me. That? That in the beginning the Word existed, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God, and everything was made by him? Can we learn from him to create the world, to fill the sky with lights, to regulate the succession of days and nights, to order the passage of time and centuries, to give strength to seeds or to populate the earth with animals? The Master tells us to learn none of this: he has done that as God. But since this God deigned to also be a man, listen to what he did as a God to recreate you, and listen to what he did as a man to imitate him. Learn from me, he said. Not to manufacture the world, nor to create natures or those other things that he, hidden God and manifest man, did. He did not even say: "Learn from me to expel fever from the sick, to cast out demons, to raise the dead, to rule over the winds and waves, to walk on the waters; Nor does he refer to this when he says: Learn from me. These gifts he granted to some of his disciples, and not to others. But learn from me says it to everyone; Let no one feel exempt from this precept: Learn from me, for I am meek and humble in heart. Why do you hesitate to carry this weight? Is humility and piety a heavy burden? Is faith, hope and charity a heavy burden? These are what make one meek and humble. Haec enim dedit quibusdam discipulis suis, quibusdam non dedit: hoc autem, Discite a me, omnibus dicit; ab hoc praecepto nemo se excuset, Discite a me quoniam mitis sum, et humilis corde (Mt 11:29). Quare dubitas hanc sarcinam ferré? Haec sarcina gravis est, humilitas et pietas? Haec sarcina gravis est, fides, spes, caritas? Istae enim humilem, istae mitem reddunt. This burden is not a weight for the one who is burdened, but wings for the one who is going to fly. Indeed, birds carry the weight of their wings. What to say? They carry it and are carried by it. Now think about a miser entering. You know he is a miser; He is standing next to you, who are not; moreover, that you are merciful, that you give what you have to the poor and do not sigh for things that you do not possess; You hear what the Apostle says: Command the rich of this world not to behave arrogantly nor to put their hope in the uncertainty of riches, but in the living God, who gives everyone everything to enjoy abundantly; Be rich in good works, give easily, distribute, treasure up a good foundation for the future to achieve true life. You have heard it, recognized it, learned it, retained it and fulfilled it. Keep doing it, don't get lazy, don't stop. Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved. You behaved well with a man, and he was ungrateful: do not regret having

done good, lest in your sorrow you spill out what you filled with your mercy. Say in your heart: "Although the one to whom I did it does not see it, the one for whom I did it sees it, because if that one had seen it and stopped being ungrateful, it would benefit him more than it would benefit me. I will cling to God from whom what I do is not hidden; and not only what I do, but even what I want to do; I will wait for the reward of him who does not need testimonies of my action. You are like that, and perhaps there is standing next to you in the people of God a miser and a thief, pining for other people's things. Although you know this to be the case, given that he is a believer or, better yet, that he calls himself faithful, you cannot expel him from the church, you have no possibility of correcting him through punishment or reproach; He will come to your side at the altar, but do not fear: Each one will carry his own burden. Remember the Apostle to approach calmly: Each one will carry his own burden. You just have to make sure that he doesn't say: "Help me carry it," because if you want to participate in his greed, the weight will not decrease, but will overwhelm both of you. Let him, therefore, strive for his burden, and you, for yours, since when the Lord lifted such a weight from your shoulders, he imposed another on you: he removed the weight of ambition, and imposed that of charity on you. Thus, each one carries his own burden, bad for the bad and good for the good, according to his ambitions. 9. Embrace the other precept as well: Carry each other's burdens. It is time to listen to this other precept: Bear your burdens mutually. Poverty does not oppress me, but my brother. Think if riches are not a more oppressive weight for you. Help him carry his and in this way you mutually carry your burdens. What does the weight of poverty consist of? In not having. And the one about riches? In having more than what is necessary. Both of you are loaded. Help him in not having, help yourself in having more than necessary, so that your burdens are equal. If you give to someone who is in need, you reduce their burden, which consisted of not having; When you give it, you begin to have: the weight of not having has been reduced. At the same time, your own burden, which we call having more than what is necessary, has decreased. You both advance along the path of the Lord while the pilgrimage of this temporal life lasts; you, burdened with large and superfluous garments; he, however, without any. He joined you wanting to be your companion: do not look at him with indifference, do not despise him, do not abandon him. Don't you notice how great the weight you are dragging is? Give a share to someone who carries nothing and has nothing, and in this way you will help the companion and you will be relieved. No doubt they tried to weaken the force of the truth and did their best to cloud its clarity with the clouds of useless disputes. But the Lord was present, and his clarity defeated his clouds. And see how without knowing it they absolved the Church from the world of the earth, in whose communion those of us who are in it rejoice. It is not ourselves, but her that we protect, defend and obtain, as we defend the threshing floor of the Lord. It is for her that I raise my voice. Don't worry who I am inside her; nicares cum illo Christi mensam. Et quid tibi obesset, si cum illo communicares Christi mensam? Apostolus dicit: Qui enim manducat et bibit indigne, iudicium sibi manducat et bibit (1 Cor 11:29). Sibi, non tibi. Sane si iudex es, si iudicandi potestatem accepisti, ecclesiastica regulates, si apud te accusatur, si veris documentis testibusque convincitur, coerce, corripe, excommunicate, degrade. Sic vigilet tolerance, ut non dormiat disciplina. CAPUT VIII.—12. Caecilianus absens et innocens damnatur. Leges Imperatorum against Donatists. Caecilianus ter absolutus. Primianus. Sed damnatus est, inquíunt, Caecilianus. Damnatus? Whoa? Primo absens, deinde a traditoribus innocens. Allegata sunt ista, gestis inserta, probata sunt. Enervare quidem vires veritatis conati sunt, et inanium nebulis prosecutionum eius serenitatem nebulare, quantum potuerunt, enisi sunt. Adfuit Dominus, vicit serenitas eius nebulas eorum. Et videte quomodo nescientes absolverunt Ecclesiam orbis terrarum, cuius communione gaudemus, qualescumque in ea simus. Non ipsos nos, sed ipsam tuemur, defendimus, obtinemus, aream dominicam defending, proarea dominica clamo.

Tu quis in ea sim, nolo cures: ventilabrum exspecto "Traitors" translates the term traditores, which in its most proper meaning means those who handed over the Holy Books to the enemies of the Christian faith in the persecution of Diocletian. It is the permanent accusation of the Donatists to the Catholics. Caecilian was condemned by a council of bishops, numbering 70, who, instead, appointed Majorinus to occupy their episcopal see. This is how the schism arose. He was then declared innocent by Catholic bishops at the councils held in Rome (313) and Arles (314). By declaring themselves in communion with Caecilian, whom the Donatists accused of having been consecrated bishop by a traditor, they are also called here traditors.

13. What do you think they responded to get out of this predicament? What could they say? Where were they going to escape, trapped in the webs of truth? What did they say in a few words, and undoubtedly in our favor, to violently break those networks? A lot, in fact, and almost everything in our favor, as the minutes that will be proposed for the reading of your charity will indicate. But I beg you and beseech you for the sake of Christ that you retain this for the moment, that you proclaim it and always keep it in your mouth. A shorter, truer and clearer sentence could not have been pronounced in our favor. What did they answer to our objection, according to which their judgment against Caecilian was of as little value as theirs against Primianus? These are the words of its defender: Neither one cause prejudges another cause, nor one person prejudges another person. Short, clear and true answer! He did not know what he said, but he prophesied in a similar way to Caiphas when he was pontiff: Neither one cause prejudges another cause, nor one person prejudges another person. If one cause does not prejudge another, nor one person another, then each person bears his own burden. Go now and stop objecting to Ceciliano; Let him object with Caecilian not to you, an individual, but to the entire globe of the earth. In doing so, he objects to innocents with an innocent. The minutes will indicate this very clearly. Caecilian was free from all taint; But suppose that he was not acquitted, suppose that he was recognized as a criminal, listen to your voice repeated throughout the world: Not one cause prejudges another cause, nor does one person prejudge another person.

CAPUT IX.—13. Donatistae sua ipsorum sententia damnati.—Quid eos putatis in hac anguish respondedise? Quid enim dicerent? Qua evaderent even retibus veritatis? Ut haec retía violenter rumperent, quid dixerunt breviter et absolute pro nobis? Et quidem fines, et penis omnia pro nobis, sicut gesta indicabunt, quae iam proposenda vestra Caritas reading est. Sed hoc loco rogo vos, et obsecro per Christum, ut teneatis, dicatis, in ore semper habeatis. Non potuit enim pro nobis brevior, et certior, et liquidior ferri sententia. Quid ergo dixit, cum hoc obiceremus: Sic non praeiudicant isti Caeciliano, quomodo nec illi Primiano. Et ille defender illorum: Nec causa causae praeiudicat, nec persona personae (Brevic. Collationis cum Donatistis, die 3, cap. 16, n. 28). O brief responsum, liquidum, verum! Non enim scivit quid dixit; sed Caiphae similis, cum esset pontifex prophetavit (cf. lo 11:49): Nec causa causae praeiudicat, nec persona personae. Si nec causa causae, nec persona personae praeiudicat, ergo unusquisque sarcinam suam portat. Eat nunc et obiciat tibi Caecilianum: non tibi cuicumque homini, sed ipsi orbi terrarum obiciat Caecilianum. Quod cum facit, innocentem, obicit innocentibus. Prorsus gesta indicabunt liquidissime. Purgatus est Caecilianus. Sed fac eum non purgatum, fac criminosum inventum; audi spokesperson tuam ab orbe terrarum: Nec causa causae, nec persona personae

praeiudicat. Anima haeretica, insanabilis, animosa, cum tu in te sententiam dicas, iudicem quid accusas? Si illum ego corrupi, ut iudicaret pro me; you want to corrupt, ut damnares you? CAPUT X.—14. Donatistas quid in errore detineat.—Utinam haec iliquando cogitent, vel sero cogitent, vel detumescente animositate cogi: ent; ad se redeant, se interrogent, se disputant, sibi responder, pro reritate non timeant eos quibus falsitatem diutissime vendiderunt. Ipsos: nim timent offendere; erubescunt humanoe infirmitati, et non erubescunt nvictissimae veritati. Utique hoc timent, ne dicatur eis: Quare ergo nos lecepistis? quare us seduxistis? quare so much bad et false dixistis? I will answer debenent, si Deum timerent: Humanum Fuit errare, dia[902]bolicum est per animositatem in errore manere. Melius quidem erat ii nunquam erraremus: sed vel quod secundum est faciamus, ut errorem aliquando emendemus. Decepimus, quia decepti eramus: false praedicavimis, qui praedicantibus false credidimus. Dicant suis: Simul erravimus, iimul ab errore recedamus. Duces vobis Fuimus ad foveam, et secuti estis: um duceremus ad foveam; et nunc sequimini cumducimus ad Ecclesiam. Possent is dicere: indignantibus dicerent, iratis dicerent, aliquando et illiponerent indignationem, amarent vel sero unitatem. 15. Patientia in ipsos exhibitenda.—We are tamen, fratres, cir-

inflamed and swollen those eyes that we heal. I'm not saying that we stop healing them, but that we avoid causing them greater bitterness with our insults. Let us explain the truth to them gently, instead of arrogantly exulting over victory 5. For it is not fitting that the servant of the Lord be quarrelsome, says the Apostle, but that he be meek towards all, docile, patient, and that he meekly correct those who think differently, in case God grants them repentance and, coming to their senses, they separate themselves from the snares of the devil, of whom they are captives of their own free will. Bear them, then, patiently, if you are healthy; bear them patiently as long as you are healthy. Well, who is totally healthy? When the righteous king sits on his throne, who will boast that he is cleansed from all sin? Therefore, as long as our condition is this, our common duty is to mutually bear our burdens. Returning to the Lord... ca illos simus. In fervore sunt et tumore oculi quos curamus. Non dico ut curare cessemus; sed ut non insultationibus ad maiores amaritudines provocemus; rationem leníter reddamus, non de victoria superbe exsultemus. Servum enim Domini litigare non oportet, Apostolus dicit, sed mitem esse ad omnes, docibilem, patientem, in modestia corrípientem diverse semientes: ne forte det illis Deus paenitentiam, et resispiscant a diaboli laqueis, a quo captivi tenentur secundum ipsius voluntatem (2 Tim 2,24-26). Patienter ergo ferte, si sani estis, patientes ferte, in quantum sani estis. Nam quis perfecte sanus? Cum Rex iustus sederit in throne, quis gloriabitur mundum se habere cor, aut quis gloriabitur mundum se esse a peccato? (cf. Prov 20:8-9). Ergo quamdiu such sumus, hoc nobis debenmus, ut invicem onera nostra portemus. Conversi ad Dominum, etc. It refers to the result of the Conference held in 411 in Carthage between Donatists and Catholics to elucidate differences and seek unity, under the presidency of the imperial agent Marcellinus. The ruling was in favor of the Catholics, and from that moment Donatism began to decline under the weight of the severe coercive measures of the civil power. However, he still survived for a long time.

There are those who think that alms should only be given to the righteous, and that it is not appropriate, on the other hand, to give anything to sinners. At the head of this error are the Manichaeans; They believe that particles of God are mixed and gathered in any food, and they believe that they must be prevented from being stained by sinners and entangled in more miserable ties. This nonsense, which offends the sensibilities of any healthy person by simply proposing it, may not even deserve to be refuted. But some, without thinking anything of this, believe that sinners should not be fed so as not to attack God, whose indignation against them is manifested in such a way that we too can be the object of his wrath if we want to help those whom he wants to punish. They even present as proof texts from the Holy Scriptures in which we read: Grant mercy and do not receive the sinner; take revenge on the wicked and sinners. The spiritual combat

Topic: Spiritual combat. Location: Unknown. Date: Unknown. Our fight is not against flesh or blood, because not only man persecutes you, but also the devil through him and, before wounding your body, he kills you in your soul. Our struggle is not against flesh or blood, of men against men, who are flesh and blood, but against the princes and powers, the rulers of this darkness, for in the same way that those who are light are governed and governed by Christ, so those who are darkness are precipitated and instigated by the devil to all evil. For this reason the Apostle exhorts us to pray, not against the evil man, but against the devil who acts together with him and to do everything possible so that the devil is expelled and man is liberated. It is the same as if in a battle one comes armed and on horseback against another on the opposite side; He is not angry at the horse, but at the rider, and what he wants to do, to the best of his ability, is to hurt the rider and keep the horse. The same must be done with bad men; You have to work with all your strength, not against them,

We have just heard the Apostle's reading and perhaps someone has been surprised by what is written there: According to the justice that comes from the law, I have lived blamelessly. What was gain to me, I have considered loss for Christ. Then he adds: I considered it not only as loss, but also as dung, in order to gain Christ and be found in him not possessing self-righteousness, that which comes from the law, but that which comes from faith in Jesus Christ. How did he equate living blamelessly according to the justice that comes from the law to loss and dung? Who, then, gave the law? Did he not anticipate with the law who later came with forgiveness for transgressors of the law? We believe, in effect, that he brought forgiveness for those whom the law designated as guilty. But did the law consider guilty those who had lived irreproachably according to the justice that comes from it? And if the Lord brought forgiveness and remission of sins for those guilty before the law, did he not bring it for the apostle Paul, who claims to have lived blameless in the law? But let us listen to him in another text: He saved us not by our works, but by his mercy, through the washing of regeneration. And again: Before I was a blasphemer, a persecutor and an insulter, but I have obtained mercy, etc. On the one hand he acknowledges having lived blamelessly according to the law, and on the other hand he confesses to having been a sinner, so that no sinner loses the hope of forgiveness, given that Paul was worthy of it.

What is further and more separated from each other than God and man, the immortal and mortals, the righteous and sinners? Remoteness that does not result from distance, but from dissimilarity. It is the same way of speaking that we use when we say of two men of different customs: "They are very far from each other." Even if they are next to each other, even if they live even closer to each other, even if they are

Bound with the same chain, the pious is far from the wicked, the innocent far from the guilty, and the just far from the unjust. If this is said about two men, what can we say about God and men? Despite the immortal and the just being far from us as mortals and sinners, he who was far away descended to us to become close to us. And what did he do? He had two goods and we had two evils; His two goods were justice and immortality; our two evils, iniquity and mortality; If he had assumed our double evil, he would have become equal to us and would have needed a liberator with us. So what did he do to be close to us? Close, that is, not like us, but almost like us. Consider these two things: He is just and immortal; In your two evils, one thing is guilt and another is punishment; Guilt is that for which you lack justice, and punishment is that which makes you mortal. He, to become close to you, assumed your pain, but not your guilt, and if he assumed it, it was to erase it, not to perpetrate it. Being just and immortal, he was far from the unjust and mortal. You, as a sinner and mortal, were far from the just and immortal. He did not become a sinner like you were, but he became mortal like you. Remaining righteous, he became mortal. Assuming the penalty, without the guilt, he destroyed guilt and penalty. Therefore, the Lord is near, do not worry about anything. Although he ascended bodily above all the heavens, he did not depart in his majesty. Whoever made everything is present everywhere. 4. Always rejoice in the Lord. What is it to enjoy

8. But pay attention to what follows: Do not be arrogant or put your hope in the uncertainty of riches. You love gold: show, if you can, that you are not afraid of losing it. You have amassed a fortune; offer yourself security. Nor put your hope in the uncertainty of riches. They come, they go; quod ad eos dictum est, ubi caput est, non superbe sapere (1 Tim 6:17). Ad hoc habentur diuitiae multumque amantur. Nídus colligitur superbiae, ubi nutriatur et crescat; et quod peius est, non uolet, sed maneat. Ergo ante omnia, non superbe sapere. Ut ínteílegat, sapiat, cogitet se mortalem, et mortalis pauperis parem. Both enim terra knots excepit, both exspectat mors, both non timet febris. Habet eam pauper in strato tierra, sed nec diues eam uenientem lecto terret argenteo. Ergo, Praecipe huius mundi diuitibus, non superbe sapere. Agnoscant pares suos pauperes: pauperes homines sunt et homines; dissimilis uestis, sed similis cutis: et si diues mortuus conditur aromatibus, non erit nulla putredo, sed sera; serius putrescit, numquid non putrescit? As soon as there are some, they perish or one lives in fear of losing them. Therefore, do not put your hope in the uncertainty of riches. He withdrew hope from them. Where did you deposit it? But in the living God. Place your hope in him, anchor your heart in him, so that the storm of this century does not rock you and cause you to perish: in the living God, who gives us everything in abundance to enjoy. If he gives us everything, how much more will he give us himself! Indeed, in order to enjoy, he will be everything to us. It seems to me that he was only referring to himself when he said: That he gave us everything in abundance to enjoy. It is easy to see that it is one thing to use and another to enjoy. Using is linked to necessity and enjoying to joy. Therefore for our use he gave us these temporal things, and for our enjoyment he gave himself himself 6. If he gave himself, why does he say everything except because it is written: May God be all in all? Let the enjoyment of the heart be put into it, so that the heart itself may be on high. Untie yourself from here, but bind yourself there; It is dangerous for you to remain without chains in the midst of these storms. 9. Do not put your hope in the uncertainty of riches. They are not told not to put it anywhere, but in the living God, who gives us everything in abundance to enjoy. What is more everything than the one who made it all? None of these things would have been done by him if he had not known them. Who will dare to say: "God did what he did not know"? He did what he knew. I had it, then, before I did it; but he had it in wonderful ways, not in the way he did them, that is, temporary and fleeting, but as is usual for the artist.

It has within it what works externally. There are, therefore, the main things, the immortal, the indeficient, the permanent, and the same God who is all in all. He will be all in all, but in his saints, in his righteous. He, therefore, is enough; Only he is enough of whom it was said: Show us the Father and it is enough for us. But he answers them: I have been with you for so long and you have not known me? Whoever sees me, also sees the Father. God, Father, Son and Holy Spirit, is everything. No wonder he alone is enough. If we are miserly, let us love him. If we wish for riches, let us wish for him. Only he of whom it was said: Who satisfies your desires with good things, can satisfy us. Is this not enough for the sinner? Is not this great and magnificent good sufficient for the sinner? Wanting to have more, you lose everything, because greed is the root of all evil. God rightly rebukes, through the prophet, the sinful and fornicating soul that turns away from him with these words. You thought that by leaving me you were going to have something more. But, like that younger son, you had to feed pigs; He sees that you lost everything, that you were left in misery and that, although late, you returned tired. Understand once and for all that what the Father gave you was safer in his custody: You thought that, by separating yourself from me, you were going to have something more. Oh sinful soul, full of fornications, clumsiness, emaciated, unclean and so beloved! Return, then, to the beautiful to recover beauty; Go back and say to the one with whom you are enough: You have lost the one who turns away from you. What is enough for you but what follows?: But,

perit mode, timetur ne pereat mode. Non ergo sperent in incerto diuitiarum. Tulit inde spem. Ubi fixit? Sed in deo uiuo. Ipse ergo sufficit, solus sufficit, de quo dictum est: Ostende nobis patrem, et sufficit nobis, sed, tanta, inquit, tempore uobiscum sum, et non cognouistis me? Solus nos satiare poterit, de quo dictum est: Qui satiat in bonis desiderium tuum (Ps 102,5). Hoc peccatori non sufficit? Hoc tantum, tam magnum bonum pecca[71]tori non sufficit? Volendo habere plus, perdidit omnia: quia radix omnium malorum auaritia est. Merito per prophetam increpat animae peccatrici et a se fornicanti, et dicit: Existimasti, si a me discessisses, aliquid te amplius habituram (?). Sed quomodo Ule filius minor, ecce porcos pauisti (cf. Lk 15:15); ecce omnia perdidisti; ecce egens remansisti, et sero fessus redisti. Iam intellege quia id quod tibi pater ibat, tutius ipse seruabat, Existimasti, si a me recessisses, aliquid amplius te habituram. For me, good consists in adhering to God. So hold your heart high; Do not leave it on earth, not in the extremely lying treasure, not in the place of poverty. For greed is the root of all sins. Even in Adam, greed was the root of all evil. He wanted more than what he had received, because God was not enough for him. 10. Pay attention now, oh rich man!, to what you have to do with what you have. You are no longer arrogant, perfect! You don't have your hope in the uncertainty of riches, extraordinary! Rather, your hope is in the living God, who gives us everything abundantly to enjoy: worthy of all praise! So do not be lazy to do what follows: Be rich in good works. Let's try to see this; and what we do not see, let us believe. He said: "I have gold, but I don't love it." Not loving him belongs to your inner core; but if I deserve something before you, give me also proof of it; What you do not hide from your God, also show it to your brother. “How, you ask, will I prove it?” As it says below: Be rich in good works, give easily. Be rich for this: to give easily. The poor want to give, but they don't have it; It is difficult for him, easy for you. Being rich is beneficial to you, because if you want to do it, you immediately do it. Give easily, distribute. Do they lose it, perhaps? Lay up a good foundation for the future. And lest we also love for the next life the same gold, silver and possessions that seem beautiful to the senses of men; and so that we do not desire jornicatur abs te (Ps 72,27). Quid ergo sufficit, nisi quod sequitur? Mihi autem adhaerere deo bonum est (ib., 28). Ergo sursum cor, non in terra, non in mendicissimo thesauro, non in loco putredínis. Radix est enim otnnium malorum auaritia. Et in ipso Adam radix omnium malorum auaritia Fuit. Plus enim uoluit, quam accepit, quia deus illi non suffecít. 10. Quid ergo sis facturus ex his quae habes, or diues, adtende. Iam non superbe sapis: recte. Non speras in incerto diuitiarum: optime. Sed speras in deo uiuo, qui praestat nobis omnia abundantr ad fruendum: laudabiliter. Noli ergo píser esse in his quae seauentur: Diuites sint in operibus bonis. Haec uideamus, et quod non uidemus, credamus. You said: Aurum habeo, sed non amo: non amare, tuum intus est; si quid de te meor, proba et mihi; quod non abscondis deo tuo, proba et fratri tuo. Unde, inauit, do I try? Ex eo quod sequitur: Diuites sint in operibus bonis, facile tribuant.

Ad hoc diues este, ut facile tribuas. Pauoer enim uult tribuere. et non potest: apud íllum dífficultas, apud you facilitate yourself. Hoc tibi prosit quod diues es, auia cum uolueris faceré, statim facis. Vacile tribuant, communicent (1 Tim 6:18). Numquid perdunt? Thesaurizent sibi fundamentum bonum in futurum (ib., 19). Et ne ipsum aurum et argentum et praedia, et ea quae pulchra uidentur in facultatíbus hominum, etiam in illo saeculo amaremus, et talia ibi desi-

for such goods because we have been told: "Take it there and place your treasure there," he warns us against those carnal thoughts saying: So that they may obtain true life, not gold, which remains on earth, nor riches subject to decay, nor fleeting goods, but true life. How then do we transfer them, if these things will not happen there, nor will we have there what we transferred from here? In a certain way, the Lord our God wants us to be merchants and makes exchanges with us: we give him what is abundant here and we receive what is abundant there, like so many who exchange goods: in one place they give one thing and receive another in the place where they arrive 7. For example, one says to his friend: "Receive this gold of mine here and give me oil in Africa"; it transfers it and does not transfer it; What he gave he already transferred, but he did not receive the same merchandise. You receive what you want. My brethren, our commerce with God is similar to this. What do we give and what do we receive? We give what we cannot take with us even if we want to, so it consequently perishes. Therefore, give yourself the lesser here to find the greater there. We give earth and receive heaven; we give temporal goods and receive eternal goods; We give them corruptible and receive them imperishable; Finally, we give what God gave us and receive God himself. Let us not be lazy to carry out this exchange of goods in this excellent and ineffable trade. Let us take advantage of being here, aprovederaremus, cum dicitur nobis: Illuc migrate, thesaurum [72] uestrum ibi ponite: admonuit nos contra carnales cogitationes, et ait: Ut apprehendant ueram uitam (ib.): non aurum, quod in terra remanet, non iacultates putribiles, non bona transeuntia, sed ueram uitam. Quomodo ergo migramus, quando hoc illuc non transit, ñeque hoc ibi haoebimus, quod hinc translerimus? Quodam modadominus deus noster mercatores nos uult esse, mutationes nobiscum facit: quod hic abundat damus, quod ibi abundat accipimus; quemadmodum plerique traiectitias merces faciunt: aliud dant alibi, et quo ueniunt aliud accipiunt. Verbi graua, dicit amico suo: Accipe a me hic aurum, et da mihi in Aírica oleum: et migrat ct non migrat: iam quod dedit transtulit, sed non hoc accepit. Quod desiderat accipit. Talis est is mutatio, quaüs, fratres meí, nostra mercatio. Quid damus, et quid accipimus? Hoc damus quod nobiscum ierre non possimus, etsi uellemus, quare ergo perit.

Hic quod minus est detur, ut quod est maius ibi inueniatur. Damus terram, et accipimus caelum; damus temporalia, accipimus aeterna; damus putrescentia, accipimus immortalia; desserto damus quod dedit deus, et accipimus ipsum deum. Non ergo pigri simus in ista mutatione rerum, in ista mercatura opima This is one of the ideas most frequently repeated by the saint. You can see, among others, the following texts: Sermons 80.5; 124.4; 130.2; 233.4; Comments on Psalms 30:3; 148.8, etc.

Let's take advantage of being born, let's take advantage of being pilgrims. Let us not return to destitution. 11. Do not let the moth of evil thoughts enter the ark of your heart. Let no one say: "I won't give in case I don't have it for tomorrow." Don't think too much about the distant future. Treasure for yourself, he says, a good foundation for the future, so that you may attain true life. As the Apostle said, it is not a matter of there being food for others and scarcity for you, but rather depending on what each one has. It only asks that you do not love, nor keep, nor treasure nor rely on created things, that is, that you do not put hope in insecure things. How many did not go to sleep rich and wake up poor! Evil are the thoughts of those who say: "If I have nothing stored up, who will give me if I begin to feel need?", or: "I have abundance or sufficiency to live; but what if a slander falls on me? How will I get rid of her? What if it is necessary for me to enter into trials; How will I cover the expenses? No matter how much time you have spent narrating and recounting all the evils that can befall the human race, often a single misfortune upsets the calculations of the person who made them, and not only does he perish, but not even anything remains of what he counted on his fingers! Therefore, after having said: Without loving it, let the measure of money be sufficient for present needs, against those evil thoughts, against this worm of thought, against the evil moth, God put something in his Scripture, in a way et ineffabilí. Prosit quia hic sumus, prosit quia natí sumus, prosit quia peregrinamur. Non inopes redeamus. 11. Non intret arcam cordis tinea malae cogitationis. Non dicatur: Non dabo, ne eras non habeam. (960) Noli multum cogitare de futuris: immo multum cogita de futuris, sed de longe futuris: Thesaurizent, inquit, sibi fundamentum bonum in futurum, ut apprehendant ueram uitam. Nec ita, quemadmodum dixit apostolus, ut aliis rejectio, uobis autem anguish, sed ex eo quod quisque babet (2 Cor 8:13). Tantum nolite amare, seruare, thesaurizare, incumbere conditis, hoc est de incertis sperare. Quam multi diuítes dormierunt, pauperes surrexerunt.

Propter istas enim cogitationes, cum dixisset: Sine amore modus pecuniae sufjiciens est praesentibus, propter malas cogitationes, quae dicunt: Si thesaurum non habuero, [73] quis mihi dabit, cum egere coepero? deinde: Abundat unde uiuam, sufficit unde uiuam; sed quid, si impingat mihi slander: unde me redeem? quid, si mihi necesse sit litigare: unde sumptus impendam? — quamdiu omnia mala quae possunt euenire generi humano narrare et computare poteris, plerumque una calamitas turbat computum numerantis, et totum quod numerabatur, non solum perit, sed nec in digitis remanebit — ideo contra istum cogitationis uermiculum, contra malignam tineam apposuit deus in scriptura sua, quo-

similar to how it is customary to put certain smells on clothes so that they do not become moth-eaten. What thing? You thought about not being short of money for that occasion and you listed an endless number of calamities. Didn't you feel afraid of the only great one? Pay attention to what follows these words: Without loving it, let the measure of money be sufficient for present needs; He himself said: I will not leave you alone, I will not abandon you; You feared I don't know what evils and thinking about them you kept the money; have me as guarantor. This is what God tells you. It is not a man, not one like you or yourself, but God who tells you: I will not leave you alone, I will not abandon you. If a man promised you, you would believe him; God promises it to you, and do you avoid it? He has made the promise, he has left it in writing, you have a guarantee: be sure. Read what you have; you have the guarantee of God; Your debtor is the one whom you asked to forgive your debts. Amen. solent mode apponi uestibus odoramenta quaedam, ne tineent. Crux? Cogitabas ne tibi desit propter illud et illud, et numerabas fines calamitates. Non timebas unam grandem? Attend quod sequitur: sine amore modus pecuniae sufficiens est praesentibus, ipse enim dixit: Non te derelinquam, non te deseram (Hebr 13:5); timebas mala nescio quae, propterea pecuniam reseruabas: me teñe fideiussorem. Hoc tibi deus illicit. Non homo, non par tuus aut ipse tu, sed deus tibi dicit: Non te derelinquam, non te deseram. Homo si promitteret, crederes; deus promittit, et dubitas? Promisit, scripsit, cautionem fecit: this is secure. Lege quod tenes, cautionem dei tenes, ipsum debitorem tenuisti, a quo tua debita relaxan petisti. Amen.

1. Reading the letter of the blessed Apostle reminded me, no doubt, that I must look at myself, and at you, who should not judge me, especially considering that we have all just heard the last phrase of the chapter of the Gospel just read: Do not judge with partiality, but according to justice. In a judgment, no one makes reference to another person other than his own. The blessed Apostle says in a certain place: I do not fight as if hitting the air, but I punish my body and reduce it to servitude, lest while I preach to others I find myself reprobate. He terrified us with his same fear. What will the lamb do when the ram trembles? Among the many things that the Apostle wrote about how a bishop should be, we also heard one that perhaps gives us enough topic to talk and dispute. Well, if I tried to discuss point by point and talk about each one of them as they deserve, neither my strength would be enough to speak nor yours to listen.
DE VERBIS APOSTOLI, TIT 1,9: «UT POTENS SIT EXHORTARI IN DOCTRINA SANA, ET CONTRADICENTES ARGUERE». ONTRA RERUM ALIENARUM RAPTORES

CAPUT I.—1. Episcoporum onus.—Beati Apostoli Epistle cum legeretur de constituendis episcopis, commemoravit nos sine dubio respicere in nos: et vos commemoravit non iudicare nos; maxime quia omnes audimus capituli Evangelii recentis lectionis novissimam sententiam: Nolite iudicare personaliter, sed iustum iudicium iudicate (lo 7,24). Personam itaque judicando nemo accipit alienam, si non accipit suam. Beatus Apostolus ait quodam loco: Non sic pugno, quasi aerem caedens: sed punishment corpus meum, et in servitutem redigo; ne forte aliis praedicans, ipse reprobus inveniar (1 Cor 9:26-27). Suo timore nos terruit. Quid enim faciet agnus ubi aries [961] tremit? Inter Fine ergo, quibus scripsit Apostolus, qualis esse episcopus debeat, etiam illud audivimus, unde moda forsitan loqui et disputare sufficiat. Si enim singula discusse, et de singulis, ut dignum est, disputare conemur; nec nostrae vires sufficiunt ad lonquendum, nec vestrae ad audiendum. Quid ergo est quod

char. What, then, do I mean by the help of the one who terrified me? Among other things, it says that the bishop must be powerful in sound doctrine so that he can refute those who contradict him. It is a great task, a heavy load, an arduous pending task. But, he says, I will wait on God because he will free me from the snare of hunters and from every harsh word. There is nothing that makes the dispenser of God more lazy to refute contradictors than the fear of a harsh word. 2. First of all, I will explain to you, to the extent that God grants it to me, what it means to refute contradictors. Contradictors are not of a single kind. There are very few who contradict us with words, but many with their bad lives. When will a Christian dare to tell me that it is good to steal other people's things, if he does not even dare to say that it is good to cling tenaciously to one's own? Was it perhaps that rich man to whom the field had given a great harvest and had no place to store his fruits, and was glad to have found the determination to destroy the old warehouses and build larger ones to fill them and say to his soul: Soul, you have abundant goods for a long time; rejoice, rejoice and be satisfied; Was this rich man looking for other people's goods? He was preparing to collect his fruits and was wondering where he was going to put them; He only thought about collecting his own, not those from the neighbor's field; without crossing the boundaries and without dispossessing any poor person or deceiving any ignorant person. Hear what he heard who so tenaciously guarded his possessions; and from here deduce what awaits them at will say, si adiuvet me qui terruit me? inter cetera ait episcopum potentem esse debenré in doctrina sana, ut contradicientes redarguere possit. Magnum opus est, gravis sarcina, clivus arduus. Sed sperabo, inquit, in Deum, quoniam ipse liberabit me from laqueo venantium, et a harsh verb (Ps 90,2.3). Nulla enim causa est, quae magís faciat hominem dispensatorem Dei pigriorem ad redarguendos contradicentes, quam timor verbi asperi. CAPOT II.—2. Avarus suorum reconditor damnatur. — Prius ergo quid sit, contradicentes redarguere (cf. Tit 1:9), ut Dominus donaverit, exponam vobis. Contradictory non uno modo intellegendi sunt. Paucissimi enim nobis contradicunt loquendo: sed multi male vivir. Quando mihi audet dicere christianus, bonum esse rappere res alienas; quandoquidem non audet dicere, bonum esse tenaciter servare res suas?

Numquid enim dives ille, cui successerat regio, et non inveniebat ubiponeret fructus suos, et se consilium invenisse gaudebat destruendi veteres apothecas, et construendi new amplores, ut impleret eas, et diceret animae suae: Anima, habes fines bona in multum tempus, laetare, iucundare, satiare (Le 12,19): numquid ergo iste dives aliena quaerebat? Fructus suos collegere disposebat, ubiponeret consulebat, non de cuiusquam vicini agris, non limite pertúrbate, non spoliato paupere, non circumvento simplice, sed tantummgdo de suis colligendis cogitabat. Audite quid au-

who steal other people's things. When he judged that he had found a very prudent determination, that is, to destroy the old and narrow deposits and build new and larger ones and collect and store in them all their fruits, without wanting or stealing those of others, God said to him: Fool, and called him a fool for the same reason that he believed himself to be wise. «You fool, he says, tonight they will require your soul; Who will this thing you prepared be for? If you keep it, it will no longer be yours; If you give it, it will be yours. Why, he says, do you put back what you are going to leave? See that the fool who guarded his wealth poorly was rebuked. If he who keeps his own is a fool, find a name for him who takes away what belongs to others. If he who keeps what is his is dirty, he who steals what belongs to others is ulcerated. Ulcerative, but not like the one who lay at the rich man's door and whose ulcers the dogs licked, for that one had ulcers on his body; the thief, however, in the heart. 3. Perhaps someone will reply saying: "It was no great punishment for that man that God called him a fool." But fool in the mouth of God is not the same as fool in the mouth of man. Such a word directed by God against someone is equivalent to a sentence. Will God give the kingdom of heaven to fools? And to those who will not be given the kingdom of heaven, what remains but the punishment of Gehenna? This seems like a guess on our part; Let's see it openly and clearly. Well, neither of that rich man before whose door lay the poor ulcedierit, qui tenaciter servabat sua; et hinc ¡intelligite quid exspectent,_qui rapiunt aliena. Cum ergo se prudentissimum consilium invenisse arbitraretur, de apothecis veteribus angustis deiciendis, et amplificaribus novis aedificandis, et ómnibus suis fructibus colligendis et recondendis_, non alienis concupiscendis atque rapiendis; ait illi Deus: Stulte: ubi tibi sapiens videris, ibi stulte. Stulte, inquit, hac nocte repetunt a te animam tuam; haec quae praeparasti cuius erunt? (ibid., 20). Si servaveris, tua non erunt: si erogaveris, tua erunt. Quid, inquit, reponis, quod relicturus is it? Ecce increpatus est stultus male recondens. Si stultus est qui recondit sua, vos invenite nomen ei qui tollit aliena. Si sordidus est reconditor suorum, ulcerosus est raptor alienorum. Sed non qualis ille ulcerosus, qui iacebat ante ianuam divitis, et cuius canes linguebant ulcera. lile enim ulcerosus erat in corpore; raptor, in corde. CA.PUT III.—3.

Theme: Putting the word into practice (James 1:19-22). Location: Carthage? Date: Before 409. 1. The blessed apostle James admonishes the assiduous listeners of the word of God, telling them: Be obedient to the word and not only listeners, deceiving yourselves. You deceive yourselves, not the author of the word nor the minister of it. Starting from that phrase that flows from the source of truth through the most truthful mouth of the apostle, I also dare to exhort you, and while I exhort you, I look at myself. He wastes time preaching the word of God externally who is not a listener of it internally. Those of us who preach the word of God to the people are not so far removed from the human condition and from reflection supported by faith that we do not notice our dangers. But we are consoled by the fact that where our danger is because of the ministry, there we have the help of your prayers. And so that you may know, brothers, that you are in a safer place than we are, I quote another phrase from the same apostle, which says: Each one of you be quick

Thinking about this phrase, in which we are admonished to be quick to listen and slow to speak, I will speak first of this our ministry; then, after having justified the ministry of which we frequently speak, I will return to what I had proposed in the first place. 2. It is convenient that we exhort you to not only be listeners of the word, but also fulfillers. Who, because we speak to you frequently, without stopping to lie in our obligation, does not judge us when he reads: Let every man be quick to listen and slow to speak? You see that concern for you does not allow us to comply with this rule. You must, therefore, pray and lift up those you force to put themselves in danger. However, my brothers, I am going to tell you something that I want you to believe, because you cannot see it in my heart. I, who so frequently speak to you at the command of my lord and brother, your bishop and because you ask me, only truly enjoy when I listen. My joy, I repeat, is only authentic when I listen, not when I preach. Then my joy is without fear, for such pleasure does not carry with it swelling. There is no place to fear the precipice of pride where the solid stone of truth is. And that you may know that this is true, listen to what is said: You will give joy and gladness to my ear. I enjoy when I listen. Then he added: The humiliated bones will rejoice. vestrum velox ad audiendum, tardus autem ad loquendum (ib., 19). CAPUT II.—2. Audire verbum Dei tutius est quam praedicare.— Oportet vos exhort us, ut non sitis auditores tantum verbi, sed etiam factors. Quod ergo saepe vobis loquimur, quis non, parum advertens necessitatem nostram, iudicat nos, cum legit, Sit autem omnis homo velox ad audiendum, tardus autem ad lo[967]quendum? Ecce studium vestrum nos non permittit istam servare sententiam. Debetis ergo orare, sublevare, quem cogitis periclitan. Verumtamen, fratres mei, dicam vobis, quod voló credatis; Quia hoc in corde meo non videtis. Ego qui vobis assidue loquor, iubente domno et fratre meo episcopo vestro, et exigentibus vobis, tune solidum gaudeo, dum audio.

Psalm that, inviting patience, says: Get up after sitting, you who eat the bread of sorrow. What does it mean: Get up after sitting? He who humbles himself will be exalted. With the words he said of Mary, who, sitting at his feet, listened to him, the Lord became a witness of the goodness of listening. When her sister, busy with service, complained that she had left everything to her, she heard from the Lord, whom she had questioned, the following: Martha, Martha, you take care of many things, and only one is necessary. Mary chose the best part, which will not be taken away from her. Was what Marta was doing bad? Who among us will have enough words to praise the goodness of serving the saints? If to any saint, how much more to the head and the main members, to Christ and the apostles! Doesn't each one of you say to himself when he hears what Martha did and has the good of hospitality before his eyes: "Oh blessed, oh happy woman, who deserved to receive the Lord; who had the apostles as guests when they walked in the flesh! » So that you do not faint because you cannot receive Christ with his apostles like Martha into your home, he himself offers you security: When you did it to one of my little ones, you did it to me. A magnificent and extremely great work is what the Apostle orders when he says: Sharing the needs of the saints, seeking hospitality; hospitality that he praises in the letter to the Hebrews with these words: Through it some, without knowing it, gave hospitality to the angels. Magnificent service, ubi admonet de paenitentia, et dicit: Surgite postquam sedistis, qui manducatis panem doloris (Ps 126,2). Quid est, Surgite postquam sedistis? Qui se humiliat, exaltabitur (Luke 14:11). Quid autem boni habeat auditorio, ipse Dominus testis est, loquens de Maria quae sedebat ad pedes eius, et verbum eius audiebat. Maria meliorem partem elegit, quae non auferetur ab ea (ib., 10,41-42). Numquid malum erat quod Martha agebat? The Lord also showed why that was the best part. Immediately after saying: Mary chose the best part, as if we were asking her to know why it was better, she added: Because it will not be taken away from her. How do we understand this, my brothers? If she chose the better part because it will not be taken away from her, then Martha had chosen something that will be taken away from her. Every man who is engaged in serving the saints as much as is necessary for the body will be deprived of his office; He will be deprived of what he does. Serving the saints, in fact, will not last forever. For what purpose is it, if not weakness? To what, if not mortality? To whom but the hungry and the thirsty? All this will cease to exist when this corruptible body has been clothed with incorruptibility and from mortal it has become immortal. Once the need has passed, there will be no reason to be of service to it. The job will disappear and the reward will be awarded. Who will be served food where no one feels hungry? To whom will drink be given, if no one is thirsty? Who will be given hospitality where there are no pilgrims? The Lord, and with him his disciples, deigned to feel need in order to reward attention to it. He also felt hungry and thirsty, but not out of necessity, but because he deigned to do so. It was good that he who made all things should feel hungry; in this way

He would make happy whoever fed him. And when someone fed the Lord, what did he give him? who gave? What did he give him? to whom did he give? what did it give? It gave food to bread. Who gave it? One who wanted to receive more. What did he give him? Perhaps yours? What did I have that I hadn't received? Who did he give it to? Did he not give it to the one who had created what he received and to the one from whom he received it? Great is this service, great this work, immense gift! And yet, Martha chose the best part, which will not be taken away from her. Martha's part, then, is transitory; but, as I said, the reward received for it is not. 5. On the other hand, Mary's part does not pass. See how. What delighted Mary as she listened? What was their food, what was their drink? Do you know what he ate and what he drank? Let's ask him. Blessed, he says, are those who hunger and thirst for justice, because they will be satisfied. From this fountain and from this granary of justice Mary received some crumbs when, hungry, she sat at the feet of the Lord. The Lord then gave him to the extent of his ability. Neither the disciples nor the apostles themselves then had the capacity to receive what was to be given to them at their future table; That's why I told them: I still have many things to tell you, but now you can't hear them. What, then, was it that delighted Mary? What did he eat, what did he drink with the greedy jaws of his heart? Justice, truth. He heard the truth, and delighted in it;

Pars Mariae melior, quia non aufertur. Marthae opus aufertur, non merces.—Ostendit tamen Dominus, unde fuerít illa pars melior. Continuous quippe cum dixisset, Mary meliorem partem elegit, quasi quaereremus, ut scire vellemus unde meliorem, subiunxit et ait, Quae non auferetur ab ea (Luke 10:42). Quid intellegímus, ftatres mei? Si ideo meliorem partem elegit, quia non auferetur ab ea, sine dubio Martha eam partem elegerat, quae auferetur ab ea. Plan auferetur ab omni homine, qui ministrat sanctis ea quae sunt corpori necessaria, auferetur ab eo quod facit. Non enim semper ministraturus est sanctis. Cui enim ministrat, nisi infirmitati? cui ministrat, nisi mortalitati? cui ministrat, nisi esurienti ac sitienti? Haec omnia non erunt, cum corruptibile hoc induerit incorruptionem, et mortale hoc induerit immortalitatem. Cum enim transierit ipsa necessitas, nullum erit ministerium necessitatis. Auferetur labor, sed reddetur merces. Cui tune ministrabitur cibus, ubi esurit nemo? cui potus, ubi sitit nemo? cui hospitium, ubi peregrinus est nemo? Dominus ergo cum discipulis suis, ut posset mercedem huius operis reddere, dignitus est indigere. Esuriebat et ipse, et sitiebat: non quia

cogebatur, sed quia dignbatur. Bonum enim erat, ut per quem facta sunt omnia, esuriret: sic enim felix esset qui pasceret. Et when Dominum quisque pascebat, quid ibat? quis dadat? Where did it go? cui dadat? Quid dadat? Cibum pañi ibat. Quis dadat? Ule utique dadat, qui plus accipere volebat. Unde dadat? numquid de suo? quid enim habebat, quod non acceperat? Cui ibat? Nonne illi qui creaverat et quod accipiebat, et a quo accipiebat? Magnum hoc ministerium, magnum hoc opus, magnum donum. Et tamen María meliorem partem elegit, quae non auferetur ab ea. Pars ergo Marthae transit: sed, ut dixi, merces pro illa data non transit. CAPUT V.—5. Pars Mariae quomodo non transit.—Pars vero Mariae non transit. Videte quomodo non transeat. We talk about serving the saints, preparing food for them, giving them drink, setting the table, washing their feet 3, making their beds and receiving them under one's own roof; Don't you see that all this is temporary? Who will dare to say that we feed on the truth now, but not when we reach immortality? If we feed on crumbs now, won't we then have a full table? but God will destroy both. Why will you destroy it? Because there will be no hunger there. The food there is not consumed. I have shown your sweetest charity, as far as I could and as far as the Lord deigned to help me, how much safer you are in listening than I am in preaching. Now you do what we will all do then. No one will then be a teacher of the word, but the Teacher will be the Word. It follows, therefore, that it is your turn to carry it out and it is our turn to admonish you to do so. You are, in fact, the hearers of the word, we are the preachers. But inside, where no one sees, we are all listeners; inside, in the heart, in the mind, where he who exhorts you to praise teaches you. I speak to you externally, he awakens you internally. We are all listeners on the inside and we must all be fulfillers of the word externally and internally in the presence of God. What does it mean to fulfill internally? Whoever sees a woman and desires her has already committed adultery with her in his heart. He can be an adulterer without any man seeing it, but not without God punishing him. What does it fulfill externally? Divide your bread with him hungry. When he does this, his neighbor also sees him, but only God sees with what spirit he does it. Therefore, my brothers, be obedient and not only listeners of the word, deceiving yourselves, not God or him who preaches. For I, or anyone else who preaches the word to you, do not see your heart; I cannot judge what you chew internally in your thoughts. Quis est foris factor? Frange panem tuum esurienti (Is 68,7). Hoc enim eum fit, videt et proximus: sed quo animo fit, non videt nisi Deus. listóte ergo, fratres mei, factors verbi, et non auditores tantum, ¡alientes vosmetipsos (Iac 1,22): non Deum, non eum qui praedicat. Ego enim, yol quisquís vobis praedicat verbum, cor vestrum non videt: quid agatis intus in cogitationibus vestris, iudicare non potest. Quia homo non potest, intuetur Deus, cui cor humanum non potest oceultari. Ipse videt quo studio audias, quid cogites, quid teneas, quantum proficias de supplcmentis suis, quam instantor ores, quemadmodum depreceris Deum ex co quod non habes, quomodo gratias agas ex eo quod habes: ille novit qui exacturus est. Nos pecuniam dominicam erogare possumus; veniet exactor qui dixit: Serve nequam, dares pecuniam meam nummulariis, et ego veniens cum usuris exigenrem (Luke 19,23). CAPUT VIII.—8. Auditores verbi aedificantes alii super petram, alii \uper arenam.—Nolite ergo, fratres mei, fallere vosmetipsos, quia venislis studiose ad audiendum verbum, si non facitis quod auditis deficienilo. Cogitate si pulchrum est audire, quanto magis faceré. Si non audis, nmlitum neglegis, nihil aedificas. Si audis et non facís, ruinam aedíficos. Domini [971] Christi est de hac re proposita congruentissima similarity: Qui audit, inquit, verba mea haec, et facit ea, similabo eum viro prudenti qui aedificat domum suam super petram. Descendit pluvia, venerunt flu-
Put the word into practice

rain, the rivers came, the winds blew, they fell against that house and it did not collapse. Why didn't it collapse? It was founded on rock. Therefore, hearing the word and fulfilling it is equivalent to building on rock. Just listening is already edifying. But, he says, whoever hears these words of mine and does not put them into practice will be like a foolish man who builds. He also builds, what does he build? See that he builds his house, but since he does not put into practice what he hears, listening he builds on sand. He who listens to it and does not put it into practice builds on sand, and he who listens to it and puts it into practice builds on rock; and whoever does not even listen to it, does not build on rock or sand. Consider, however, what follows: The rain fell, the rivers came, the winds blew and beat against that house, and it fell to the ground and became a great ruin. Lamentable spectacle! 9. But someone will say, "What need do I have to hear what I am not going to put into practice?" Well, he says, if I listen and don't put it into practice I will build a ruin. Isn't it safer to stay without listening to anything? In the similarity proposed by the Lord, he did not want to expressly touch on what he proposes, but he implied it. Indeed, in this world the rains, the winds and the rivers never cease. Do you refuse to build on rock, knowing that in that case, even if they come, they will not affect you? Don't you build on sand to prevent the elements from destroying the house? Then you will be left without a roof over your head if you listen to nothing. The rain is coming, the

rivers; Will you feel safe because they will drag you naked? Consider, then, which part you are going to choose. Even if you think so, you will not have security by avoiding listening; If you find yourself homeless, you will necessarily be buried, dragged and submerged. Therefore, if it is bad for you to build on sand, it is also bad not to build anything; It only remains good to build on rock. It is a bad thing, then, not to listen; It is also bad to listen and not act; The only thing left is to work too. Be, then, keepers of the word and not just listeners deceiving yourselves. 10. I fear that, after this exhortation, instead of having lifted your spirits with my word, I have plunged it into despair. It is possible that someone, one or two or possibly many, among those who regularly attend, formulate judgments about me and say: "I would like to know if the person who speaks to me fulfills everything that he himself hears or what he says to others." To him I answer: I don't care about being judged by you or in this human time. For I myself may partially know what I am now, but I do not know what I will be tomorrow. But as for me, the Lord gave you security, you who are worried about it. In fact, if I fulfill what I say or hear: Be imitators of me, as I am of Christ; If, however, I say it, but do not do it, listen to the Lord: Do what they tell you, but do not do what they do. Consequently, if you think well of me, you praise me; If you think badly, you accuse me, but that doesn't make you excuse yourself. How is reversing the situation going to serve as an excuse for you?

mina, flaverunt venti, et impegerunt in domum Mam, et non cecidit. Quare non cecidit? Found it enim erat super petram. Ergo audire et faceré, aedificare est super petram. Ipsum enim audire aedificare est. Qui autem, inquit, audit verba mea haec, et non facit ea, similabo eum viro stulto qui aedificat. Et ipse aedificat. Quid aedificat? Ecce aedificat domum suam: sed quia non facit quod audit, et audiendo aedificat super arenam. Ergo super arenam, qui audit et non facit, aedificat: super petram, qui audit et facit: nec super arenam, nec super petram aedificat, qui omnino non audit. Vide autem quid sequatur: Descendit pluvia, venerunt flumina, flaverunt venti, et impegerunt in domum Mam, et cecidit; et facía est ruina eius magna (Mt 7,24-27). Spectaculum miserabile! HOOD IX.—9. Non audire, quasi non aedificare, malum est.—Ait ergo aliquis: Quod non sum facturus, quid mihi opus est audire? Audiendo enim, inquit, et non fazando, ruinam aedificabo. Norme tutius est nihil audire? Ipsam quippe partem Dominus in its similarityine purpose attingere noluit, sed intellegendam dedit. In hoc enim saeculo, pluvia, venti, flumina non quiescunt. Non aedificas super petram, ut veniant, et non te deiciant? Non aedificas super arenam, ne cum venerint, domum deiciant? Ergo sine ullo tecto, quia nihil audis, sic remanebis. Venit pluvia, veniunt flumina: numquid ideo tutus, quia raperis nudus?

Consider ergo, qualem tibi elegeris partem. Non eris, ut putas, non audiendo securus: necesse est te nudam sine ullo tecto obrui, tolli, submergi. Si ergo malum est super arenam aedificare, malum est nihil aedificare; restat ut non sit bonum nisi in petra aedificare. Malum est ergo non audire; malum est audire et non faceré; restat audite et faceré. This is ergo factors verbi, et non auditores tantum, fallantes vosmetipsos (Iac 1,22). HOOD X.—10. Auditor neglegens praedicatoris vitia ne causetur.— Post hanc exhortationem timeo ne non verbo erigam, sed desperatione confringam. Fortassis enim aliquis, vel unus, vel duo, vel certe plures, in ista vestra frequenti praesentia iudicat me, et dicit: Vellem scire, si iste qui mihi loquitur, omnia facit quae vel ipse audit, vel ceteris dicit. Huic responds: Mihi autem minimum est ut a vobis diiudicer, aut ab humano die. Quoníam et ego ipse ex aliqua parte, quid nunc sim, possum scire; Quid you were futurus sim, nescio. Be warm with me, or quisquís itamovis, Dominus securitatem dedit. Si enim fació quae dico vel quae audio, imitatores mei estote; sicut et ego Christi (1 Cor 4,3.16). Si autem dico, et non fació, Dominum audite: Quae dicunt, facite; quae autem faciunt, faceré nolite. Ergo if you feel good, praise me: if bad

Well, they say and they don't do. They are his words. They speak good, but do evil; You listen to good and do not do evil. Perhaps you will answer this: "How can I hear good things from a bad man?
