given his mercy, we will not even be able to mention the same danger or evaluate it with greater intensity. Do not enter into judgment with your servant, says a certain man; holy yes, but man; do not enter into judgment with your servant, for no living person is righteous in your presence. He therefore did not want a trial to be entered into with him. The judgment will be without mercy for him who has no mercy. Let us understand, by contrast, the other phrase and see where we should place our hope. If judgment will be without mercy for him who has no mercy, it will certainly be merciful for him who has mercy. This phrase, that is, that judgment will be without mercy for those who have no mercy, was uttered by the apostle James, to whose letter the same terrible reading mentioned above belongs. On the other hand, the statement that we made, by contrast, namely: that judgment will be merciful to him who has mercy, was expressed by the Lord when he said: Blessed are the merciful, for they will obtain mercy. Our hope is, then, in the mercy of God if our misery does not desert the works of mercy. What do you ask the Lord? Mercy. Give and it will be given to you. What do you ask the Lord? Forgiveness. Forgive and you will be forgiven. 2. But it is often asked how this is to be understood: Anyone who keeps the entire law, but stumbles over one precept, has become guilty of all. We must fear and guard against judging that the thief is to be compared with the murderer and the adulterer; This is a dangerous and harmful error;

1. Before the psalm a terrible reading sounded in our ears, namely: Anyone who keeps the entire law, but stumbles over one precept, has become guilty of all. In the face of such great danger, who is there who does not cry out: Have mercy on us, Lord; have mercy on us? Well, retisentis, accuse me, sed no excuses. Quomodo enim te excusabis, si in malum praedicatorem veritatis verbum Dei tibi dicentem, et sua [972] mala opera facientem contorqueas accusationem; cum Dominus tuus, redemptor tuus, effusor pretii, aggregans te militiae suae, et faciens de servo suo fratrem suum, non te desinat commonere, et dicat: Quae dicunt, facite; quae autem faciunt, faceré nolite? Dicunt enim, inquit, et non faciunt (Mt 23,3). Bona dicunt, mala faciunt: tu audi bona, et noli faceré mala. Hic responded: What good audio mode ab homine bad? Numquid colligunt of spinis grapes? (ib., 7,16).
CLXXIX A (Wilmart 2) [PLS 2,708] (MA 1,673)
FROM EPISTLE IACOBI UBI AIT: «QUICUMQUE TOTAM LEGEM SERVAVERIT, OFFENDAT AUTEM IN UNO, FACTUS EST OMNIUM REUS» (IAC 2,10)

1. Terribilis lectio ante psalmum sonuit in auribus nostris, quoniam quicumque totam legem servaverit, offendat autem in uno, factus est omnium reus (Iac 2,10). In tant ergo periculo quis non clamet: miserere nostri, domine, miserere nostri? (Ps 122.3). Non enim subtracta eius mi~

sericordia nos ipsum periculum commemorare vehementius, et vehementius commendare poterimus. Ne intres in iudicio cum servo tuo, ait quidam, sanctus licet, sed tamen homo; ne intres in iudicio cum servo tuo, quoniam non iustificabitur [709] in conspectu tuo omnis vivos (Ps 142,2). Noluit ergo secum intrari in iudicium. ludicium autem sine Misericordia Mi, qui non facit Misericordiam (Jac 2:13). Acontra intellegamus aliam sententiam, et videamus ubi spem will put debenamus. Si enim iudicium sine Misericordia Mi, qui non facit Misericordiam, procul dubio iudicium cum Misericordia illi qui facit Misericordiam. Hanc sententiam Iacobus apostolus protulit, ex cuius epistle eadem lectio terribilis recitata est, quia iudicium sine misericordia illi, qui non facit misericordiam. Hanc vero acontrary, quam nos diximus, ludicium cum misericordia illi qui facit misericordion, dominus expressit, ubi (674) ait: beati misericordes, quoniam ipsi misericordion consequentur (Mt 5:7). Spes est ergo in dei misericordia, si ab opere misericordiae non sit arida nostra miseria. What do you want to dominoes? Mercy. Date, et dabitur vobis (Luke 6:38). What do you want to dominoes? Indulgentiam. Dimittite, et dimittetur vobis (ib., 37). 2. Verumtamen quaeri solet quomodo accipiendum sit, quicumque totam legem servaverit, offendat autem in uno, factus est omnium reus. Metuendum est enim et cavendum, ne arbitremur furem homicidae apt

great is the difference between robbery and homicide. But we are objected: It is clear that whoever keeps the entire law, but stumbles over a single precept, has become guilty of all. Beware of murder, adultery, false testimony, idolatry and any condemnable sacrilege. Heist; Should he already be considered a murderer, adulterer, false witness, idolater and sacrilegious, for having stolen? It is not true that just because he has stolen he has already become everyone's culprit. Explaining this, the apostle, the author of the letter, added the following: He who said: "You shall not commit adultery," also said: "You shall not kill." So if you do not kill, but commit adultery, you have become a transgressor of the law. After having presented this danger before their eyes, and having made everyone tremble, as if wishing to console, he added: Speak and judge as those who begin to be judged by a law of freedom. The judgment will be without mercy for him who has no mercy. Therefore, whether we can unravel the knot of this question, whether our attempt perhaps succumbs to the difficulty it contains, or whether I am unable to think of anything worthy to say or perhaps to say what I have been able to think, in either case, give yourself ardently to the works of mercy. This is evident; It is so clear that it does not need someone to explain it, but rather someone who listens to it and hears it. However, I will try to decipher that anyway; Help me your prayer before God. Surely now is the time to listen, not pray; But if you expect from God what I am going to tell you, you are already praying.

3. The law contains many precepts; That same law that is called the decalogue has ten. But they are like the ten general precepts to which all the others must refer, innumerable indeed. However, it would be a matter of never ending to explain how those other precepts that seem countless can be reduced to the small number of ten. Similarly, with the help of the Lord, we will be able to demonstrate that, as all the other precepts are contained in these ten - to speak of which would involve, as I said, enormous fatigue - so these ten are reduced to two. These ten precepts are the following: One precept orders worship of the only God and no other: You shall not make for yourself any idol, nor the image of any thing, neither of those that are in heaven above nor of those that are on the earth below. The Lord your God is the only Lord. The second precept reads: You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain. The third: Keep the Sabbath day. These precepts refer to God. It is almost superfluous to teach the Christian anything concerning the observance of the Sabbath; rather, not only is it not superfluous, but it has a solid foundation: it is a shadow of the future. The people are prohibited from servile works on the Sabbath. Aren't they also forbidden to us? Listen to the Lord: Everyone who commits sin is a servant of sin. However, expecting this same thing from God, that is, that we do not commit sin, is equivalent to observing the Sabbath; That is why it is written: God rested on the seventh day from all his works. God rested: God makes you rest. In

adulterous comparandum; error quippe iste periculosus est et molestus: multum interest inter furtum et homicidium. Sed opponitur nobis: Certe ergo qui totam legetn servaverit, ofjendat autem in uno, factus est omnium reus. Servat se ab homicide, servat ab adultery, servat a false testimony, servat ab idololatry, servat a quolibet damnabili sacrilege. Furatus est: iam tenebitur et homicida et adulter et falsus testis et idololatres et sactilegus, quia furtum fecit? Non certe ergo, qui in uno offendit, factus est omnium reus. Exponens autem hoc ipsum idem apostolus, cuius epístola est, subiunxit adque ait: qui enim dixit, non moechaberis, dixit et, non occides. Quod si non occidis, moecharis autem, factus es transgressor legis (Iac 2,11). Hoc periculum cum ante oculos posuisset, omnesque tremuissent, velut consolaturus adiunxit: sic loquimini et sic facite, sicut per legem libertatis incipiientes iudicari. ludicium enim sine Misericordia illi qui non facit Misericordiam (ib., 12-13). Sive ergo nodum quaestionis huius explicare possimus, sive conatus noster difficultati eius fortasse subcumbat, et aut vel cogitare digne non possim quod dicam, aut forte dicere quod potuero cogitare, fervete in operibus misericordiae. Hoc pla[710]num est, hoc apertum est, hoc non expositore indiget, sed auditore atque factore. Tamen etiam illud aperire utcumque conabor; adiuvet nos apud deum oratio vestra. Tempus quidem audiendi est, non orandí; sed si quod dicturus sum a deo expectatis, oratis.

3. Lex fines praecepta continet; et quidem illa lex, quae decalogus dicitur, decem praecepta habet. Decem vero praecepta quasi generalia (675) sunt, quo cuneta cetera innumerabilia referantur. Verumtamen, quomodo praecepta cetera, quae videntur innumerabilia, ad istam paucítatem deceni numeri redigantur, infinitum est disputare. Hoc sane moda, quantum dominus adiuvat, demonstrare poterimus, quia, quo moda cetera praecepta omnia ad ista referuntur — quod dixi disputare esse operosissimum — íta ista decem ad duo referuntur. Decem vero ísta quippe sunt. De uno deo colendo, alio non colendo, unum praeceptum ibi est: non facies tibi idolum, nec cuiusquam similarityinem, ñeque quae in cáelo sursum, ñeque quae in terra deorsum (Ex 20,4). Dominus deus tuus dominus unus est (Deut 6,4). Secundum praeceptum est: non accipies in vanum nomen domini dei tui (Ex 20,7). Tertium praeceptum est: observe diem sabbatorum (Deut 5,12, sec. LXX). Ista praecepta ad deum pertinent. De sabbati observatione quasi superfluum est aliquid docere christianum. Immo non solum superfluum non est, sed hoc solidum est: nam illa umbra est. A servilibus enim operibus populus sabbato prohibetur. Do we not prohibit servilibus operibus? Audi dominum: omnis qui facit peccatum, servus est peccati (lo 8,34). Tamen idipsum, ut peccatum non faciamus, a deo sperare, hoc est sabbatizare; ideo enim scriptum est: deus requievit in die seventh ab omnibus operibus S.Ag. 23

Why did God, who created everything with his word, tire himself to have to rest? Therefore, these three precepts refer to God. The remaining seven refer to man: Honor your father and mother; you will not commit adultery; you shall not kill \- you shall not bear false witness; you will not steal; you shall not desire your neighbor's wife; you will not desire your neighbor's goods. If you love God, you will not worship anyone else nor take his name in vain, and you will dedicate the Sabbath to him to rest in you when he makes you rest. If, on the other hand, you love your neighbor, you will honor your parents, and you will not commit adultery, nor kill, nor harm anyone with your false testimony, nor steal, nor desire the wife or property of any other person. And, therefore, you will love the Lord your God with all your heart, with all your soul and with all your mind; and you will love your neighbor as yourself. In these two precepts all the law and the prophets are fulfilled. Also listen to the apostle: The fullness of the law, he says, is charity. He did not send you to fulfill many precepts: not even ten, not even two; Charity alone fulfills them all. But charity is twofold: towards God and towards one's neighbor. Towards God, to what extent? Yet. What does this all refer to? Not to the ear, or the nose, or the hand, or the foot. What can you love yourself totally with? With all the heart, with all the soul, with all the mind; you will love the source of life with everything that has life in you. If, then, I must love God with all that is alive in me, suis (Gen 2:2). Deus requievit: deus te requiescere facit. Ut enim requiesceret deus, ubi laboravit, qui cuneta verb creavit? Ergo tria ista ad deum pertinent. Septem cetera ad hominem pertinent: honora patrem et matrem: non moecbaberis: non occides: non falsum testimonium dices: non iuraberis: non concupisces uxorem proximi tui: non concupisces rem proximi tui (Ex 20:12-17). Si diligis deum, nec alterum colis, nec nomen eius in vanum accipis, et ei sabbatizas, ut in te requiescat, cum te requiescere facit. Si autem diligis proximum, et honoras parentes, et non moecharis, et non occidis, et neminem false [711] testimony laedis, et nemini furtum facis, et nullius uxorem concupiscis, et nullius rem concupiscis. Ac per hoc diliges dominum deum tuum (676) ex toto corde tuo, et ex tota anima tua, et ex tota mente tua (Mt 22,37); et diliges proximum tuum tamquam teipsum (ib., 39). In his duobus praeceptis tota lex impletur et prophetae (ib., 40). Audi et apostolum: plenitudo, inquit, legis caritas (Rom 13:10).

Non te misit in fines, nec in decem, nec in duo: una caritas totum implet. Sed ipsa caritas gemina est: in deum, et in proximum. In deum, how much? Ex toto. What toto? Non enim aure, et naso, et manu, et pede. Unde diligi potest ex toto? ex toto corde, ex tota anima, ex tota mente: ex toto, quod in te vivit, diliges fontem vitae. Si ergo ex toto quod in me vivit diligere deben deum, quid mihi reíin3 This order in the series of commandments is not occasional; We have seen it appear relatively frequently. See, for example, sermons 8,8; 32.2.

What do I reserve to be able to love my neighbor? When you were given the precept to love your neighbor, you were not told: With all your heart, with all your soul and with all your mind, but: as yourself. You must love God with all your being, because he is better than you, and your neighbor as yourself, because that is what you are. 4. The precepts are, therefore, two; three, however, the objects of love. Two precepts have been given: love God and love your neighbor; However, I see that three things are to be loved. For it would not be said: and your neighbor as yourself, if you did not love yourself. If there are three objects of love, why then are there two precepts? Because? Listen to it. God did not consider it necessary to exhort you to love yourself, because there is no one who does not love themselves. But since many go to perdition for loving themselves badly, telling you to love your God with all your being, you were at the same time given the standard of how you should love yourself. Do you want to love yourself? Love God with all your being, for there you will find yourself, so that you do not lose yourself. If you love yourself in yourself, you must also fall from yourself and your search outside of yourself must be long. For this reason, the Apostle began the enumeration of all evils from there, when he says: There will be men who love themselves. Behold, you chose to love yourself; Let's see if you at least stay within yourself. It is false, you do not remain there; you fell from God and you will fall from yourself. There is the foundation; You should have adhered to him, in him you should have put your strength and your place of refuge. Now, however, have you loosened the bond of your love or have you withdrawn it? Hiarn unde diligam proximum? De proxima enim diligendo cum tibí praeciperetur, non tíbi dictum est, Ex toto corde, et ex tota anima, et i-K tota mente; sed tamquam teipsum. Deum ex toto te, quia ule est inelior te; proximum tamquam te, quia hoc est quod tu. 4. Duo sunt ergo praecepta; tamen tria sunt diligenda. Ibi est enim liniiamcntum: ibi haerere debuísti, illum tíbi faceré locum munitum et diiinum refugíi. I never see the bond of love between you and your relax, as soon as you dirupisti.

from him to put into you; but not even in you do you remain. Finally listen to the apostle himself. After having said: There will be men who love themselves, he then added: lovers of money. Didn't I just say that you wouldn't even remain in yourself? Or are you and money the same thing? Behold, you have turned away even from yourself because you have turned away from God. What is left for you but to waste all the heritage of your mind living with prostitutes, that is, among frivolities and a variety of perverse desires, and being forced by necessity to feed swine, that is, since filthy greed dominates you, to be the food of filthy demons? But that son, having experienced misery and crushed by hunger, returning to himself said... He returns to himself because he had distanced himself from himself, and now in himself he found himself poor; He looked everywhere for happiness, and found it nowhere. What did he say when he came back to himself? I'll get up and go. Where to? To my father. Having come to himself, but still lying on the ground, he says: I will arise and go; No lying down, no staying here! You have, therefore, been given the standard according to which you must love yourself: love him who is better than you and loved yourself. And I'm talking about the one who is better by nature, not by will. Many men find themselves better than you by will, but only God is better by nature: he is the creator, the founder, the maker, who was made by no one. Hold on to it. Understand once and say: For me, on the other hand. For you, however, what? It is a good thing to adhere to God. Because? Pay attention to what he said before: You caused to perish everyone who turned away; non remanes nec in te. Audi denique ipsum apostolum. Topic: Avoid swearing (James 5:12). Location: Unknown. Date: Year 415.

1. Today's first reading, taken from the apostle James, gives us and in a way prescribes to us the theme of this sermon. He caught your attention by exhorting you not to swear above all else. It is a difficult question. If swearing is a sin, who is free from it? No one doubts that perjury is a sin, and a great sin. But the apostle from whom the reading has been taken does not say: First of all, my brothers, do not perjure, but rather: do not swear. The Lord Jesus Christ himself had already advanced in the Gospel with a similar exhortation: You have heard, these are his words, that it was said to the ancients: "Thou shalt not perjure"; But I tell you: "Do not swear by heaven, which is the throne of God; nor for the earth, which is the footstool of his feet; not even for your head, because you have no power to turn one of your hairs white or black. Your word be: Yes, yes; No no; Whatever happens from there comes from evil. Iuret ergo Deus, qui iurat securus, quem nihil fallit, quem mihil latet, qui omnino fallere ignorat, quia nec fallí potest. Cum enim iurat, se adhibet testem. Quomodo tu cum iuras, Deum adhibes testem; sic ipse cum iurat, se testem adhibet. Tu quando illum adhibes testem, forte [974] supra mendacium tuum, accipis in vanum nomen Domini Dei tui (Ex 20:7). Ne ergo mendacium iures, noli iurare. Ipsa this anguish. Periurium praecipitium. Qui iurat, iuxta est: qui non iurat, longe est. Peccat et graviter qui falsum iurat: non peccat qui verum iurat'; sed nec ille peccat, qui omnino non iurat. Sed qui non iurat, et

freckle. But whoever does not swear does not sin and is far from sin; On the other hand, he who swears the truth does not sin; but it is close to sin. Suppose you are walking through a certain place, to the right of which there is a wide space without any narrowness and to the left, a precipice. Where do you prefer to walk: along the edge of the cliff or away from it? I think far from him. In the same way, he who swears walks right on the edge and, furthermore, with weak feet because he is human. If you stumble, you go down; If you slip, same thing. And who receives you? The punishment for your perjury. You really wanted to swear; listen to God's advice: "Do not swear." 4. If the oath were a sin, it would not have been said in the old law either: You shall not swear falsely, but rather you shall fulfill your oath to the Lord. We would never be prescribed what sin is. But your God says to you: “I will not condemn you if you swear, if you swear the truth. But will I condemn you if you do not swear? There are two things that I never condemn: swearing the truth and not swearing; I do condemn, however, the false oath. Swearing falsely is pernicious; swearing in truth carries danger; "Not swearing is the safe thing." I know it is a difficult question and, I confess to your charity, I have always avoided it. This time, however, when the same reading was read at the time of preaching this Sunday's sermon, I believed I was inspired by God to talk to you about it. God wanted him to speak to you about this and for you to listen to him. I ask you not to despise it, to affirm your heart and transform the lightness of your tongue. It is not without meaning that

Having always wanted, as I said, to avoid this question, it has been imposed on me; It is so that it is also imposed on your charity. 5. So that you can see that swearing the truth is not a sin, we find that the apostle Paul also swore: For your glory, which I have in Christ Jesus, our Lord, I die day by day. For your glory it is an oath. He does not say: I die for your glory, as if it were that glory that causes him to die, in an identical way to how it is said: "He died by poison, or was killed by the sword, by a beast or by an enemy", that is, the enemy, the sword, the poison and similar things causing death. He did not say in that sense: For your glory. The Greek text eliminates all ambiguity.' If the letter is examined in the original Greek, there is also an oath that leaves no room for doubt: Ny¡ TÍ¡V úu.exépav xaópjatv. NYJ TÓV 6sóv. It is a form of oath in the Greek language. non peccat, longe est a peccato: qui autem verum iurat, non peccat, sed prope est ad peccatum. Si offenderis, deorsum is; si lapsus fueris, deorsum is. And what excited you? Periurii poena. Ergo volebas verum iurare; audi consílium Dei: Noli iurare. CAPOT IV.—4. Obsecro ne contemnatis, obsecro ut cor stabiliatis, linguae mobilitates mutetis. Nonfrustra est omnino, non vacat

quod cum eam, ut dixi, quaestionem semper devitare voluerim, imposita est necessitati meae, ut imponatur et Caritati vestrae. CAPOT V.—5. See vestram gloriam, iuratio est. to you. And in another text from the letter to the Galatians: Regarding what I write to you, I assure you by the presence of God that I am not lying. 6. Pay attention, then, and concentrate; and although my words are not worthy of applause due to the difficulty of the question, they will nevertheless be useful if they penetrate your hearts. Behold, the Apostle swore. Do not be deceived by those who, wanting, I do not know in what way, to make distinctions between oaths, or rather, without understanding what they are about, affirm that there is no oath at all in words like these: "God knows," "God is witness," "I call upon God upon my soul that I speak the truth." «All that has been done is to invoke God, he says; put him as a witness; "Can you call that an oath?" Those who say this only want to lie, putting God as a witness. So, whoever you are, you man of wicked and perverse heart, if you say, "By God," do you swear; If, however, you say: "God is my witness," do you not swear? What does "By God" mean, but rather "God is a witness"? Or what else is meant by “God is a witness” but “By God”? 7. What is swearing but doing justice to God when you swear by him? Do justice to health when you swear by it; Do justice to your children when you swear by them. And what justice should we do to our health, to our children, to our God, if not that of charity, that of truth and never that of falsehood? The true oath is given above all when one swears by God. For even when one says: "For my health," he pledges his health to

God; When he says: "For my children," he gives his children as a pledge to God, so that what comes out of the mouth of him who swears may fall on their heads: if the truth, the truth; If the lie, the lie. If, then, when a man mentions his children, or his head, or his health in his oath, he pledges all of this to God, how much more so when he swears directly by God! Are you afraid to swear falsely by your child and are you not afraid to do so by your God? You may say in your mind, “I am afraid to swear falsely by my son, lest he die; But what evil can befall God, who does not die, even if one swears falsely by him? You say well that no evil can befall God when you swear falsely by Him, but great is that which befalls you, who deceive your neighbor by making God your witness. If you had done something in the presence of your son, and you said to your friend, your neighbor or to any man: "I did not do it," and placing your hand on the head of the son, witness of your action, you insisted: "On the health of my son I swear that I did not do it," it is possible that he, trembling under the hand of the father, but fearing not the hand of the father, but that of God, would say: "No, father; Don't let my health be such a despicable thing to you; you called upon God upon me; I saw you, you did it, do not swear falsely; It is true that you are my father, but I fear the creator more, yours and mine. 8. When you swear by him, God does not say to you: "I saw you, do not swear, you did it." You fear that someone will kill you, and you start by killing yourself. Do you think he didn't see you because he doesn't say, "You

meam, quia parcens vobis nondum veni Corinthum (2 Cor 1:23). Et alio loco ad Galatas: Quae autem ¡cribo vobis, ecce coram Deo, quia non mentior (Gal 1,20). CAPUT VI.—6. Varii modi iurandi.—Intendite, quaeso, et advertite: et si non tam plausibilis sermo vobis sit, propter anguishes quaestionis, utilis tamen est, si ad viscera vestra perveniat. Ecce iuravit Apostolus. Non vos fallant, qui nescio quomodo volentes ipsas iurationes discernere, vel potius non intellegere, dícunt non esse iurationem, quando dicit homo: Scit Deus, Testis est Deus, Invoco Deum super animam meam verum me dicere. Invocavit, inquit, Deum, testem fecit Deum: numquid iuravit? Qui haec dicunt, nihU aliud volunt, nisi invoketo Deo teste lieri. Itane vero, quisquís is pravi cordis, et perversi cordis, if you say: Per Deum, iuras; yes you say: Testis est Deus, non iuras? Quid est enim: Per Deum, nisi: Testis est Deus? Aut quid est: Testis est Deus, nisi: Per Deum? 7. lurare quid sit.—Quid est autem iurare, nisi ius Deo reddere, quando per Deum iuras; ius saluti tuae reddere, quando per salutem tuam iuras; ius filiis tuis reddere, quando per filios tuos iuras? Quod autem ius debenmus saluti nostrae, filiis nostris, Deo nostro, nisi caritatis, veritatis, et non falsitatis? Máxime autem per Deum cum fit, ipsa est vera iuratio: quia et cum dicit quisque: Per meam salutem, salutem

suam Deo obligat: quando dicit: Per filios meos, oppignorat Deo filios suos, ut hoc veniat in caput eorum, quod exit de ore ipsius: si verum, verum; if falsum, falsum. Cum ergo filios suos, vel caput suum, vel salutem suam quisque in iuratione nominans, quidquid nominat obligat Deo; quanto magis quando peierat per ipsum Deum? Timet enim falsum iurare per íilium suum, et non timet falsum iurare per Deum suum? Fortassis hoc dices in animo suo, Timeo per filium meum falsum iurare, ne moriatur: Deo autem qui non moritur, etsi falsum per eum iuretur, quid mali contingit? Bene quidem dicis, nihil mali contingit Deo, quando falsum iuras oer Deum: sed contingit mali multum tibi, qui fallís proximum, cui testem adhibes Deum. Si aliquid teste filio tuo facetes, et amico vel proxima tuo vel cuilibet homini díceres: Non feci, et tangeres filio tuo caput, quo teste fecisti, et díceres, Per huius salutem, quia non feci: exclamaret forte filius tuus sub paterna manu tremens, nec tamen paternam manum, sed divinam tremens: Noli pater, non tibi vilis sit salus mea; Deum super me invokesti, ego te vidi, fecisti, noli peierare: te quidem habeo genitorem, sed plus et tuum et meum timeo Creatorem. CAPUT VII.—8. Períurium animae morttfemm. Vita corporis anima, vita animae Deus.—Sed quia Deus, quando per eum iuras, non tibi dicit, Ego te vidi, noli [976] iurare, fecisti: sed times ne te iste occidat, tu te ante occidis: qua ergo non dicit: Ego te vidi, putas quia non vidit?

“I saw”? And where is what is written: I was silent, I was silent; Do I always have to be silent? However, very frequently he tells you: "I saw you," but in a different way, when he punishes perjury. But it does not punish everyone, and that is why men build their lives on such examples. «I know that he swore falsely to me and continues to live; that other did the same with you and lives. He swore falsely and lives; he swore falsely. You are deceived. If you had eyes with which to see his death, if you too were wrong about what it is to die and not die, you would see his death. And now set your eyes on the Scripture; There you will see that the person you think lives lies on the ground. You think it is alive because it walks with its feet, touches with its hands, sees with its eyes, hears with its ears and uses the functions of the other members. He lives, but his body; On the other hand, his soul is dead; its most noble part is dead. The house lives, but whoever lives in it is dead. How, you will say, is the soul dead if the body lives, since the body would not have life if it were not vivified by the soul? How then is the soul that gives life to the body dead? Listen, therefore, and learn: the body of man is a creature of God just like the human soul. Through the soul, God vivifies the body; To the soul, however, he gives life himself, not itself. Consequently, the life of the body is the soul, and the life of the soul is God. When the soul withdraws, the body dies; The soul dies if God withdraws. The soul is withdrawn when the body is wounded by the sword; And do you think that God does not withdraw when the soul receives the wound of perjury? Do you want

see that the one you speak of is dead? Read the Scripture: A lying mouth kills the soul. But you think that God currently takes revenge only if you see the one who deceived you with a false oath fall and expire. If he had expired before your eyes, his flesh would have expired. What does it mean that his flesh expired? That cast out the spirit that gave him life. That is, he expired by casting out the spirit by which the flesh lived. He perjured himself: he cast out the Spirit by which the soul lived. He expired, but you ignore it; It expired, but you don't see it. You see, in fact, the flesh lying without a soul, but you cannot see the miserable soul deprived of God. Believe, then; apply the eyes of faith. No perjurer goes unpunished; absolutely none. Perjury is worth it. If he had an executioner for the flesh in his house, he would be punished; He has in the secret of his heart the executioner of his conscience, and do you consider him unpunished? Still, what are you saying? «Live, enjoy, give yourself over to lust who swore falsely against me; "Why do you refer me to invisible things?" For the same God, by whom he swore, is invisible; He swore by the invisible and is wounded with an invisible punishment. "But it lives, he says, and in a certain way it abounds and bubbles in the midst of pleasures." If this is really the case, that abundance and bubbling between pleasures are the worms of the dead soul. Finally, every prudent person who sets his sights on such perjured men given over to excesses, thanks to the healthy sense of smell of his heart, turns away, he does not want to see or listen. Why does this healthy person withdraw? That the dead soul smells bad.

Et ubi est quod dicit: Tacui, tacui; numquid semper tacebo? (Is 42,44). Et tamen plerumque dicit: Ego te vidi: sed aliter when vindicat in periurum. Sed non in omnes vindicat: ideo homines aedilicantur ad exemplum. Ego scio, Ule mihi falsum iuravit, et vivit. Ule tibi falsum iuravit, et vivit? Falsum iuravit, et vivit: ille falsum iuravit. You will fail. Si tu oculos haberes unde mortem huius videres, si et tu in eo quod est morí, et non morí, non fallereris, videres huius mortem. Et moda intende Scripturam; et ibi inventes iacentem, quem putas vivostem. Quia pedibus ambulat, quia maníbus contrectat, quia oculis videt, et audit auribus, officiis ceteris membrorum satis utitur, vivostem putas. Vivit, sed corpus eius: mortua est autem anima eius, mortuum est quod melius est eius. Vivit habitaculum, mortuus est habitator. Quomodo, inquies, cum vivat corpus, mortua est anima; cum corpus non viveret, nisi vivificatum ab anima? What mode ergo mortua est anima, de qua vivit corpus? Audi ergo, et disce: corpus hominis creatura Dei est, et anima hominis creatura Dei est. De anima Deus vivificat carnem; ípsam item animam vivificat de se ipso, non de se ipsa. Vita ergo corporis anima est; vita ergo animae Deus est. Moritur corpus, cum recedit anima: moritur ergo anima, si recedit Deus. Recedit anima, cum corpus percutitur gladio: et putas quía non recedit Deus, cum ipsa anima feritur periurio? Vis videre

quia mortuus est, what are you talking about? Lege Scripturam: Os quod mentitur, occidit animam (Wis 1:11). Sed tu praesentem Deum ultorem whores, si ille qui te iuratione false deceperit, continuous exspiret. If he died before your eyes; exspiravit caro ipsius. Quid est, exspiravit caro ipsius? Spiritum quo vivificabatur, eiecit. Hoc est, exspiravit excluso spiritu, quo vidabat expensive. Peieravit, exclusit spiritum quo vivebat anima. Exspiravit, sed nescis; exspiravit, sed non vides. Carnem enim iacentem sine anima vides, animam miseram sine Deo videre non potes. Crede ergo, adhibe oculos fidei. Nemo periurus impunitus; prorsus nemo, cum illo est poena sua. Si haberet in cubicle suo tortorem carnis, punitus esset: habet in secreto cordis sui tortorem conscientiae suae, et impunitus vocatur? And also what are you saying? Vivit, gaudet, luxuriatur qui mihi mendacium iuravit: quid est, quod me mittis ad invisibilia? Quia et ipse Deus, per quem iuravit, invisibilis est. Iuravit per invisibilem, feritur poena invisibili. Sed vivit, inquit, et quodam moda scatet et bullit luxuriis. Si hoc ita est, quod scatet luxuriis, quod bullit luxuriis, vermes sunt animae mortuae. Denique omnis homo prudens, qui such luxuriantes periuros attendit, healthy cordis olfactu avertit se, non vult videre, non vult audire. Unde se is sanitas avertit, nisi quia putet anima mortua?

9. Listen to me, then, my brothers, a few seconds more; I will conclude the sermon by piercing your hearts with a healthy concern: First of all, do not swear. Why first of all? Why does he say: First of all, do not swear, if, although it is a great crime to perjure, there is no guilt in swearing the truth? According to this, he should have said: "First of all, do not perjure." First of all, don't swear, he said. So is swearing worse than stealing? Is swearing worse than committing adultery? I'm not talking about false swearing, but simple swearing: is swearing worse than killing a man? In no way. Killing a man, committing adultery, stealing is a sin; not, however, swear; but swearing falsely. Why then does he say: First of all? With these words he wanted to put us on guard against our own language. He said: First of all, so that first of all you are attentive and alert so that the habit of swearing does not creep towards you. He put you before yourself as before a mirror; By telling you first of all he raised you above other things so that you can look at yourself. He notices that you swear: "By God, by Christ, I'll kill him!" —and how many times a day, how many times an hour!—. You don't open your mouth unless it's to swear. Would you have wanted to see away that first thing, which forces you to pay close attention to that habit, to examine all your things, to diligently monitor all the movements of your tongue and to be the guardian of your bad habit in order to master it? Listen: First of all. You were asleep and I pricked you;

First of all..., I bring you the pins. What does it mean first of all? First of all, be awake; Above all, be attentive. 10. I also swore at every moment; I also had this horrible and deadly habit 2. I confess it to your charity: Since I began to serve God and saw the evil that perjury contains, a strong fear took hold of me and with it I stopped such a deep-rooted habit. Once stopped, it is contained; contained, languishes; languishing, it dies, and the bad habit gives way to the good. I am not telling you, then, that I did not swear, because if I said so I would be lying. As for me, I swear; but, at least it seems to me, driven by a strong need. When I see that I am not given credit unless I swear, and that not giving credit harms the one who does it, after thinking and weighing it well, with no little fear, I say: "In the presence of God," or "God is witness," or "Christ knows that this is what I think." I realize that it is more than just Yes, yes; No, no and what happens from there comes from evil, if not from the evil of those who swear, yes from the evil of those who do not believe. Finally, he does not say that it is bad who says something else; He does not say: “Your word be: Yes, yes; No no; If anyone says more, it is bad", but: Your word be: Yes, yes; No, no, and what happens from there comes from evil. But ask whose evil it is. But, nevertheless, this terrible human custom has another aspect.

[977] CAPOT VIII.—9. Cur dicitur a iuratione ante otnnia abstinendum.—Breviter ergo audite, fratres mei, concludam sermonem, figens in cordibus vestris curam salubrem: Ante omnia nólite turare (Iac 5,12). Quare, Ante omnia? Si magnum est facinus peierare, nulla autem culpa est verum iurare, quare, Ante omnia nólite itirare? Debuit ením dicere, Ante omnia nólite peierare. Ante omnia, inquit, nólite iurare. Iurare ením peius est, quam furari? Iurare peius est, quam adulterare? Non dico falsum iurare; iurare dico: iurare peius est, quam hominem occidere? absit. Hominem occidere, adulterare, furari, peccatum est: iurare non est peccatum; sed falsum iurare peccatum est. Quare ergo, Ante omnia? This verb quod ait: Ante omnia, cautos nos fecit adversus linguam nostram. Ante omnia, ait, ut attendatis prae ceteris, ut vigiletis ne subrepat vobis consuetudo iurandi. Tanquam in speculo ita te possuit contra te: Ante omnia, levavit te super cetera, unde te attendees. Considerat enim te iurare: Per Deum, per Christum occido illum: et haec quoties per diem, quoties per horam? Non aperis os, nisi ad talem iurationem. Nolles ut dicetet tibi: Ante omnia, ut te adversus consuetudinem intentissimum redderet, ut omnia tua inspiceres, omnes motus linguae tuae diligentissime custodires, esses custos malae consuetudinis tuae, ad eam constringendam? Audi: Ante omnia. You slept, pungo; Ante omnia,

spinas admoveo. Quod est, Ante omnia? Ante omnia vigila, ante omnia try this. HOOD IX.—10. Iurandi consuetudini aliquando obnoxius Augustinus. luratio qua conditione adhibenda.—Iuravimus et nos passim, habuimus istam teterrimam consuetudinem et mortiferam. I say Caritati vestrae: ex quo Deo serve coepimus, et quantum malum sit in periurio vidimus, timuimus vehementer, et veterosissimam consuetudinem timore frenavimus. Frenata restrictitur, restricta languescit, languescens emoritur, et malae consuetudini bona succedit. Denique non vobis dicimus, non nos iurare. Si enim hoc dicimus, liemur. Quantum ad me pertinet, iuro; sed quantum mihi videtur, magna necessitate compulsus. Cum videro non mihi credi nisi faciam, et ei qui mihi non credit non expediré quod non credit, hac perpensa ratione et consideratione librata, cum magno timore dico: Coram Deo; aut: Testis est Deus; aut: Scit Christus sic esse in animo meo; et video quia plus est, id est, quia amplius est quam: Est, est; No, no; sed quod amplius est, a malo est; et si non a malo iurantis, a malo est non credentis. Denique non ait: Si amplius facit, malus est; et: Sit in ore vestro: Est, est; No, no; si quis amplius facit, malus est: sed, Sit in ore vestro: Est, est; No, no; quod autem amplius est, a bad est (Mt 5:37). Sed quaere cuius. Be also aliud habet pessima humano consuetudo. Et cum tibi creditur, iuras; et cum nemo exigit, iuras; et horrentibus hominibus iuras; non taces iurando, The same confession appears in sermon 307,5. However, as far as we know, he makes no mention of such a custom in the Confessions.

You swear even when they give you credit and when no one demands it from you; you fight even if men are horrified; If you do not stop swearing, you will hardly be healthy and free from perjury. Unless you judge, brothers, that if the Apostle had known that the Galatians were going to believe him, he would have added the oath that says: Regarding what I write to you, I assure you in the presence of God that I do not lie. He saw there those who believed him; He also saw others who did not believe him. So do not say: "I will not swear, even if perhaps I am required to do so." What you do comes from evil certainly, but from the evil of those who demand it of you. In fact, you have no other way to justify yourself, you can't find a way to resolve a pressing matter. If the required oath and the one offered are different things, even in the latter case it is different to offer it to someone who does not believe you than to someone who believes you. 11. Celestio was one of many young people from a noble family who were attracted to the ascetic ideal of Pelagius. Augustine defines him as a man of "very keen wit" (Against the Two Letters of the Pelagians II 3,5). He, and not Pelagius, was the one who caused the crisis in Africa by arriving in Carthage and beginning to defend strange theories in that environment, such as the no need for the baptism of children. He was denounced when he tried to be ordained a priest, and six of his proposals were then condemned, which he did not want to retract.

Redi ergo, haeretice, ad orationem, si obsurduisti contra veram fidei rationem. Dimitte nobis debita nostra, dicis, an non dicis? If you do not say, etsi praesens fueris corpore, foris tamen es ab Ecclesia. Ecclesiae enim oratio est, vox est de magisterio Domini veniens. Ipse dixit, Sic orate (Mt 6:9-14); discipulis dixit: Sic orate; discipulis dixit, Apostolis dixit, et nobis qualescumque agniculi sumus dixit; arietibus gregis dixit: Sic orate. Videte quís dixerit, et quibus dixerit. Veritas discipulis, Pastor pastorum arietibus: Sic orate, Dimitte nobis debita nostra, sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris. Rex militibus, Dominus servis, Christus Apostolis, veritas hominibus loquebatur, sublimitas humilibus loquebatur. Scio quid in vobis agatur: ego vos appendo, ego de trutina mea renuntio, prorsus dico quid in vobis agitur. Hoc enim ego plus quam vos scio. Say to yourself: Dimitte nobis debita nostra, sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris. CAPUT V.—7. Iota Ecclesia hic petit sibi dimitti peccata. Hic agitur ut Ecclesia in caelis sit sine macula et ruga.—Interrogo te, homo iuste, sánete, homo sine macula et ruga; I interrogate you, inquam: Oratio ista Ecclesiae est, fidelium est, an catechumenorum? Certe utique regenera-

Without a doubt, it is typical of the regenerated, that is, of the baptized; In short—and this is worth more than anything else—it is typical of children. In fact, if it is not the prayer of children, with what face is it said: Our Father, who art in heaven? Where are you then, you righteous and holy ones? Are you or are you not among the members of this Church? You were one of their number, but you are no longer one. May those who are separated, seeing why, listen and believe! Consequently, if the entire Church says: Forgive us our debts, whoever does not say it is a reprobate. Even we, who talk about our debts, until we receive what we ask for are reprobates because we are sinners; But by doing what you do not do, that is, confessing our sins, we purify ourselves, provided we fulfill what we say: Just as we also forgive our debtors. Where are you then, heretic, Pelagian or Celestian whoever you are? Behold, the whole Church says: Forgive us our debts. From which it is concluded that it has spots and wrinkles. But with confession the wrinkle is stretched and the stain is washed away. The Church is kept standing by prayer to be purified by confession, and as long as it lives here, it stays that way. And at the moment of leaving the body, each one is forgiven all his debts that needed forgiveness, since it is also obtained through daily prayer; then it comes out purified and the Church, like pure gold, passes into the treasures of God; That is why there will be no spot or wrinkle there. And if there he will not have even a stain torum est, id est, baptizatorum: desserto, quod totum superat, filiorum est. Nam si non est filiorum, qua fronte dicitur: Pater noster, qui est in caelis? Ubi ergo estis, or iusti et sancti? In membris Ecclesiae huius estis, an non estis? Ibi eratis, sed iam non estis ibi. Et utinam iam praecisi accepta ratione audiant et credant. Ergo si tota Ecclesia dicit: Dimitte nobis debita nostra, reprobus est qui hoc non dicit. Et nos quidem cum dicimus, debita nostra, quousque id quod petimus accipiamus, reprobi sumus, quia peccatores sumus: sed quod vos non facitis, nos fazando, id est peccata nostra confitendo, mundamur; si tamen faciamus quod dicimus: Sicut et nos dimittimus debitoribus nostris. Ubi is ergo, haeretice Pelagiane vel Caelestiane? Ecce tota Ecclesia dicit: Dimitte nobis debita nostra. Habet ergo maculas et rugas. Sed confessíone ruga extenditur, confessione macula abluitur.

Stat Ecclesia in oratione, ut mundetur confessione: et quamdiu hic vívitur, sic stat. Et cum de corpore exierit unusquísque, dimittuntur ei omnia, quae talia habebat ut dimitterentur debita; quia et quotidianis precibus dimittuntur: et tune [985] exit mundatus, et thesaurizatur Ecclesia in thesauros Domini aurum purum; ac per hoc in thesauros Domini Ecclesia est sine macula et ruga. Et si ibi sine macula et ruga est, hic quid orandum est? Ut venia percipiatur. Qui dat veniam, maculara extergit: qui ignoscit, rugam extendit. Et ubi extenditur ruga nostra? Tanquam in tendicula magni fullonis, in crossing
Forgiveness of confessed sins

nor wrinkle, why do we have to pray here? To receive forgiveness. He who grants forgiveness washes away the stain; He who forgives, straightens the wrinkle. And where does our wrinkle stretch? On the cross of Christ, like the great fuller's hanger. On the same cross, that is, on that hanger, he shed his blood for us. You, the faithful, know what testimony you give to the blood you have received. Truly you say: "Amen" 2. You know what blood was shed for the remission of the sins of many. See how the Church becomes without spot or wrinkle: how, well washed, it is stretched on the clothesline of the cross. But that can only be done here. The Lord places in his own presence the glorious Church without spot or wrinkle. He does this here too, but he shows it there. What it does is this: that we have neither spot nor wrinkle. Great is he who does it; He heals well, he is a very learned doctor. He stretches us on the wood and leaves those who, by washing us, had removed the stains without wrinkles. He, who came without spot or wrinkle, stretched himself out on the hanger, but for us, not for himself, that we might become without spot or wrinkle. Let us ask him, then, to do it and, after having done it, to take us to the granaries and deposit us there, where there will be no press to oppress us. 8. You, then, who spoke, are you without spot or wrinkle? What are you doing here, in a Church that says: Forgive us our debts, that confesses to having debts that must be forgiven? Those who don't recognize them, that doesn't mean they stop having them, Christi. In ipsa enim cruz, id est, in ipsa tendicula pro nobis sanguinem fudit._ Et nostis fideles quale testimonium perhibatis sanguini quem accepistis. Certe enim dicitis: Amen. Nostis qui sit sanguís qui pro multis effusus est in remissionem peccatorum. Ecce quomodo fit Ecclesia sine macula et ruga, tanquam bene mundata in tendicula crucis extenditur: sed hic omnino potest id agi. Exhibet sibi Ecclesiam gloriosam Dominus, non habentem maculara aut rugam. Agit hoc et hic, exhibit ibi. Hoc enim agit, ut non habeamus maculam aut rugam. Magnus est qui agit, bene curat, doctissimus artifex est. Extendit in ligno, et facit nos sine ruga, quos abluendo fecerat sine macula. Ipse qui venit sine macula et sine ruga, extensus est in tendicula; sed propter nos, non propter se, ut nos faceret sine macula et ruga. Rogemus ergo eum ut faciat, et postquam fecerit, ad horrea nos ducat, ibique nos reponat, ubi pressorium non erit. CAPUT VI.—8. Remedia peccatorum sine quibus vivi non potest.

Mortifera non facit bonae fidei et bonae spei Christianus. Conditio qua nobis relaxantur quotidiana peccata.—Tu ergo qui loquebaris, sine macula et ruga es? Quid hic facis in Ecclesia, quae dicit: Dimitte nobis debita nostra? Debita se habere confitetur, quae relaxentur. Qui non It refers to the "Amen" that was pronounced when receiving the Eucharist, as is also done today, after the restoration of Vatican II.

but for that they will not be forgiven. Confession and prudent living, humble living, prayer with faith, heartfelt contrition, unfeigned tears that flow from the heart to ask for forgiveness of our sins, without which we cannot be, heal us. Confession, I repeat, heals us according to the words of the apostle John: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and cleanse us from all evil. Not because he said that we cannot live here without sin, we should commit murder, or adultery or other mortal sins that result in death with a single stroke. Such sins are not committed by the Christian who believes and hopes rightly, but only by those others who are covered with the brush of daily prayer. With humility and devotion let us say every day: Forgive us our debts, but only if we do the following: As we also forgive our debtors. It is a contract with God: a true contract with an explicit clause. You are a man and you have debtors, at the same time you are also a debtor. You appear before God, who has debtors without being a debtor himself, to ask him to forgive you your debt. But he tells you the following: «I don't have debts, you do; You owe me, but your brother also owes you something. You are my debtor and, in turn, my creditor. You are my debtor because you sinned against me; You are your brother's creditor because he sinned against you. Whatever you do to your debtor, that is what I will do to mine; That is, if you forgive, I forgive; If you retain, I retain. You hold it against you if you do not forgive confitentur, non ideo non habent: sed ideo eis non relaxabuntur. Confessío nos sanat, et vita cauta, vita humilis, oratío cum fide, contritio cordis, lacrimae non fictae de vena cordis profluentes, ut dimittantur nobis peccata, sine quibus esse non possumus. Confessio, inquam, nos sanat, they say te apostólo loanne: Si confiteamur peccata nostra, fidelis est et tustús, ut dimittat nobis peccata, et mundet nos ab omni iniquitate.^ Non autem, quia dico quod non possumus hic esse sine peccato, homicidia faceré debenmus, aut adulteria, vel cetera mortifera peccata, quae uno ictu perimunt. Talia non facit bonae fidei et bonae spei christianus: sed illa sola, quae quotidiano orationis penicillo tergantur. Humiles et devoti dicamus quotidie: Dimitte nobis debita nostra: sed si faciamus quod sequitur, Sicut et nos ditnittimus debitoribus nostris. Sponsio haec cum Deo, vera sponsio et fixa conditío est.

Tu homo es, et habes debitorem, et debitor etiam tu es. Accedis ad Deum, qu habet debitores, et debitar non est, ut postulas tibi debita relaxad. Sed hoc tibi dicit: Ego debita non habeo, tu habes debita; you must enim mihi: sed etiam frater tuus debent tibi. Debi [984] tor meus es, habes et tu debitorem. Debitor meus es, quia peccasti in me: habes debitorem fratrem, quia peccavit in te. Quod feceris cum debitare tuo, fació et ego cum meo: id est, si dimittis, dimitto; If you have, I have. You have yourself against yourself, qui alteri non dimittis. Nemo ergo dicat se esse sine sine: sed non tamen ideo must-
Discernment of spirits

the debt to the other. Let no one say, therefore, that he is without sin; but that does not mean we should love sin. Let us hate him, brothers; although we do not lack them, let us hate them; and above all, let us abstain from the most serious sins; Let us abstain, as far as possible, from light sins. «I, says I don't know who, have no sins». He deceives himself and the truth does not dwell in him. Let us pray, then, that God forgives us, but let us do what he commands us: let us also forgive our debtors. When we forgive, we are also forgiven. Every day we repeat it, every day we do it and every day it becomes reality in us. We are not without sin here, but we will get out of here without it.
Topic: Discernment of spirits (1 Jn 4,1-3). Location: Unknown. Date: After 416.

1. When we read the apostle John, we heard the Holy Spirit speaking through him and saying: Dearly beloved, do not give faith to just any spirit; but examine the spirits to see if they come from God. I insist on it, because it is mus amare peccatum. Oderimus ea, fratres; etsi non sumus sine peccatis, oderimus tamen ea: et máxime a criminibus nos abstineamus; abstineamus, quantum possumus, a levibus peccatis. Ego, ait, nescio quis, non habeo peccata. Se ipsum decipit, et veritas in eo non est. Prorsus oremus, ut Deus dimittat; sed faciamus quod dicitur, dimittamus et nos debitoribus nostris. Cum dimittimus, et dimittitur nobis. Quotidie dicimus hoc, et quotidie facimus, et quotidie fit in nobis. Non hic sumus sine peccato, sed exibimus hinc sine peccato.
DE VERBIS EPISTOLAE 1 IOANNIS, 4,1-3: «CARISSIMI, NOLITE OMNI SPIRITUI CREDERE; SED PROBATE SPIRITUS, SI EX DE O SUNT”, ETC. AGAINST MANICHAEOS

CAPUT I.—1. Non cuilibet spiritui credendum.—Quando Ioannes apostolus legebatur, audivimus loquentem per eum Spiritum sanctum, et dicentem: Carissimi, nolite omni spiritui credere; sed probate spiritus, si ex Deo sunt. Repeto, quia necessarium est ut repetam, et hoc men-
Discernment of spirits

It is necessary that I repeat it to you and instill it strongly in your minds, to the extent that God helps me. Dearly beloved, do not give faith to just any spirit; but examine the spirits to see if they come from God, because many false prophets have gone out into the world. The Holy Spirit has commanded us not to give faith to any spirit, and He showed us the reason for this command. Which is it? Because many false prophets have come out into the world. Therefore, whoever despises this command and thinks that he must believe every spirit, will necessarily fall into the hands of false prophets and, what is worse, will blaspheme against the authentic ones. 2. Now, the man put on guard by this precept will say to me: "I have heard it, I maintain it and I wish to fulfill it, since I too do not want to end up among the false prophets. Well, who is there who wants to be deceived by mendacious people? Indeed, a false prophet is a lying prophet. Present me a pious man: he does not want to deceive; Present me another impious, sacrilegious: he wants to deceive, but not be deceived. If the good do not want to deceive, and both the good and the bad hate to be deceived, who is there who wants to fall into the hands of false prophets? I repeat the words of the one who gives me advice; But the truth is that no one, except involuntarily, gives himself over to false prophets. I have heard the precept of John, better, from the Lord through the mouth of John: Do not give faith to just any spirit. I accept it and that's how I want to act. He goes on to say: Rather, examine the spirits to see if they come from God. How to do it? I would like to examine them,

If I had no chance of making a mistake. On the other hand, if I do not find out which spirits come from God, I will necessarily find those that do not come from him and, consequently, I will be seduced by false prophets. What can I do? How to distinguish them? Oh, if holy John, in the same way he told us: Do not give faith to any spirit; rather, distinguish those that are from God, he would have also deigned to tell us the way to know if they come from God! Cease your worry and listen: By this you know the spirit that comes from God: here is what you wanted to hear to find out which spirits are from God. In this the spirit that proceeds from God is known; They are Juan's words, not mine; Thus the reading that I am commenting on continues. After making us cautious and cautious so that we do not give faith to just any spirit, but rather find out which ones come from God, since there are many false prophets who came out into this world, he immediately saw what our desire would be; He meets our expectations and focuses his gaze on our hidden thoughts. Thank God that he has also deigned to show us this through Juan. In this we know the spirit that is from God. Hey, then, listen; listen, understand and distinguish; Adhering to the truth, resist falsehood. In this the spirit that proceeds from God is known. «In what, I beg you? This is what I wanted to hear. Every spirit that confesses that Jesus Christ came in the flesh proceeds from God; and every spirit that does not confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh does not come from God. In the meantime, then, dearly beloved, put away from your ears

tibus vestris, quantum Dominus adiuvat, vehementer inculcem. Carissimi, nolite omni spiritui credere; sed probate spiritus, si ex Deo sunt. Quoniam multi pseudoprophetae prodierunt in hunc mundum (1 lo 4,1). Praecepit Spiritus sanctus, ne omni spiritui credamus: et causam cur hoc praeceperit, dixit. What is the cause? Quoniam multi, inquit, pseudoprophetae prodierunt in hunc mundum. Quisquís ergo ista praecepta contempserit, et omni spiritui credendum putaverit, necesse est incurrat in pseudoprophetas, et quod peius est, blasphemet veros Prophetas. CAPUT II.—2. Ex Deo non est, qui negat Christum in carne venisse.—Hic iam ex isto praecepto homo cautus effectus dicturus est mihi: Audivi, teneo, obtemperare desidero, quia et ego in pseudoprophetas nolo incurrere. Quis enim hoc veüt, a mendacibus decipi? Siquidem pseudopropheta est mendax propheta. Da mihi hominem religiosum, non vult fallere: da mihi hominem impium, sacrilegum, fallere vult, falli non vult. Cum ergo nolint fallere boni, falli autem nec boni velínt nec mali, quis est qui in pseudoprophetam velit incurrere? Verba dico consultentis me: sed utique ín pseudoprophetam nemo nisi invitus incurrit. Audivi praeceptum loannis, immo Domini per Ioannem: Nolite omni spiritui credere. Ecce accipio, ita flew. Addit, et dicit: Sed probate spiritus, si ex

[985] Deo sunt. Where did I try? I will try again, if I err, I will not possem. Certe nisi probavero spiritus qui ex Deo sunt, incurram necesse est in spiritus qui ex Deo non sunt, et ex hoc seducar a pseudoprophetis. Quid agam? How do we observe? Or si sanctus Ioannes, quomodo nobis dixit, Nolite omni spiritui credere, sed probate spiritus, si ex Deo sunt; dicere digretur, quomodo probentur spiritus qui ex Deo sunt! Noli esse sollicitus, et hoc audi. Hinc cognoscitur spiritus Dei: hoc certe exspectabas audire, ut proveres spiritus qui ex Deo sunt. Hinc cognoscitur spiritus Dei: Ioannes dixit, non ego: hoc sequitur in lectione quam tracto. Cum enim nos propterea faceret sollicitos et cautos, ne omni spiritui credamus, sed probemus spiritus qui ex Deo sunt, quia multi pseudoprophetae prodierunt in hunc mundum; continuous vidit quid desideraremus, occurrit exspectationi, iniecit oculum tacitae cogitationi. Gratias Deo, quia et hoc per illuní loqui dignitus est. Hinc cognoscitur spiritus Dei. Eia audite; audit, intellegite, discern; inhaerete veritati, resistite falsitati. Hinc cognoscitur spiritus Dei. Well, do I ask you? Hoc est quod audire cupiebam. Omnis spiritus qui conjitetur lesum Christum in carne venisse, ex Deo est: et omnis spiritus qui non conjitetur lesum Christum in carne venisse, ex Deo non est (1 lo 4,2-3). Interim ergo, carissimi,

to any charlatan, preacher, writer or whisperer who denies the coming in the flesh of Jesus Christ. Therefore expel from your houses, your ears and your hearts the Manichaeans, who openly deny that Jesus Christ came in the flesh.' Therefore, his spirit does not come from God. 3. I am now seeing where the wolf wants to sneak in; I warn it, and, to the best of my ability, I will show how it is to be avoided. In what I said, or rather in the words of the Apostle mentioned by me, that every spirit that denies that Jesus Christ came in the flesh does not come from God, the Manichaean sets his trap and says: "Behold, the spirit that denies that Jesus Christ came in the flesh does not come from God; Where does it come from, then? If it does not come from God, then where from? Can it exist without coming from somewhere? Therefore, if it does not come from God and comes from somewhere else, there you have the two natures." 2. We have encountered the wolf; let's lay out the saving snares to him, let's hunt him down, apprehend him and, once captured, let's tear him to pieces. Let's tear it apart, yes; Let error die and long live man! In the words I just said: “Let us seize him, let us tear him to pieces; Let error die and long live man! », is the solution to the problem. But remember what I proposed to you, lest, having forgotten the problem, you do not understand the solution. Every spirit that does not confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh does not come from God. repellite ab auribus vestris omnem disputatorem, praedicatorem, scriptorem, whisperatorem, who negat Iesum Christum in carne venisse. Ergo repellite Manichaeos a domibus, ab auribus, a cordibus vestris. Manichaei enim Christum in carne venisse apertissime negant. Spiritus ergo illorum non sunt ex Deo. 3. Manichaeorum in ipso loco Ioannis insidiae. Duabus naturis error.—Hic video unde velit lupus obrepere; agnosco, et quantum valeo, devitandum esse demonstro. Hinc, in eo quod dixi, vel potius ab Apostólo dictum commemoraví; quia Omnis spiritus qui negat lesum Christum in carne venisse, ex Deo non est; insidiatur Manichaeus in hoc verbo, et dicít mihi: Ecce spiritus qui negat Iesum Christum in carne venisse, ex Deo non est; where is ergo? If ex Deo non est, inquit, where is it? Numquid enim potest esse, nisi aliunde? Si ergo, inquit, ex Deo non est, et aliunde est, vides esse duas naturas. Invenimus lupum: retia salubria tendamus, venemur, capiamus, captum trucidemus. Trucidemus plane; moriatur error, vivat homo.

Ecce in eo quod dixi, Capiamus, trucidemus; moriatur error, vivat homo; ibi solvitur quaestío. Sed recolite quod proposed, ne obliti quaestionem, non intellegatis solutionem. Omnis spiritus qui non confitetur lesum Christum in carne venisse, ex Deo non est. Manichaean Christology was fully doctrinal. See supplementary note 3: The 2Manichean Christology vol. VII p.743-744. He is referring to the Manichean doctrine of two principles, one good and one bad.
Discernment of spirits

And the Manichean continues: «Where does it come from, then? If it does not come from God, it comes from somewhere else. If it comes from somewhere else, that is my demonstration that there are two natures. Hold this objection and return your minds to those words of mine spoken a short time ago: “Let us seize him, let us tear him to pieces; Let error die and long live man! » The error does not come from God, but man does. Return to the objection: Every spirit that does not confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh does not come from God. I also say: All things were made by him. Let every spirit praise the Lord. But if not all spirits come from God, how does he who does not come from God praise the Lord? Absolutely let every spirit praise the Lord. I see both; I notice that one is sick. Let the evil be cured and nature be liberated. Evil is not a nature, but the enemy of nature. Eliminate the cause of your illness and the reason for praise remains. Medicine pursues evils, not nature. Any spirit that does not confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh does not come from God. It does not come from God as long as it does not confess that Jesus Christ came in the flesh, because this error, that is, the statement that Jesus Christ did not come in the flesh, does not come from God. Brothers, why are we reborn? If we were born well, why are we reborn? That corrupted nature may be repaired, that fallen nature may be raised, and nature that lay deformed be reformed by grace. For there is only one creator: the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit; triune unity and one trinity; immutable and unchangeable nature, not subject even to CAPUT III.—Et Manichaeus continuo: Et unde est? If ex Deo non est, aliunde est. Si aliunde est, docui duas esse naturas. Hanc quaestionem tenete, et mentes ad illa mea verba revócate, ubi dixi: Capiamus, trucidemus; moriatur error, vivat homo. Error non est ex Deo, homo ex Deo est. Redite ad [986] quaestionem: Omnis spiritus qui non confitetur Iesum in carne venisse, ex Deo non est. Dico et ego, Omnia per ipsum facta sunt (lo 1,3). Omnis spiritus laudet Dominum (Ps 150.6). Sed si non omnis spiritus ex Deo est, quomodo spiritus qui ex Deo non est laudat Dominum? Prorsus omnis spiritus laudet Dominum. Utrumque video, languidum intellego; vitium sanetur, natura liberetur. Vitium natura non est, sed naturae inimicum est. Sana unde langues, remanet unde laudes. Medicine vitia persequitur, non naturam.

Omnis spiritus qui non confitetur lesum Christum in carne venisse, ex Deo non est. In quantum non confitetur Christum in carne venisse, in tantum ex Deo non est; quia iste error qui non confitetur Christum in carne venisse, ex Deo non est. Fratres, quid est quod renascimur? Si bene nati sumus, quid est quod renascimur? Natura quae corrupta fuet, reparatur; natura quae lapsa fuet, erigitur; natura quae deformis iacebat, gratia reformatur. Solus enim Creator, Pater, Filius et Spiritus sanctus; trill unitas, one

return or progress, it is the only one that neither declines until it becomes less nor surpasses itself until it becomes more: it is the only perfect, everlasting and absolutely immutable nature. The creature, on the other hand, is good, but without comparison with the Creator. Trying to make creatures equal to the creator is equivalent to adhering to the deserted devil. 4. Let the soul recognize its own condition: it is not God 3. When it considers itself God, the soul offends God, and does not find in him a savior, but a condemner. In fact, when God condemns perverse souls, he does not condemn himself, which would happen, however, if the souls were God. Let us pay honor, brothers, to our God, to whom we cry: Deliver us from evil. And if someone, to turn your prayer into temptation, whispers to you: "Why have you cried out: Deliver us from evil?" Isn't it true that there is no evil? 4, answer him: «I am the bad one; and if he delivers me from evil, I will go from evil to good; Let him free me from myself so that I do not end up in you. This is what the Manichean must say: «If God frees me from myself, I will not end up in you, because if God frees me from myself, who is bad, I will become good; If I become good, I will also become wise; If wise, I will not err and, if I do not err, I will not be able to be deceived by you. May God free me, therefore, from myself and so I will not end up in you. To err and believe you is my vice, since my soul is full of fantasies. I am not a light to myself, trinitas; sola illa natura immutabilis, incommutabilis, nec defectui, nec profectui obnoxia, nec cadit, ut minus sit; nec transcendit, ut plus sit; perfect, everlasting, omni moda immutabilis, sola illa natura. Creatura vero bona, sed Creatori odd valde. Vis adhaerere diabolo desertori, si aequare contendis condita Conditori. CAPUT IV.—4. Manichaeorum error, animam esse partem Dei, confutatur.—Agnoscat anima conditionem suam: non est Deus. Cum se anima putat Deum, offendit Deum: non invenit salvatorem, sed invenit damnatorem. Quoniam Deus quando animas malas damnat, non se damnat: si autem anima hoc est quod Deus, se damnat. Demus honorem Deo nostro, fratres, cui clamamus: Deliver us evil (Mt 6,13). Et si susurret tibi, ut in oratione invenías temptationem, et dicat tibí: Quid est quod clamasti: Libera nos a malo? Certe non est malum? illi answers: Ego sum malus; et si Iiberaverit me a mal, ero de mal bonus: liberet me a me, ne incurram in te.

Hoc dic Manichaeo: Si Deus Iiberaverit me a me, non incurram in te: quia si Deus Iiberaverit me a me bad, ero bonus; yes bonus ero, sapiens ero; If sapiens ero, I do not err; If I don't err, I'll tell you no potero. 10. More subtle is the dispute about those who confess the same as we do: that the only begotten son is equal to the Father, of the same substance, co-eternal with the eternal, and yet they are Donatists. We call Christ the one of whom John the Baptist says: He who has the wife, he is the husband. Good marriage! Holy nuptials! Christ is the husband, the Church is the wife. Donatistae plurimí hoc confitentur de Filio quod nos, quod aequalis sit Patri Filius, eiusdemque substantiae: alii vero eorum, eiusdem quidem substantiae confitentur, sed aequalem negant. What opus is disputere de his qui negant aequalem? Si enim negant aequalem, negant Filium. Si negant Filium, negant Christum. Si negant Christum, quomodo confitentur in carne venisse Christum? Donatism is another of the heresies (officially considered since 405) omnipresent in Augustinian sermons. The reader will have already noticed what its main doctrinal points are. In Letter 185,1,1 Augustine says: «The Donatists, on the other hand, do not teach this error (of the Arians), but admit in the Trinity a single and identical substance. Although some of them affirm that the Son is inferior to the Father, they do not deny the identity of substance with the Father; most of them profess the same Catholic faith. Also in the work The Heresies he attributes the Arian error to Donatus with these words: 'There are his writings where it is clear that his statements about the Trinity were not truly Catholic, because although he considered it to be of the same substance, he admitted that the Son was inferior to the Father, and the Holy Spirit less than the Son. However, the crowd of Donatists hardly paid attention to this his Trinitarian error and it is not easy to find one who knows that he thought this way" (69,2). These statements of Augustine

Additional notes

[1] Function of the humanity of Christ.—For Saint Augustine, the appropriate food for man as a rational being is the Word. But, as a result of the fall, that man has spiritually become a child and is incapable of receiving the solid food that is the Wisdom of God, unless it is transformed into milk. What the mother does: she takes solid food and gives it to the child converted into milk, that is what the Wisdom of God has done, giving itself to us as food through its flesh. Thanks to the incarnation, Wisdom nourishes our spiritual infancy with the milk of her humanity (Comments on Psalms 8:5; 33:6; 119:2; 130:9-11; Confessions VII 18, 24). In this, Augustine is in no way original, since he limits himself to interpreting Saint Paul (1 Cor 3:1-2; 2:6; Heb 5:12-13). In this way, through his humanity, the Word has become accessible to man (Commentary on Psalm 109-12). Faith in the incarnation is the appropriate means to our weakness to approach it; It is the only path we have to follow and we cannot abandon (The Customs of the Catholic Church I 7,11-12). Obviously, this is nothing more than a transitory stage. Man must grow to reach spiritual adulthood and be able to take solid food, the bread that is the Word of God, since one cannot always live on milk alone. Beyond the humility of Christ is his divinity, to which every man has been called. [2] Verbum-vox.—The theme of the human word and voice, of the inner and outer word, appears repeatedly in Augustinian pages and in different contexts. Sometimes to indicate the relationship between Christ and John the Baptist (Sermons Frangipane 8,2; Guelf. 22,3; 288; 289), others to explain, as a similarity, the incarnation. The consideration of this verbum-vox binomial is not original to Augustine, who picks it up from the previous tradition. In a Christian environment it dates back to the apologists. Such an assumption, however, is not purely passive, but transforms it in its application. While they referred it to the moment of the birth of the Word in the bosom of the Father, distinguishing two moments (logos endiathetos and logos prophorikós), Augustine applies the first to the pre-existing Word, and the second moment to the incarnation. This is a symbol of the humanity of Jesus, which reveals the divine mystery as the external word transmits the invisible riches of the concept formed by intelligence.

On this, with other parallel texts of Augustinian work, the advantage of this application over that of the apologists and what imperfection remains in the comparison, see G. BAVAUD, Un théme augustinien: le mystére de l'incarnation, h lamiere de la distinction entre le Verbe intérieur et le Yerbe proferé: «Revue des Études Augustiniennes» 9 (1963) 95-101. The expression vehiculum carnis also appears in sermons 120,2; Denis 2,2, etc. [3] Praeceptum et exemplum.—The binomial praeceptum-exemplum appears frequently in Augustinian texts. We remember, in addition to the present, sermons 273,1; 305.2; 325.1. To these we must add others

in which instead of praeceptum he speaks of verbum (word): sermons 62,1; Guelf. 3.4; 32.5; 284.6; Treatises on the Gospel of Saint John 59,1, etc. In this way of expressing himself we can see how Augustine is fully immersed in the classical world. In effect, education at that time advanced on the two rails that are praecepta and exempla, two different concepts, but never separated. The use of exemplum was common to the Greeks and Romans. But it was typical of the Roman spirit to give greater weight to the exemplum than to the praeceptum (QUINTILIAN, Oratory Institute When Augustine insists that Jesus teaches not only by word, but also by example, praeceptis et exemplo, he wants to present him to us as an ideal teacher. All the more so since the exemplum is his personal life; In addition to prescribing, he himself carries out what he prescribes; He himself does what he orders others to do. It can be deduced from Augustine's way of expressing himself that many times, when he speaks of the exemplum of Christ, he is not so much proposing the Christian an example to imitate as presenting Christ as the ideal teacher. Insisting that he was a doctor verbo et opere (of word and deed), he manifests an essential condition for this: the coherence of his own life. Phrases like this go in this direction: «He did not want to teach what he himself was not; He did not want to order what he himself did not do (Holy Virginity 35); "who did not teach what he himself did not perform" (Commentary on Psalm 18:19); "He himself did what he taught" (Commentary on Psalm 56:1); "He does what He warns must be done." The authority of his praeceptum comes from the authority of his exemplum; That is to say, the precept that is not accompanied by example lacks force. See P. de Luis VIZCAÍNO, THE acts of Jesus in the preaching of Saint Augustine. Classical rhetoric at the service of patristic exegesis (Valladolid 1983) p.260ff. [4] The temptations of Jesus.—Augustine speaks about the temptations of Jesus in different passages: Sermons 12,12; 210.3; Commentary on Psalms 90:11; 90.11 1.6-7; 30.11 1.10; 60.3; 63.18; Commentary on the Letter of Saint John to the Parthians 2,14; The city of God IX 21.

In these texts, temptations are rarely the central theme, and it is normal for them to enter the discourse in passing. What is most surprising is the character that Augustinian reflection invariably takes. The normal thing would be to contemplate, in fidelity to the biblical text, Jesus and Satan as the most important actors in the drama. In the Augustinian commentary, on the other hand, Satan takes a backseat and the "dialogue" develops between Jesus and the Christian, but not as a dialogue-discussion, but as a teacher-authority who teaches and a Christian-student who learns how he should behave. Certainly, the devil is necessary for this purpose, but he is no longer the protagonist. If other ancient commentators (SAINT JERONIMO, Commentary on Matthew I 305ss; SAINT HILARIO, Commentary on Matthew III lss; SAINT AMBROSIO, Exposition of the Gospel according to Saint Luke IV 25-35) are greatly interested in the deep reasons for the devil's actions, Augustine seems to be interested only in the reasons why Jesus allows himself to be tempted. That other type of exegesis is not unknown to him, but it takes second place in his intentions, because above all he wants to make Jesus a teacher of the Christian. One text states this: «He (the devil) saw him as mortal, capable of being tempted; so that the Christian, having been tempted, might be taught" (Commentary on the Psalm
