The temptations of Jesus hardly contribute to clarifying Augustine's Christology, regardless of this magisterial aspect. Certainly, in this way the commentary on the evangelical text is very impoverished. [5] The power of the will.—Saint Augustine clearly distinguishes between the velle and the posse, the will and the power, in the context of the means for salvation (The spirit and the letter 53). For him, the idea that the will, the desire to do good, is required as a necessary condition to do it (Nature and Grace 18,20). Without our will the justice of God will not exist in us (Sermon 169,13). The need for collaboration and human will is even deduced from the designation of God as a "helper", because "if you did nothing that came from your will, God would not be called a helper, for the helper helps those who do something" (Commentary on Psalm 143:6). The fact that salvation is not the work of man who runs or who wills, but of God who has compassion (Rom 9:16) does not mean that it occurs without the help of our will, but only that it is incapable of achieving it if it lacks divine help (The Perfection of Man's Justice 19:40). From what has been said, another aspect is already clear, namely: that the will, necessary, has its limits and its own scope. It is not sufficient to fulfill the precepts (Grace and Free Will 13,26) nor to avoid sin (Nature and Grace 18,20; Letter 177,5; 179,3). That is when it does not reach more radical formulations according to which good will cannot do anything good (Grace and Free Will 5,12; Sermon 156,12), since, according to the confession of the Pehgianos themselves, the human will lost the strength to do good (Unfinished Work against Julian II 10). The effort of the will, without God, is nothing (Commentary on Psalm 26,11 17), and this is not because the will is bad, but because even though it is good, it is small and invalid and needs to be great and robust, which is a fruit of grace (Grace and free will 17',33). Without grace, then, the will is not moved to good. A double gift from God is required, therefore: first the will of the good, and then the realization of that desired good.

The summary of everything is given to us by this force from letter 177,5: "Neither would the law command anything if the will did not exist, nor would grace help if the will were sufficient alone." [6] Augustinian interpretation of Rom 7.—The famous text of Rom 7:7-25 has occupied Augustine on repeated occasions, and the interpretation he has given of it has not always been uniform. In the first period, which reaches the Questions to Simplician (I 1,7), the saint believes that the famous "I" describes the man who lies under the law before receiving grace; that is, the Apostle personifies the man who groans under the law. This interpretation also appears in Exposition of some propositions of the Letter to the Romans 44 and in 83 various questions 66,5. Then there is a long period of approximately twenty years in which the saint continues to use certain verses to describe the captivity of the Christian and his inner struggles, but without commenting on them in their global context and without being interested in knowing who the person who is speaking there is. This use occurs predominantly in sermons, although with the emergence of the Pelagian controversy it also moves, and preferably, to letters and treatises. Indeed, with this controversy a change is already beginning to be noticed. The Pauline text is already interpreted in The Consequences and Forgiveness of Sins II 12,17 depending on the interpretation that will be imposed later, that is, he sees in the Pauline text the just man who delights in the law of God according to the inner man,

even experiencing within himself the law of the members that opposes that of his mind. The last step will be to see in the text the apostle Paul who speaks about himself. But before reaching the apodictic affirmation of the new interpretation, which appears in Against Julián (VI 23,70), a work composed around 421, and earlier in Against the two letters of the Pelagians (I 8,13-14), from a year earlier, Augustine is somewhat cautious, perhaps due to the literary genre, that is, because it is about sermons to the people and not polemical treatises. We can observe this caution in sermon 154 preached in 418 or 419, where he speaks in the conditional, expressly admitting the possibility (n.2 and 4). The saint justifies the change as a yielding to the opinion of other better and more intelligent authors and, ultimately, to the truth. These authors are none other than the saints Hilary of Poitiers, Gregory of Nazianzus and Ambrose (see Against Julian VI 23,70); can be read M. F. BERROUARD, L'exegése augustinienne de Rom 7,7-25 entre 396 et 418 avec des remarques sur les deux premieres périodes de la crise «pelagienne», in «Recherches Augustiniennes» XVI [1981] 101-195). [7] Function of the law.-—The doctrine of Saint Augustine on the law is a faithful reflection, if not a mere repetition, of the thought of Saint Paul. First of all, it must be affirmed that the law is good; good in its origin, as given by God, and good in its content, as it prohibits evil and commands good. Yet he is incapable of justifying man; Although it grants him a certain carnal justice, it does not have the strength to justify it before God. The law has a double face or function: one negative and one positive. Negative function. It is expressed in the Pauline statement that the letter kills, which admits of a double interpretation. The letter kills when what is to be interpreted spiritually is taken in a carnal sense, a danger that must always be avoided: which the Jews had to avoid and which the Christians must avoid. But it also kills in another sense: insofar as it turns man into a transgressor. If the life-giving Spirit is lacking, the law, good in itself, becomes an occasion for sin and death: by prohibiting sin it makes it known and increases the desire for it. Before the prohibition formulated by the law, the desire for evil is less; after it, it is greater if grace is not present. In other words: without the law sin is practically ignored.

The law has, therefore, the function of manifesting the sin that previously lay hidden in the person, but it has no force against it; What's more, it makes him older. Before the law, man realizes that he is dead, he recognizes that he cannot observe the precepts and, transgressing them, he sins greatly (see in this regard The Spirit and the Letter 4,6). Positive function. Still, the law is a providential gift. For what purpose was it given? In the Exposition of the Letter to the Galatians 24, it says this: "Since without grace they could in no way fulfill the precepts of the law and that grace could only be received through humility, that proud people received the law so that the transgression of it would make them humble to the point of asking for grace, and thus they would not think that salvation was the fruit of their own merits." "The transgression of the law forced him to recognize that he needed the grace and mercy of the Lord so that his sins would be forgiven and he would be reconciled to God in the new life through him who had shed his blood for them." That is to say, the purpose of the law was to break the arrogance of those who, boasting of being children of Adam, boasted of having a quasi-natural justice and put themselves before the Gentiles for the merits of their circumcision, all the more pernicious as they were more arrogant (ibid., 25).

and 26). The law is, therefore, an instrument given by God to prepare us to receive grace. This condition for justification requires humility as a fundamental disposition, which is manifested in the recognition of one's own weakness. This is precisely what the law does: it reveals to man his own weakness, demanding ideals superior to his strength that leave him in sin, deserving of condemnation. In short, although it increases man's misery and occasionally kills him, the law puts man on the path to redemption, disposing him to expect it only from faith and divine grace. The weight that crushes him makes him ask for help; The knowledge of one's own weakness makes one long for the doctor. The more sinful and worthy of punishment man recognizes himself, the more he humiliates himself and requests the help of the liberator who can save him by allowing him to fulfill the law. The law has, therefore, this positive purpose: to unmask man, not to abandon him condemned in his condition as a sinner, but to make him aware of his limits, which will lead him to humbly address the savior. In summary: «The law was given so that grace could be sought; grace was given that the law might be fulfilled” (The Spirit and the Letter 19:21). [8] Anti-Donatist legislation.—Imperial legislation against Donatism is abundant and dates back to early times. Virtually no emperor, except Julian the Apostate, has exempted himself from legislating directly or indirectly against the followers of Donatus. Let's mention the most important thing about it. Emperor Constantine; At the end of 316 or beginning of 317, he published the "edict of unity", the first law of prohibition against Donatism, made ineffective by the same emperor's edict of tolerance in the year 321. Constantine himself published four constitutions (in 319, 320—February and December—• and 328), referring to defamatory libels against Catholics. In 326 and 330 he also legislates excluding the Donatists from those privileged from tax immunity, which is reserved for the Catholic clergy. Constant: In 347 he published an edict that reestablished Constantine's law of 317 and which was repealed by another of Emperor Julian in 362. Valentinian again legislated on defamatory libels, and in 373 he prohibited rebaptism and punished any bishop who did not pay attention with deposition.

Gratian: In 376 he prescribed, through a constitution, confiscating the meeting places of heretics, and in 377 he again prohibited rebaptism, ordering the transfer to the Catholic Church of any Church where it was rebaptized. Theodosius: Among the abundant anti-heretical legislation of this emperor, we can remember the constitution of 392, with which any heretic who was ordained as a clergyman or who had acted as an orderer and anyone who had favored those illegal meetings was punished with a fine of 10 pounds of gold. In the year 392, Theodosius prescribed that anyone who caused inconvenience to the Catholic Church be deported; in 394 he forbids heretics to ordain bishops; three months later, every meeting, every organization and propaganda. Two months after his death, all these laws are confirmed by his sons Honorius and Arcadio, who continue to legislate without ceasing. In 395 they prohibited heretics from meeting, celebrating worship and ordaining. On September 3 of the same year, they legally assimilate heretics to those who do not fully admit Catholic doctrine. In January 404, imperial agents were prohibited from attending such tumultuous meetings under penalty of confiscation of property; In September it is specified that, under penalty of fine, masters must prevent their slaves from attending them; In November, governors are ordered to close all places of illicit assembly. Specifically addressed to African governors were the following laws: in March 395, the

Emperor Honorius confirms the privileges of the Catholic Church, and again in June 399. In 405 he promulgates the edict of union, which broadly reproduced those of Constantine and Constans, adding something very important: the equation of schism with heresy, which meant that the Donatists fell under the weight of all anti-heretical legislation. In November 408, a constitution dictated the penalty against dissidents who disturbed Catholic celebrations; Three days later he ordered that all gatherings of heretics be prevented, their assembly places confiscated, and all those guilty exiled. In January 409, a new constitution decreed capital punishment for those who looted Catholic churches or insulted their bishops or clerics. On August 25, 410, another imperial constitution, which annulled an edict of tolerance a few months earlier, punished heretics convicted of having held meetings with capital punishment or banning. Finally, we must mention the edict of union promulgated by Honorius on January 30, 412, which meant the definitive confirmation of the sentence pronounced by Marcellinus and his edict of June 26, 411 against the Donatists, after the celebration of the Conference of Carthage between both Churches, the Catholic and the Donatist. The imperial legislation still continued, but we are not going to continue with it because we have already exceeded the period of time to which Augustine refers in the sermon. More widely it can be seen in P. MONCEAUX, Histoire littéraire de l'Afrique chrétienne depuis les origines ¡usqu'al'invasion arab IV (Paris 1912) p.193ff. [9] Saint Augustine and religious coercion.—This is one of many points regarding which the bishop of Hippo experienced a notable change in his views. During his priestly period and at the beginning of his episcopate, Augustine explicitly rejects all religious coercion; then, in a short space of time, he began to accept and defend it. In his Revisions, mentioning the two books Against the Party of Donatus, written around 397 and now lost, he writes: «In the first of them I have written that I do not like that schismatics are forced to enter into communion by any kind of violence coming from the force of secular power.

It is true that I did not like them then, because I had not yet experienced the evil that their impunity caused or how much timely correction could serve in order to change them for the better" (Rev. II). The truth is that, in May 404, at the Council of Carthage, he still maintains that no one should be forced to believe if he does not want to; But when the emperor promulgated, on February 12, 405, the edict of union, with severe penalties for the Donatists, the saint accepted it and defended it. The reasons for the change are explained by him as follows: «Impressed by the examples that my colleagues have presented to me, I have changed my mind. My first ruling was that no one should be forced to accept the unity of Christ; that we had to act by word, fight in the dispute, triumph in reason so as not to turn those we knew as declared heretics into feigned Catholics. But this opinion of mine has been defeated, not by the words of my competitors, but by these obvious examples. I was first made aware that my own hometown, which belonged to Donato's party, was converted to Catholic unity out of fear of the imperial laws. Now we see her detest the prejudices caused by your animosity, so that it seems as if she was never on your side. This is how many other cities have been mentioned nominally to me... How many there are, and I know with certainty, who even before wanted to be Catholics because they were moved by the obvious truth! Every day they deferred being one in fact because they feared their own,

How many were bound not by the truth about which you have never had any illusions, but by the strong bond of inveterate custom!... How many thought that Donatus' party was the true Church, because its security hindered them from seeking the Catholic truth and filled them with laziness and boredom! How many were blocked by the rumors of slanderers, who spread that we were placing I don't know what on the altar of God! How many believed that it mattered little in which party they were Christians, and they remained in Donato's because they were born there and no one forced them to leave it and become Catholic!... Could I oppose and contradict my colleagues by preventing such gains from the Lord? (Letter 93,5,17-19). At the same time, Augustine finds biblical support for his new thesis in the compelle intrare, compel them to enter, of Luke 14,23 (Letters 173,10; 185,6,24). Despite appearances, the change is not abrupt. Agustín himself has been evolving in his way of conceiving the action and purpose of State intervention. Basing himself on the theology of Paul (Rom 13,1-4), he sees in power a minister of God to repress evil (Against the Letter of Varmeniano I 8,13ff); Imperial laws and sanctions were an auxiliary means at the service of truth and justice, and although they cannot force anyone to do good, they can prevent him from doing evil. At the same time, his fight against Manichaeism has put him in constant contact with the Old Testament, which he had to defend, and specifically its pedagogy of fear, which would be extremely useful from our perspective (see P. BROWN, L'atteggiamento di sant'Agostino verso la coerzione religious, in Religione e societh nell'etá di sant'Agostino [Turin 1972] p.245-263). Despite Agustín's change of attitude, we must never forget his specific way of acting, which can clarify the way of thinking. Augustine always rejects the death penalty; In addition, he frequently appeals to the authorities so that the laws are not applied or done in a spirit of moderation (SAINT POSIDIUS, Life of Saint Augustine 20). [10] The resurrection of the Lord as "exemplum."—For Saint Augustine, the entire life of Jesus is a continuous magisterium that develops in two ways: verbo et exemplo, with the word and with the example (Sermones 218C, 4 [ = Guelf. 3 ]; 119,7; 273,1; 305,2; 325,1; etc.). But when talking about an example we must distinguish two cases, correlative to two specific meanings of the term.

In the meaning of exemplum, the notion of exhorting prevails, and in relation to it we can speak of the pedagogical or moral example, considering it as that property of the facts by which they are proposed for imitation by other people. It is the exemplum as an invitation to act in the same way. This use is very frequent in Augustinian texts, in which we frequently see the Lord appear as an example of humility (Sermons 50,11; 52,1; 210,3; Treatises on the Gospel of Saint John 5,3; 13,4.7; 59,1; etc.), of patience (Sermons 218,1; 309,3; Treatises on the Gospel of Saint John 3,3; 50:11; 88:1; etc.), of strength (Commentary on Psalm 63:12), of how to live (Commentary on Psalm 56:2), etc. But in another meaning the notion of demonstrating, proving prevails. We are, therefore, faced with the example-proof. In this precise meaning, the term also appears frequently in Augustinian texts, although referring almost exclusively to the resurrection and ascension of the Lord. When Augustine claims that Jesus rose from the dead to show us an example, he is trying to give us proof that the resurrection will actually occur. The texts are numerous (Sermons 113A, 1 [ = Denis 24 ]; 169,12; 175,3; 263,1 [ = Guelf. 21 ]; 2290, 1 [ = Morin 17]; 242A, 1 [ = Mai 87 ]; (Comments on Psalms 55,3; 61,22; etc.) and almost They all wear one

temporal connotation, expressed in the verb praecessit, anteceded, which is equivalent to saying: "what happened before will happen later" (Sermons 223D, 2 [ = Wilmart 4 ]; 242.1; 336.5; etc.). But in these texts it is not simply an example-proof, as rhetoric conceived it, that is, a proof outside the cause and whose force lies in purely external comparison. The resurrection of Jesus cannot be reduced to that, since the relationship between it and the future of the Christian is much closer and more intimate. Starting from. Since Christ, even in his individual human nature, represented all human nature, the resurrection of his flesh is no longer just an announcement, but also a foretaste of our resurrection. In other words: we will not only be resurrected as he was resurrected, but we will be resurrected because he was resurrected. In his flesh he resurrected our flesh; It is not just a question of similarity, but of a certain identity (Commentary on Psalm 70:11 10). Obviously, Augustine does not think of the simple bodily resurrection, but of the resurrection-glorification, the resurrection for the kingdom (Sermons 223D, 2 [ = Wilmart 4]). [11] Original sin and human generation.—Original sin is a fact of faith regarding its existence. But there are many other aspects that can be considered and that are open to theological discussions. One that was raised to Agustín was that of its transmission. The solution to the problem is related to the conception of sin itself and what its main consequence is. In his early period, Augustine had emphasized mortality as the main consequence of Adam's sin, a mortality that was felt in the weakness of the flesh, which required particular attention from man to avoid falling into sin. Later, the saint speaks especially of concupiscence as the inheritance and manifestation of Adam's sin in man; a concupiscence that is a sinful quality and that, therefore, makes us guilty. By disobeying God's commandment, Adam and Eve receive as punishment the lack of control over their body, which has its evident manifestation in the generative faculty (Against the two letters of the Pelagians I 15,31; Marriage and concupiscence I 5,6-6,7). The proof of this is that, despite having sinned with their hands and mouth, what they covered with the fig leaves were the members through which generation is carried out.

Having lost control over their generative faculties, parents transmit being to their children only through carnal concupiscence or that new sensation that had its beginning in the sin of Adam and Eve. «The new sensation is located in the part they covered. This is where original sin comes from; This is why no one is born without sin” (Sermon 151,5). Man cannot have that sensation at will. Even Christians have to engender through the power of the pleasure that it produces, pleasure prohibited by God (The perfection of man's justice 5,11; 11,28) and transmit to their children the same carnal disobedience that remains in them (The consequences and forgiveness of sins I I 9,11; Original sin 40,45). Through disobedience, human flesh becomes sinful flesh under the law of sin, which seeks only the good and pleasure of the flesh (Nature and Grace I 23,25); Thus, the law of sin that resides in the flesh generates flesh of sin (The consequences... I I 23,37; 36,58). Augustine, then, identifies in the carnal concupiscence that works in generation the agent of its own transmission. A further proof is found in the person of Christ: he is the only one who was born without original sin, because he is the only one who was not generated through carnal lust, the only one who was not born from the union of the two sexes; only his flesh is not the flesh of sin (The consequences...
